en: Now begins the *Kātantra*, together with the commentary composed by Śrī Durgasiṃha.
Homage to Gaṇeśa!

Having first prostrated before the God of gods, the omniscient and all-seeing one, I shall proclaim the commentary on the *Kātantra* composed by Śarvavarman. The traditional collection of phonemes is established. (Kāt 1.1.1)
The meaning is that the traditional enumeration (*samāmnāya*) of the phonemes must indeed be understood as established (*siddha*), and not taught otherwise.

Here, the word *siddha* has the sense of "eternal" (*nitya*), "accomplished" (*niṣpanna*), or "well-known" (*prasiddha*), as in the expressions "space is established," "food is prepared," or "Kāmpilya is established.
The phonemes are *a* and so forth; their *samāmnāya* is the sequence of recitation.
In that regard, there are fourteen vowels at the beginning [of the alphabet]. Kāt_1.1.2:

Within this subject matter of the traditional enumeration of phonemes (*varṇasamāmnāya*), those fourteen phonemes which stand at the beginning receive the designation "vowel" (*svara*): *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au*.
According to the view held by some, just as there is a short *ḷ*-phoneme in imitation (*anukaraṇa*), there is likewise a long one.
The rules concerning vowels include such statements as "vowels" (*svara-pradeśāḥ*) and "the vowel *a*, excluding the letter *a*, is called *nāmī*" (*svaro ’varṇavarjo nāmī*).

There are ten *samāna* vowels. According to Kāt 1.1.3, those ten letters which stand at the beginning of the phonemic inventory (*varṇasamāmnāya*) receive the technical designation *samāna*: *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ*.
[The rules] beginning with "those occupying the same place, when followed by a homogeneous vowel, become long and the subsequent one is elided" (Kāt 1.2.1) and so forth.
Among these, each pair is mutually homogeneous.
According to Kāt 1.1.4, among those very ten vowels, each pair of letters is designated as mutually homogeneous: a, ā; i, ī; u, ū; ṛ, ṝ; ḷ, ḹ.
The inclusion of these [terms] is for the sake of clarity; by this, the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is established for both pairs of short and long vowels.
The instances where *savarṇa* applies include such rules as: "When a homogeneous vowel follows, the former becomes long and the latter is elided" (Kāt 1.2.1), and so forth.
The preceding [vowel] is short (Kāt 1.1.5).
Of each pair of phonemes designated as *savarṇa*, whichever phoneme is the first is designated as *hrasva* (short): namely, a, i, u, ṛ, and ḷ.
The applications (*pradeśa*) of the term *hrasva* include such rules as "a vowel is short in the neuter" [Kāt 2.4.52], and so forth.
The subsequent [phoneme in each pair] is *dīrgha* (long). [Kāt 1.1.6]
Among each pair of vowels designated as *savarṇa*, whichever vowel is the latter is designated as *dīrgha* (long): namely, ā, ī, ū, ṝ, and ḹ.

It is understood from the manner of pronunciation that a short vowel is *laghu* (light) and a long vowel is *guru* (heavy); likewise, when a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) follows, even a short vowel is *guru*. This is also evident from the exclusion [of *ṛcch*] in the rule *gurumato ’nṛcchaḥ*.
Instances where the term *dīrgha* is applied include: *ro re lopaṃ svaraś ca pūrvo dīrghaḥ* [Kātantra 1.5.17], and so forth.
A vowel, excluding *a*-vowels, is called *nāmin*.
(Kāt_1.1.7) A vowel other than *a*-vowels bears the technical designation *nāmin*: *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*.
The applications of the term *nāmin* include such rules as "when followed by a *nāmin*, *r* [is doubled]" (Kāt_1.5.12), and so forth.
The diphthongs (sandhyakṣara) begin with *e*. According to Kāt.
1.1.8, the names of vowels beginning with *e* are the diphthongs: *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
Passages concerning the diphthongs include, for example, Kāt. 3.6.38: "and in the case of a diphthong," and so forth.

*Kādīni vyañjanāni* (The consonants beginning with *ka*). From *Kāt_1.1.9*: those beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ha* are designated as consonants (*vyañjana*). They are: *ka kha ga gha ṅa; ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma; ya ra la va; śa ṣa sa ha*.
Passages concerning consonants include such rules as: "A consonant that lacks a vowel should lead to the following phoneme" (*Kāt_1.1.21*), and others like these.

[Proofread by ZXS up to this point, 2018.9.20] Those groups are five, five, and five. Kāt_1.1.10: Those phonemes beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* become five each; thus, those five constitute the technical term "varga" (group). [They are: *ka kha ga gha ṅa*, *ca cha ja jha ña*, *ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa*, *ta tha da dha na*, *pa pha ba bha ma*.

The *aghoṣa* (voiceless) sounds are the first and second members of each *varga* (consonant class), as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*. [Kāt 1.1.11] The first and second members of the *vargas*, along with *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, are designated as *aghoṣa*. [Kāt 1.1.11] The letters that are the first and second of the *vargas*, as well as *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*, receive the technical name (*saṃjñā*) *aghoṣa*: namely, *ka kha*, *ca cha*, *ṭa ṭha*, *ta tha*, *pa pha*, *śa ṣa sa*. The points of application (*pradeśa*) for this term include [rules such as]: "in place of an *aghoṣa*" [Kāt 2.3.61], and so forth.

Others are voiced (*ghoṣavant*). Kāt_1.1.12: Those remaining consonants other than the unvoiced (*aghoṣa*)—namely *ga* and so forth—are designated as "voiced" (*ghoṣavat*). They are: *ga gha ṅa ja jha ña ḍa ḍha ṇa da dha na ba bha ma ya ra la va ha*.
Applications of the term "voiced" include such rules as Kāt_1.5.11: "There is elision [of a preceding vowel] before a voiced [consonant]," and others.

The *anunāsika* (nasalized) sounds are *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*. According to Kāt_1.1.13, these phonemes—*ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*—bear the technical designation *anunāsika*. Instances where this term is applied include Kāt_2.1.13: "A *dhuṭ* consonant, except for a semivowel (*antaḥstha*), is nasalized (*anunāsika*)," and so forth.
The semi-vowels (*antaḥsthā*) are *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*. According to Kāt_1.1.14, these phonemes—*ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—bear the technical designation *antaḥsthā*.

The rules concerning *antaḥsthā* include such passages as Kāt_3.3.27: "In place of *u*-vowel, [there is substitution] when followed by a *jha*-class consonant, a *antaḥsthā*, or an *apavarga* [consonant], provided that the following vowel is not an *a*-vowel," and so forth.

The *ūṣman* sounds are *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*. According to Kāt_1,1.15, these phonemes—*ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*—bear the technical designation *ūṣman*. Furthermore, by the rule "those beginning with *ś* are called *śiṭ*" (Kāt_3,8.32), they also bear the designation *laghu*. These terms, well-established by former teachers, are here made known as being significant (*anvartha*). The sound *aḥ* is the *visarjanīya*. (Kāt_1,1.16)

The letter *a* here serves the purpose of pronunciation; thus, the phoneme shaped like a young girl’s pair of breasts is designated as *visarjanīya*. The rules concerning *visarjanīya* include such passages as: “*visarjanīya* followed by *c* or *ch* optionally becomes *ś*” (Kāt. 1.5.1), and so forth. *ẖka* is the *jihvāmūlīya*. (Kāt. 1.1.17)
The letter *ka* here serves the purpose of pronunciation; thus, the phoneme in the form of a vajra is designated as the *jihvāmūlīya*.
Regarding the locations of the *jihvāmūlīya*, there are rules such as "the *jihvāmūlīya* occurs before *k* and *kh*, or not" (Kāt 1.5.4), and so forth.
*ḫpa* is the *upadhmānīya* (Kāt 1.1.18).
The letter *pa* here is for the purpose of pronunciation; thus, the phoneme shaped like an elephant’s frontal globe (*gajakumbha*) is termed *upadhmānīya*.
The rules governing the *upadhmānīya* include such passages as "the *upadhmānīya* optionally replaces *p* and *ph*" (Kāt.
1.5.5). The syllable *aṃ* is the *anusvāra*. (Kāt. 1.1.19)
The letter *a* here serves the purpose of pronunciation; thus, the phoneme consisting of a mere dot (*bindu*) is termed *anusvāra*.
The applications of *anusvāra* include such rules as "the *m* becomes *anusvāra* before a consonant" (Kāt. 1.4.15) and others.
A word (*pada*) is that which brings about the comprehension of meaning through the combination of preceding and following elements (Kāt. 1.1.20).

When the meanings of the preceding and following base and suffix are perceived, the aggregate is designated as a *pada*. In [the examples] *te atra* and *yajante atra*, the inclusion of the term "perception" (*upalabdhi*) is for the sake of the suffix-meaning.
Instances of the term *pada* include [rules] such as *edotparaḥ padānte lopam akāraḥ* (Kātantra 1.2.17) and others.
A consonant that lacks a vowel should be joined with the following phoneme. (Kātantra 1.1.21)

One should lead a consonant (*vyañjana*) to the following vowel (*varṇa*), but not a vowel; for a consonant follows [another], whereas a vowel shines by itself. Thus, *tad gacchati*, *ṣaḍ atra*, and *kaẖ khanati*—in these cases, [the sandhi] occurs because of the quality of being a carrier (*yogavāha*). One should separate [the letters] without overstepping [their natural order]. (Kāt.

1.1.22) One should separate—that is, disjoin—the letters that are joined and combined without overstepping them. This rule (*yoga*) is for the sake of avoiding confusion, as in the examples *vaiyākaraṇaḥ* and *uccakaiḥ*.
The establishment of inclusion [of certain items] is due to worldly convention (*lokopacāra*). (Kāt.

1.1.23) "Convention" (*upacāra*) refers to the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of people; from that, it should be understood that the inclusion of even those not explicitly mentioned is established—such as the elision of particles (*nipāta*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), prefixes (*upasarga*), case-roles (*kāraka*), tense (*kāla*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and so forth.

Likewise, *Varaṇā* is a name for a city, and *Pañcālāḥ* is a name for a region; the grammatical connection (*yoga*) [of these names with their referents] is not perceived, because they are words functioning as proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*).

Regarding "harītakyaḥ phalāni" (myrobalans are fruits), the feminine form occurs even for fruits. Similarly, other derivative words (*taddhita*) are established in common usage like proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*), such as "khalatikaṃ vanāni" (the grove of Khalatika); the name of those forests ends in the singular number.

Even when the referent is the same, there is a difference in gender and number among words, as in: *āpaḥ* (feminine plural), *jalam* (neuter singular), *dārāḥ* (masculine plural), *kalatram* (neuter singular), and *bhāryā* (feminine singular).

"Those [words] which have been stated by Vedic scholars and those who know worldly usage, exactly as they are, should be understood as having their meanings determined; there is no inclusion of them from common usage.
Thus ends the first quarter on euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the commentary of Durgasiṃha.
When a homogeneous vowel (*samāna*) is followed by another homogeneous vowel (*savarṇa*), it becomes long, and the subsequent vowel is elided. (Kātantra 1.2.1)

A vowel designated as *samāna* (homogeneous) becomes long when followed by another homogeneous vowel, and the subsequent vowel undergoes elision (*lopa*). Examples: *daṇḍāgram*, *sāgatā*, *dadhīdam*, *nadīhate*, *madhūdakam*, *vadhūḍham*, *pitṝṣabhaḥ*, *kṝkāraḥ*, *kḹkāreṇa*.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] even in cases such as *hotṝkāraḥ*.
The inclusion of the term *samāna* is for the purpose of causing the elision of a homogeneous vowel following a long vowel even when it is not explicitly heard; thus, [we have] *vṛkṣāḥ*.

*Kāt_1.2.2*: An *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*) becomes *e* (*er*) before an *i*-vowel (*ivarṇa*), and the subsequent [vowel] undergoes elision (*lopa*). In the mention of a specific vowel (*varṇagrahaṇa*), there is the inclusion of its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). Thus: *tavehā*, *seyam*.

The inclusion of the letter *ca* is for the purpose of collecting what has not been explicitly stated; therefore, in some cases, even the preceding [vowel] is elided: *halīṣā*, *lāṅgalīṣā*, *manasa īṣā* → *manīṣā*.
Kātantra 1.2.3: Before a vowel *u*, an *a*-vowel becomes *o*, and the subsequent [vowel] undergoes elision; e.g., *tavohanam* (tava + ūhanam), *gaṅgodakam* (gaṅgā + udakam).
Kātantra 1.2.4: Before a vowel *ṛ*, [an *a*-vowel becomes *ar*].
When followed by a vowel of the *ṛ*-class (*ṛvarṇa*), the vowel *a* becomes *ar*, and the subsequent [vowel] undergoes elision; for example: *tavarkāraḥ*, *sarkāreṇa*.
In certain cases, when the word *ṛṇa* follows, there is also lengthening of the vowel *a*; for example: *ṛṇārṇam*, *prārṇam*, and so forth.
Furthermore, in a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*) involving the word *ṛte*, [the same applies]; for example: *śītena ṛtaḥ* → *śītārtaḥ*.
The substitution of *al* occurs for the *ṛ*-vowel of a verbal root when preceded by a prefix; e.g., *prārchati*.
Or, in the case of a nominal stem, as in *prārṣabhīyati* or *prarṣabhīyati*.
According to Kātantra 1.2.5, this substitution of *al* occurs when an *ḷ*-vowel follows.

When followed by the vowel *ḷ*, an *a*-vowel becomes *al* and the subsequent [vowel] undergoes elision: *tavalkāraḥ*, *salkāreṇa*. Optionally, when followed by *ḷ*, a long vowel may replace the final *a* of a prefix before a verbal root: *upālkārīyati* or *upalkārīyati*. In the case of *e* and *ai*: Kāt_1.2.6.
When followed by *e* or *ai*, an *a*-vowel becomes *ai* and the subsequent [vowel] undergoes elision: *tavaiṣā*, *saindrī*.

Due to the governing influence of the word *ca* ("and"), in some instances even the preceding [particle] is elided; furthermore, *eva* is used when there is no restriction (*aniyoga*), as in *adyaiva* ("this very day") and *iheva* ("right here").

However, when there is a restriction (*niyoga*), it is used as in *adyaiva gaccha* ("go this very day") and *ihaiva tiṣṭha* ("stay right here"). It should also be stated that the substitution of *ai* occurs for *sva* before the suffixes *era* and *erin*, as in *svairam* ("at will") and *svairī* ("one who acts at will").
In the case of *o* and *au*:

when an *a*-vowel (*avarṇa*) is followed by *o* or *au*, it becomes *au*, and the subsequent vowel is elided. Examples: *tavaudanaṃ* (your rice), *saupagavī* (the daughter of Upagu). Because of the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*), there is also the elision of the *a*-vowel of a prefix (*upasarga*) before the *e* or *o* of a verbal root (*dhātu*): *prelayati*, *parokhati*.
The substitution of *ai* for *e* does not occur after the roots *iṇ* and *edh*: *upaiti*, *upaidhate*.
Or, it may optionally occur after a nominal stem: *upekīyati* / *upaikīyati*, *proṣadhīyati* / *prauṣadhīyati*.
In a compound, the substitution of *au* for *o* is optional when the members are *oṣṭha* and *ūt*: *bimboṣṭhaḥ* / *bimbauṣṭhaḥ*, *sthūlotuḥ* / *sthūlautuḥ*.
What is the purpose of the term "compound" (*samāsa*)? [Examples of non-compounds: *he chāttrauṣṭhaṃ paśya* ("O student, look at the lip"), *adyautuṃ paśya* ("look at the sun").
[The rule] "and before *om*, it is always [substituted]" applies: *adyom* ("today, Om"), *som ity avocat* ("he said, 'Om'").
[The substitution of] *au* for *akṣa* occurs before *ūhinī*: *akṣauhiṇī* ("an army").
In the case of *prasyoḍha* and *prasyoḍhya*, [the substitution] of *au* occurs: *prauḍhaḥ*, *prauḍhiḥ*.

In the case of *eṣa* and *eṣya*, the substitution of *ai* is an exception to [the elision of the semivowel]; thus, *praiṣaḥ* and *praiṣyaḥ*. But for the root *īṣ*, it is *preṣaḥ* and *preṣyaḥ*. When a semivowel (*i-varṇa*) follows a vowel that is not homogeneous (*asavarṇa*), it is not to be elided. (Kātantra 1.2.8)
When an *i*-vowel encounters a non-homogeneous vowel, it undergoes substitution [with *y*], and the subsequent vowel is not elided: *dadhy atra*, *nady eṣā*.
Why "an *i*-vowel"? [Observe: *pacati*.
Why "non-homogeneous"? [Observe: *dadhi*.
*vam* is for the *u*-vowel. Kāt_1.2.9:
An *u*-vowel becomes *vam* when followed by a non-homogeneous vowel, and the subsequent vowel is not elided; as in *madhv atra* and *vadhvāsanam*.
*ram* is for the *ṛ*-vowel. Kāt_1.2.10.

The vowel *ṛ* becomes *ra* when followed by a dissimilar vowel, and the subsequent [vowel] is not elided; e.g., *pitrarthaḥ*, *krarthaḥ*. The vowel *ḷ* becomes *la*; Kāt_1.2.11: the vowel *ḷ* becomes *la* when followed by a dissimilar vowel, and the subsequent [vowel] is not elided; e.g., *lanubandhaḥ*, *lākṛtiḥ*.
e ay. Kāt_1,2.12: The vowel *e* becomes *ay*, and the following [vowel] is not to be elided; as in *nayati* and *agnaye*. ai āy. Kāt_1,2.13.
The vowel *ai* becomes *āy*, and the subsequent [vowel] is not elided: *nāyakaḥ*, *rāyaindrī*.
*o* becomes *av*: Kāt_1.2.14. The vowel *o* becomes *av*, and the subsequent [vowel] is not elided: *lavaṇam*, *paṭav otuḥ*.
Before *au*, [the word-final *o*] becomes *āv*, and the subsequent [vowel] is not elided: *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*.

In these cases, the absence of euphonic combination (*visandhi*) and the separate rule are for the sake of clarity; however, where euphonic combination is intended, it occurs: *gavājinaṃ* or *go'jinam*, as there is an optional insertion of the vowel *a* before a vowel-sound. But in *gavākṣaḥ* and *gavendraḥ*, the insertion of the vowel *a* is obligatory.

There is optionally the elision of *y* and *v* at the end of a word for [stems] beginning with *ay*, and when there is elision, the original form (*prakṛti*) is maintained. (Kātantra 1.2.16) For those ending in *ay* and so forth occurring at the end of a word, there is optionally the elision of *y* and *v*. When there is elision, however, the original nature remains. Thus: *ta āhuḥ* or *tay āhuḥ*; *tasmā āsanam* or *tasmāy āsanam*; *paṭa iha* or *paṭav iha*; *asā induḥ* or *asāv induḥ*.
Why say "beginning with *ay*"? [To exclude cases such as: *dadhy atra*, *madhv atra*.
What is the purpose of the condition "at the end of a word" (*padānta*)? [Consider] *nayanam* and *nāyakaḥ*. *Kāt_1.2.17*:
"An *a*-vowel following *e* or *o* at the end of a word undergoes elision. [Examples: *te atra*, *paṭo atra*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "edodbhyām" (from *e* and *o*)? [The answer is: *tāv atra* (those two here).

The mention of "end of a word" (*padānta*) is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the end of a word; therefore, in *citam* and *stutam*, the vowels are not to be combined when a consonant follows. (Kātantra 1.2.18)

Vowels are certainly not subject to euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) when followed by a consonant, as in: *devīgṛham*, *paṭuhastam*, *mātṛmaṇḍalam*, *jale padmam*, *raidhṛtiḥ*, *vāyo gatiḥ*, *nauyānam*. That which is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-obligatory; therefore, [the following are exceptions]: *pitryam*, *gavyūtiḥ*, and the term *adhvamāne* is to be understood as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Thus ends the second quarter on euphonic combination in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.

Nipātas ending in *o*, as well as *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ā* when standing alone, remain in their original form (*prakṛtyā*) before a vowel. (Kātantra 1.3.1) Nipātas ending in *o*, and the solitary vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, and *ā*, remain unchanged when followed by a vowel. Examples: *no atra* ("not here"), *aho āścaryam* ("oh, what a wonder!"), *atho evam* ("and thus"), *a apehi* ("go away!"), *i indraṃ paśya* ("look at Indra!"), *u uttiṣṭha* ("stand up!"), *ā evaṃ kiṃ manyase* ("Ah, do you think so?"), *ā evaṃ nu tat* ("Is that really so?"). Why does it say "thus" (*evam*) [in the rule]? [To exclude cases like: *na vā u*.
The mention of "end" (*anta*) is for the sake of including *a* and the other vowels exclusively; therefore, [the rule applies] here to *cetīti*, *nanu*, or *veti*.
What is the purpose of saying "particles" (*nipātāḥ*)? [Consider: *paṭa iha*, *paṭav iha*, *īṣatuḥ*, *ūṣatuḥ*, *āṭatuḥ*.
The doubling [of the consonant] does not occur when *an* follows. (Kātantra 1.3.2)

A dual ending that has not undergone modification remains in its original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by a vowel; the meaning is that it abandons the form of *au* and assumes another form. Examples: *agnī etau*, *paṭū imau*, *śāle ete*, *māle ime*.
Why "dual ending"? [Consider: *citranv atra*. Why is this a *paryudāsa* (exclusion)? [Consider: *ayajāvahy āvām*, *devayor atra*.
What is meant by "not experienced"? It refers to those two cases here. Regarding the plural form *amī*:
according to Pāṇini 6.1.3, the plural form *amī* remains in its original state (*prakṛti*) when followed by a vowel; for example, *amī aśvāḥ* (those horses) and *amī eḍakāḥ* (those sheep).
What is the purpose of the term *bahuvacanam* (plural)? [Example: *amī atra*. What is the purpose of the term *amīrūpam* (the form *amī*)? [Example: *tay āhuḥ*.
And those not explicitly taught [are also included]. (Kātantra 1.3.4)

Furthermore, those protracted vowels (*pluta*) which are not taught individually within the scope of the traditional list of phonemes (*akṣarasamāmnāya*), but are designated by their class (*jāti*) as having the name "vowel" (*svara*), remain in their original form (*prakṛti*) when followed by another vowel. For example: *āgaccha bho Devadatta3 atra* ("Come here, O Devadatta!"), *tiṣṭha bho Yajñadatta3 iha* ("Stay here, O Yajñadatta!"). These protracted vowels are established in common usage for calling from a distance, singing, and weeping. Thus ends the third section on euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.

The first letters of the classes [of consonants], when at the end of a word, become the third letters [of their respective classes] before vowels and voiced consonants. (Kātantra 1.4.1) The first letters of the classes at the end of a word undergo the change to the third letters when followed by vowels or voiced sounds, as in *vāg atra* and *ṣaḍ gacchanti*. Why say "the first letters of the classes"? [Consider: *bhavān āha*.
Why "at the end of a word"? [Consider: *śakanīyam*. Why "in vowels and voiced consonants"? [Consider: *vāk pūtā*, *ṣaṭ kurvanti*.
In the fifth [class], the fifth [consonant] optionally becomes the third [consonant]. (Kāt. 1.4.2)

The first letters of the classes (varga-prathama), when standing at the end of a word, optionally become the fifth letter of their respective class when followed by a fifth letter; or they may become the third letter. Examples: *vāṅmatī* or *vāgmatī*; *ṣaṇmukhāni* or *ṣaṇmukhāni*; *tannayanam* or *tannayanam*; *triṣṭubminoti* or *triṣṭubminoti*. When the first letter of the *dhuṭ* group follows at the end of a word, [the rule applies]: *dṛśannayanam*, or *jñānabhunnāthaḥ*.
By way of a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), when a fifth letter of a suffix follows, the fifth letter is obligatory in the common language (*bhāṣā*): e.g., *vāṅmayam*, *yanmātram*.
After the first letters of the [five] classes (*varga*), a *śakāra* followed by a vowel, *y*, *v*, or *r* optionally becomes a *chakāra*. (Kāt.

1.4.3) After the first letters of the classes occurring at the end of a word (*padānta*), a *śakāra* followed by a vowel, *y*, *v*, or *r* optionally undergoes the change to *chakāra*: *vāk chūraḥ* / *vāk śūraḥ*; *ṣaṭ chyāmāḥ* / *ṣaṭ śyāmāḥ*; *tac chvetam* / *tac śvetam*; *triṣṭup chrutam* / *triṣṭup śrutam*.
Why "after the first letters of the classes"? [Observe: *prāṅ śete*.
What is the purpose of the rule "svarayavarapara" (followed by a vowel, *y*, *v*, or *r*)? [Examples: *vāk ślakṣṇaḥ* and *tac śmaśānam*.
Others also desire [the substitution] before nasalized vowels (*lānunāsika*).
From those very [nasalized vowels], the letter *h* becomes the fourth letter of the preceding class, or not. (Kātantra 1.4.4)

The letter *ha*, when following those same word-final consonants belonging to the first class [the gutturals], optionally becomes the fourth letter of its own preceding class, or it does not. Examples: *vāgghīnaḥ* / *vāg hīnaḥ*; *ajjhalau* / *aj-halau*; *ṣaḍḍhalāni* / *ṣaḍ halāni*; *taddhitam* / *tad-hitam*; *kakubbhāsaḥ* / *kakub-hāsaḥ*.
Why specify "the letter *ha*"? [Consider: *tatkṛtam*.
The mention of "those [consonants]" is for the purpose of excluding vowels (*svara*), semivowels (*yara*), and the letter *pa*; therefore, in *vāg ghlādayati*, the change does not occur.
The word *eva* is used for the purpose of excluding a third alternative.
The letter *ta* is the "subsequent form" (*pararūpa*) when followed by the *la*, *ca*, or *ṭa*-vargas. *Kāt 1.4.5*:

A *ta* at the end of a word becomes the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) when followed by the *la*, *ca*, or *ṭa*-vargas. Examples: *tal lunāti* (it cuts), *tac carati* (it moves), *tac chādayati* (it covers), *taj jayati* (it conquers), *taj jhāsayati* (it causes to shine), *tañ ñakāreṇa* (with the letter *ña*), *taṭ ṭīkate* (it explains), *taṭ ṭhakāreṇa* (with the letter *ṭha*), *taḍ ḍīnam* (flight), *taḍ ḍhaukate* (it approaches), *taṇ ṇakāreṇa* (with the letter *ṇa*).
When a *dhuṭ* [consonant] follows at the end of a word (*padānte*) and the first [consonant] is present, that [first consonant] is dropped: as in *taj jayaḥ*, *dṛśallekhā*, and *jñānabhuṭṭīkanam*.
Why does it say "in the case of the *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta* groups"? [Consider: *tat pacati*. *Caṃ śe*: Pāṇini 8.2.6.

The letter *takāra* at the end of a word becomes *cam* when followed by *śe*; as in *tac ślakṣṇaḥ* and *tac śmaśānam*. This rule applies to the alternative where it does not become *chatva*. When preceded by a short vowel, the letters *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na* are doubled before a vowel; Kāt_1.4.7.

The phonemes *ṅ*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *m* at the end of a word, when preceded by a short vowel (*hrasva-upadhā*), become doubled before a vowel. For example: *kruṅṅ atra*, *sugaṇṇ atra*, *pacann atra*. Why specify "the phonemes *ṅ*, *ṇ*, *n*, and *m*"? Consider: *kim atra*. Why specify "at the end of a word"? Consider: *vṛtrahaṇau*.

What is the purpose of the rule "when there is a short vowel in the penultimate position" (*hrasvopadhā*)? [Example: *prāṅ āste* (he sits facing east). [Rule Kāt_1.4.8: "A final *n* at the end of a word becomes *ś*, preceded by an *anusvāra*, when followed by *c* or *ch*. Examples: *bhavāṃś carati* (you move), *bhavāṃś chādayati* (you cover), *bhavāṃś cyavate* (you fall), *bhavāṃś chyati* (he cuts). Because of the traditional rule regarding fixed application (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), this does not apply in *praśāñ carati*; the same applies in subsequent cases as well.
Likewise, "end" means cessation; by that, you cross over.
Regarding the rule for *ṭa* and *ṭha*:

according to Pāṇini 8.3.29 (*naś ca apadāntasya jhali*), a *n* at the end of a word becomes a *ṣ* when followed by *ṭa* or *ṭha*, provided it is preceded by an *anusvāra*. Thus: *bhavāṃṣ ṭīkate* (you cross), [or] *bhavāṃṣ ṭhakāreṇa* (by the letter *ṭha*).

In the case of *t* and *th*, [the rule applies]. According to Pāṇini 8.3.10 (*nakāraḥ padāntas tathayoḥ sakāram āpadyate 'nusvārapūrvam*), a *n* at the end of a word becomes *s* when followed by *t* or *th*, preceded by an *anusvāra*: *bhavāṃs tarati*, *bhavāṃs thuḍati*.
[Examples include: *puṃskokilaḥ*, *puṃskhananam*, *puṃścakoraḥ*, *puṃśchattram*, *puṃṣṭiṭṭibhaḥ*, *supuṃś carati*.

In the case of the word *puṃsaḥ*, because the elision of a final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) is not mandatory when followed by a non-śit (non-aspirated) voiced sound, it remains exactly as it was obtained [by the previous rule]. Why does [the rule] specify "not followed by a śit"? [Consider: *puṃsaraḥ*.
*le lam* (Kātantra 1.4.11).

The letter *na* at the end of a word becomes *la*, provided it is not followed by an *anusvāra*, when *la* follows: *bhavāṃl lunāti*, *bhavāṃl likhati*. Because of the absence of the *anusvāra*, it becomes nasalized (*anunāsika*). Before the letters *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, and *śa*, it becomes *ña*: Pāṇini 8.4.12.

A *nakāra* at the end of a word becomes a *ñakāra* when followed by *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, or *śa*: as in *bhavāñ jayati*, *bhavāñ jhāṣayati*, *bhavāñ ñakāreṇa*, and *bhavāñ śete*. Regarding the rule that there is a substitution from the *ca*-class or *ṭa*-class within the middle of a word, this prescribes the *ñakāra* for [the *na*] before *ja*, *jha*, and *ña*. *Śi* is optionally [retained] before *ñcau*. (Kātantra 1.4.13)

The letter *n* at the end of a word optionally becomes *ñ* when followed by *c* that is itself followed by *ś*. Thus: *bhavāñc chūraḥ*, *bhavāñc śūraḥ*, *bhavāñ śūraḥ*; *kurvañc chūraḥ*, *kurvañc śūraḥ*, *kurvañ śūraḥ*; *praśāñc chayanam*, *praśāñc śayanam*, *praśāñ śayanam*.

In these cases, there is neither the substitution of *ṇ* nor the substitution of *g*; rather, there is simply the *anusvāra* or the nasal of the respective class (*vargānta*). The particle *vā* here denotes conjunction (*samuccaye*).
But when followed by *ḍa*, *ḍha*, or *ṇa*, the *n* becomes *ṇ*. [Kāt.

1.4.14] "That which has *ḍa*, *ḍha*, or *ṇa* following it" is *ḍaḍhaṇapara*; the *n* that is followed by *ḍa*, *ḍha*, or *ṇa* undergoes the change to *ṇ*. Examples: *bhavāṇ ḍīnam*, *bhavāṇ ḍhaukate*, *bhavāṇ ṇakāreṇa*.
The word *tu* is for the purpose of excluding the alternative (*vā*).

*mo 'nusvāraṃ vyañjane* (Kāt_1.4.15): The letter *m*, when it occurs at the end [of a word], undergoes the change to *anusvāra* when followed by a consonant. For example: *tvaṃ yāsi* ("you go"), *tvaṃ ramase* ("you delight"). Why does it say "at the end"? [Consider: *gamyate* ("it is gone").
The rule "anusvāra" is non-obligatory because it is preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*); therefore, [we have] *samrāṭ*, *samrājau*.

Or, when a class-consonant (*varga*) follows, the fifth letter of that same class may optionally [be substituted]. (Kātantra 1.4.16) When a class-consonant follows, a final *anusvāra* becomes optionally the fifth letter of that same class; thus: *tvaṅ karoṣi* or *tvaṃ karoṣi*, *tvañ carasi* or *tvaṃ carasi*, *pumbhyām* or *puṃbhyām*.
What is the purpose of the word *varga*? [Example: *tvaṃ lunāsi*. Thus ends the fourth quarter on euphonic combination (*sandhi*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi. *Kāt_1.5.1*:
The *visarjanīya* is optionally changed to *ś* before *c* and *ch*.
When followed by *cha* or *cha*, the *visarjanīya* undergoes the change to *śa*: as in *kaś carati* ("who moves? and *kaś chādayati* ("who covers?").

When followed by *ṭa* or *ṭha*, it becomes *ṣa*. According to Kāt_1.5.2, the *visarjanīya* becomes *ṣa* when followed by *ṭa* or *ṭha*: as in *kaṣ ṭīkate* ("who explains? and *kaṣ ṭhakāreṇa* ("by the letter *ṭha*").
Alternatively, in this case, the conjunction (*vā*) is for the purpose of instructing beginners.
[The rule] *te vā the vā sam* (Kāt. 1.5.3) means that the *visarjanīya* becomes *sam* when followed by *te* or *the*. Examples:
*kas tarati*, *kas thuḍati*.

Words such as *kāraskara* and others are conventional terms established by common usage. Regarding the rule *Kāt. 1.5.4*: "The *visarjanīya* optionally becomes the *jihvāmūlīya* before *ka* and *kha*. Thus, one may say *kaḥ karoti* or *kaḥ karoti*, *kaẖ khanati* or *kaḥ khanati*.
The *upadhmānīya* is optionally substituted for [the *visarjanīya*] before *pa* and *pha*.
(Kāśikā 1.1.5) When followed by *pa* or *pha*, the *visarjanīya* becomes the *upadhmānīya* or not: *kaḥ pacati*, *kaḥ pacati*; *kaḥ phalati*, *kaḥ phalati*.

By the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), when a sibilant (*śit*) follows that is not voiced (*aghoṣa*), the letters beginning with *śa* (i.e., *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*) do not undergo this change: *puruṣas tsarukaḥ*, *vāsaḥ kṣaumam*, *adbhiḥ psātam*.

*Śe ṣe se vā vā pararūpam* (Kāt_1.5.6): When *śe*, *ṣe*, or *se* follows, the visarga optionally undergoes the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*), or it does not. Examples: *kaḥ śete* / *kaś śete*; *kaḥ ṣaṇḍaḥ* / *kaṣ ṣaṇḍaḥ*; *kas sādhuḥ* / *kaḥ sādhuḥ*. Because the rule for the substitution of the visarga is not included among the sounds beginning with *ca*, *ṭa*, and *ta*, the first [unaspirated, voiceless stop] would not occur in place of the visarga before a voiceless sound; thus, in cases such as *kaś carati*, the same [rule of non-substitution] applies.
Between two *a*s: According to Kāt_1,5.7, a *visarjanīya* becomes *um* when situated between two *a*s, as in *ko 'tra* and *ko 'rthaḥ*.
Furthermore, regarding the word *atra*, because of the subsequent rule [Kāt_1,5.14] stating that it has *ra* as its base, the *repha* (the sound *r*) would [otherwise] occur.

Kāt_1.5.8: Between two unvoiced consonants, a *visarjanīya* undergoes the substitution of *u*. (Examples: *ko gacchati*, *ko dhāvati*. Why "between two unvoiced consonants"? (Counter-example: *kaḥ śete*. Kāt_1.5.9:
In another case, when followed by a vowel other than [a voiced consonant], it is either elided or becomes *y*.
A *visarjanīya* following the vowel *a* is to be elided before a vowel other than those already mentioned, or it optionally becomes *y*. Examples: *ka iha*, *kay iha*, *ka upari*, *kay upari*.
Why does it say "other"? [Observe: *agnir atra*.
The word *vā* here signifies conjunction; thus, in this case, the *y* is slightly more articulated (*īṣatspṛṣṭatara*).

The same rule applies after *ā* and *bhoḥ* before a vowel. (Kāt. 1.5.10) A *visarjanīya* following the words *ā* and *bhoḥ* remains unchanged when a vowel follows: *devā āhuḥ*, *devāy āhuḥ*; *bho atra*, *bhoy atra*.
Some hold that the word *bhoḥ* is an illustration for any vocative ending in *o*: *bhago atra*, *bhagoy atra*; *agho atra*, *aghoy atra*.

The *yakāra* following the vowel *au* is slightly more closed (*īṣatspṛṣṭatara*) than that following *ā*. The inclusion of the word "exactly" (*evam eva*) is for the purpose of excluding its obligatory elision. *Kāt_1.5.11*:
A *visarjanīya* following the vowels *ā* and the word *bhoḥ* undergoes elision when followed by a voiced sound (*ghoṣavat*). Examples: *devā gatāḥ*, *bho yāsi*, *bhago vraja*, *agho yaja*.

The mention of *lopagrahaṇa* (the elision) is for the purpose of excluding the rule *yaṃ vā* [Kāt_1.5.10]. *nāmiparo ram* [Kāt_1.5.12]: A *visarjanīya* following a vowel with a nasal marker (*nāmin*) becomes *ram*, independently; as in *supīḥ* and *sutūḥ*. This statement is made for the sake of the vowels *ī*, *ū*, and *ṛ*.
*Kāt_1.5.13*: A *visarjanīya* following a vowel (*nāmin*) becomes *ra* when followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*) or a vowel. Examples:
*agnir gacchati*, *agnir atra*, *paṭur vadati*, *paṭur atra*.
Why specify "followed by a voiced consonant or a vowel"? [Observe: *agniḥ śete*.

The *repha*-originated *visarjanīya*, whether followed by a vowel with a nasal (*nāmin*) or not, becomes *ra* when followed by a voiced consonant or a vowel, regardless of whether that following sound is nasalized or not. For example: *gor patiḥ* or *goḥ patiḥ*; *dhūr patiḥ* or *dhūḥ patiḥ*. However, it is obligatory when followed by a vowel that is both voiced and nasalized: *pitar atra*, *pitar yātaḥ*.
Even when the *arepha* is the base form: "O wise King" (*he pracetā rājan*) or "O wise King" (*he praceto rājann*), [as in] "awakening at dawn" (*uṣarbudhaḥ*).
When there is no *repha* after the word *ahan*: "lord of the day" (*aharpatiḥ*), "a collection of days" (*ahargaṇaḥ*), "day here" (*ahar atra*).
But when there is a *repha*: "day and night" (*ahorātram*), "the form of the day" (*ahorūpam*), "the *rathantara* chant of the day" (*ahorathantaraṃ sāma*).

This *visarjanīya* following *eṣa* or *sa* is to be elided before a consonant. (Kātantra 1.5.15) The *visarjanīya* following *eṣa* or *sa* is elided when a consonant follows: *eṣa carati*, *sa ṭīkate*, *eṣa śete*, *sa pacati*. Because it is a subsequent rule (*paratva*), it supersedes the preceding ones, either because of the governing context (*adhikāra*) or because the specific form itself is being grasped. Thus: *eṣakaḥ karoti*, *sakaḥ karoti*, *aneṣo gacchati*, *aso gacchati*. However, this would not apply in the case of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), such as *akī*. Furthermore, once the *visarjanīya* has been elided, there is no further euphonic combination (*sandhi*). (Kātantra 1.5.16)

When the elision (*lopa*) of the *visarjanīya* has been performed, euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) does not take place again; however, it certainly does occur when another [sound] is elided, as in *ka iha*, *devā āhuḥ*, and *bho atra*.

Within the section concerning the *visarjanīya*, the repeated mention of the *visarjanīya* is for the purpose of terminating that section hereafter; by this means, the doubling [of the consonant] in *eṣa cchātreṇa* is established.
*R* followed by *r* undergoes elision, and the preceding vowel becomes long. (Kātantra 1.5.17)
When *r* or *re* follows, [the preceding *r*] undergoes elision, and the preceding vowel becomes long: *agnī rathena*, *punā rātriḥ*, *uccai rauti*.
*Kāt_1.5.18*: A *ch* following a vowel undergoes doubling. [Examples:
*vṛkṣacchāyā*, *icchati*.
Also [the doubling of *c*] occurs after a long vowel at the end of a word, optionally: *kuṭīcchāyā*, *kuṭīchāyā*. After *āṅ* and *mā*, it is obligatory: *ācchāyā*, *mā cchidat*.
Thus ends the fifth section on euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.

Now, regarding the fourfold [classification] within a name: that which possesses meaning, excluding verbal roots and case-endings, is designated as a *liṅga* (grammatical gender). Kātyāyana 2.1.1 states: "The *artha* is the denoted object; that which possesses meaning, excluding verbal roots and case-endings, receives the technical designation of *liṅga*. Examples: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *kuṇḍam*, *kumārī*, *ḍitthaḥ*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *aupagavaḥ*, *kārakaḥ*."

What is the purpose of excluding those ending in case-suffixes (*dhātuvibhaktivarjam*)? [Examples: *ahan* (day), *vṛkṣān* (trees). What is the purpose of excluding those that are meaningful (*arthavat*)? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to each individual phoneme in the word *vṛkṣa*—namely, *v*, *ṛ*, *k*, *ṣ*, *ām*—nor to the speech of a madman such as *rājan*. The applications of the term "gender" (*liṅga*) include [rules] such as *liṅgāntanakārasya* [Kāt 2.3.56].

Therefore, the case-endings follow. (Pāṇini 4.1.2) Following that meaningful stem, the case-endings (*vibhakti*) beginning with *syat* occur: *si*, *au*, *jas*; *am*, *au*, *śas*; *ṭā*, *bhyām*, *bhis*; *ṅe*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*;
*ṅasi*, *bhyām*, *bhyas*; *ṅas*, *os*, *ām*; *ṅi*, *os*, *sup*.

*dṛśat*, *dṛśad* (nominative singular), *dṛśadau*, *dṛśadaḥ* (plural); *dṛśadam*, *dṛśadau*, *dṛśadaḥ* (accusative); *dṛśadā*, *dṛśadbhyām*, *dṛśadbhiḥ*, and so forth. Likewise: *kumārī*, *kumāryau*, *kumāryaḥ*; *khaṭvā*, *khaṭve*, *khaṭvāḥ*.
They are called "case-endings" (*vibhakti*) because they divide (*vibhañjana*) the meaning.
*Pañcādau ghuṭ*. (Kātantra 2.1.3) The first five case-endings among *sy*-beginning suffixes are designated as *ghuṭ*: *si*, *au*, *jas*, *am*, and *au*.
The applications (*pradeśa*) of the term *ghuṭ* include such rules as *ghuṭi cāsaṃbuddhau* (Kātantra 2.2.17), and so forth.
*Jas* and *śas* are *ghuṭ* in the neuter.
(Kātantra 2.1.4) In the neuter gender, *jas* and *śas* receive the technical designation *ghuṭ*; for example: *sāmāni tiṣṭhanti*, *sāmāni paśya*.
Because of the restrictive rule that in the neuter only *jas* is *ghuṭ*, [the forms] are *vāriṇi* and *jatunī*.

The suffix *si* is called *saṃbuddhi* when used in address (*āmantrita*). According to Kāt_2.1.5, that which has been established and is made to face [the speaker] is "addressed" (*āmantrita*); the suffix *si* prescribed for that purpose receives the technical name *saṃbuddhi*, as in *he amba* and *he vṛkṣa*. The applications of *saṃbuddhi* include such rules as Kāt_2.1.39: *saṃbuddhau ca*, and others.

An augment (*āgama*) having *u* as its indicatory letter (*ud-anubandha*) follows the final vowel. (Kāśikā 2.1.6) An augment is that which does not affect either the base (*prakṛti*) or the suffix (*pratyaya*).
An augment with the indicatory letter *u* is defined as following the final vowel, as in *padmāni* and *payāṃsi*.
What is an *āgama*? For example, *vidyutvān*. A vowel with an *u* as its marker (*ud-anubandha*) is the sign of an *āgama*.
However, from the third case-ending onwards, it is treated as if beginning with the subsequent element (*parādi*). (Kātantra 2.1.7)

The augment *ud* following an *ā* in a stem becomes the initial element when followed by a case ending beginning with the third case (*tr̥tīyā*) and those that follow; as in *sarvasyai*, *sarveṣām*, and *vṛkṣāṇām*.
The word *tu* serves to terminate the governing scope of the third case and subsequent endings. [In the case of *agni*,] *id* is substituted for *u*; *agniḥ*. (Kātantra 2.1.8)
The vowels *i* and *u* are designated as "fire" (*agni*), as in *agnim* and *paṭum*.
Why [specify] *id* and *ud*? [Consider] *senānyam* and *yavalvam*.
The rules concerning "fire" include such [sūtras] as: "The vowel *a* of the case-ending *am* after 'fire'... (Kātantra 2.1.50), and so forth.
Feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū* are designated as *nadī*.
(Pāṇini 1.4.3) Feminine stems ending in *ī* and *ū* are termed *nadī*, as in *nadyai* and *vadhvai*. The inclusion of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity.
Why is it stated "called feminine" (*stryākhyau*)? [Examples are: *senānye*, *yavalkve*.
The rules for rivers and regions (*nadīpradeśāḥ*) include such forms as *nadyāḥ*, *ai*, *ās*, *ās*, *ām* (Kātantra 2.1.45), and so forth.
*ā śraddhā* (Kātantra 2.1.10).
That form which is designated as feminine is termed *śraddhā*; that is, *śraddhā* and *mālā*.
Why is it specified as "designated as feminine"? [Consider] *kīlālapāḥ*.
These are instances of *śraddhā*: such forms as *śraddhāyāḥ* [in the genitive singular], where the rule *sir lopam* [Kātantra 2.1.37] applies, and so forth.
The penultimate letter. Kāt. 2.1.11:

That letter which precedes the final letter of a stem or a verbal root is designated as the *upadhā* (penultimate). For example, the vowel *a* in *rājan*, the vowel *i* in *bhid*, and the vowel *ṛ* in *vṛt*.

Applications of the term *upadhā* include such rules as Kāt. 3.6.5: "There is lengthening of the *upadhā* of this [root], provided it is a *nāmin* vowel, before suffixes beginning with *nām*, *ni*, *ca*, and *ṭ*," and so forth.
The *vyañjana* (consonant) is not included [in this definition]. According to Kāt.

2.1.12, the *nakāra* (the letter *n*) that precedes the final *vyañjana* of either a *liṅga* (nominal stem) or a *dhātu* (verbal root) is designated as *anuṣaṅga*. Examples include *viduṣaḥ* and *śrasyate*. Why specify "the *nakāra*"? Consider *ūrgbhyām*.
Instances where the term *anuṣaṅga* is applied include Kāt. 2.2.39: *anuṣaṅgaś cākruñcet*, and others such as these.
A consonant, excluding the semivowels and the nasals, is designated as *dhuṭ*. (Kāt.
2.1.13) A consonant, with the exception of the semivowels and nasals, bears the technical name *dhuṭ*, as in *payāṃsi* and *apakta*.
Why specify "excluding the semivowels and nasals"? [Consider] *catvāri* and *amaṃsta*.
The rules concerning *dhuṭ* are such as "the *dhuṭ* [augment] before a *dhuṭ* [consonant]" (Kāt 3.6.51) and others.
Regarding the rule "the vowel *a* becomes long before a voiced sound" (Kāt 2.1.14):
the vowel *a* at the end of a nominal stem (*liṅga*) undergoes lengthening when followed by a voiced case-ending (*vibhakti*), as in *ābhyām*, *vṛkṣāya*, and *vṛkṣāṇām*.
What is an example of "vocalized" (ghoṣavat)? *vṛkṣaḥ*.
Regarding the suffix *jas*: Pāṇini 6.1.103 states that a final vowel of a stem (*liṅgānta*) becomes long when followed by *jas*; thus, *vṛkṣāḥ*.
This is a rule intended to prevent the elision of the letter *a*. In the case of the nominative-accusative plural ending *śas*, the final *s* is also replaced by *n*. According to Kāt_2.1.16:
when the suffix *śas* follows, the vowel at the end of a nominal stem undergoes lengthening, and the *s* of the suffix becomes *n*; thus, *vṛkṣān*.
What is the governing rule? It is "in small measure" (alpaśaḥ).

[Kātantra 2.1.17] The vowel *a* at the end of a nominal stem (*liṅga*) undergoes elision when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*) that begins with a general *a*. Examples: *vṛkṣam*, *yuṣmad*, *yaḥ*, *saḥ*, *uśanā*.
*bhis* or *ais*. (Kāt_2.1.18) After a nominal stem ending in *a*, the suffixes *bhis* or *ais* optionally occur; as in *vṛkṣaiḥ*.
The word *vā* indicates an alternative option: [the suffix] *es* or *ais*.
Some say [the form] is *atijarasaiḥ* because of the elision of the suffix *-ais*. However, according to Kāt_2.1.19, *dhuṭi bahutve tv e*:

"In the case of a plural ending beginning with a *dhuṭ* sound, the final vowel *a* becomes *e*. Thus, in forms such as *eṣu* and *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, the substitution of *e* would occur due to the subsequent rule.
What is excluded by the word *dhuṭ*? [The answer is: *vṛkṣāṇām*.
The word *tu* is for the purpose of excluding the optionality (*vibhāṣā*). And [the substitution occurs] before *osi*. (Kātantra 2.1.20)
The letter *e* occurs in place of the letter *a* at the end of a nominal stem (*liṅga*) when followed by the case-ending *osi*; [as in] *vṛkṣayoḥ*.
[The suffix] *ṅasi* becomes *āt* after a nominal stem ending in *a*; [as in] *vṛkṣāt*. (Pāṇini 7.1.12 and 7.1.13)
Due to the prolonged pronunciation, there is excessive weariness.
[The rule] *ṅasi sya* (Pāṇini 7.1.12) [is applied]: according to Kātyāyana 2.1.22, *sya* is substituted for *ṅasi* after a stem ending in the vowel *a*; thus, *vṛkṣasya*.

*Ina ṭā* (Pāṇini 7.1.23): The suffix *ṭā* becomes *ina* after a nominal stem ending in the vowel *a*. Although [the form] *vṛkṣeṇa* is established by [the rule] *ṭā*, the explicit mention of *ina* is for the sake of what follows; that is, *ina* itself [is substituted] in forms such as *tena* and *atijarasina kulena*.
The separate formulation of the rule is for the purpose of facilitating understanding for beginners.
Ṅer yaḥ. (Kāt_2.1.24) The substitution of *ya* occurs for the singular case-ending *ṅe* following a nominal stem ending in the vowel *a*, as in *vṛkṣāya*.
Smai sarvanāmnaḥ. (Kāt_2.1.25) [The substitution of *smai* occurs for the singular case-ending *ṅe*] following a pronominal stem.
The substitute *smai* occurs for the dative singular (*ṅe*) following a pronominal stem ending in *a*. For example: *sarvasmai*, *viśvasmai*.
Why is it said "of all names" (*sarveṣāṃ nāmnaḥ*)? [To exclude cases such as: *viśvo nāma kaścit* ("someone named Viśva"), *viśvāya* (in the sense of "having transcended Viśva," i.e., *ativiśvāya*).
It should be stated that the substitution is optional after ordinal numbers: *dvitīyasmai* or *dvitīyāya*; *tṛtīyasmai* or *tṛtīyāya*.

What is that "all-name" (sarvanāman)? It consists of: *sarva*, *viśva*, *ubha*, *ubhaya*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *itara*, *ḍatara*, *ḍatama*, *vṛt* (words ending in -vṛt), *tva*, *nema*, *sama*, *simā*; and *pūrva*, *apara*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *para*, *adhara* when used in the sense of relative position (*vyavasthā*) and not as a proper name (*asaṃjñā*). Also *sva* when it does not denote a kinsman or wealth.
The [suffixes] *antara*, *bahiḥ*, *yoga*, and *upasaṃvyāna* [are used in the locative].
*vṛt*, *tyad*, *tad*, *yad*, *etad*, *adas*, *idam*, *kim*, *eka*, *dvi*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and *bhavantaḥ* [are used in the genitive].
For *ṅasi*, [the substitute] *smāt* is used after *kā*. (Pāṇini 7.1.26)
The suffix *ṅasi* becomes *smāt* after a masculine or neuter noun ending in the vowel *a* that is a pronominal base: *sarvasmāt*, *viśvasmāt*.
Why "after one ending in *a*"? [Observe: *bhavataḥ*.
The suffix *ṅi* becomes *smin*. (Pāṇini 7.1.15)
After a pronominal stem ending in the vowel *a*, the locative suffix *ṅi* becomes *smin*; for example, *sarvasmin* and *viśvasmin*.
Why is it said "of all names" (*sarveṣāṃ nāma*)? [To exclude cases such as: "He sacrifices on level ground" (*same deśe yajati*).
According to Kātyāyana 2.1.28, these two forms are optional after stems beginning with *pūrva* and others.

In place of the *ṅasi* and *ṅi* [case endings] following the group beginning with *pūrva*, *smāt* and *smin* are optionally substituted; this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) because they would otherwise be applicable. Thus: *pūrvasmāt*, *pūrvāt*; *pūrvasmin*, *pūrve*.
It should be stated that this applies after ordinal numbers (*tīya*): *dvitīyasmāt*, *dvitīyāt*; *dvitīyasmin*, *dvitīye*; *tṛtīyasmāt*, *tṛtīyāt*; *tṛtīyasmin*, *tṛtīye*.
After all [words], *su* is substituted for *ām* (the genitive plural ending). (Pāṇini 7.1.52–54)
The augment *sur* is inserted after a pronominal stem ending in *a*, before the suffix *ām*, in all genders; as in *sarveṣām*, *viśveṣām*, *yāsām*, and *tāsām*.
The letter *u* is for the purpose of indicating that the augment follows the end of the word (*parāditva*).
Because of the rule regarding the mention of specific forms (*pratipadokta*), it does not apply in cases such as *tvām* or *yuvām*.

*Jas* becomes *ir* after a neuter noun ending in *a*. (Kāt. 2.1.30) After a neuter noun ending in *a*, the suffix *jas* becomes *ir*. Examples: *sarve*, *viśve*. Why "after one ending in *a*"? [Consider: *sarvāḥ*.

Or [the substitution occurs] after the group beginning with *alpa*. (Kāśikā 2.1.31) After the group beginning with *alpa*, the nominative plural suffix *jas* optionally becomes *ir*; for example, *alpe* or *alpāḥ*, *prathame* or *prathamāḥ*. However, in the case of *ubhaya*, it is always [substituted] in the common language (*bhāṣā*).

The [words] *alpa*, *prathama*, *carama*, *taya*, *aya*, *katipaya*, *nema*, and *ardha*—as well as those beginning with *pūrva*—[are included]. Also, after a neuter base ending in /a/ that occurs within a *dvandva* compound, the suffix *jas* optionally becomes *ir*. Examples: *katarakatame*, *katarakatamāḥ*; *dvandvakatame*, *dvandvakatamāḥ*.

Nothing else [is called] *sārvanāmika*. (Kāt_2.1.33) The word "ca" (and) is carried over [from the previous rule]. For a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) situated in a *dvandva* compound, the gender that has been stated applies, and no other operation pertaining to a pronominal (*sārvanāmika*) occurs; for example: *pūrvāparāya*, *pūrvāparāt*, and *dakṣiṇottarapūrvāṇām*.
And [this also applies] in a compound with the third case (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). (Kāt_2.1.34)

In the case of the third [case-ending], whether in a compound or not in a compound, the aforementioned rule applies, and furthermore, no other operation pertaining to a pronoun (*sārvanāmika*) takes place: *māsena pūrvāya* / *māsapūrvāya*, *māsenāvarāḥ* / *māsāvarāḥ*. Because it is explicitly stated [in the rule], the compound here would occur with the pronoun itself: *tvayakākṛtam*, *mayakākṛtam*. [This applies] in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. (Kātantra 2.1.35)
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the grammatical operation pertaining to pronouns (*sārvanāmika*) does not take effect; thus, in *tvatkapitṛkaḥ* and *matkapitṛkaḥ*, the suffix *ak* would not occur.
Alternatively, in *vastrāntara-vasanāntaraḥ*, it would not occur because of the rule "only from a non-principal [member], and from that which stands in a *dvandva*" (Kātantra 2.1.32).
Or else, it applies to the names of directions (Kātantra 2.1.36).
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the operation pertaining to pronouns (*sārvanāmika*) regarding words for the cardinal directions is optionally not applied: *uttarapūrvasyai*, *uttarapūrvāyai*.
[The rule] "in a *bahuvrīhi* of words for the cardinal directions" (diśāṃ bahuvrīhau)—why is this stated? [Consider: *dakṣiṇapūrvāyai mugdhāyai* ("to the deluded woman who is south-eastern").
[By the rule] "there is elision of the *si* of *śraddhā*" (Kāt. 2.1.37).
The *s* following that which is designated as *śraddhā* undergoes elision (*lopa*); for example, *śraddhā*, *mālā*.
Why [is it said] "of *śraddhā*"? [Consider] *kīlālapāḥ*.
When [the rule] *sir ad* is applied, *jarā* would become *jaras*.
When the [nominative] dual endings *ṭā* and *aus* follow, the substitution of *e* occurs for *śraddhā*; as in *tulayā*, *tulayoḥ*. And also in the vocative singular. Kāt_2.1.39.
In the vocative singular of *śraddhā*, the form becomes *śraddhe* or *māle*. [Pāṇini 7.3.106] states:

"The short vowel is substituted for words meaning 'mother' (*ambārtha*) in the vocative. [Kātantra 2.1.40] states: "For words meaning 'mother' (*ambārtha*), when designated as *śraddhā* [by the rule], a short vowel occurs in the vocative: *he amba*, *he akka*."

Since the rule *ad ambārthānām* already establishes [the short vowel], the mention of *hrasva* (short) is for the sake of ease, as it is based on a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*). Because they consist of many syllables, the [shortening] would not apply to those containing *ḍa* or *la*, such as: *he ambāḍe*, *he ambāle*, *he ambike*.
[The rule] *aur īm* [applies]. (Kātantra 2.1.41)
After *śraddhā*, the vowel *ī* is substituted [for the case endings]; thus, *śraddhe*, *śraddhe*, *māle*.
Why "long" (*dīrgha*)? Some say it is for the forms *jarasī* etc. [The feminine endings] *ṅi*, *n*, *bhyām*, *bhis*, *bhyas*, *bhyām*, *sup* [are applied]. (Kātantra 2.1.42)

The nine case-endings following *śraddhā*—namely *yai*, *yās*, *yās*, and *yām*—occur in their respective order: *mālāyai*, *mālāyāḥ*, *mālāyāḥ*, *mālāyām*. However, for a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), [the endings] *sasu* and those preceded by a short vowel [are substituted]. (Kātantra 2.1.43) For a pronoun, the nine case-endings following it—namely *yai*, *yās*, *yās*, and *yām*—occur in their respective order together with the suffix *su*, and they are preceded by a short vowel. The marker *u* is for the purpose of making [the suffix] initial. [Examples: *sarvasyai*, *sarvasyāḥ*, *sarvasyāḥ*, *sarvasyām*.

The word *tu* serves to terminate the jurisdiction of its own [previous] rule. Or, according to *Kātantra* 2.1.44, *aprāpte vibhāṣā*: the case-endings beginning with *ṅ* following the second and third [feminine stems], namely *yā*, *yās*, *yās*, and *yām*, optionally become identical to the nominative (*su*) respectively, provided they are preceded by a short vowel. Thus: *dvitīyasyai* or *dvitīyāyai*; *tṛtīyasyai* or *tṛtīyāyai*.
Since the rule would have been established by *tīyāt vā*, the formulation *dvitīyātṛtīyābhyām* is for the sake of clarity.

Regarding *nadyā ai ās ās ām*: according to Kāt_2.1.45, the case-endings beginning with *ṅ* that follow a word designated as *nadī* (feminine) are replaced by *ai*, *ās*, *ās*, and *ām* respectively; alternatively, this substitution is not prescribed, resulting in *nadyai*, *nadyāḥ*, *nadyāḥ*, *nadyām*; and likewise *vadhvai*, *vadhvāḥ*, *vadhvāḥ*, *vadhvām*.
In the vocative singular, there is shortening. According to Pāṇini 6.1.69, the final vowel of a word ending in *nadī* becomes short in the vocative singular: *he nadi*, *he vadhu*.
Why is it specified "of *nadī*"? [To exclude cases such as: *he grāmaṇīḥ*, *he khalapūḥ*.
The initial [sound] of the case-endings *am* and *śas* undergoes elision. (Kāt.
2.1.47) When *am* and *śas* follow a word ending in *nadī*, their initial [sound] undergoes elision: *nadīm*, *nadīḥ*; *vadhūm*, *vadhūḥ*.
After a word ending in long *ī*, the nominative singular suffix *si* [is applied]. (Kāt. 2.1.48)
The *si* [case-ending] following a word ending in the vowel *ī* that is designated as a "feminine noun" (*nadī*) undergoes elision; for example: *nadī*, *mahī*.
Why specify "that which has *ī* as its final letter"? Consider *lakṣmīḥ*.
And [the *si* is elided] after a consonant as well. (Pāṇini 6.1.68)
A *s* following what is designated as a consonant (*vyañjana*) undergoes elision (*lopa*), as in *vāk* and *taḍit*.
If it were established by the rule for the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*), then there would be no elision of an initial *dhuṭ* [consonant].
Furthermore, the governing word (*liṅga*) continues to apply.
The *amo* [ending] after a word designated as *agni* undergoes elision (*lopa*). Examples: *agnim*, *paṭum*;
*buddhim*, *dhenum*. (Kāśikā 2.1.50)
The vowel *au* is the preceding [augment]. (Kāt. 2.1.51) After the word *agni*, the vowel *au* becomes the preceding vowel: *agnī*, *paṭū*, *buddhī*, *dhenū*.
The vowel *a* of the suffix *śas* becomes *n* when it follows a word that is not feminine. (Kāt. 2.1.52)

In the word *agni*, the letter *a* following the *śas* ending undergoes the vowel of the preceding sound, and it becomes nasalized (*nu*), provided it is not in the feminine gender—as in *agnīn* and *paṭūn*.
Why is it specified "not in the feminine"? [Consider] *buddhīḥ* and *dhenūḥ*.
The suffix *ṭā* becomes *nā*. (Kātantra 2.1.53)

The substitution of *na* occurs for the *ṭā*-case ending of the word *agni*, provided it is not feminine: *agninā*, *paṭunā*. Why is it specified "not feminine"? [Because in the feminine we have] *buddhyā*, *dhenvā*. *Kātantra 2.1.54*:
For the word *adas*, the substitution of *amu* occurs, and for the *ṭā*-case ending, the substitution of *nā* occurs, provided it is not feminine: *amunā*.
Why does it say "not feminine" (*astriyām*)? [Because in the feminine form] *amuyā* [the rule does not apply].
*Kāt_2.1.55*: *ir ed ur oc jasi*. When *jasi* follows, the final vowel of the stem becomes *ir*, *ed*, *ur*, or *oc*. For example: *agnayaḥ*, *paṭavaḥ*, *buddhayaḥ*, *dhenavaḥ*.
And in the vocative singular. (Kātantra 2.1.56) In the vocative singular, *i* becomes *e* for a stem ending in *i*, and *u* becomes *o* for a stem ending in *u*: he agne, he dheno.
Some say that this applies only to the word *agni* in the vocative: he nadi, he vadhu.

When *ṅe* follows, *iṛ* becomes *eṭ* for a stem ending in *iṛ*, and *uṛ* becomes *oṭ*; [e.g.,] *agnaye*, *paṭave*, *buddhaye*, *dhenave*. Because of the mention of the unmodified form *ṅe*, [the forms] *buddhyai* and *dhenvai* [are also included]. Kāt_2,1.58: In *ṅasi* and *ṅas*, there is also the elision (*lopa*) of the final vowel (*al*).

The *a* of the genitive singular endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas* is elided after the word *agni*; furthermore, *i* becomes *e*, and *u* becomes *o*. Thus: *agneḥ*, *agneḥ*; *dhenoḥ*, *dhenoḥ*. And [the same applies] after *go*: Kātantra 2.1.59 states that the *a* of the genitive singular endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas* is elided after the word *go*. Thus: *goḥ*, *goḥ*.

*Ṅi* with its preceding vowel becomes *au* after a term designated as *agni*. (Kātantra 2.1.60) After a word named *agni*, the case-ending *ṅi* together with its preceding vowel becomes *au*: *agnau*, *dhenau*.
*Ṅi* [becomes *au*] after *sakhi* and *pati*. (Kātantra 2.1.61)

The suffix *ṅi* following the words *sakhi* and *pati* becomes *aur*. Thus: *sakhyau*, *patyau*. The repetition of the mention of *ṅi* is for the purpose of excluding [the rule] when preceded by another word.
Regarding *ṅasi* and *ṅas*: "um aḥ" (Kātantra 2.1.62).
The vowel *u* (*um*) is substituted for the *a* of *ṅasi* and *ṅas* following the words *sakhi* and *pati*. Thus: *sakhyuḥ*, *sakhyuḥ*, *patyuḥ*, *patyuḥ*.
The mention of *agrahaṇa* (non-grasping) is for the purpose of preventing [the application of the rule] according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).

From a stem ending in *ṛ*, provided it has a preceding vowel: Pāṇini 6.1.63 states that after a nominal stem (*liṅga*) ending in *ṛ*, the *a* of the endings *ṅasi* and *ṅas* undergoes *um*-āgama together with the preceding vowel. Thus: *pitur*, *pitūḥ*; *mātuḥ*, *mātuḥ*.

What is the purpose of [the rule] "after that which ends in ṛ"? [It is to show: "ā is substituted for the feminine stem ending in ṛ before the nominative singular suffix *su*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of *su*. (Pāṇini 7.1.94). When *su* follows, *ā* is substituted for a nominal stem ending in ṛ, and *su* is elided; e.g., *pitā* (father), *mātā* (mother).
It is like *agni* before the suffix *śas*. (Kāt. 2.1.65) A stem ending in *ṛt* becomes like *agni* when *śas* follows; for example, *pitṝn*.
However, because of the prohibition "not in the feminine" (*tatrāstriyām*), it is *mātṝḥ*.

*ar ṅau*. Kāt_2,1.66: The substitute *ar* occurs for a stem ending in *ṛ* when the locative singular suffix *ṅi* follows; as in *pitari* and *mātari*. Due to the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), [the form] *pitaras tarpayāmāsa* is also established. *ghuṭi ca*. Kāt_2,1.67.

The substitute *ar* occurs for a stem ending in *ṛ* when a *ghuṭ* suffix follows: *pitarau*, *pitaraḥ*. Why is it specified "when a *ghuṭ* [suffix] follows"? [To exclude cases such as] *pitṝn*. This separate rule (*pṛthag-yoga*) is for the sake of what follows. The substitute *ar* occurs for the element *tṛ* belonging to a verbal root. (Kātantra 2.1.68)

The *ṛ* of the suffix *tṛ* prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes *ār* when a *ghuṭ* ending follows; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the rule for] *ar*. Examples: *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*.
Why specify "prescribed after a verbal root"? [Consider] *yātarau*, *yātaraḥ*; here, the suffix *ṛn* is applied and the vowel is lengthened.
Why specify "of the suffix *tṛ*"? [Consider] *nanāndarau*, *nanāndaraḥ*; here, the suffix is applied after the root *nand* with the prefix *nañ*.

In the *ghuṭ* [case endings], there is *tun* for the masculine and none for the feminine because it is derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes; thus, *kroṣṭā* (masculine nominative singular) and *kroṣṭrī* (feminine nominative singular). This is established by the suffix *tṛc*. However, in the case of *śas* and the following [endings], there is the usage of both the form ending in *tṛc* and the form ending in *tun*: *kroṣṭṝn*, *kroṣṭūn*; *kroṣṭrā*, *kroṣṭunā*, and so forth. And the same applies to *svasṛ* and the others. According to Pāṇini 7.1.89 (*Kāt_2,1.69*), for *svasṛ* and the others, *ār* replaces *ṛ* when a *ghuṭ* ending follows:
*svasārau*, *naptārau*.

*Svasṛ*, *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *kṣattṛ*, as well as *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ*—these eight beginning with *svasṛ* are traditionally taught [to form their vocative singular] with *ā*. However, this does not apply when they are in the state of being fully awakened (*saṃbuddhi*). (Kāt. 2.1.70)

In the vocative singular of a neuter stem ending in *ṛ*, the substitution of *ār* does not occur; rather, by implication, only *ar* is applied: *he kartar*, *he svasar*. *Kāt_2.1.71*: After a short vowel (*hrasva*), a *nadī* stem, or *śraddhā*, the *s* of the vocative (*saṃbuddhi*) undergoes elision (*lopa*). Examples: *he vṛkṣa*, *he agne*, *he dheno*, *he nadi*, *he vadhū*, *he śraddhe*, *he māle*.

What is meant by "perfectly awakened" (*saṃbuddhi*)? For example: *vṛkṣaḥ*. The inclusion of the terms *nadī* (feminine), *śraddhā*, and *grahaṇa* is for the sake of subsequent rules and for the present purpose as well. Regarding the rule *āmi ca nuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.54): after a stem ending in a short vowel, a *nadī* stem, or *śraddhā*, when the case-ending *ām* follows, the augment *nuṭ* is inserted before *ām*. Examples: *vṛkṣāṇām*, *agnīnām*, *dhenūnām*, *nadīnām*, *vadhūnām*, *śraddhānām*, *mālānām*.

Or, because of the inclusion of *āma* as accompanied by *śraddhā*, [the forms] are *nadyām* and *yuvām*. Regarding *tri*: Kāt_2.1.73 states that when *ām* follows, *tri* undergoes the substitution of *traya* and the augment *nu* is added; thus, [the forms are] *trayāṇām* and *paramatrayāṇām*.

Regarding *caturaḥ*: by Pāṇini 7.1.54 (*caturo 'ś*), the augment *nuṭ* is inserted before the genitive plural ending *ām* after the word *catur*; thus, *caturṇām*. This occurs only when [the stem] is not the principal member of a compound; hence, *aticaturām*.

*Kāt_2.1.75: After a numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n*, the augment *nuṭ* is inserted before the genitive plural suffix *ām*. [Examples: *ṣaṇṇām* ("of six"), *pañcānām* ("of five"). Because of the mention of "ending" (*anta*), it also applies to those that previously ended in *n*, such as *aṣṭānām* ("of eight").
Why specify "after a numeral"? [Counter-examples: *vipruṣām* ("of droplets"), *yajvanām* ("of sacrificers").

There is elision (*luk*) of *jas* and *śas* after *kati*. (Kāt. 2.1.76) After the word *kati*—which is a numeral ending in *ṣ* or *n*—there occurs elision of *jas* and *śas*: *kati*, *kati*; *ṣaṭ*, *ṣaṭ*; *pañca*, *pañca*.
There is *ṅi* [and] *ām* after *ni*. (Kāt. 2.1.77)
The *ni* [suffix] becomes *ṅi*, as in *niyām* and *grāmaṇyām*.
Thus ends the first quarter on the four types of nouns in the Daurgasimhī Vṛtti.
[The rule] *na sakhiṣ ṭādāv agniḥ* (Kāt_2.2.1) [applies].
In the forms *sakhi* and *pati*, when followed by the suffixes beginning with *ṭa* or a vowel, the substitution of *nā* for the final *i* does not occur. Thus: *sakhyā*, *sakhye*.

Regarding *pati* when not in a compound (*asamāse*): in the forms *pati* and *pati*, when followed by the suffixes beginning with *ṭa* or a vowel, the substitution of *nā* for the final *i* does not occur. Thus: *patyā*, *patye*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not in a compound"? [Example: *narapatinā* (by the king).
A feminine word is treated like a river-stem (*nadī*). According to Pāṇini 1.4.3, the feminine word behaves like a river-stem before a case-ending: *he stri*, *striyai*, *strīṇām*.
It also sublates the alternative view.

[The rule] *stryākhyāv iyuvau vāmi* (Kātantra 2.2.4) states: "When followed by the case-ending *ām*, the feminine nouns (*stryākhya*) that have *i* and *u* as their substitutes may optionally behave like the *nadī* class. Thus we have: *śrīṇām* or *śriyām*; *bhrūṇām* or *bhruvām*.

What is the purpose of the rule *stryākhyau*? [Examples: *yavakrīyam*, *kaṭaprūvam*. And when a *ṅit* suffix follows, there is also a short vowel. (Kātantra 2.2.5) When a *ṅit* suffix follows, the feminine designations (*stryākhya*) whose substitutes are *iy* and *uv* optionally become like the *nadī* [vowels], provided they are short *i* or *u*: *buddhyai*, *buddhaye*; *dhenvai*, *dhenave*; *śriyai*, *śriye*; *bhruvai*, *bhruve*; *paṭvai*, *paṭave*.

Some say [the rule applies] "to a feminine [noun]. Why [is it said] "it is not [so] in the vocative"? [Examples are: *he śrīḥ*, *he bhrūḥ*. [In these cases,] the object of comparison (*upameya*) is not well-known. Regarding the neuter [nouns], there is no elision of the nominative and accusative singular endings (*syamoḥ*), and that has already been stated. (Kātantra 2.2.6)

The elision of *si* and *am* occurs after a neuter stem, and the grammatical operation prescribed for it does not take place; as in *payaḥ*, *payaḥ*; *tat*, *tat*; *susakhi*, *susakhi*. Why "after a neuter [stem]"? [Consider] *supayā gauḥ* ("a cow with good milk"). And after a [neuter stem ending in] *a*, when it is not the vocative singular, *mu* is also substituted. (Kāt. 2.2.7)

The suffixes *si* and *am* following a neuter noun ending in *a* undergo elision (*lopa*), and the augment *mur* is added, except in the vocative singular; e.g., *kuṇḍam*, *atijaram*. Why "except in the vocative singular"? [Observe: *he kuṇḍa*.
But for a stem beginning with *anya*, the substitute is *tu*; Pāṇini 7.1.28.

After the neuter gender forms of the group beginning with *anya*, there is elision of the case endings *si* and *au*, and the augment *tu* is inserted; thus: *anyat*, *anyatarat*, *itarat*, *katarat*, *katamat*.
The word *tu* is for the purpose of excluding the vocative; [therefore] not *he anyat*.
[The rule] *aur īm* [applies]. (Kātantra 2.2.9)
After every neuter [stem], the vowel *au* undergoes the substitution of *īm*, as in *kuṇḍe* (in the pot) and *payasī* (in the two milks). *Kāt_2.2.10*:
After every neuter [stem], in place of the dual endings *jas* and *śas*, the substitute *śi* occurs, as in *padmāni* (lotuses) and *payāṃsi* (milks).

*Kāt_2.2.11: dhuṭ-svarād ghuṭi nuḥ.* Before a *ghuṭ* [consonant], after a vowel that precedes a *dhuṭ* [consonant], the augment *nu* is inserted for a neuter gender [stem] when a *ghuṭ* follows. Examples: *payāṃsi*, *padmāni*, *sukartṛṇi*, *susakhīni*.
How is it that [the forms] *sukruñci*, *gomanti*, and *suvalgi* are formed? [They are so] because the *dhuṭ* is separated [from the vowel by the augment].
Because *dhuṭ* is a class [of consonants], there is no fault in [the form] *goraṅkṣi*.
One should rather say *bahūrji* or *bahūrñji*.
[The rule] "after a vowel-stem, before a vowel" (Kāt_2.2.12) applies.
The augment *nu* is added after a neuter stem ending in a *nāmin* vowel when followed by a vowel; for example, *vāriṇā*, *vāriṇe*. Why specify "after a *nāmin* vowel"? [Observe: *kulayoḥ*.

In the case of *asthi*, *dadhi*, *sakthi*, and *akṣi*, the suffix *an* is substituted for the final vowel before suffixes beginning with *ṭa* (the fourth case ending and those following). (Kātantra 2.2.13)

In the case of neuter stems ending in *an* belonging to the *asthi*-class and so forth, *an* is substituted for the final vowel before a vowel beginning with the suffixes starting with *ṭa*. For example: *asthnā*, *dadhnā*, *sakthnā*, *akṣṇā*, *atyasthnā*, *atidadhnā*, *chāttreṇa*.
Why is the vowel *a* pronounced [in the rule]? [To show that] it might otherwise be *asthni* or *asthanī*.
When a word has been previously used as masculine (*bhāṣitapuṃska*), it optionally becomes like the masculine (*pumvat*). (Kātantra 2.2.14)

A neuter noun ending in a vowel that has a corresponding masculine form becomes optionally like the masculine before case endings beginning with *ṭa* (the fourth case) and vowels; for example, *kartrā* or *kartṛṇā kulena*, *mṛdave* or *mṛdune vastrāya*.
Why "having a corresponding masculine form"? [As in] *vāriṇe*.
Why "ending in a vowel"? [As in] *somapena kulena*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "neuter"? [Example: *kalyāṇyai*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "the meaning has been expressed as masculine"? [Example: *pīlune phalāya*. Regarding the rule *Kāt_2.2.15*: "A stem ending in a vowel (*nāmyanta*) becomes long before the genitive plural suffix *ām* when it follows the suffix *san*. [Examples: *agnīnām*, *dhenūnām*, *kartṝṇām*.

The inclusion of *san* is for the sake of subsequent rules, and here it is also for the sake of lengthening when the augment *nu* has been applied. [Kātantra 2.2.16] "In a stem ending in *n*, the penultimate vowel becomes long before *san*, *āmu*, and *ām*: as in *pañcānām* and *saptānām*. Why say 'before *san*'? As in *varmaṇām*.

*Kāt_2.2.17*: In the presence of a *ghuṭ* [suffix], except for the vocative singular (*asaṃbuddhau*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of a stem ending in *n* becomes long. For example: *rājā*, *rājānau*, *sāmāni*. Why specify "of a stem ending in *n*"? Consider: *janam*, *janau*.

What is meant by "except in the vocative singular" (*asaṃbuddhau*)? [The rule applies] to words ending in *s* and to the word *mahat*, provided the penultimate vowel is not long. (Kātantra 2.2.18) In these two cases—namely, those ending in *s* and *mahat*—the penultimate vowel becomes long before a *ghuṭ* suffix, except in the vocative singular: *śreyān*, *śreyāṃsau*; *mahān*, *mahāntau*.

What is the purpose of the condition "not being followed by a *saṃbuddhi* (vocative singular) ending"? [Consider: *he śreyan*, *he mahan*. What is the purpose of the condition "ending in a final *s*"? [Consider: *haṃsam*, *haṃsau*.
Due to its association with the word *mahat*, the rule would not apply to the verbal root; thus, [we have] *suhin*, *suhiṃsau*.
And [the rule] regarding *āp*. Kāt_2.2.19:

In the case of this [stem] *āp*, whether its penultimate vowel is *an* or not *an*, a long vowel occurs before a *ghuṭ* [consonant], except in the vocative singular; as in *āpaḥ* and *svāmpi taḍāgāni*. Why "except in the vocative singular"? [As in: *he śucy ap*.

*Kāt_2.2.20*: "And for that which ends in *antu* or *as*, provided it is not a verbal root, when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*, the long vowel occurs in place of the audible *at*, except in the vocative case. For example: *bhavān*, *gomān*, *suśrotāḥ*. Even in the masculine, there is the long vowel in *dīrghāho nidāghaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not when [the stem] ends in a suffix"? [Examples: *piṇḍagraḥ*, *carmavaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not in the vocative singular (*asaṃbuddhau*)"? [Example: *he suśrotaḥ*.
[The rule] *inhanpūṣāryamṇāṃ śau ca* (Kātantra 2.2.21) [applies].

In the case of these words—*daṇḍin*, *vṛtrahan*, *pūṣan*, and *aryaman*—the penultimate vowel becomes long when followed by the nominative plural suffix *śas* or the nominative singular suffix *su*, provided they are not in the vocative case. Examples: *sudaṇḍīni*, *suvṛtrahāṇi*, *supūṣāṇi*, *svaryamāṇi*; [and in the singular: *daṇḍī*, *vṛtrahā*, *pūṣā*, *aryamā*. Why "not in the vocative"? Because of the restriction that this occurs only before *śas* and *su*, we have [in the dual] *daṇḍinau*, *vṛtrahaṇau*, *pūṣaṇau*, *aryamaṇau*. Why "not in the vocative"? [Because the rule does not apply there]: *he daṇḍin*. Because of the restriction that it applies only to *śas* and *su*, [we have the following forms].
Precisely for this reason, there is no lengthening of the penultimate vowel in *han* when followed by the suffix *kvip*.

[The rule] "In the case of *uśanas*, *purudaṃśas*, and *anehas*, the suffix *an* is added at the end before the nominative singular ending *s* (except in the vocative)" (Kātantra 2.2.22) means that for these words—*uśanas*, *purudaṃśas*, and *anehas*—the suffix *an* occurs at the end before the nominative singular ending *s*, provided it is not the vocative: *uśanā*, *purudaṃśā*, *anehā*.
What is the purpose of the condition "not being a *saṃbuddha*"? [Examples: *he uśanaḥ*, *he purudaṃśaḥ*, *he anehaḥ*.

How is it that we have *he uśanan* and *he uśana*? Because the negative particle (*nañ*) is not invariably applied here; the inclusion of the letter *a* is for the sake of subsequent rules. And [the rule applies] after *sakhi*. (Kātantra 2.2.23)
The suffix *an* occurs in place of the final portion of the word *sakhi*; this [substitution] takes place before case endings other than the vocative singular (*asaṃbuddhau*), resulting in *sakhā*.
Why specify "before endings other than the vocative singular"? [To exclude forms such as] *he sakhe*.
However, before *ghuṭ* endings, *ai* is substituted [for the final vowel]. (Kātantra 2.2.24)
Before a *ghuṭ* suffix, the final [sound] of *sakhi* becomes [the substitute *sakhā*]. Thus: *sakhāyau*, *sakhāyaḥ*, *sakhāyam*, *sakhāyau*.
Why is it specified as "before a *ghuṭ*"? [To exclude cases like: *sakhīn*. The word *tu* is for the purpose of excluding the vocative (*asaṃbuddhi*) in the subsequent rules.
*diva ud vyañjane* (Kāt_2.2.25): The *v* of *div* becomes *u* when followed by a consonant (*vyañjana*). Examples: *dyubhyām*, *dyuṣu*, *dyugataḥ*, *dyutvam*.
It would not be so [i.e., the *v* would not become *u*] in the case of *divyam*.
Kāt_2,2.26: In the presence of the [nominal] suffix *su*, the *v* of *div* becomes *au*; thus, *dyauḥ*, and in the vocative, *he dyauḥ*.
Kāt_2,2.27: Or, when followed by a vowel (*am*), [the *v* of *div* becomes *au*].
The substitution of *v* for the *v* of *div* occurs optionally when the case ending *am* follows: *dyām*, *divam*, *atidyām*, *atidivam*.
According to Kāt_2.2.28, the nasal *n* of the root *yujir* is substituted by *ghuṭ* when it occurs at the end of a non-compound (*asamāsa*) before a *ghuṭ* suffix:
*yuṅ*, *yuñjau*, *yuñjaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not in a compound"? [Consider] *aśvayuk*.

From Kātantra 2.2.29, it will be stated that "the reduplicated (*abhyasta*) [root], except for the final vowel, [receives the augment *an*]" and that "the group beginning with *jakṣ* is also reduplicated."
After a reduplicated (abhyasta) root, the suffix *anta* becomes *anakāraka* when followed by a *ghuṭ* case-ending: *dadat*, *dadhat*, *jakṣat*, *jāgrat*.
Why say "after a reduplicated root"? [Observe: *lihan*.
Optionally so in the neuter gender. (Pāṇini 7.1.78–80)

After [a stem] ending in *tu* or *bhā*, the suffix *anti* becomes optionally *anakāraka* (lacking the augment *a*) when followed by a neuter *ghuṭ* case-ending: *dadati*, *dadanti*; *jāgrati*, *jāgranti* (the families).

Regarding the rule *tudabhādibhya īkāre* (Pāṇini 7.1.31): the form *tuda* ending in *ad* is repeated [as the base]. After stems beginning with *tuda* and *bhā*, the suffix *anti* becomes optionally *anakāraka* when followed by the feminine suffix *īkāra*: *tudatī*, *tudantī* (the woman); *tudatī*, *tudantī* (the family); *bhātī*, *bhāntī* (the woman); *bhātī*, *bhāntī* (the family). Why "after *tuda* and *bhā* etc. (*tudabhādibhyaḥ*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to: *pacantī*, *dīvyantī*.

*Kāt_2,2.32*: *haner her ghir upadhālope*. When the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) of the root *han* is elided, *ghi* is substituted in place of *hi*; e.g., *vṛtraghnaḥ*, *vṛtraghnā*. Why specify "when there is elision of the penultimate vowel"? [Observe: *vṛtrahayati*. *Kāt_2,2.33*: *gor au ghuṭi*. [The substitution of *ghu* occurs for *go* before a *ghuṭ* suffix.]
The substitution of *au* occurs for the word *go-* when a *ghuṭ* suffix follows: *gauḥ*, *gāvau*, *gāvaḥ*.
Why is it specified "when a *ghuṭ* [suffix follows]"? [Observe: *he citrago*, *he citragavaḥ*.
[In the case of] *am* and *śas*, the substitution of *ā* [occurs]. (Pāṇini 7.1.9–10)
The vowel *ā* occurs at the end of the word *go* when the suffixes *am* or *śas* follow: *gām*, *gāḥ*.
Why is the long vowel specified? [To indicate that] in the masculine, the rule "the substitute *ād* occurs in place of the feminine [suffix]" would not apply.
For *panthin*, *manthin*, and *ṛbhukṣin*, [the substitution of *ā* occurs] before the nominative singular suffix (*su*). (Kātantra 2.2.35)

In the case of *pathin* and other such stems, the final vowel becomes *ā* when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*: *panthāḥ*, *he panthāḥ*; *manthāḥ*, *he manthāḥ*; *ṛbhukṣāḥ*, *he ṛbhukṣāḥ*.
In the strong cases (*ghuṭ*), the final vowel of *pathin* and others becomes *an*:
*panthānau*, *manthānau*, *ṛbhukṣāṇau*. (Kātantra 2.2.36)

In a non-ghuṭ vowel, there is elision [of the final syllable]. (Kātantra 2.2.37) For *pathin* and the others, the final [syllable] undergoes elision before a non-ghuṭ vowel: *pathaḥ*, *pathā*; *mathaḥ*, *mathā*; *ṛbhukṣaḥ*, *ṛbhukṣā*.
And before a consonant, *niḥ* is substituted for these. (Kātantra 2.2.38)

In these words beginning with *pathin*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the nasal [anusvāra] before a consonant that is not a *ghuṭ* sound and before a vowel. Thus: *pathaḥ*, *pathikaḥ*, *pathayati*; *mathaḥ*, *mathikaḥ*, *mathayati*; *pathibhyām*, *pathitvam*; *mathibhyām*, *mathitvam*. The mention of "these" is for the purpose of elision only before vowels and consonants that are not *ghuṭ*; therefore, one has *pathigataḥ*, *pathyuttamaḥ*, *mathigataḥ*, and *mathyuttamaḥ*. And the *anuṣaṅga* [nasal] remains except when followed by *kruñc*. (Kātantra 2.2.39)

The word *kruñced* is a compound consisting of *kruñcaḥ* and *ic*, with the case-ending elided. A nasal (*n*) designated as an *anuṣaṅga* undergoes elision before a vowel that is not *ghuṭ* (i.e., a non-nasal stop or a sibilant). However, this does not occur for the nasal of the root *kruñc-* which has *it* as its indicatory letter, as in *viduṣaḥ*, *viduṣā*, *viduṣī*, *vaiduṣyam*; nor for the nasal of *mahat-*, as in *mahataḥ*, *mahatā*, *mahadbhyām*, *mahatsu*, *mahattā*. Why "not after *kruñc-*"? [Consider] *kruñcaḥ*, *kruṅbhyām*, *sukaṃsaḥ*, *sukanbhyām*.

The elision of the word *pumān*. (Kātantra 2.2.40) The elision of the word *pumān* occurs before suffixes beginning with vowels other than those called *ghuṭ*, and before consonants; [as in] *puṃsaḥ*, *puṃsā*, *puṃbhyām*, *puṃstvam*, *pauṃsnam*.
