Why "before suffixes beginning with vowels other than *ghuṭ* and before consonants"? [Consider: *pumāṃsau*.
The substitution of *u* for the vowel of *catvār* is optional. (Kāt.

2.2.41) The substitution of *u* occurs optionally for the vowel of the word *catvār* before suffixes beginning with consonants other than those called *ghuṭ*, as well as before vowels; e.g., *caturaḥ*, *cāturikaḥ*, *caturthaḥ*, *priyacatayati*, *caturbhiḥ*, *cāturyam*.
And [the substitution of *u* occurs] for the vowel of *anaḍuh* as well. (Kāt. 2.2.42)

In the word *anaḍvāh*, the vowel *u* replaces the sound *v* before a suffix beginning with a non-*ghuṭ* vowel or a consonant: *anaḍuhaḥ*, *anaḍuhā*, *ānaḍuhikaḥ*, *anaḍudbhyām*, *anaḍuhyam*, *anaḍuhī*, *anaḍvāhī*.
Some maintain that there is an option regarding the feminine form.
After the nominative singular (*su*), *nu* is substituted [for the final syllable]. (Kātantra 2.2.43)
The augment *nu* is added to the word *anaḍvāh* when the nominative singular suffix *s* follows; thus, *anaḍvān*.
Why specify "in the nominative singular" (*sāv*)? [Observe that] *anaḍvāhau* [does not take the augment].
In the vocative singular, both [the final vowel and the augment *nu*] become short. (Kātantra 2.2.44)
In the vocative case, the vowel of both *catur* and *anaḍuh* becomes short: *he priyacatvaḥ*, *he anaḍvan*.
According to Kātantra 2.2.45, when *adas* occurs as a word (*pada*), the *da* is replaced by *ma* before a case-ending:
*amuṣmāt*, *amuṣmin*.
What is the purpose of the condition *vibhaktau* ("in a case-ending")? [Examples where it does not apply: *adas-yati*, *adas-tvam*, *adaḥ-putraḥ*.
It should be stated that *adamuyaṅ*, *amudryaṅ*, *amumuyaṅ*, and *adadryaṅ* [are formed].
When a suffix beginning with a vowel other than *ghuṭ* follows, the substitution of *u* for the syllable *va* occurs even in the case of *vaṃśi* when it takes the augment *iṭ*. (Kātantra 2.2.46)

When a suffix beginning with a non-guttural vowel follows, the substitution of *u* occurs for the syllable *va* of the root *vaś*, whether it takes the augment *iṭ* or not; as in *pecuṣaḥ*, *pecuṣā*, *pecuṣī*, *paicuṣam*; and *viduṣaḥ*, *viduṣā*, *viduṣī*, *vaiduṣam*.
It should also be stated that [the suffix] *yañ* follows these, as in *paicuṣyam* and *vaiduṣyam*.
And [the same applies] to *śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan*. (Kātantra 2.2.47)

In the case of these words—*śvan*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan*—the substitution of *u* for the vowel *va* occurs when a suffix beginning with a non-*ghuṭ* vowel follows: *śunaḥ*, *śunā*, *śunī*; *yūnaḥ*, *yūnā*, *yūnī*; *maghonaḥ*, *maghonā*, *maghonī*. By virtue of the governing rule (*apyadhikārāt*), we have: *śauvanaṃ māṃsam* (dog meat), *yauvanaṃ vartate* (youth exists), and *māghavanaḥ sthālīpākaḥ* (an offering for Maghavan). When a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix follows, the change is observed: *upaśunam* (near the dog), *śunaḥ saṃkocaḥ* (contraction of the dog), and *śauvaḥ* (belonging to the dog). According to Kātantra 2.2.48, in the word *vāh* (ox), the vowel *va* is optionally changed to *u*.

The vowel *au* replaces *vāh* before suffixes beginning with a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ* (i.e., a non-nasal consonant or a semivowel), as in *praṣṭhauhaḥ*, *praṣṭhauhā*, *praṣṭhauhī*, and *prāṣṭhauhyam*. In the case of the root *añc*, there is elision of the final *a* and lengthening of the preceding vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ* (Kātantra 2.2.49). This occurs due to phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*). Thus: *pratīcaḥ*, *pratīcā*, *pratīcī*, *prātīcyam*; *gocaḥ*, *gocā*, *gocī*, *gaucyam*.

*tiryaṅ* becomes *tiraścir* [before vowels and consonants other than semivowels and nasals], except when followed by a *ghuṭ* (a strong case-ending) or a vowel. Thus: *tiraścaḥ*, *tiraścā*, *tiraścī*, *tairaścyam*.
*udaṅ* becomes *udīciḥ* [in the same conditions]. *Kāt_2,2.50–51*
The word *udac* becomes *udīc* before suffixes beginning with a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ*. Thus: *udīcaḥ*, *udīcā*, *udīcī*, *audīcyam*.

The rule *pāt padaṃ samāsāntaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.63) states that the word *pad* at the end of a compound becomes *pada* before suffixes beginning with a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ*. Thus: *vyāghrapadaḥ*, *vyāghrapadā*, *vyāghrapadī*, *vaiyāghrapadyam*; *ekapadaḥ*, *supadaḥ*, *kumbhapadī*.
The rule *asamāsānta* [is also applicable here]. Consider the word *padaḥ*; it is held that there is also a form *pād*, which has the same meaning as *pāda*.
*Kāt_2.2.53*: *avamasaṃyogād ano 'lopo 'luptavac ca pūrvavidhau*.

There is elision (*lopa*) of the vowel *a* of the suffix *an*, provided it does not follow a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) ending in *v* or *m*, and this elision is treated as if it had not occurred (*aluptavat*) when a grammatical operation is to be applied to a preceding sound. Examples: *rājñaḥ*, *rājñā*, *dadhnaḥ*, *dadhnā*, *pratidīvnaḥ*, *pratidīvnā*.
What is meant by "due to connection with *avama*"? As in *parvaṇaḥ* and *carmaṇaḥ*.

[Kātantra 2.2.54: When *ī* or *īṅ* follow, there is optionally the elision of the vowel *a* of the suffix *an* that follows a word connected with *avama*; and that [elided vowel] is treated as if not elided when an operation is to be performed on the preceding phoneme. Examples: *sāmnī*, *sāmanī*; *rājñi*, *rājani*.
By virtue of constant association (*sāhacarya*), [the word] *rājñī* is always [feminine].
Why [is it said] "due to connection with something inferior" (*avamasaṃyogāt*)? [Consider the examples: *parvaṇī*, *carmanī*.
[The rule] "before a suffix beginning with a vowel other than *ghuṭ*" (*ā dhātor aghuṭ-svare*) applies from Kāt. 2.2.55.

The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs after a nominal stem (*dhātu*) before a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ* [i.e., a case-ending beginning with a vowel], as in *kīlālapaḥ* and *kīlālapāḥ*. The repetition of the phrase "before a vowel that is not a *ghuṭ*" is for the purpose of terminating the jurisdiction of the section on the vocative singular (*saṃbuddhi*); therefore, we have *śaṅkhadhmaḥ* and *śaṅkhadhmāḥ*. Before a vowel, the short vowels *ī* and *ū* become *iy* and *uv*, respectively. (Kātantra 2.2.56)

The vowels *ī* and *ū* of a nominal stem (*dhātu*) become *iy* and *uv*, respectively, before a vowel-initial case ending (*vibhakti-svara*), as follows: *niy-au*, *niy-aḥ*; *luv-au*, *luv-aḥ*. Why specify "before a vowel-initial case ending"? [Observe: *ny-arthaḥ*, *lv-arthaḥ*.
It should be stated that this applies to *svāyaṃbhuvam*.
Regarding the word *sudhī*: by Pāṇini 6.1.198 (*Kāt_2,2.57*), this [vṛddhi] applies to the word *sudhī* in the accent of the case endings (*vibhaktisvara*): *sudhiyau*, *sudhiyaḥ*.
Why "the word *sudhī*" (*sudhīr iti*)? [Consider: *pradhyau*, *pradhyaḥ*.

*bhūḥ* becomes *bhū-* [before a case ending with a vowel], as in *avarṣābhūḥ*, *apunarbhūḥ*. By rule Kāt_2.2.58, *bhū-* attains *uvaṃ* [the substitution of *u* for *bhū*] before a case-ending vowel: *avarṣābhūḥ*, *apunarbhūḥ*; *mitrabhuv-au*, *mitrabhuvaḥ*; *atibhuv-au*, *atibhuvaḥ*.
Why specify *avarṣābhūḥ* and *apunarbhūḥ*? [To exclude cases such as: *varṣābhv-au*, *punarbhv-au*.

Kātyāyana 2.2.59: *anekākṣarayos tv asaṃyogād yavau*. When two bases consisting of more than one syllable end in the vowels *ī* or *ū*, provided they are not preceded by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), the sounds *y* and *v* are substituted for them respectively when followed by a case-ending that bears an accent (*vibhaktisvara*). For example: *grāmaṇy-au*, *grāmaṇyaḥ*; *yavalv-au*, *yavalvaḥ*. Why does it say "consisting of more than one syllable"? [Counter-examples: *niy-au*, *luv-au*. Why does it say "provided they are not preceded by a consonant cluster"? [Counter-examples: *yavakriy-au*, *kaṭapruv-au*.
This rule applies only after indeclinables and kārakas.
*Bhrū* is like a verbal root (dhātu). According to Kātantra 2.2.60, the word *bhrū* behaves like a verbal root regarding the accent of case endings: *bhruvau*, *bhruvaḥ*.
This is an extended application (*atideśa*).
[Kātyāyana 2.2.61 states: "And *strī*.
The word *strī* is treated like a verbal root (*dhātu*) with respect to the accent of case endings (*vibhakti-svara*); thus: *striyau*, *striyaḥ*.

Before the suffixes *am* and *śas*, the word *strī* optionally becomes like a verbal root (*dhātuvat*). [Examples: *striyam*, *strīm*; *striyaḥ*, *strīḥ*. *Kāt_2,2.63*: In the vocative singular, the substitution of *u* for the final vowel of words beginning with *bhū* optionally occurs.
The substitution of *u* for the *ava* of *bhavat* occurs optionally before the vocative suffix (*saṃbuddhi*); thus, *he bhoḥ* or *he bhavan*.
Because the vocative suffix is characterized by its occurrence in conjunction [with the preceding element], its elision would not otherwise take place.
After an indeclinable or a pronoun, the suffix *ka* is added before the final vowel. (Pāṇini 5.3.71)

The suffix *ak* optionally occurs before the final vowel of indeclinables and pronouns; furthermore, the suffix *kap* occurs frequently. Examples: *uccakaiḥ*, *uccaiḥ*; *nīcakaiḥ*, *nīcaiḥ*; *sarvakaḥ*, *sarvaḥ*; *viśvakaḥ*, *viśvaḥ*; *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, *yuṣmābhiḥ*; *asmakābhiḥ*, *asmābhiḥ*.
It is also desired that it occur before a case-ending: *tvayakā*, *mayakā*. It also occurs after a verb: *pacataki*, *pacati*; *bhinddhaki*, *bhinddhi*.
The suffix *ka* is also applied: *yāvakaḥ* (barley gruel), *maṇikaḥ* (a water-jar).

In the sense of ignorance or contempt: *aśvakaḥ* (a miserable horse). In the sense of compassion: *vatsakaḥ* (a dear little calf). [In the vocative: *ehaki*, *ehi*, or *iha nu te dhānākāḥ* ("Come here, here are your parched grains").
Do not go far from home.
A small amount of oil is *tailakam*. A short tree is *vṛkṣakaḥ*.

In the case of *saṃjñā*, [the name] is *Devadattaka*. Regarding the suffix *ka*: when the suffix *ka* follows a feminine form ending in the vowel *ā*, the preceding *a* becomes *i*. (Kāt_2.2.65) When the suffix *ka* follows a feminine form ending in the vowel *ā*, the preceding *a* undergoes the change to *i*: *sarvikā*, *uṣṭrikā*, *pācikā*, *pāṭhikā*.
What is *ka*? *cetanā*. What is *pratyaya*? *takā*. What is *strī*? *pācakābhyām*.
What is the purpose of the word *kṛta*? [Examples include: *putrakāmyā*, *yakā*, *sakā*, *jīvakā*, *nandakā*, and *āśiṣyakaḥ*.
This concludes the second quarter of the section on names in the fourth chapter of the *Daugasiṃhī-vṛtti*.

*Kāt_2.3.1*: After a word (*pada*), the forms *vas* and *nas* optionally replace *yuṣmad* and *asmad* respectively when followed by a case ending in the sixth, fourth, or second case, provided they denote the plural. For example: *putro yuṣmākam*, *putro 'smākam*; *putro vaḥ*, *putro naḥ*; *putro yuṣmabhyam*, *putro 'smabhyam*; *putro vaḥ*, *putro naḥ*; *putro yuṣmān*, *putro 'smān*; *putro vaḥ*, *putro naḥ*. Why specify "of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" (*yuṣmadasmadoḥ*)? [Consider: *putras teṣām* ("the son of them"). (In this case, the replacement does not occur.)
What is the purpose of the condition "after a word" (*padāt*)? [Consider: *yuṣmākam*, *asmākam*.
[The rule] *vām nau dvitve* (Pāṇini 7.2.95) states:

after the word *pada* following the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when they occur in the dual number and are followed by the sixth, fourth, or second case endings, the forms *vām* and *nau* respectively are optionally substituted. For example: *grāmo yuvayoḥ*, *grāma āvayoḥ*; or *grāmo vām*, *grāmo nau*. Likewise: *dīyate*, *pātu*.
Why does [the sūtra] say "in these [cases]" (*āsu*)? [Consider: *bhadrau yuvām* (you two are auspicious), *bhadrāv āvām* (we two are auspicious).

Regarding *tvad* and *mad*, when used in the singular: *te* and *me*; but *tvā* and *mā* in the second case. *Kātantra 2.3.3*: When *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occur in the singular, having become *tvad* and *mad*, a word following a preceding word [ending in a case suffix] undergoes, respectively, the forms *te* and *me* in the sixth, fourth, and second cases when they have been produced in the singular; however, *tvā* and *mā* occur in the second case. Examples: *putras tava* (your son), *putro mama* (my son); [alternatively] *putras te*, *putro me*. Likewise: *dāsyati* (he will give), *putras tvā*, *putro mā pātu* (may the son protect you/me).

Not at the beginning of a verse-quarter (*pāda*). According to Kātantra 2.3.4, forms such as *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurring at the beginning of a verse-quarter do not undergo these substitutions. For example: "The god Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, is the family deity of you all; he alone, the Blessed One, is our protector and destroyer of sins.
Why specify "at the beginning of a verse-quarter"? [Consider: "May Narasiṃha protect you," and so forth.

And in connection with *ca* and so forth (*cādiyoge*). According to Pāṇini 8.1.24 (*Kāt_2,3.5*), the substitutes [of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] do not apply to words such as *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when they are joined with *ca* and so forth; for example: *putro yuṣmākaṃ ca*, *putro 'smākaṃ ca*, and so on.
[The particles are: *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, *eva*.
In a figurative application (*gauṇayoga*), [the elision] would not occur: "the village is yours" (*grāmaś ca te svam*) and "the city is mine" (*nagaraṃ ca me svam*).

In these cases, there is the elision of the final sound (*antalopa*) before a case ending (*vibhakti*). According to Pāṇini 7.1.27–28 (*Kāt_2,3.6*), the elision of the final sound occurs for these [pronouns] when followed by a case ending: *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*, *atitvān*, *atimān*, *tvayi*, *mayi*.

What is the purpose of the condition "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*)? [Examples where it does not apply: *yuṣmatputraḥ* ("your son"), *tvadīyaḥ* ("belonging to you"). *Kāt_2.3.7*: "In place of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *yuva-* and *āva-* occur when followed by dual endings.
Thus: *yuvābhyām*, *āvābhyām*, *atiyuvābhiḥ*, *atyāvābhiḥ*. (The substitution occurs according to their respective order.)
Why [is it specified] "when two forms are heard" among those with dual endings? [For example: *atitvām* (one who has surpassed you) and *atiyuṣmān* (those who have surpassed you).
*yuvayoḥ putraḥ* (the son of the two of you). *yuṣmatputraḥ* (your son).

This [suffix] *am* belongs to you two (*yuvayoḥ*), as it is yours (*yuṣmadīya*); it follows from the elision of the final vowel by way of the elision of the suffix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇena*). Regarding the rule *am au cām* (Kātantra 2.3.8): after the words *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, etc., the suffix *ām* occurs in place of both *am* and *au*. Thus, we have *tvām*, *mām*, *yuvām*, and *āvām*. Because this falls under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning dual expressions, there would be no association with the singular forms (*vā-sāhacaryam na syāt*).
*Ām* replaces *śas*. (Kāt. 2.3.9) After *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and so forth, *śas* becomes *ān*; thus: *yuṣmān*, *asmān*, *atitvān*, *atimān*.
*Tvam* and *aham* replace [the forms of] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* when followed by the nominative singular (*su*) along with its case endings. (Kāt. 2.3.10)

In the case of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when followed by the nominative singular (*su*) along with its case-ending, these two forms *tvam* and *aham* respectively take their place—namely, *tvam* and *aham*. Examples: *tvam*, *aham*, *atitvam*, *atyaham*. Why specify "along with its case-ending"? [To exclude cases where the ending is elided: *adhitvat*, *adhimat* (where the ending is dropped). In the nominative plural (*jas*), [the forms become] *yūyam* and *vayam*. (Kātantra 2.3.11)

In the case of *tvad* and *mad*, as well as *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when followed by the nominative plural suffix (*jas*) along with its case endings, these two forms *yūyam* and *vayam* are substituted respectively: *yūyam*, *vayam*, *atiyūyam*, *ativayam*. In the case of the dative singular suffix (*ṅe*), according to Pāṇini 7.2.95 (*Kāt_2,3.12*), *tvad* and *mad*, as well as *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, when followed by the suffix *ṅe* along with its case endings, these two forms *tubhyam* and *mahyam* are substituted respectively: *tubhyam*, *mahyam*, *atitubhyam*, *atimahyam*.

*tava* and *mama* [are substituted] for *ṅasi*. According to Pāṇini 7.2.96 (*tvamāvekavacane*), for the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad* ending in the singular case-suffix *ṅasi*, the substitutes *tava* and *mama* respectively take their place: *tava*, *mama*; *atitava*, *atimama*.
Once the substitutions *yuvā-* and *āvā-* have been applied, the suffix *ak* is added afterwards: *yuvakābhyām*, *āvakābhyām*.

Regarding the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) when not expressing duality (*advitve*): According to Kātantra 2.3.14, the fifth case ending following *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and so forth, when they do not express duality, becomes *ad*. Thus: *tvat*, *mat*, *yuṣmat*, *asmat*, *atiyuvat*, *atyāvat*. Why "when not expressing duality"? [Consider: *yuvābhyām*, *āvābhyām*.
*bhyas* becomes *abhyam*. According to Kāt_2.3.15, *bhyas* following *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and so forth, becomes *abhyam*: *yuṣmabhyam*, *asmabhyam*, *atitvabhyam*, *atyasmabhyam*.
Why is the vowel *a* pronounced [in the rule]? So that the substitution of *e* does not occur before a consonant (*dhuṭ*).
*sām ākam*. (Pāṇini 7.1.33) Following these two [pronouns], *ām* becomes *ākam* when not joined with *sva*. For example: *yuṣmākam*, *asmākam*.
Why does it say *sām* ("following these two")? [To exclude cases such as: *priyayuṣmayām*, *atitvayām*.

*Etva* occurs for these [pronouns] when they are *asthānin*. (Kāt_2.3.17) *Sthāna* means occasion (*prasaṅga*). When they are *asthānin*—that is, when they do not have an occasion [for substitution] and are not subject to an *ādeśa*—there is *etva* at the end of these [stems] before the case endings beginning with *si* (the nominative singular). For example: *tvayā*, *mayā*, *yuvayoḥ*, *āvayoḥ*, *tvayi*, *mayi*, *atitvayi*, *atimayi*.

What is the purpose of the restriction "not when there is a substitute" (*asthāninī*)? [Consider: *yuṣmān*, *asmān*. [The rule] "the substitution of *ā* occurs before a consonant-initial [suffix]" (*ātvaṃ vyañjanādau*, Pāṇini 7.2.94) means that the substitution of *ā* for the final of these [pronominal bases] occurs before a case-ending (*syāt*) beginning with a consonant when it is not a substitute (*asthānin*). [Examples: *yuvābhyām*, *āvābhyām*; *atiyuvābhiḥ*, *atyāvābhiḥ*; *atitvāsu*, *atimāsu*.
The inclusion of the word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of direct application; by that [rule], *yuṣmatputraḥ*, *asmatputraḥ*, *adhitvat*, *adhimat* [are formed, with] elision (*luk*).
*Kāt_2.3.19*: The word *rai* undergoes the substitution of *ā* before case-endings (*syādi*) beginning with a consonant; thus: *rāḥ*, *rābhyām*, *atirābhyām* [from] *kulābhyām*.
What is the meaning of "directly" (*sākṣāt*)? [As in: *atiri kulam*.
[The rule] *aṣṭanaḥ sarvāsu* (Kāśikā 2.3.20) states:
the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel of *aṣṭan* occurs in all case endings; thus, *aṣṭābhiḥ*, *aṣṭābhyaḥ*, *aṣṭāsu*, *priyāṣṭāḥ*, *priyāṣṭau*.

Regarding *au tasmāj jasśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.21): after the word *aṣṭan*, when it has taken the form *aṣṭā*, the substitute *aur* occurs in place of both *jas* and *śas*. Thus, one forms *aṣṭau* and *aṣṭau*. The inclusion of the term *tasmāt* (after that) is for the sake of making the substitution of *āt* non-obligatory; by virtue of this, one may optionally have *aṣṭabhiḥ* or *aṣṭasu*.
*Arvann* becomes *arvanti* when followed by a suffix that is not *anañ*.

(Kāt_2.3.22) The word *arvan* becomes *arvanti* when a suffix follows, provided that it is not *anañ*: *arvantau*, *arvantaḥ*, *arvatsu*, *ārvatam*, *ārvatyam*, *arvatī*. Why does it say "when followed by a suffix" (*asau*)? [Observe: *arvā*.
What is the meaning of *anañ*? [It means] not ending in a case-ending (*anarvāṇau*).

And when followed by the nominative singular suffix *su*, the word *maghavan* optionally becomes *maghavant*: *maghavān*, *maghavā*; *maghavantau*, *maghavantau*; *maghavantaḥ*, *maghavantaḥ*; *maghavatsu*.

(Kātantra 2.3.23) When followed by a case-ending or the nominative singular suffix *su*, the word *maghavan* optionally becomes *maghavant*. [Examples: *maghavān*, *maghavā*; *maghavantau*, *maghavantau*; *maghavantaḥ*, *maghavantaḥ*; *maghavatsu*.

In the context of *taddhita* suffixes, when a vowel follows, and also in the case of the feminine form, [the substitution of] *māghavata*, *māghavatyam*, and *maghavatī* occurs. Optionally, [the forms] *maghavan* and *maghavantau* are used. In the context of vowels, the substitution of *jaras* for *jarā* is optional. (Kātantra 2.3.24)
The word *jarā* optionally becomes *jaras* before a case-ending that bears an accent; thus: *jare*, *jarasau*, *jarāḥ*, *jarasaḥ*.
Furthermore, due to its inclusion in the *gaṇa*-list, the form *upajarasam* is obligatory.
For the words *tri* and *catur* in the feminine, *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* are substituted before a case-ending. (Kātantra 2.3.25)

When the feminine suffixes *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* occur in place of *tri* and *catur*, they become *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* respectively before a case-ending (*vibhakti*): *tisraḥ*, *catasraḥ*, *tisṛbhiḥ*, *catasṛbhiḥ*; as in *priyatisṛ* or *priyacatasṛ kulaṃ*. In these two, *raṃ* [is substituted] before a vowel. According to Kātantra 2.3.26, those two—*tisṛ* and *catasṛ*—attain the substitution of *raṃ* before a vowel that is part of a case-ending: *tisraḥ*, *catasraḥ*.

This rule is for the purpose of preventing the application of [the substitution of] *dīrgha* (long vowel) in place of *ām*. According to Kāt. 2.3.27, the forms *tisṛ* and *catasṛ* do not undergo the substitution of *dīrgha* when *san* or *ām* follows, as in *tisṛṇām* and *catasṛṇām*.
*nṛ* or: Kāt_2,3.28: The word *nṛ* optionally undergoes lengthening when followed by the genitive plural suffix *ām*, as in *nṛṇām* or *nṝṇām*. Kāt_2,3.29:
The words beginning with *tyad* (the pronouns) undergo substitution [with *t*] before a case ending (*vibhakti*).
The final vowel of the pronouns beginning with *tyad* becomes *a* when followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*): *syaḥ*, *tyau*, *saḥ*, *tau*, *yatra*, *tatra*.
In this context, the group of pronouns beginning with *tyad* consists of those ending in *d* and *p*.
Why specify "when followed by a case-ending"? [Observe: *tyadīyaḥ*.
*kim* becomes *ka*. According to Pāṇini 7.2.103, the word *kim* becomes *ka* when followed by a case ending (*vibhakti*): *kaḥ*, *kau*, *kadā*.
Why does it say "when followed by a case ending"? [Consider: *kiṃvān*.
There are two exceptions.
According to Kāt_2.3.31, the *m* replaces the *d* of the pronouns beginning with *tyad* when followed by a case-ending, except after *advi*; thus, *imau* and *imakau*.
Why specify "except after *advi*"? [Observe that] *dvau* remains unchanged.

*sau saḥ*. (Kāt_2.3.32) In the case of the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, the *d* becomes *s* when followed by the nominative singular suffix *sau*; thus, *asau* and *asakau*. Why [is it specified] "when followed by *sau*"? [Consider: "this is his son," i.e., *adaḥputraḥ*.
And for that [word], by *Kāt_2.3.33*, the *t* of the pronouns beginning with *tyad* becomes *s* when the nominative singular (*sau*) case-ending follows: *syaḥ*, *syakaḥ*, *saḥ*, *sakaḥ*.
Why specify "when followed by *s*" (*sākṣāt sāv*)? [Consider: *tatputraḥ*.

*idam*, *iyam*, and *ayam* [are used] for the masculine. According to Pāṇini 7.1.11 (*kā-t-ād-as-śas-ī-tā-t*), *idam* becomes *iyam* and *ayam* in the masculine when the nominative singular suffix *su* follows; thus, *iyam* is for the feminine and *ayam* for the masculine.
However, in the case of *idaṃ kulam* ("this family"), it is because of the prohibition stated for that [neuter gender].
Why is it stated "directly *sā*"? [Consider] *idaṃputraḥ*.

[The rule] *ad vyañjane 'nak* (Pāṇini 7.1.28) states that *idam-* becomes *ad-* before a case-ending beginning with a consonant, except for the nominative singular (*su*). [Examples: *ābhyām*, *ebhiḥ*.
What is the meaning of *anag*? [It means] "by these" (*imakaiḥ*).
Why is it specified that it must occur "in direct contact with a case-ending" (*sākṣād vibhaktau*)? [Consider: "his son" (*asya putraḥ*), which becomes *idaṃputraḥ*.
[The rule] *ṭausor anaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.25) applies.

The substitution *an* occurs for the case endings *ṭā* (instrumental singular) and *ṅasi~* (ablative singular) when they follow this pronoun *idam*, provided it is not preceded by *ag*. [Examples: *anena*, *anayoḥ*. Why "not preceded by *ag*"? [Counter-example: *imakena*, *imakayoḥ*.
Furthermore, in the case of subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), the substitution *en* occurs for the second case ending (*dvitīyā*). (Kātantra 2.3.37)

The substitute *enad* occurs for the forms *etad* and *idam* when followed by the dual endings *ṭā* and *auṣ*, as well as in the second case (*dvitīyā*), provided they refer to something already mentioned, in the context of a subsequent restatement. For example: *etaṃ vyākaraṇam adhyāpaya, atho enaṃ vedam adhyāpaya* ("Teach this grammar, and also teach him this Veda");
*imaṃ ghaṭam ānaya, atho enaṃ parivartaya* ("Bring this jar, and also turn it over");
*etena rātrir adhītā, atho enenāhar apy adhītam* ("By him the night was studied, and by him the day was also studied").
"The conduct of these two is beautiful, and moreover, their wealth is abundant," and so forth—this is how the construction is to be applied.
Therefore, by [the rule] *bhis bhir* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), after the form *idam* which has been changed to *etad*, the suffix *bhis* becomes *bhir*; thus, *ebhiḥ*.
Some [say] "from that" (tasmāt): what [is meant]? By means of these qualities, the Seven Sages went to heaven.
And from *adas* [Kāt_2.3.39]:
after *adas*, provided it is not followed by *ag*, the form *bhis* becomes *bhir*; thus, *amībhiḥ*.

What is meant by "anag"? [The example is] *anukaiḥ*. The letter *c* is for the purpose of preventing the application of the rule in subsequent sections. [The rule states: "When *s* follows, *au* is substituted [for the final vowel of the stem], and there is elision of *si*. (Kātantra 2.3.40)
The vowel *au* is substituted for the final syllable of *adas-* when followed by the nominative suffix *su*, and there is also elision (*lopa*) of the *s*. Thus: *asau*, *asakau*.
*Kāt_2,3.41*: The substitution of *u* occurs for the single phoneme following the *m* of *adas-*. Thus: *amum*, *amū*, *amūn*.
What is excluded by the condition "not after *m*"? As in *amukābhyām*.
However, when there is plurality, *ī* [is substituted]. According to Kāt_2.3.42, when there is plurality, the *eta* that results from what follows *m* in *adas-* becomes *ī*; as in *amī*, *amībhyaḥ*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "plurality"? [As in: *amū*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "from this"? [As in: *amukebhyaḥ*.
The word *tu* (but/however) serves to exclude plurality in the subsequent [rule].
*apām bhe daḥ*. (Kāt_2.3.43) When *bh* follows a case-ending (*vibhakti*), *da* is substituted for *ap*; as in *adbhiḥ* and *svadbhyām*. Why specify "in a case-ending"? [Observe: *abbhāraḥ*.

*Kāt_2.3.44*: In the case of words ending in *anaḍuh*, *nadi*, and *vans*, when there is a pause (*virāma*) or when followed by a consonant, the final letter of these stems becomes *d*. For example: *svanaḍut* (vocative), *anaḍudbhyām*; *upānat*, *upānadbhyām*; *suvidvat*, *vidvadbhyām*. Here, "consonant" (*vyañjana*) is intended in its general sense, as seen in *anaḍuttā*, *upānattā*, and *vidvattā*, as well as in *anaḍuhyam* and *upānahyam*.

In the case of the two stems *sras* and *dhvas*, the final [consonant] becomes *d* at the pause (*virāma*) and before consonants; e.g., *ukhāsrat*, *ukhāsradbhyām*, *ukhāsratkalpaḥ*; *parṇadhvat*, *parṇadhvadbhyām*, *parṇadhvaddeśyaḥ*.
*Kāt_2,3.46*: For those ending in *ha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, or *cha*, and for those beginning with a vowel (*ijādi*), [the final consonant] becomes *ḍ*.

For roots ending in *ha*, *ṣa*, *cha*, or *śa*, as well as for those beginning with *yaj* and so forth, the final consonant becomes *ḍ* at the end of a word (*virāma*) and before consonants. Examples: *madhuliṭ*, *madhuliḍbhyām*, *madhuliṭpāśaḥ*; *suviṭ*, *suviḍbhyām*, *suviṭtaraḥ*; *ṣaṭ*, *ṣaḍbhyām*, *ṣaḍbhyaḥ*, *ṣaṭtvam*; *śabdaprāṭ*, *śabdaprāḍbhyām*, *śabdaprāṭtvam*; *deveṭ*, *deveḍbhyām*, *deveṭtvam*; *rajjusṛṭ*, *rajjusṛḍbhyām*, *rajjusṛṭtvam*.
The roots *yaj*, *sṛj*, *mṛj*, *rāj*, *bhrāj*, *vraśc*, *bhrasj*, and *parivrāj* are included among those beginning with *yaj*.
[Furthermore,] *ga* replaces *ha* after a root beginning with *da*. (Kātantra 2.3.47)

The substitution of *go* occurs for a word ending in *ha* that begins with a voiced consonant (*gha*, *ja*, *ba*, *da*, *dha*), at the pause (*virāma*) and before consonants; as in *godhuk*, *godhugbhyām*, *godhuktamaḥ*.

And [the substitution of *go* occurs] for words ending in the *ca*-class (palatals) such as *dṛś* and others. Kātantra 2.3.48: For stems ending in the *ca*-class and for words such as *dṛś* and others, the substitution of *go* occurs for the final sound at the pause and before consonants; as in *vāk*, *vāgbhyām*, *vākkalpaḥ*; *tṛṣṇak*, *tṛṣṇagbhyām*, *tṛṣṇaktvam*; *dṛk*, *dṛgbhyām*, *dṛktvam*.

*dṛś*, *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *dadhṛṣ*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, *ṛtvij*, *sraj*, *asṛj*—these are the *dṛgādayaḥ*. According to Pāṇini 8.2.49 (*muhādīnāṃ vā*), for words beginning with *muh*, the final consonant optionally becomes a guttural (*ku*) before a pause (*virāma*) or when followed by a consonant. Thus: *muk*, *mugbhyām*, *muktvam*; or *muṭ*, *muḍbhyām*, *muṭtvam*.

*muh*, *druh*, *ṣṇuh*, *ṣṇih*, and *naś*—these are the roots beginning with *muh*. For a root ending in a fourth-class *ha*-consonant (*ha, ya, ra, va*) and beginning with a third-class consonant (*ja, bha, ga, gha*), the initial [third-class consonant] becomes a fourth-class consonant (*jha, bha, gha, dha*) as if it had not occurred [as a substitute]. (Kāt. 2.3.50) When a part of a root ends in a fourth-class *ha*-consonant and begins with a third-class consonant, that [third-class consonant] becomes a fourth-class consonant at a pause (*virāma*) and before consonants; and that [change] is treated as if it had not occurred. Examples: *nighuṭ*, *nighuḍbhyām*, *nighuṭtvam*; *jñānabhut*, *jñānabhudbhyām*, *jñānabhuttvam*.
From the verbal root *gardabhayati*, with the suffix *kvip*, we have *gardhab* (nominative singular), *gardhabbhyām* (instrumental dual), and *gardhaptvam* (abstract noun).
Why specify "from a verbal root"? [Consider] *dāmaliṭ*.
Why specify "starting from the third case" (*tṛtīyādi*)? [Consider] *vikrut*.
What is the meaning of "as if not performed" (*akṛtavat*)? *godhuk*.

[Regarding the rule] *sajuṣāśiṣo raḥ* (Kātantra 2.3.51): for the final sound of *sajuṣ* and *āśis*, the substitution of *r* occurs at the pause (*virāma*) and before consonants. Thus: *sajūḥ*, *sajūrbhyām*, *sajūḥṣu*, *sajūstā*; *āśīḥ*, *āśīrbhyām*, *āśīḥṣu*, *āśīstā*.

*Kāt_2.3.52*: For the roots *ir* and *ur*, when followed by consonants at the end of a word (*virāma*) or at the beginning of a suffix, the vowels *ī* and *ū* are substituted respectively; e.g., *gīḥ*, *gīrbhyām*, *gīrṣu*, *gīstarā*; *dhūḥ*, *dhūrbhyām*, *dhūrṣu*, *dhūstarā*.
*Kāt_2.3.53*: For the word *ahan*, the substitution of *s* [occurs].
The substitution of *s* occurs for the word *ahan* at the pause (*virāma*) and before consonant-initial suffixes: *ahaḥ*, *ahobhyām*, *ahastvam*. *Kāt_2,3.54*:
There is elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) at the pause and before consonant-initial suffixes: *vidvān*, *kaṭacikīḥ*, *puṃbhyām*, *puṃsu*.

*Saṃyogāder dhuṭaḥ* (Kātantra 2.3.55): There is elision of a *dhuṭ* consonant that begins a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) at the pause (*virāma*), as well as before consonants. For example: from *masj*, *sādhumak*, *sādhumagbhyām*, *sādhumaktvam*;
from *takṣ*, *sādhutaṭ*, *sādhutaḍbhyām*, *sādhutaṭtvam*.

In the rule *virāme vyañjanādiṣu*, what is the purpose of [specifying] "at the pause"? [Consider] *gorakṣau*. The repeated mention of *saṃyoga* here and in the preceding rule is for the sake of making them optional; therefore, [we have] *māṃsapipak*. Furthermore, in the preceding rule, the elision of *s* occurs only after *r*; thus, [we have] *ūrk* and *ūrgbhyām*. [This applies to] the *n* that is part of a stem (*liṅgānta*). (Kātantra 2.3.56)
The *n* at the end of a stem (*liṅga*) is elided at the pause (*virāma*) and before consonant-initial suffixes: as in *sakhā*, *rājabhyām*, *rājabhiḥ*, *rājasu*, and *rājatvam*.
Why specify "at the end of a stem"? [To exclude cases such as] *ahan*. The repetition of the word "stem" (*liṅga*) is for the sake of the general rule that follows.
Not in the vocative singular.
According to Pāṇini 8.2.8, the *n* at the end of a stem is not elided in the vocative singular; thus, *he rājan*.
Because it is mentioned separately, for the neuter gender it is optional: *he sāma*, *he sāman*.

A word ending in a conjunct consonant containing *n* is treated as if it were not elided when a preceding rule is to be applied, such as the lengthening of the penultimate vowel before a gender-ending (*liṅga-anta*) or similar operations.

(Kātantra 2.3.58) Even though the *n* at the end of a conjunct is elided, it is considered non-elided when a preceding operation—such as lengthening the vowel before a gender-ending—is to be performed. Examples: *rājabhyām*, *rājabhiḥ*, *rājasu*, *vidvān*, *sukanbhyām*.
In the case of suffixes ending in *is*, *us*, or *doṣ*, the *s* becomes *r* before a voiced sound. (Kātantra 2.3.59)

The *r* is substituted for the final *is*, *us*, and the word *dos* when followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*); as in *sarpirbhyām*, *dhanurbhyām*, and *dobhyām*. Why specify "when followed by a voiced consonant"? [Observe] *sarpiḥṣu*, *dhanuḥṣu*, and *doḥṣu*.
Although the rule would have been established by the previous rule *bhe ra*, the mention of "voiced consonant" is for the sake of subsequent rules.

The third of the *dhuṭ* sounds. (Kāt 2.3.60) Among the *dhuṭ* sounds, the third occurs when there is a voiced (*ghoṣavat*) general category: as in *yoṣidbhyām*, *citraliṅgaiḥ*, *majjati*, *lajjate*, and *bhṛjjati*.
When there is an unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) sound, the first [of the *dhuṭ* sounds] occurs. (Kāt 2.3.61)
When followed by a voiceless consonant (*aghoṣa*), the first of the *dhuṭ* consonants is substituted for the [final] consonants in the following six cases: *jñānabhutsu*, *icchati*, and *gacchati*.

Optionally (*vā*) before a pause (*virāma*). According to Kāt_2.3.62, in a pause (*virāma*), the third of the *dhuṭ* consonants optionally replaces the first of the *dhuṭ* consonants: *vidhap* or *vidhab*; *vāk* or *vāg*.

*Repha* becomes *visarjanīya*. (Kātantra 2.3.63) The *visarjanīya* occurs in place of *repha* and *sakāra* at the pause (*virāma*), at the word-break (*śabdaccheda*), and before both voiced (*ghoṣavat*) and unvoiced (*aghoṣa*) sounds; as in *gīḥ*, *dhūḥ*, *vṛkṣaḥ*, *payobhyām*, and *payaḥsu*. Because of the governing rule [of optionality], it may not occur before a consonant of a case-ending (*vibhakti-vyañjana*); thus, one says *gīrṣu* and *dhūrṣu*, yet it does occur in *sajūḥṣu* and *āśīḥṣu*.

Regarding what was stated concerning the pause (*virāma*) and the beginning of a consonant (*vyañjanādau*): even when *si* and *am* are elided after a neuter noun, that which was prescribed for the pause and for the beginning of a consonant applies. This is because that [rule] alone was explicitly mentioned in the sūtra: *Kāt_2.3.64*. Thus: *suvāk*, *suvāg*; *supathi*; *suvidvat*; *supum*; *sucatuh*; *sudyu*. Likewise:
*ukhāsrat*, *deveṭ*, and so forth.
The inclusion of the word *api* is for the purpose of indicating deviation; therefore, this [rule] would not apply to the form *atvam*.
Thus ends the third quarter on the fourfold types of names in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.
[Kātantra 2.4.1: After an indeclinable compound ending in *a*, the case endings [are replaced] by *am*, except for the ablative.
After an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *a*, the suffix *am* replaces the case endings (*vibhakti*), except for the fifth case (*pañcamī*). For example: *upakumbham*.
Why "after an *avyayībhāva*"? Consider: *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*. Why "of the case endings"? Consider: *upakumbhatā*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not after the fifth case"? [Example: *upakumbhāt*.
*Kāt_2.4.2*: After an *avyayībhāva* compound ending in *a*, the suffix *am* optionally occurs in place of the third and seventh cases. Thus: *upakumbham*, *upakumbhena*, *upakumbham*, *upakumbhe*.

*Anyasmāl luk*: Kātyāyana 2.4.3. Elision of case endings occurs after an *avyayībhāva* compound other than that which ends in the vowel *a*, as in *upavadhu* and *upakartṛ*. And [elision occurs] after an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Kātyāyana 2.4.4.
An indeclinable (avyaya) is that which is innumerable; furthermore, there is elision of case-endings after an indeclinable: *svaḥ*, *prātaḥ*, *ca*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, and others as well.
This [definition] is for the purpose of establishing the technical designation "word" (*pada*).
[The rule applies] to established forms (*rūḍha*) in the plural, provided they are not feminine, and when the suffix denoting offspring (*apatya-pratyaya*) is absent. (Kātantra 2.4.5)

There is elision (*luk*) of the patronymic suffix prescribed after names of *kṣatriyas* whose names are identical with those of their territories (*janapada*), provided that the name is conventional (*rūḍha*) and the plurality is expressed, and the referent is not feminine. For example: the descendants of Pañcāla are the Pañcālas; likewise, the Videhas, Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Magadhas, and Sūramasas. Here, there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*. The Pratyagrathas, Kalakūṭas, and Aśvakas: here, there is elision of the suffix *iṇ*. Why "in the plural"? Consider: *āṅgaḥ* (singular), *āṅgau* (dual), and *priyavāṅgāḥ* (a compound); in these cases, even though plurality is present, the suffix is not elided.
Why is it specified "not feminine"? [Consider: *kāliṅgyaḥ*.
Why is it specified "of a secondary suffix denoting offspring" (*apatyapratyaya*)? [Consider: these servants belong to the Pañcālas; thus, *pāñcālāḥ* (referring to the servants).
[The rule applies] also to the *garga*, *yaska*, *vida*, and so forth. (Kāśikāvṛtti 2.4.64)

The elision (*luk*) occurs of the patronymic suffix prescribed after the classes beginning with *garga*, *yaska*, and *vida* when they denote a plurality and do not refer to females. Thus: *gargāḥ*, *vatsāḥ*—here there is elision of the suffix *ṇya*.
*Yaskāḥ*, *lahyāḥ*—here there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*.
*Vidāḥ*, *urvāḥ*—here too there is elision of the suffix *aṇ*.

Words such as *yaska* and others end in various patronymic suffixes (*apatyapratyaya`); words such as *vida* and others also end in the suffix *aṇ* derived from grandsons and further descendants. In cases such as *priyagargaḥ*, *priyayaskaḥ*, and *priyavidaḥ*, the suffix should indeed be elided when plurality is expressed. Thus we have *gārgyakulam* and *gargakulam*; for the family of Gārgya is the same as the family of Garga or even of the Gargas, and is thus spoken of without distinction. [This applies] also after the names Bhṛgu, Atri, Aṅgiras, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, and Gotama. (Kātantra 2.4.7)

The patronymic suffix prescribed after Bhṛgu and others in the plural sense is elided when not denoting a female; [specifically], the suffix *eyaṇ* is applied after Atri, and the suffix *aṇ* after other sages: *bhṛgavaḥ*, *atrayaḥ*, *aṅgirasaḥ*, *kutsāḥ*, *vasiṣṭhāḥ*, *gotamāḥ*.
Why "not denoting a female"? [Consider] *bhārgavyaḥ*.
That from which fear departs or which one takes up is the *apādāna* (ablative point). (Pāṇini 1.4.24)

That from which something moves away, that from which fear arises, or that from which something is received—that *kāraka* is designated as the *apādāna*. For example: "A leaf falls from the tree," "He fears the tiger," "He trembles before the thief," "He studies from the teacher," and "He learns from the teacher."

The word *yataḥ* is used merely to indicate the limit (*avadhi*). Thus: "He fell from a running horse"; likewise, "he feels aversion toward unrighteousness," "he desists from unrighteousness," "he is negligent regarding dharma," "he fails in his studies," "he disappears from the presence of the teacher," "an arrow is produced from the horn," "the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat," "he looks out from the palace," "he looks out from the seat," "where are you from? "from Pāṭaliputra.
And [the ablative is used] for that which is desired in connection with verbs meaning "to protect" (*rakṣa*). (Pāṇini 1.4.24–29)

When roots meaning "to protect" (*rakṣ*) are employed, that *kāraka* which is intended or even unintended [as the object of protection] receives the technical designation *apādāna*. For example: *yavebhyo gāṃ rakṣati* ("He protects the cow from the barley"), *yavebhyo gāṃ niṣedhati* ("He restrains the cow from the barley"), *śālibhyaḥ śukān vārayati* ("He wards off the parrots from the rice"), *ahibhya ātmānaṃ rakṣati* ("He protects himself from snakes"), and even *kūpād andhaṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the blind man away from the well").
This [designation] sets aside the designation *karman* when [the object] is intended.
The rules concerning the *apādāna* include such statements as "the fifth case ending is used for the *apādāna*" (*apādāne pañcamī*), and so forth.
That for whom there is a desire to give, or who accepts [the gift], is the recipient (saṃpradāna). Kāt_2.4.10.

That for whom one desires to give, that which pleases someone, or that which someone maintains [in mind], is called the *saṃpradāna* (recipient) *kāraka*. Examples: "He gives a cow to the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya gāṃ dadāti*); "The sweetmeat pleases Devadatta" (*devadattāya rocate modakaḥ*); "The curd is pleasing to Yajñadatta" (*yajñadattāya svadate dadhi*); "He keeps the cow in mind for Viṣṇumitra" (*viṣṇumitrāya gāṃ dhārayate*). How is it that [the following] are also included? "He praises Devadatta" (*devadattāya ślāghate*); "He begs from the student" (*chāttrāya hnute*); "The young girl stands [waiting] for the student" (*chāttrāya tiṣṭhate kumārī*); "She swears at the student" (*chāttrāya śapate*); "He longs for flowers" (*puṣpebhyaḥ spṛhayati*); "He seeks counsel from the student" (*chāttrāya rādhyati*); "He looks toward the student" (*chāttrāyekṣate*).

[The forms] *chāttrāya pratiśṛṇoti* ("he promises to the student") and *chāttrāya śṛṇoti* ("he listens for the student") are established by the fourth case (*caturthī*) expressing purpose (*tādarthya*). [The following are also examples: *chāttrāya krudhyati* ("he is angry with the student"), *mitrāya druhyati* ("he bears malice toward the friend"), *mitrāyerṣyati* ("he envies the friend"), *mitrāyāsūyati* ("he finds fault with the friend"). It should be stated that [the fourth case is used] for one with whom one is angry. Why say "he wishes to give"? [Because it would otherwise be ambiguous; e.g.,] *rājño daṇḍaṃ dadāti* ("he gives the king a staff"). The applications of the term *saṃpradāna* (recipient) are such as "the fourth case is used for the recipient" (*saṃpradāne caturthī*), and so forth.
That which is the support (ādhāra) is the locus (adhikaraṇa). [Kātantra 2.4.11] That in which actions are supported is called the support (ādhāra).

Whatever is a support receives the technical designation of locus (adhikaraṇa): "he sits on a mat" (kaṭe āste), "oil in sesame seeds" (tileṣu tailam), "the gods in heaven" (divi devāḥ), likewise "a hamlet on the Ganges" (gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ), and "a hundred elephants on the tip of a finger" (aṅgulyagre kariśatam).
The locative case endings [are used] in the sense of locus (*adhikaraṇa*), such as in the rule "the seventh case ending is used for the locus" (*adhikaraṇe saptamī*);
that by which something is performed is the instrument (*karaṇa*). (Kātantra 2.4.12)

That instrument by which an action is performed by the agent is designated as the *karaṇa* (instrumental) *kāraka*. For example: "He cuts grain with a sickle" (*dātreṇa dhānyaṃ lunāti*); "He goes to Mount Meru with his mind" (*manasā meruṃ gacchati*); likewise, "He worships Rudra with an animal" (*paśunā rudraṃ yajate*). Also: "He is handsome by nature" (*prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ*); "He is mostly a ritualist" (*prāyeṇa yājñikaḥ*); "He is a Gārgya by lineage" (*gotreṇa gārgyaḥ*); "He runs on level ground" (*samena dhāvati*); "He runs on uneven ground" (*viṣameṇa dhāvati*); "He buys grain for two *droṇas*" (*dvidroṇena dhānyaṃ krīṇāti*); "He buys animals for five" (*pañcakena paśūn krīṇāti*); "He was hired for a hundred" (*śatena parikrītaḥ*). In the case of "You have been hired for a hundred; you shall perform work for a month," the status of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is in relation to the principal action.
The locative case endings [denote] the locus of the instrument (*karaṇapradeśāḥ*), as in "the third [case ending] is used for the instrument" (*karaṇe tṛtīyā*), and so forth.
That which is performed is the object (*karman*). (Kāt_2.4.13)

That which is performed by the agent (*kartṛ*) is called the *karman* (object) *kāraka*. For example: "he makes a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karoti*), "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), "he sees the sun" (*ādityaṃ paśyati*); likewise, "he leaps over a snake" (*ahiṃ laṅghayati*), "while going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees" (*grāmaṃ gacchan vṛkṣamūlāny upasarpati*); likewise, "he cooks a little" (*stokaṃ pacati*), "he milks milk from the cow" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), "he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru" (*pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate*), "he shuts the cow in the pen" (*gām avaruṇaddhi vrajam*), "he asks the student the way" (*chāttraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati*), "he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru" (*pauravaṃ gāṃ bhikṣate*), "he gathers fruits from the tree" (*vṛkṣam avacinoti phalāni*), "he tells the duty to the disciple" (*śiṣyaṃ dharmaṃ brūte*), [and] the disciple...

He instructs in the Dharma; he leads the goat to the village; he carries the load to the village; he carries the jar, [that is,] the load; he conquers a hundred students for the village; he fines the Gargas a hundred [pieces]; he lies upon the village; he occupies the village; he sits upon the tree; he applies himself to the Dharma; he fasts for three nights; he dwells near the village; he dwells upon the mountain; he dwells in the lodging; he plays with dice; "he plays with dice"—here the instrument is intended to be expressed; "jaggery-roasted grains for a month"; "the river is winding for the distance of a *krośa*"; because the root *bhū* (to be) is understood [as "existing"].

That which is performed by the agent is called the *karman* (object) *kāraka*. For example: *kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat), *odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice), *ādityaṃ paśyati* (he sees the sun); likewise, *ahiṃ laṅghayati* (he leaps over a snake), *grāmaṃ gacchan vṛkṣamūlāny upasarpati* (while going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees); likewise, *stokaṃ pacati* (he cooks a little), *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (he milks milk from the cow), *pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate* (he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru), *gām avaruṇaddhi vrajam* (he shuts the cow in the pen), *chāttraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* (he asks the student the way), *pauravaṃ gāṃ bhikṣate* (he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru), *vṛkṣam avacinoti phalāni* (he gathers fruits from the tree), *śiṣyaṃ dharmaṃ brūte* (he tells the student the Dharma).

He instructs the disciple in the Dharma; he leads the goat to the village; he carries the burden to the village; he carries the jar, [that is,] the burden; he conquers a hundred students for the village; he fines the Gargas a hundred [pieces]; he lies down upon the village; he presides over the village; he sits upon the tree; he applies himself to the Dharma; he fasts for three nights; he dwells near the village; he dwells upon the mountain; he dwells in the lodging; he plays with the dice; "he plays with the dice"—here there is the intention to express the instrument (*karaṇa*); "jaggery-roasted grains for a month."
The river is crooked for the distance of a *krośa*, because it is being traversed (*bhavateḥ gamyamānatvāt*).
"Objects" (*karmapradeśāḥ*), "the second case ending is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*)—these and others [are examples].
"He who acts is the agent" (*yaḥ karoti sa kartā*). (Kātantra 2.4.14)
He who performs an action receives the designation *kartṛ* (agent), as in: *chātreṇa hanyate* ("he is struck by the student") and *caitreṇa kṛtam* ("it was done by Caitra").

He who causes that very agent to act is called a *hetu* (cause/instigator). [Kāt_2.4.15] He who causes that same agent to act receives the designation *hetu*, and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, he also receives the designation *kartṛ*; as in: *hārayati* ("he causes to take away") and *pācayati* ("he causes to cook").
There are rules concerning the cause as the agent, such as *dhātoś ca hetau* (Kāt. 3.2.10) and others.
An agent (*kāraka*) established by worldly convention is that which is the cause of action.
Among these, the subsequent rule applies when both [possibilities] are applicable: *teṣāṃ param ubhayaprāptau* (Kāt. 2.4.16).

When two [kārakas] are simultaneously applicable among those [six], that which is subsequent [in the order of enumeration] prevails: having given wealth to the village (*grāmāya*), he went to the sacred ford (*tīrtham*); here it is only the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
He eats from a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātryām*); here it is only the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). He shoots arrows with a soft bow (*mṛdunā dhanuṣā*); here it is only the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The bird leaves the tree—just as [one says] "he milks the cow for milk"—the staff-bearer leaves the staff; thus, it is the agent alone who acts. So it is with others as well.

The first case ending (*prathamā vibhakti*) occurs when the meaning of gender (*liṅga*) is expressed. (Kātantra 2.4.17) When the meaning of gender is expressed as non-distinct [from the word itself], the first case ending is employed: *uccaiḥ*, *nīcaiḥ*, *vṛkṣaḥ*, *kuṇḍam*, *kumārī*, *droṇaḥ*, *khārī*, *āḍhakaḥ*, *hastaḥ*, *vitastiḥ*, *dīrgham*, *kāṣṭham*, *ghṛtam*, *palam*, *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*. All these are meanings of gender because they are concomitant [with the word]. By virtue of this etymological designation—since it expresses one, two, or many objects—one uses the singular number for a single object, the dual for two, and the plural for many.

The term *saṃpanno yavaḥ* ("the barley has ripened") is the singular number used for a genus (*jāti*); *saṃpannā yavāḥ* ("the barley grains have ripened") is the plural number used for distinct individuals (*vyakti*). The word *vayam* ("we") is used for external and internal entities; likewise, *aham* ("I") is used in the singular when there is no intention to express distinction among teachers. And [it is used] in address (*āmantraṇe*). (Kātantra 2.4.18) The first case ending occurs in the sense of address: *he putra*, *hā putra*, *dhik putrau*, *hai putrāḥ*. This is an exception to the sixth case.
The remaining [case endings] are used for the objects, instruments, recipients, sources, possessors, and loci. (Kāt.

2.4.19) The remaining six case endings, beginning with the second, occur respectively in the six meanings starting with the object: in the sense of the object, as in *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat");
in the sense of the instrument, as in *paraśunā chinatti* ("he cuts with an axe").
In the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*): he gives a cow to the teacher (*gurave gāṃ dadāti*). In the sense of the source (*apādāna*): fear from a wolf (*vṛkād bhayam*).

In the sense of ownership and so forth (*svāmy-ādi*): the owner of Devadatta (*Devadattasya svāmī*), the property of Yajñadatta (*Yajñadattasya svam*), the relation of Viṣṇumitra (*Viṣṇumitrasya saṃbandhaḥ*).

In the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*), [the seventh case is used], as in *kaṭe āste* ("he sits on a mat"), *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("proficient in grammar"), and likewise *sādhur mātari* ("virtuous toward his mother"), *asādhuḥ pitari* ("unvirtuous toward his father"), and so forth.

When there is a connection with an action (*karmasaṃyoga*) based on a cause (*nimitta*), the seventh case should be stated: *carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti* ("he kills the leopard for its skin"), *dantayor hanti kuñjaram* ("he kills the elephant for its tusks"), *keśeṣu camarīṃ hanti* ("he kills the yak for its hair"), and *sīmni puṣkalako hataḥ* ("the musk deer is killed for its musk-gland").
With the prepositions *pari*, *apa*, and *āṅ*, the fifth case is used. (Kātantra 2.4.20)
When used in conjunction with these—*pari*, *apa*, and *āṅ*—the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs by virtue of the indicator (*liṅga*).
Here, *apa* and *pari* signify exclusion (*varjana*), while *āṅ* signifies both limit-inclusive (*maryādā*) and limit-exclusive (*abhividhi*). Examples:
*pari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (It rained outside the Trigarta country); *apa pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (It rained away from Pāṭaliputra); *ā pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (It rained up to Pāṭaliputra).
[The word *pañcamī*] is [also used] with *dig*, *itará*, *ṛté*, and *anyá*.

(Kāśikā 2.4.21) When these—*diś*, *itará*, *ṛté*, *anyá*—are employed, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occurs by virtue of the rule; for example: *pūrvo grāmāt* ("east of the village"), *uttaro grāmāt* ("north of the village"), *pūrvo grīṣmād vasantaḥ* ("spring is before summer"), *iyam asyāḥ pūrvā dik* ("this is the eastern direction of that"), *itaro devadattāt* ("other than Devadatta"), *ṛte devadattāt* ("without Devadatta").
[In the expression] *ṛte Devadattam*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is also desired.

"Other than Devadatta," "different from Devadatta. [The word] ending in the suffix *ena* [is used]. According to Pāṇini 2.3.29, when used in conjunction with a word ending in the suffix *ena*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs by virtue of the gender [of the rule]; for example, *dakṣiṇena grāmam* ("to the south of the village"), *uttareṇa himavantam* ("to the north of the Himalayas"). [In this context], *ena* signifies "not far," provided it does not end in the fifth case (*apañcamyāḥ*).

By virtue of the governing rule [of the preceding sūtra], the second case ending is employed when joined with *nikaṣā*, *samayā*, *hā*, *adhik*, *antarā*, and *antareṇa*: *nikaṣā grāmam* (near the village), *samayā grāmam* (near the village), *hā Devadattam* (shame on Devadatta), *dhig Devadattam* (fie on Devadatta), *antarā gārhapatyam āhavanīyaṃ ca vediḥ* (the altar is between the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya fires), and *antareṇa puruṣakāraṃ na kiṃcil labhyate* (nothing is obtained without human effort). And [this applies] also when joined with words designated as *karmapravacanīya*. (Kāśikāvṛtti 2.4.23)

When used in conjunction with *karmapravacanīya*s, the second case (*dvitīyā*) occurs by virtue of the [inherent] gender [of the rule]. For example: *vṛkṣam abhividyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward the tree"), *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam abhi tiṣṭhati* ("He stands facing each tree"), *sādhur devadatto mātaram abhi* ("Devadatta is kind toward his mother"). Also: *yad atra māṃ pari syāt* ("Whatever may be on my side here"), *yad atra māṃ prati syāt* ("Whatever may be against me here"), *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes along the tree"), *parvatam anu vasitā senā* ("The army is encamped along the mountain"), *anvarjunaṃ yoddhāraḥ* ("The warriors are inferior to Arjuna"), *upārjunaṃ yoddhāraḥ* ("The warriors are inferior to Arjuna"). It is taught that *abhi* is used in the senses of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), desire (*vīpsā*), and state of being (*itthaṃbhūta*), as well as for a share (*bhāga*). *Parī* and *prati* are used in these same senses. *Anu* is said to be used in these senses as well as in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). *Upa* is said to be used in the sense of inferiority (*hīna*).

The locative case should be prescribed when used with words having the sense of "excess" (ādhikya) or with the prefix *upa*; for example, *upa khāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("A droṇa measure is slightly more than a khārī").

It is also used with the prefix *adhi* when it has the sense of "lordship" (*svāmyartha*); for example, *adhi brahmadatteṣu pañcālāḥ* ("The Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta") and *adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ* ("Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas").

According to Pāṇini 2.3.12, the accusative and dative cases are used for the object of a verb meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) when there is physical movement (*ceṣṭā*), provided it is not a path (*anadhvan*). *Kātantra* 2.4.24.

For verbal roots meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) that denote physical movement (*ceṣṭākriyā*), the second and fourth case endings are used when the object (*karman*) is not a road (*adhvan*). For example: *grāmaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to the village"), *grāmāya gacchati* ("he goes to the village"), *grāmaṃ vrajati* ("he goes to the village"), and *grāmāya vrajati* ("he goes to the village"). Why is it specified "denoting physical movement"? Consider: *manasā meruṃ gacchati* ("he goes to Mount Meru by mind"). Why is it specified "not a road"? Consider: *adhvānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the road"), *panthānaṃ gacchati* ("he goes along the path"), and *panthānaṃ vrajati* ("he goes along the path"). Here, the word *adhvan* refers to the primary sense of a road.
Kātyāyana 2.4.25:

In the sense of contempt regarding the object of the verb *man* (to think), provided the object is not a living being, both the second and fourth cases occur when contempt is implied. For example: *na tvā tṛṇaṃ manye*, *na tvā tṛṇāya manye*; *na tvā busaṃ manye*, *na tvā busāya manye*. Why "in the sense of contempt"? [Observe: *aśmānaṃ dṛśadaṃ manye* ("I consider the stone to be a grindstone").
The notion of "sentient being" applies to [the word] *nau* (boat) and so forth; thus one says: *na tvā nāvaṃ manye*, *na tvā kākaṃ manye*, *na tvānnam manye*, *na tvā śṛgālaṃ manye*.
In this context, it would indeed be so: *na tvā śvānaṃ manye*, *na tvā śune manye*.
If the dative case were used for the pronoun *yuṣmad*, then disregard (*anādara*) would not be understood.

The dative case is used in connection with *namaḥ* (salutation), *svasti* (well-being), *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alam*, and *vaṣaṭ*. (Kāt. 2.4.26) When joined with words such as *namas* and the rest, the dative case occurs by virtue of this indicative mark (*liṅga*). Examples: *namo devebhyaḥ* (salutation to the gods); *svasti prajābhyaḥ* (well-being to the subjects); *svāhāgnaye* (svāhā to Agni); *svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ* (svadhā to the ancestors); *alaṃ mallo mallāya* (the wrestler is a match for the wrestler); *samartho mallo mallāya* (the wrestler is capable against the wrestler); *vaṣaḍ indrāya* (vaṣaṭ to Indra).
[The dative is also used] in the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthye*). (Kāt. 2.4.27)
That which has this as its purpose, or that for which this [is intended], is called *tadartha*.

When the state of having that as its purpose (*tadarthabhāva*) is to be expressed, the fourth case ending occurs after a word denoting a gendered noun (*liṅga*). Examples: *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post), *randhanāya sthālī* (a pot for cooking), *śrāddhāya nigalhati* (he swallows for the sake of a funeral rite), *yuddhāya saṃnahyate* (he arms himself for battle), *patye śete* (she lies down for her husband). Likewise: *mūtrāya saṃpadyate yavāgūḥ* (the gruel turns into urine), *mūtrāya saṃkalpate* (it is intended for urine), *vātāya kapilā vidyut* (a reddish lightning flash portends wind). And [the fourth case occurs] after a word expressing an action (*bhāvavācin*) that has the sense of the suffix *-tum*. (Kātantra 2.4.28)

The fourth case ending occurs after a nominal stem that expresses the state of having the same purpose as the action denoted by a suffix meaning *tum*, provided it is followed by a word expressing the action itself—as will be stated later. For example: *pākāya vrajati* (he goes for the sake of cooking), *paktaye vrajati* (he goes for the sake of cooking).

Why is it said "after a suffix meaning *tum*"? Consider: *pākasya* (of cooking), *tyāgasya* (of abandoning). In the cases *edhebhyo vrajati* (he goes for fuel) and *phalebhyo vrajati* (he goes for fruits), the intention is to express the purpose (*tādarthya*).
The third case ending is used in connection with a companion (*sahayoga*). (Pāṇini 2.3.19)

When there is a connection with the meaning of *saha* ("together with"), the third case ending occurs by virtue of the grammatical indicator (*liṅga*). For example: *putreṇa sahāgataḥ* ("he has come together with his son"), *putreṇa saha sthūlaḥ* ("he is stout together with his son"), *putreṇa saha gomān* ("he possesses cows together with his son"), as well as *putreṇa sākam*, *putreṇa sārdham*, and *putreṇa samam*. Likewise, in *putreṇāgataḥ sthūlo gomān*, the third case ending, like the sixth, occurs only from that which is not the primary factor (*apradhāna*). Regarding the sense of cause (*hetvartha*): *Kātantra 2.4.30* states that the third case ending occurs after a word expressing the sense of cause. For example: *dhanena kulam* ("the family [is great] because of wealth"), *annena vasati* ("he dwells because of food").
It is established by the instrument (*karaṇa*) when there is a desire to express mere capability.

Regarding "in a defective limb" (Kāt. 2.4.31): the third case ending occurs after a word denoting a defective limb; for example, *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye"), *pādena khañjaḥ* ("lame in the foot"), *pṛṣṭhena kubjaḥ* ("humpbacked in the back"). However, in the expression *asyākṣi kāṇam* ("his eye is blind"), only the first case ending occurs because [the eye] is the primary object.

Regarding the rule *viśeṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.32): when a word expressing a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is used as a noun, the third case ending occurs. For example: *jaṭābhis tāpasam adrākṣīt* ("He saw the ascetic by his matted hair"), *śikhayā parivrājakam apaśyat* ("He saw the wandering mendicant by his topknot").
Why say "when it is a qualifier"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotanam* ("Lightning flashes toward the tree").
It would not occur in the case of a mere characteristic, such as "a blue lotus"; rather, when denoting merely the meaning of gender, only the nominative case is used.

And [the third case is used] for the agent (*kartṛ*). (Kātantra 2.4.33) When the suffixes expressing gender refer to the agent (*kartṛ*) among the kārakas, the third case occurs: *devadattena kṛtam* ("done by Devadatta"), *caitreṇa hanyate* ("is being killed by Caitra").

The seventh case (*saptamī*) is used for time and state (*kāla-bhāva*). [Pāṇini 2.3.34] When time or state functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the seventh case occurs after a word expressing that [time or state]. For example: *śaradi puṣpyanti saptacchadāḥ* ("In autumn, the saptacchada trees flower"); *goṣu duhyamānāsv āgataḥ* ("He arrived while the cows were being milked"); *dugdhāsv āgataḥ* ("He arrived when they had been milked"). Why specify "time and state"? [Consider: *yo jaṭābhiḥ sa bhuṅkte* ("He who has matted hair eats") and *yo bhoktā sa Devadattaḥ* ("He who is the eater is Devadatta"). Or rather, by association (*sāhacarya*), it is the well-known action itself that serves as the qualifier. Furthermore, in the expression *rudataḥ prāvrājīt* ("He went forth into homelessness while [someone] was weeping"), there is also an intended expression of a relationship [between the weeping and the renunciation].
The sixth case ending is also used in connection with *svāmin*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, *pratibhū*, and *prasūta*.

(Pāṇini 2.3.39) In connection with these words—*svāmin*, *īśvara*, *adhipati*, *dāyāda*, *sākṣin*, *pratibhū*, and *prasūta*—the sixth case ending occurs optionally alongside the seventh case ending according to the gender [of the word]. Examples: *gavāṃ svāmī*, *goṣu svāmī* (the owner of cows); *gavām īśvaraḥ*, *goṣv īśvaraḥ* (the lord of cows); *gavām adhipatiḥ*, *goṣv adhipatiḥ* (the master of cows); *gavāṃ dāyādaḥ*, *goṣu dāyādaḥ* (the heir of cows); *gavāṃ sākṣī*, *goṣu sākṣī* (the witness of cows); *gavāṃ pratibhūḥ*, *goṣu pratibhūḥ* (the surety for cows); *gavāṃ prasūtaḥ*, *goṣu prasūtaḥ* (born of cows).

The statement "the connection here is clear" refers to the rule *Kāśikā* 2.4.36: *nirdhāraṇe ca*. When a word expressing a genus (*liṅga*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and the seventh case (*saptamī*) both occur. Examples: *puruṣāṇāṃ kṣatriyaḥ śūraḥ* (among men, the Kṣatriya is brave), *puruṣeṣu kṣatriyaḥ śūraḥ*; *gavāṃ kṛṣṇā saṃpannakṣīrā* (among cows, the black one is rich in milk), *goṣu kṛṣṇā saṃpannakṣīrā*; *gacchatāṃ dhāvantaḥ śīghrāḥ* (among those walking, the runners are fast), *gacchatsu dhāvantaḥ śīghrāḥ*.

The sixth case ending occurs when used in connection with a word expressing a cause (hetu). According to Pāṇini 2.3.26, the sixth case ending is applied to a nominal stem when it is employed in the sense of a cause; for example: *annasya hetor vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food").
This rule is stated because the third case ending would otherwise have been required by virtue of its meaning as a cause.
Regarding the rule for the object of verbs meaning "to remember" (Kāt.

2.4.38): when verbs having the sense of remembering are employed, the sixth case ending occurs for their object, as in *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother") and *pitur adhyeti* ("he studies from his father").
Because the word "always" (*nitya*) is mentioned in the subsequent rule, the usage in this section is not invariably so; thus one also finds *mātaraṃ smarati* ("he remembers his mother").

How is the mother remembered? Since the meaning has already been stated, the first case ending alone is used. If the relationship "the mother is remembered" is intended here, then [the genitive applies]. Likewise in *sarpiṣo dayate*, *madhuna īṣṭe*, *sarpiṣo jānīte*, and *madhuno jānīte*; because in the case of confused cognition (*saṃbhrāntijñāna*), there is no status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for the non-existent ghee (*sarpiṣaḥ*), the genitive expresses only the relationship. So it is with others as well. Regarding the root *kṛ* (to do/make) in the sense of "effort toward improvement" (*pratiyatna*): *Kātantra 2.4.39* states that "effort toward improvement" (*pratiyatna*) is the imparting of another quality to something that already exists.

When the sense of "careful preparation" (*pratiyatna*) is understood, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the object (*karman*) of the root *kṛ*. For example: *edhodakasyopaskurute* (he prepares fuel and water) or *edhodakam upaskurute*.

Regarding roots meaning "injury" (*hiṃsārtha*), with the exception of *jvari*: according to Kātantra 2.4.40, the sixth case ending is used for the object when employing roots meaning injury, excluding *jvari*. For example: *caurasya rujati* (he injures the thief), *dāsyā āmayati* (he afflicts the maidservant), *caurasyojjāsayati* (he terrifies the thief), *caurasya nihanti*, *caurasya prahanti*, *caurasya praṇihanti*, *caurasyonnāṭayati*, *caurasyotkrāthayati*, *caurasya pinaṣṭi*.
"Even though it is impermanent, it afflicts the thief," and so forth.
Why [is the phrase] "of those meaning 'to injure'" (hiṃsārthānām) used? [Consider: "He grinds the grains.

Why [is the phrase] "except for *jvari*" (ajvarer) used? "He causes the thief to suffer fever" (*cauraṃ jvarayati*)—this is indeed intended as a case where the thief is the object of the action of causing distress (*saṃtāpayati*).

*Kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti nityam* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). When a *kṛt* suffix is employed, the sixth case ending is invariably used for both the agent and the object. For example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down") and *bhavata āsikā* ("your sitting"). Regarding the object: *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters") and *purāṃ bhettā* ("the destroyer of cities").

What is the purpose of the condition "having been formed" (*kṛti*)? It is so that [the genitive] does not occur in the employment of *taddhita* suffixes, as in *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat").
[The rule] "not in the case of *niṣṭhā* and so forth" (Kāśikā 2.4.42) states:

the genitive does not occur for the agent or the object when used with *niṣṭhā* suffixes and the like, as in *devadattena kṛtam* ("done by Devadatta"), *odanaṃ bhuktavān* ("having eaten rice"), *odanaṃ pacan* ("cooking rice"), and *odanaṃ pacamānaḥ* ("in the process of cooking rice").

In this context, the suffixes beginning with *niṣṭhā*—namely, *kta*, *ktavantu*, *śantṛṅ*, *āna*, *vansu*, *ki*, *udanta*, *ukañ*, and the *avyaya-khal-arthā-tṛn*—are [governed by the rule]. It should be stated that for the root *dviṣ* ("to hate"), the genitive case is optionally used when it denotes an enemy; e.g., *cauraṃ dviṣan* or *caurasya dviṣan*. For the root *ṣaḍ* ("to destroy"), the substitution of *ṇa* for *na* does not occur. (Kātantra 2.4.43)
*ṣaḍ* becomes *ṣaṇ* before a case-ending (*vibhakti*) beginning with *n*; for example, *ṣaṇṇām*. Why specify "before a case-ending"? [Observe: *ṣaḍnayanam*.
In the word *manas*, an *anusvāra* is substituted before a consonant (*dhuṭ*). (Kātantra 2.4.44)
An *anusvāra* occurs before a *dhuṭ* consonant following two non-final vowels, as in: *puṃsaḥ*, *śāntiḥ*, *uñchitā*, *yuñjau*, *svāmpi*.
Why specify "non-final"? [To exclude cases like] *praśān karoti*.
Before a *dhuṭ* suffix beginning with *syādi*, the word-final position applies (*padāntavat*): *pumbhyām*, *puṃbhyām*, *praśānbhyām*, *sukanbhyām*.
What is meant by *dhuṭ*? [The roots] *gam* (to go) and *han* (to kill).

In a consonant group (*varga*), a final consonant of that group [is applied]. According to Kāt_2.4.45, a non-final *anusvāra* becomes the final consonant of the group when followed by a consonant group; as in *śaṅkitā*, *uñchitā*, *vañcitā*, *yuñjau*, and *svāmpi*.

What is the purpose of the term *varga* [in the rule]? [Consider: *ākraṃsyate*. When a *tavarga* [dental stop] comes into contact with a *caṭavarga* [palatal or retroflex stop], it becomes a *caṭavarga*. According to Kātantra 2.4.46, a *tavarga* that is not final, when in contact with a *caṭavarga*, would become a *caṭavarga* due to *āntaratamya* (phonetic proximity), as in: *majjati*, *lajjate*, *bhṛjjati*, *yajñaḥ*, *yācñā*, *rājñaḥ*.

And when there is a conjunction with the *ṭa*-class [consonants], as in *ṣaṇṇām*, *aḍḍati*, *aṭṭati*, and *aṭṭate*. Why "in conjunction with the *ca*- and *ṭa*-classes"? [Consider] *viśnaḥ* and *praśnaḥ*.
Why "not final"? [Consider] *madhuliṭ tarati*.

A *si* [the letter *s*] following a nasal (*nāmika*) or a *k*, situated in a suffix, a substitute, or an augment, becomes *ṣ*, even when separated by *nu*, *visarjanīya*, or *ṣ*. (Kāt. 2.4.47) A *si* that follows a nasal or a *k*, which is not final and is situated in a suffix, a substitute, or an augment, undergoes the change to *ṣ*, provided it is separated by *nu*, *visarjanīya*, or *ṣ*; according to the word "even" (*api*), this applies even when there is no separation. First, regarding those followed by a nasal: *agniṣu*, *vāyuṣu*. Regarding those followed by *k*: *dikṣu*.
In *raparaḥ*, *gīrṣu*, and *dhūrṣu*, it resides in a modification (*vikāra*). In *eṣaḥ*, it resides in a suffix (*āgama*). In *sarveṣām*, it resides in a suffix (*āgama*).

[The substitution of *s* occurs] when followed by a *visarjanīya* or a *ṣ*. Examples: *sarpīṃṣi*, *dhanūṃṣi*, *supīḥṣu*, *sutūḥṣu*. Since it is stated that "the *ra*-base [is substituted] even when not followed by *ām*," there is optionally the substitution of *r* (before *su*), after which *ī*, *ū*, and *au* are substituted; examples: *parpiṣṣu*, *dhanuṣṣu*. Because the word "even" (*api*) has the sense of "variously" (*bahulam*), it applies in compounds: from *aṅguli-saṅga* comes *aṅguliṣaṅgaḥ*; likewise, from *bhīru-sthāna* comes *bhīruṣṭhānam*; from *agni-stuta* comes *agniṣṭut*; after a long vowel, from *somasya* comes *agnīṣomau*; and from *jyotis* and *āyus* before *stoma*, [the *s* is substituted]: *jyotiṣṭomaḥ*, *āyuṣṭomaḥ*, and *agniṣṭomaḥ*.
This applies specifically within a compound; examples include *jyotiḥstomam*, *darśayati*, and so forth.

*Kāt_2.4.48*: After the letters *repha* (r), *ṣakāra* (ṣ), and *ṛvarṇa* (ṛ/ṝ), a non-final *nakāra* (n) becomes *ṇa*, even when there is an intervening vowel (*svara*), *ha*, *ya*, *va*, the *ka*-group (*kavarga*), or the *pa*-group (*pavarga*).

That is to say, a *nakāra* that follows *repha*, *ṣakāra*, or *ṛvarṇa* and is not at the end of a word is changed to *ṇa*, provided there is an intervening vowel, *ha*, *ya*, *va*, a letter from the *ka*-group, or a letter from the *pa*-group.
Regarding the intervals of vowels: [the example] is *haraṇam* with *puruṣeṇa*, and with *mātṛkeṇa*.
Regarding the interval of *ha*: with *arheṇa*. Regarding the interval of *ya*: with *āryeṇa*.
Separated by the *va*-group: with *parvaṇā*.
Separated by the *ka*-group: with *arkeṇa*, with *mūrkheṇa*.
Separated by the *pa*-group: with *darpeṇa*, with *repheṇa*.
Even when immediately following [the preceding vowel], as in *śīrṇam*; in the case of the three [nasals].
Because of their being vowels, [the rule applies] even after an *anusvāra* and a *visṛṣṭa*, as in *vṛṃhaṇam*, *uraḥkeṇa*, and *uraḥpeṇa*.
Due to the treatment of the *visarjanīya*, [it applies] even after the *jihvāmūlīya* and *upadhmānīya*, as in *uraẖkeṇa* and *uraḫpeṇa*.
What is the purpose of [the term] *anantya* (“non-final”)? [Consider: *vṛkṣān*.
How does the fire lead [them]? Only for that [word] whose final letter is *n*, are the sounds *r* and *ṣ* taken [as causes of doubling], because they are explicitly heard [in the rule].

Because the word *api* has the sense of “often,” there are exceptions such as *sūrpaṇakhā* and others, where [doubling occurs] after letters situated in the preceding member when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*).

*Kāt_2,4.49*: The suffix *āp* occurs after a nominal stem ending in *a* that denotes a feminine. Gender—whether feminine, masculine, or neuter—is understood from worldly convention and grammatical instruction; examples are *ajā*, *eḍakā*, *caṭakā*, and *mūṣikā*.
*Kāt_2,4.50*: The suffix *ī* occurs after stems beginning with *nadī*, after those ending in *añc*, *vāh*, *ya*, *ant*, *tṛ*, and *sakhi*.
The suffix *ī* is applied in the feminine gender after words ending in *nad*, *anc*, *vāh*, *u*, *i*, *ansi*, *ant*, *ṛ*, *sakhi*, and those ending in *n*. Examples: *nadī*, *mahī*, *bhaṣī*, *plavī*;
*anci*: *prācī*, *atiprācī*;
*vāh*: *praṣṭhauhī*.
Feminine forms ending in -ud: *paṭvī*. Feminine forms ending in -id: *dākṣī*. Feminine forms ending in -ans: *viduṣī*, *atividuṣī*.
Feminine nouns ending in *a*: *pacantī*, *atipacantī*, *bhavatī*, *maghavatī*. Feminine nouns ending in *ṛ*: *kartrī*, *atikartrī*. The word *sakhi* becomes *sakhī*.

Not so for words ending in *n* or *t*, such as *daṇḍinī*. Furthermore, after a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) that does not end in *kharu* or have a conjunct consonant as its penultimate (*upadha*), [the feminine suffix *ī* is applied]; thus, from *paṭu* comes *paṭvī*.
However, *bahvī* may also occur.

From this [rule], there would not be forms such as *kharuḥ* (this is rough) or *pāṇḍuḥ* (this is pale). Furthermore, from roots other than those ending in *ktin*, we have *dhūliḥ* or *dhūlī*. However, from a root ending in *ktin*, there would not be [the feminine form], as in *paṅktiḥ*.

In the case of *svasā*, *duhitā*, *nanāndā*, *yātā*, *mātā*, *tisraḥ*, and *catasraḥ*, the feminine gender is expressed even without a suffix; whereas in the case of *pañca* and *sapta*, it does not occur precisely because of the absence of feminine gender. The word *sakhī* is for the sake of establishing the rule as permanent (*nitya*). The class beginning with *nadī* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*.
When the vowel *ī* is applied to form a feminine noun, the preceding *a* is not elided. (Kāt.
2.4.51) When the vowel *ī* is applied in the feminine, the letter *a* becomes subject to elision; for example: *nadī*, *mahī*.
Why specify "in the feminine"? [Because it does not apply] in cases such as *kuṇḍe*.
What is the purpose of the word *kṛte* [in the rule]? [Example: *kuṇḍehā*.
*Svaro hrasvo napuṃsake* (Pāṇini 1.2.47):
A vowel at the end of a neuter [stem] becomes short. Examples: *somapam*, *senāni*, *yavalu*, *atiri*, *atinu* [when referring to] a family (*kulam*).

By means of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the vowel is short" (*svaro hrasvaḥ*), there is a short vowel for the final [member] of a subordinate [compound] in the feminine, as well as for those beginning with *ā* and so on; thus: *citraguḥ*, *atisvaṭvaḥ*, *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*, *atikarabhoruḥ*.

Thus ends the section on the case-roles (*kārakapāda*) within the fourfold category of nouns (*nāmni catuṣṭaye*) in the commentary by Durgasiṃha. A compound of nouns (*samāsa*) is that whose meaning is joined [with another]. (Kātantra 2.5.1)
Names denote things. That which is combined is called "joined" (*yukta*).

The joined meaning of names is designated as a compound (*samāsa*); anything other than that is established as a sentence (*vākya*). Alternatively, the rule is explained by means of its technical designation itself. Furthermore, due to the nature of expression, this [compound] is in some cases optional, in some cases obligatory, and in some cases it does not occur; and so he will state later.

The case endings (*vibhakti*) situated therein are to be elided. (Kātyāyana 2.5.2) Case endings situated therein—that is, residing solely in the joined meaning—are to be elided, as in *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king's man), *rājatā* (kingship), and *putrīyati* (he desires a son).

In some instances, they are not elided due to specific linguistic usage (*abhidhāna*), such as *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (the one with a dark throat) and *urasilomā* (the one with hair on the chest), and so forth.
And the base form of that which ends in a vowel [is used]. (Kāt.
2.5.3) When the case endings have been elided, the base form of a gendered word ending in a vowel that stands in a compound sense also occurs; for example, "he whose friend is dear" is *sakhipriyaḥ*.
"He who has reached a friend" is *sakhiprāptaḥ*.
One who is good toward his father is *pitṛsādhuḥ*. One who has gone to a cow is *gogataḥ*.
The letter *ca* (in the rule) refers to the case of elision; thus, compounds such as *devendraḥ* and *kharoḍhaḥ* would indeed undergo euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

*Vyañjanāntasya yat subhoḥ* (Kātantra 2.5.4). When the case-endings (*vibhakti*) have been elided, that which has been prescribed for a nominal stem (*liṅga*) ending in a consonant and standing in its primary sense—namely, what is stated for both *su* and *bh*—should apply simultaneously; for there is no primary grammatical operation (*kārya*) in the presence of *sup*. Thus, it would be stated for both *su* and *bh*: *vidvadgamanam*, *diggataḥ*, *ṣaḍākṛtiḥ*, *jñānabhudāśrayaḥ*.
This is an extended application (*atideśa*).
When there are two words in apposition, it should be understood as a *karmadhāraya* compound (Kāt.

2.5.5). In a compound where two words have the same grammatical referent (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), that is to be understood as a *karmadhāraya*; for example, "it is blue and it is a lotus" becomes *nīlotpalam*.
In some cases, it is an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*): *kṛṣṇasarpaḥ* (black snake), *lohitaśāliḥ* (red rice).
In some cases there is no compound: *dīrghaś cārāyaṇaḥ*, *rāmo jāmadagnyaḥ*, *vyāsaḥ pārāśaryaḥ*, *arjunaḥ kārtavīryaḥ*.
