Likewise, because they share a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatvāt*): *kṛṣṭamadīkṛtaḥ*, *chinnaprarūḍhaḥ*, *ekapuruṣaḥ*, *sarvānnam*, *jaraddhastī*, *purāṇadhānyam*, *navodakam*, *kevalānnam*.
Similarly, *pūrveṣukāmasamī* is a technical name (*saṃjñā*).
Even when a numeral stands as the prior member of a compound, [the feminine suffix *ī* is applied]: *saptarṣayaḥ* (the Seven Sages), *pañcāmrāḥ* (five mango trees).
Likewise: *yājñikakitavaḥ* (a fraudulent sacrificer), similarly *pāpakulālaḥ* (an evil potter), *anakanāpitaḥ* (a barber without a son).
In some cases, the qualifier functions as a standard of comparison: *śastrīva śyāmā* (dark like a knife), resulting in *śastrīśyāmā*.

In some cases, the qualifier may stand as the object of comparison: *puruṣo vyāghra iva* (a man like a tiger), resulting in *puruṣavyāghraḥ* (a tiger-like man); likewise, *puruṣasiṃhaḥ* (a lion-like man).
Similarly: *pūrvapuruṣaḥ*, *aparapuruṣaḥ*, *prathamapuruṣaḥ*, *caramapuruṣaḥ*, *jaghanyapuruṣaḥ*, *samānapuruṣaḥ*, *madhyapuruṣaḥ*, *madhyamapuruṣaḥ*, *vīrapuruṣaḥ*.
Likewise, those who were not rows (*aśreṇayaḥ*) are made into rows (*śreṇayaḥ*), resulting in *śreṇīkṛtāḥ* (made into rows).

Likewise: *kṛtākṛta* (done and not done), *bhuktāpabhukta* (eaten and not eaten), *gatapratyāgata* (gone and returned), *yātānuyāta* (traversed and followed after), *aśitānaśita* (eaten and not eaten), *kliṣṭākliśita* (afflicted and not afflicted), *krayākrayikā* (buying and selling), *phalāphalikā* (fruit and non-fruit), *puṭāpuṭikā* (fold and non-fold), *mānonmānikā* (measuring and weighing). Likewise: *satpuruṣa* (good person), *mahāpuruṣa* (great person), *paramapuruṣa* (supreme person), *uttamapuruṣa* (excellent person), *puruṣottama* (best of persons)—these may be further qualifiers—or *utkṛṣṭapuruṣa* (superior person).
Likewise: *govṛndārakaḥ*, *gonāgaḥ*, *aśvakuñjaraḥ*;
*katarakaṭhaḥ*, *katamakaṭhaḥ*;
*kiṃrājā*.
Or rather, there may be a further qualification, such as *ibhyapoṭā* (the young female of a wealthy man), *ibhyayuvatiḥ* (a young woman of a wealthy man), or *agnistokaḥ* (a small fire).

Likewise: *dadhikatipayāni* (a few portions of curd), *gogṛṣṭiḥ* (a cow that has calved once), *godhenuḥ* (a milch cow), *govaśā* (a cow that miscarries), *govehat* (a cow that has lost her calf), *gobaṣkayaṇī* (a cow with a calf of the same age), *kaṭhapravaktā* (one who recites the Kaṭha texts), *kaṭhaśrotriyaḥ* (a learned Kaṭha), *kaṭhādhyāpakaḥ* (a teacher of the Kaṭhas), *kaṭhadhūrtaḥ* (a rogue of the Kaṭhas), *goprakāṇḍam* (an excellent cow), and *aśvamatallikā* (an excellent horse).
*yuvakhalatiḥ*, *yuvakhalatī*, *yuvapalitaḥ*, *yuvapalitā*, *yuvabalinaḥ*, *yuvabalinā*, *yuvajaran*, *yuvajaratī*;
*bhojyoṣṇam*, *tulyaśvetaḥ*, *sadṛśaśvetaḥ*, *śuklakṛṣṇaḥ*, *śuklaśuklaḥ*;
she is both a maiden (*kumārī*) and a Śravaṇā, thus *kumāraśravaṇā*; *kumārapravrajitaḥ*, *kumārapravrajitā*, *kumārapaṇḍitaḥ*, *kumārapaṇḍitā*.

*gogarbhiṇī* (a cow pregnant with a calf), *ajagarbhiṇī* (a goat pregnant with a kid). Like a peacock, he is a deceiver; thus, *mayūravyaṃsakaḥ*. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "one whose shoulders are gone like those of a peacock. Similarly, *chāttravyaṃsakaḥ* (a student-deceiver). Like a Kamboja, he is shaven; thus, *kambojamuṇḍaḥ*. That which is both high and low is *uccāvacam*; similarly, *uccanīcam* (high and low). *Na kiṃcana*, *akiṃcanam*: "nothing at all" or "one who has nothing"; that is, one for whom there is not even a little bit, hence *akiṃcanam*.

That which is both "prior" (*pūrva*) and "body" (*kāya*) is "the prior body" (*pūrvakāya*). In the case of a single part of the body, it is designated as "the body," just as one speaks of the "lower body," "upper body," "middle body," "central body," or "midday.

Similarly, that which is both "half" (*ardha*) and "long pepper" (*pippalī*) is "half a long pepper" (*ardhapippalī*); for a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) such as *pippalyardha* is also observed, as in "the southern half of Meru," "half an arrow," "half a bow," or "half a hearth"—even when the division is not equal, for one cannot accept the principle of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*).

In this manner: *dvitīyabhikṣā* (second alms), *bhikṣādvitīyam* (alms that are second); *tṛtīyabhikṣā* (third alms), *bhikṣātṛtīyam* (alms that are third); *caturthabhikṣā* (fourth alms), *bhikṣācaturtham* (alms that are fourth); *turīyabhikṣā* (quarter-alms), *bhikṣāturīyam* (alms that are a quarter); *turyabhikṣā* (quarter-alms), *bhikṣāturyam* (alms that are a quarter).
*Māsajātaḥ* (born after a month) and *saṃvatsarajātaḥ* (born after a year) are established by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. *Na brāhmaṇaḥ* (not a Brāhmaṇa) is *abrāhmaṇaḥ*.
The section on *karmadhāraya* compounds includes rules such as "in the technical designation of *karmadhāraya*, the masculine form is prescribed" (Kāt. 2.5.20), and so forth.

It should be understood that a compound preceded by a numeral is a *dvigu*. This is connected with the term *karmadhāraya* in Kāt. 2.5.6. Examples include: *pañcakapāla odanaḥ* ("rice prepared in five dishes"), *pañcagavadhanam* ("wealth consisting of five cows"), and *pañcapūlī* ("a collection of five bundles"). This latter is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) used in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a subsequent member of a compound, or a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).
Both are *tatpuruṣa*. According to Kātantra 2.5.7, both *dvigu* and *karmadhāraya* compounds are to be understood as having the designation *tatpuruṣa*.
The rules concerning *tatpuruṣa* are found under the governing heading beginning with Kātantra 2.5.22: "In a *tatpuruṣa*, [the final vowel of the first member] is elided."
In the case of *kūṣṭra*, the substitution of *kaṭ* would not occur in a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Case endings beginning with the second case are compounded with a word that follows them; this compound should be known as a *tatpuruṣa*. (Kātantra 2.5.8)

"Resorted to hardship" (*kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ*) becomes *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*; likewise, "gone beyond the wilderness" (*kāntārātītaḥ*), "fallen into hell" (*narakapatitaḥ*), "gone to the village" (*grāmagataḥ*), "passed over the waves" (*taraṅgātyastaḥ*), "attained happiness" (*sukhaprāptaḥ*), "fallen into suffering" (*duḥkhāpannaḥ*), "one who goes to the village" (*grāmagamī*), "one who comes from the village" (*grāmāgāmī*), "desirous of eating rice" (*odanabubhukṣuḥ*), "the rogue who has mounted the couch" (*khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ*), "moments elapsed during the day" (*aharatisṛtā muhūrtāḥ*), "transitions occurring during the day" (*ahaḥsaṃkrāntāḥ*), "mounted upon the night" (*rātryārūḍhāḥ*), "the moon measured by the month" (*māsapramitaś candramāḥ*), "happiness for a moment" (*muhūrtasukham*), "auspicious throughout the entire night" (*sarvarātrakalyāṇī*).
In some cases, it remains a sentence alone, as in: "He has eaten rice" (*odanaṃ bhuktavān*).

The third [type of compound] consists of words such as *giriṇā kāṇaḥ* (blind from a mountain), *girikāṇaḥ*; likewise *dhānyārthaḥ* (wealth consisting of grain), *māsapūrvaḥ* (preceded by a month), *pitṛsadṛśaḥ* (resembling a father), *pitṛsamaḥ* (equal to a father), *māsonaḥ* (less than a month), *māsavikalaḥ* (deficient by a month), *asikalahaḥ* (a sword-fight), *vāṅnipuṇaḥ* (skilled in speech), *guḍamiśraḥ* (mixed with molasses), *vākślakṣṇaḥ* (gentle in speech); and similarly *rājahataḥ* (killed by a king), *nakhanirbhinnaḥ* (pierced by nails), *kākapeyā nadī* (a river drinkable by crows), and *bāṣpacchedyāni tṛṇāni* (grass that can be cut with dew).
In some cases it does not occur, as in *kākena pātavyā* (drinkable by a crow).

In other cases it does occur, as in *buṣopendhyam* (to be ignited by chaff), *ghanaghātyam* (to be struck by a mallet), *dadhnopasikta odanaḥ* (rice sprinkled with curd), *dadhyodanaḥ* (curd-rice), *guḍena miśrā dhānāḥ* (parched grains mixed with molasses), and *guḍadhānāḥ* (molasses-grains).

The fourth [case-ending] [is used]: *gobhyo hitam* (beneficial for cows), *go-hitam*; likewise *go-sukham* (comfortable for cows), *kuvera-baliḥ* (an offering for Kubera), *go-rakṣitaḥ* (protected by a cow); *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post), *yūpa-dāru*; *deva-deyam puṣpam* (a flower to be given to a god), *brāhmaṇa-deyam dhanam* (wealth to be given to a Brahmin), *vara-pradeyā kanyā* (a maiden to be given as a bride). In some cases it may not occur: *brāhmaṇāya dātavyam* (to be given to a Brahmin), *brāhmaṇārthaḥ pūpaḥ* (a cake for the sake of a Brahmin), *brāhmaṇārthā prapā* (a water-stall for the sake of a Brahmin), *brāhmaṇārthaṃ payaḥ* (milk for the sake of a Brahmin); [in these cases] there is always a compound and the word takes all genders.

The fifth [case]: *vṛkād bhayam* (fear from a wolf), *vṛkabhayam* (wolf-fear), *vṛkabhītaḥ* (frightened by a wolf), *vṛkabhītiḥ* (the fear of a wolf), *vṛkabhiḥ* (by means of a wolf); *grāmanirgataḥ* (gone out from the village), *sukhāpetaḥ* (deprived of happiness), *kalpanāpoḍhaḥ* (free from conceptual construction), *cakramuktaḥ* (released from the wheel), *mañcapatitaḥ* (fallen from the bed), *taraṅgāpatrastaḥ* (terrified by the waves).

The sixth [case]: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king-man), *ātmaṣaṣṭhaḥ* (with oneself as the sixth), *bhikṣādvitīyaḥ* (with alms as the second); proximity to the present time; *candanagandhaḥ* (the scent of sandalwood), *nadīghoṣaḥ* (the sound of a river), *kanyārūpam* (the beauty of a maiden), *stanasparśaḥ* (the touch of the breast), *phalarasaḥ* (the juice of the fruit).

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in composition (*samāsa*) when it expresses a relationship, as in the following examples: *brāhmaṇasya kartavyam* ("the duty of a Brahmin"), *brāhmaṇasya vṛttir apīṣyate* ("even the livelihood of a Brahmin is desired"), *brāhmaṇasya kurvan* ("doing for a Brahmin"), *brāhmaṇasya kurvāṇaḥ* ("doing for a Brahmin"), and *vākyam eva* ("only the sentence itself"). Likewise, in cases such as *phalānāṃ tṛptaḥ* ("satisfied with fruits"), *chāttrasyoccair gṛham* ("the student's high house")—because these involve dependence [on another word]—and in *palāśaśātanam* ("the plucking of Palāśa leaves"), *mātṛsmaraṇam* ("remembering one's mother"), *sureśvaraḥ* ("Lord of the Gods"), and *rājapūjitaḥ* ("honored by the king"), the genitive of relationship (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*) indeed forms a compound.

The seventh [case] is as follows: *akṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ* (skilled at dice), *akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*, *akṣadhūrtaḥ*, *akṣakitavaḥ*; *vane 'ntarvasati* (he dwells within the forest), *vanāntarvasati*; likewise, *kāmpillasiddhaḥ* (perfected in Kāmpilla), *chāyāśuṣkaḥ* (dried in the shade), *kumbhīpakvaḥ* (cooked in a pot), *cārakabandhaḥ* (bound in prison), *tīrthadhvāṅkṣaḥ*, *tīrthakākaḥ*; likewise, *pūrvāhṇageyaṃ sāma* (the Sāman to be sung in the forenoon), *māsadeyam ṛṇam* (a debt to be paid after a month), *pūrvāhṇakṛtam*, *aparāhṇakṛtam*, *pūrvarātrakṛtam*, *apararātrakṛtam*, and others of this kind.

What is the purpose of the phrase "with a subsequent word" (*parapadena*)? [Examples: *gato grāmam* ("gone to the village"), *kathaṃ prāpto jīvikām* ("how has he obtained a livelihood?"), *prāptajīvikaḥ* ("one who has obtained a livelihood"), and likewise *āpannajīvikaḥ*.

Words beginning with *ati* are compounded with a word in the second case when they have the sense of "having surpassed," as in *atikrāntaḥ khaṭvām* ("having surpassed the bed"), resulting in *atikhaṭvaḥ*.

Words beginning with *ava* are compounded with a word in the third case when they have the sense of "called out by," as in *avakruṣṭaṃ kokilayā* ("called out by a cuckoo"), resulting in *avakokilaṃ vanam* ("a forest called out by cuckoos"), and likewise *avamayūram*.
The group beginning with *pari* is used with the fourth case (*caturthī*) in the sense of being weary of something, as in *pariglāno ’dhyayanāya* (weary of study) or *paryadhyayanaḥ*.
The group beginning with *nis* is used with the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of having departed from something, as in *nirgataḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī) or *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*.

This is correct; once the compound is formed, the prior placement [of the subordinate member] occurs by virtue of conventional usage (*abhidhāna*), just as in *dantānāṃ rājā* (king of teeth) becoming *rājadantaḥ*, while examples such as *kubrāhmaṇaḥ* (a bad Brahmin) are *karmadhāraya* compounds.

Whether there be two words or even many, when they [express] the meaning of another word, that is a *bahuvrīhi*. (Kātantra 2.5.9) The connection is "where there is a compound": this monkey has climbed it, thus "the tree with the climbed-monkey" (*ārūḍhavānara*); that person by whom a salutation was performed is "the person who has performed a salutation" (*kṛtapraṇāma*); likewise, a guest to whom food was given is "a guest to whom food was given" (*dattabhojana*); a country whose inhabitants have perished is "a country with its people destroyed" (*ucchannajanapada*); Devadatta [possesses] variegated cows is "Devadatta with variegated cows" (*citragu*); a river with much water is "a river with abundant water" (*bahūdaka*). Even with many words: a forest with many intoxicated elephants is "a forest with many-intoxicated-elephants" (*mattabahumātaṅga*); likewise, those to whom ten have approached are "those with ten-approached" (*upadaśa*), similarly "those with ten-attained" (*āpannadaśa*), and "those with ten-near" (*āsannadaśa*).
Those whose state (*daśā*) is not far [from ten] are *adūradaśāḥ*; those whose state is more than [ten] are *adhikadaśāḥ*, and these are again nine or eleven.
Those whose measure (*parimāṇa*) is three tens are *tridaśāḥ*. The word *daśa* functions here as a number because of its proximity to a word denoting measure (*parimāṇa*).
For example, those whose measure is five are "five-ers" (*pañcakāḥ*), such as birds.
Two or three is their measure; thus, *dvitrāḥ* (two or three).
Even when the referents are different, as in *urasilomā* (hair on the chest), *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (Kāla [Śiva] on the throat), and *uccairmukhaḥ* (high-mouthed).

Even when the first member ends in the nominative case, as in the sense of another word (*anyapadārthe*): *saha putreṇāgataḥ* (he came with his son) becomes *saputrakaḥ*; *saha lomnā vartate* (it exists with hair) becomes *salomakaḥ*, meaning "possessing hair. Similarly, *sapakṣakaḥ* (having wings) and *sakaṣṭakaḥ* (having thorns).
A she-donkey carries its load together with ten sons; such a usage is not recorded [in the lexicons].
Furthermore, when a battle has taken place by seizing each other by the hair, it is called *keśākeśi*; when a battle has taken place by striking each other with sticks, it is called *daṇḍādaṇḍi*.
Instances of the *bahuvrīhi* compound include those beginning with the rule *bahuvrīhau* (Pāṇini 6.2.1).
"Likewise, *vidik*.

(Kāt 2.5.10) Likewise, a *bahuvrīhi* compound should be understood as denoting an intermediate direction (*vidig*), provided that two words expressing directions are combined in a compound; for example, that which lies between the southern and eastern directions is the "southeastern" (*dakṣiṇapūrvā*) direction.
"A *dvandva* [compound] occurs when there is a conjunction of two names, or even of many. (Kāt 2.5.11)

In a compound where there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of two names or even many names, that is a *dvandva*. Examples are: *Devadattayajñadattau* (Devadatta and Yajñadatta), *dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ* (the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees), *vāgdṛśadam* (speech and sight), and *pīṭhacchattrōpānaham* (a seat, an umbrella, and sandals).
Both *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection) and *samāhāra* (aggregation) are merely varieties of conjunction.
In such cases, the word with the fewer syllables (*alpasvaratara*) comes first. (Kātantra 2.5.12)
In that regard, within a *dvandva* compound, that member which has fewer syllables (*alpasvaratara*) is placed first: as in *plakṣanyagrodham* and *dhavāśvakarṇam*.
The inclusion of the term "more" (*tara*) is for the purpose of establishing a restriction regarding two-word compounds; by this, [the rule does not apply to] *śaṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ*.
Furthermore, there are exceptions: *udūkhalamuṣale*, *taṇḍulakiṇve*, *citrarathabāhlīkau*, and so forth.

And regarding that which is honored (*arcita*) between two [in a *dvandva* compound]: Kātyāyana 2.5.13 states that in a *dvandva* compound, that which is more honored of the two is placed first—e.g., *devadaityau* (gods and demons), *vāsudevārjunau* (Vāsudeva and Arjuna).
However, this rule is subject to exceptions, as in *naranārāyaṇau* (Nara and Nārāyaṇa), *umāmaheśvarau* (Umā and Maheśvara), and *kākamayūrau* (crow and peacock).
That which is to be expressed first is desired as an *avyayībhāva* compound (Kāt. 2.5.14).
The connection is with the word "of the compound" (*samāsasya*). For example: "The discourse proceeded concerning women" (*kārake strīṣv adhikṛtya kathā pravṛttā*) becomes *adhistri*;
"in the vicinity [of the jar]" (*samīpe*) becomes *upakumbham*.
In the sense of prosperity, *sumadram*.
In the sense of absence, *nirmakṣikam*. Likewise, the disappearance of the prosperity of ox-carts is *durgavadikam*.
The passing of the cold seasons; extreme cold; excessive frost; the time for the enjoyment of *taisṛka* coverings has not yet arrived.
Even when a word appears [as a compound], according to Pāṇini, it is *tat-pāṇini*.
In the sense of "behind" or "after," there is *anu-ratha*.

In the sense of "according to the object" (yathārthe): *anurūpam* (suitable), *rūpasya yogyatvam* (fitness of form); *pratyartham* (with respect to each object), meaning according to capacity (*yathāśakti*), according to seniority (*anujyeṣṭham*), that is to say, without exceeding one's capacity and in order of seniority.

In the sense of "similarity" (*sādṛśye*): *sakikhi* (like a partridge), meaning similar to a partridge (*kikhyāḥ sadṛśam*). In the sense of "entirety" (*sākalye*): *satṛṇam abhyavaharati* (he eats even grass), *sāgny adhīte* (he studies even including the fire-chant); other examples are likewise formed.

The rules concerning *avyayībhāva* compounds are as follows: "After an *avyayībhāva* ending in *a*, the case endings (*vibhakti*) take the suffix *am*, except for the fifth case" (Kāt 2.4.1), and so forth.

That [compound] shall be neuter gender. Kāt 2.5.15: "That *avyayībhāva* compound shall be neuter gender. This has been illustrated and is being illustrated further: *samatvaṃ bhūmeḥ* ("the levelness of the ground"), *samambhūmi* ("level with the ground"), *samaṃpadāti* ("level with the foot"); likewise, *suṣamam*, *viṣamam*, *niḥṣamam*, *duḥṣamam*; and such sentences as *aparatvaṃ śobhanatvaṃ samasya* ("the state of being subsequent or the state of being beautiful belonging to the *samāsa*").
Likewise, [the forms] *pramṛgam*, *praratham*, and *pradakṣiṇam* [are established].
Since the preceding member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), the absence of gender would have been obtained [by rule]; therefore, this statement is made.
[The neuter singular form] for a *dvandva* compound is prescribed. (Kātantra 2.5.16)

The singular neuter gender applies to a copulative compound (*dvandva*): *pratyaṣṭhāt kaṭhakālāpam* (the Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have established themselves), *udagāt kaṭhakauthumam* (the Kaṭhas and Kauthumas have risen), *arkāśvamedham* (the Arka and Aśvamedha sacrifices), *padakakramakam* (the Pada and Krama texts), *ārāśastri* (the bow and the sword), *gaṅgāśoṇam* (the Gaṅgā and Śoṇa rivers), *kurukurukṣetram* (Kuru and Kurukṣetra), *mathurāpāṭaliputram* (Mathurā and Pāṭaliputra), *ahinakulam* (the snake and the mongoose), *takṣāyaskāram* (the carpenter and the blacksmith), *pāṇipādam* (the hand and the foot), *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummer and the player of the *pāṇava*), *hastyaśvam* (the elephant and the horse), *yūkālikṣam* (the louse and the nit), *badarāmalakam* (the jujube and the myrobalan), *plakṣanyagrodham* (the *plakṣa* and the banyan tree), *dhavāśvakarṇam* (the *dhava* and the *aśvakarṇa* trees), *kuśakāśam* (the *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses), *tilamāṣam* (sesame and beans), *rurupṛṣatam* (the *ruru* and the spotted deer), *haṃsacakravākam* (the swan and the ruddy goose), *dadhighṛtam* (curd and clarified butter), and *sukhaduḥkham* (pleasure and pain).

In the Anuvāda section, [the following are excluded]: verbs of the root *sthā* used in the sense of the present tense (*adyatanī*), Yajus formulas and sacrificial rites that are recited in close proximity,
and names of rivers, countries, and cities whose genders differ from those of non-living species.
Furthermore, regarding those who are eternal enemies, artisans, and the components of musical instruments;

and when there is a plurality of the components of an army, as well as of small creatures, fruits, and specific types of trees, grasses, grains, animals, and birds, the rule is indeed optional (*vibhāṣā*).

The equality of specific consonants that possess substance and are mutually opposed, and the combination of those [consonants], indeed constitutes something else in the case of curd and milk. What is meant by "oneness"? For example: *hastyaśvau* (elephant and horse), *dadhighṛtāḥ* (curd and ghee).
Likewise for a *dvigu* compound.
(Kātyāyana 2.5.17) Likewise, even for a *dvigu*, there shall be the singular number and the neuter gender, as in *pañcagavam*, *catuṣpatham*, because of the qualifier "beautiful" (*śobhanam*).
Why "the singular number"? [Consider: *pañcakapāla odanaḥ*.

This [compound] beginning with *apātra* ends in a short vowel; likewise, a *dvigu* ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) or one that does not end in a suffix (*ananta*) is declared to belong to the *nadādi* group when it is a collective (*samāhāra*). *Kāt_2.5.18*: A word denoting a female (*striyāṃ vartamānaḥ*) that has been previously stated to denote a male (*bhāṣitapuṃskaḥ*) and does not contain the suffix *ūṅ*, becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*), provided it occurs in grammatical apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇe*) with another word denoting a female, excluding words such as ordinal numbers (*pūraṇī*) and the like. For example: *śobhanabhāryaḥ* (one who has a beautiful wife) and *dīrghajaṅghaḥ* (one with long shanks).

That is to say, because of the qualification "in the feminine" for both the preceding and the following [rules], we have *grāmaṇidṛṣṭiḥ* (meaning "one whose view is that of a village headman") from *grāmaṇi-kulam*, and *kalyāṇīpradhānāḥ* (meaning "those for whom a beautiful woman is the chief") from *kalyāṇī-pradhānam eṣām*. Why specify "the meaning is one that has a corresponding masculine form"? Consider *droṇībhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a wooden trough"). Why specify "not ending in *-ūṅ*" (*anūṅ*)? Consider *brahmabandhūbhāryaḥ* ("one whose wife is a woman of the Brahmin class").
What is the purpose of the phrase "in the case of non-pūraṇī [words] and so forth"? [Example: *kalyāṇīpañcamā rātrayaḥ* ("five nights, the fifth of which is auspicious").
Because of the inclusion of the primary *pūraṇī* [words], [we have] *kalyāṇapañcamīkaḥ pakṣaḥ* ("a fortnight having an auspicious fifth day").
Because of the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), [we have] *kalyāṇīpriyaḥ* ("one who loves an auspicious woman").

*priyā*, *manojñā*, *subhagā*, *durbhagā*, *bhaktiḥ*, *sacivā*, *svā*, *kāntā*, *samā*, *bālyā*, *duhitā*, *vāmanā*. However, those with a *saṃjñā* as their prior member or those having a *pūraṇī* (ordinal) as their *upadhā* do not [take the masculine form]. (Kāt. 2.5.19). Here, the mere masculine form applies; however, those with a *saṃjñā* as their prior member or those having a *pūraṇī* as their *upadhā* do not take the masculine form: *dattābhāryaḥ*, *guptābhāryaḥ*, *pañcamībhāryaḥ*, *pañcamīyate*, *pañcamīmāninī*, *pācikābhāryaḥ*, *madrikābhāryaḥ*.
How is it that [the forms] *pākabhārya*, *bhekabhārya*, and *śuṣkabhārya* are designated? [The rule states:

"There is no substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) for a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) ending in *-ī* which is the cause of a vowel-increment (*vṛddhi*), nor for a word denoting a bodily limb (*svāṅga*) that does not undergo a visible change, provided it does not end in a suffix expressing measure (*mānin*); likewise for a genus (*jāti*).
However, when these are designated as *karmadhāraya* compounds, the substitution of the masculine form is prescribed. (Kātantra 2.5.20)

This [rule] is an exception to the prohibition of the suffix *ūṅ* for words that have a corresponding masculine form (*bhāṣitapuṃska*). For example: *kaṭhī ca sā bhāryā* (she is both a Kaṭha woman and a wife) becomes *kaṭhabhāryā*; likewise, *dattabhāryā*, *pañcamabhāryā*, and *pācakabhāryā*.

Why is it specified "having a corresponding masculine form"? Consider *khaṭvāvṛndārikā* (a young girl who is a bedstead). Why is it specified "not having the suffix *ūṅ*"? Consider *brahmabandhūdārikā* (a young girl who is a low Brahmin woman).
The substitution of *ā* occurs for the final vowel of the word *mahat* when it stands in grammatical apposition with another word.

(Kāt. 2.5.21) Examples: *mahādevaḥ*, *mahāvaktraḥ*. Because the rule for the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *ā* takes place after that elision has occurred; however, it does not apply to a form ending in the suffix *cv-*: *mahadbhūtaś candramāḥ*. Due to a formal separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), the substitution also applies in cases such as *mahatyā ghāsaḥ* → *mahāghāsaḥ*; likewise, *mahākaraḥ* and *mahāviśiṣṭaḥ*.
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the *n* [of the first member] is to be elided. According to Kāt.

2.5.22, in a *tatpuruṣa* related to *na*, the *nakāra* (the letter *n*) related to *na* is to be elided; or rather, there is a reading with two *n*s. *Na savarṇaḥ* = *asavarṇaḥ*; those which possess no resonance (*ghoṣa*) or sound are "voiceless" (*aghoṣāḥ*); the absence of a Brahmin is *abrāhmaṇam*.
In this context, *tatpuruṣa* is used as an illustration.
Regarding vowel [substitution], there is a reversal of syllables. Kāt_2.5.23:
In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, when a vowel follows, there occurs a reversal of syllables for the suffix *-na*, as in *anajaḥ*, *anajam*, and *anajakaḥ*.

*Koḥ kat* (Pāṇini 6.3.104). In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *ku-* becomes *kad-*. For example, "a contemptible horse" is *kadaśvaḥ*; likewise, *kaduṣṭraḥ*. Why specify "in a *tatpuruṣa*"? [Consider] *kūṣṭro deśaḥ* ("the country of Kuṣṭra"), where it does not apply.

But what [is the case] when *kā* is used in the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*)? According to Pāṇini 6.3.104 (*ku-gati-prādayaḥ*), the substitution of *kā-* for the word *ku-* occurs when it is used in the sense of "slight" within a *tatpuruṣa* compound, provided that the word *akṣa-* follows. Examples include: *īṣallavaṇam* (slightly salty) becomes *kālavaṇam*; *kāmḷam* (slightly sour); and *kākṣeṇa vīkṣate* (he looks with a squint).
However, in the case of accentuation (*svara*) when the sense is "slight," the substitution of *kā-* alone applies because it has higher priority.

In the case of *puruṣa*, however, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). According to Pāṇini 2.5.26, when the word *ku* is followed by the word *puruṣa* in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the substitution of *kā* for *ku* occurs optionally. Thus we have *kāpuruṣaḥ* or *kupuruṣaḥ*. This is an optional rule applied where [the previous rule] would not otherwise apply. It should be stated that [the same applies to] *īṣaduṣṇam*, *koṣṇam*, *kavoṣṇaḥ*, and *kaduṣṇam*.

The *y* and *ā* sounds, when treated as feminine, are sometimes short [in a compound]. (Kāt. 2.5.27) Both the letter *ī* and the letter *ā* are referred to as *yākārau*. In a compound, the *y* and *ā* sounds are sometimes short when they are treated as feminine, according to the requirements of usage (*lakṣya*). Examples include *revatimitraḥ*, *rohiṇimitraḥ*, and *bharaṇimitraḥ*;
*iṣṭakacitam*, *iṣīkatūlam*, and *mālabhāriṇī kanyā*; and other similar cases as well.

The lengthening of a short vowel. According to Kātantra 2.5.28, the lengthening of a short vowel occurs in a compound in certain instances, in accordance with usage: *dātrākarṇaḥ*, *dvividhākarṇaḥ*, *dviguṇākarṇaḥ*, *dvyaṅgulākarṇaḥ*; here, the vowel is long only when it refers specifically to a mark on the ear.
In some cases, it does not occur: *piṣṭakarṇaḥ*, *aṣṭakarṇaḥ*.

In the case of words ending in *kvip* derived from the roots *nah*, *vṛt*, *vṛṣ*, *vyadh*, *ruc*, *sañj*, and *niṣ*, there is lengthening of the vowel only when a preposition (*prādi*) functions as the *kāraka*. Examples include: *upānat*, *upāvṛt*, *prāvṛṭ*, *marmāvit*, *nīruk*, *ṛtīṣaṭ*, *parītat*; other similar cases are also to be understood in this way. However, when not following an indeclinable (*anavyaya-visṛṣṭa*), [the final *s*] becomes *sakāra* before the *ka*-class and the *pa*-class consonants. (Kātantra 2.5.29) When not following an indeclinable, [the final *s*] undergoes the change to *sakāra* when followed by the *ka*-class or *pa*-class consonants; in some compounds, this occurs in accordance with observed usage (*lakṣya*). Examples are: *ayaspāśam*, *ayaskalpam*, *ayaskāmyati*, *ayaskam*. This change is seen before the suffixes *pāśa*, *kalpa*, and *kāmyaka*.
In the case of *kāmya*, it does not occur after a non-rap-prakṛti [stem]: *gīḥkāmyati*, *dhūḥkāmyati*. [Examples with rap-prakṛti stems are:
*ayaskāraḥ*, *ayaskāmaḥ*, *ayaskaṃsaḥ*, *ayaskumbhaḥ*. In a compound with *kṛñ*, *kāmin*, *kaṃsa*, and *kumbha*, this [suffix] follows the letter *a*.

In the *Anuttara* [grammar], [the suffix] is observed after words such as *kuśa* and *karṇī* when preceded by *bhāskara* and others. That which is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-eternal; examples include *namaskartum*, *puraskartum*, and so forth.
Thus ends the section on compounds within the fourfold treatment of nouns in the *Daurgasimhī-vṛtti*.

Regarding *vāṇ apatye* (Kātantra 2.6.1): after a noun ending in the genitive case, when the meaning to be expressed is "offspring" (*apatya*), the suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied. For example: the offspring of Upagu is *aupagavaḥ*, *pāṇḍavaḥ*, *āśvapataḥ*, *śaivaḥ*, or *prauṣṭhaḥ*. When there is a desire to express the offspring in general, it is derived from the very first base [of the lineage]. However, regarding the offspring of a grandson (*pautra*) and so forth, the suffixes *aṇ* and others are prescribed specifically for the offspring of one who is praiseworthy, excluding females. Because of the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*), both "the offspring of Upagu" (*upagor apatyam*) and "Upagu’s offspring" (*upagvapatyam*) would be possible.

The suffix *ṇya* is applied after [the names] beginning with *garga*. According to Pāṇini 4.1.105 (*gargādibhyo yañ*), when a descendant is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇya* occurs after the group of words beginning with *garga*. For example: the descendant of *Garga* is *Gārgya*; likewise, *Vātsya*.
Since this applies only to descendants such as the grandson and beyond who have become members of a *gotra*, in other cases it is *Gārgi*.
Anantara, Rāma Jāmadagnya, Vyāsa Pārāśarya, and Arjuna Kārtavīrya—
[these are examples of the names] Jāmadagna and Pārāśara.
This [list] beginning with Garga is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class).
The suffix *āyanaṇ* is prescribed after the group beginning with *kuñja*.

(Kātantra 2.6.3) After the group beginning with *kuñja*, when it functions as a *gotra* [patronymic], the suffix *āyanaṇ* occurs to denote a descendant such as a grandson (*pautra*) and so forth; and *ṇya* is also prescribed after that [group]. Before the group beginning with *naḍa*, when there is no plurality and not in the feminine, [the suffixes apply]. This is because the mention of "prescribed" (*smṛta*) indicates a restricted scope of application. Thus: *kauñjāyanyaḥ*, *kauñjāyanyau*; *vrādhnāyanyaḥ*, *vrādhnāyanyau*. But in the feminine: *kauñjāyanī*.
In the case of plurality, however, they are called Kauñjāyanas.
From the *naḍa* group, however, we have Nāḍāyana, Cārāyaṇa, and Mauñjāyana.
There was a certain person named Kuñja; his descendant is Kauñji, and the first-born descendant is also Kauñji.
*Kuñja* and so forth constitute an *ākṛtigaṇa*.

[The suffix] *eyaṇ* is applied after *strī*, *atrya*, and so on. According to Pāṇini 4.1.120 (*striyāṃ vihitatvāt strī*), the word *strī* [is used here]. By Pāṇini 4.1.121 (*stryādibhyo ḍhak*), when the offspring is to be expressed, *eyaṇ* occurs after words beginning with *strī* and after *atrya*; for example: *vainateyaḥ*, *sauparṇeyaḥ*, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *yauvateyaḥ*.
Ātreya, Śauceya.
By the inclusion of "etcetera" (ādi), [we have] Śaubhreya, Vaiṣṭapureya.

This *atri* is an indicator for dissyllabic bases ending in the suffix *-an* that lack a secondary suffix (*apratyaya*); therefore, the offspring of Marīci is Mārīca, and the offspring of Dākṣi is Dākṣāyaṇa.

The group beginning with Atri is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. [Kāśikā 4.1.95] states: *iṇ ataḥ*. The suffix *iṇ* occurs after a name ending in the vowel *a* when the meaning to be expressed is "offspring. For example: the offspring of Dakṣa is *Dākṣi*; likewise, *Plākṣi*; the offspring of Asita is *Asiti*.
What is the meaning of "ataḥ" (from this)? [The suffix does not apply] after *kailālapaḥ*.

It does not occur after *śata*, *sarva*, *kāka*, *śukla*, *vṛddha*, *rājapuruṣa*, *māthuraka*, or *kāraka*, because of the absence of such usage (*anabhidhānāt*). How is it that one says, "Let Maithilī be given to the son of Daśaratha" (*pradīyatāṃ dāśarathāya maithilī*)? [In this case, the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to him").

And [the suffix] *iṇ* is prescribed after the group beginning with *bāhu*. (Kāśikā 4.1.96) The suffix *iṇ* occurs after the class of words beginning with *bāhu* when a descendant is to be expressed: *bāhaviḥ*, *aupabāhaviḥ*, *bindaviḥ*, *aupabindaviḥ*.
It is desired that this applies only when the word has become part of a *gotra* (clan name) and so forth; for example, if there is someone named Bāhu, his descendant is *bāhavaḥ*.

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (open class) beginning with *bāhu*. The suffix *aṇ* is desired after [stems ending in] *rāga*, *nakṣatrayoga*, *samūha*, *sāsya devatā*, *tad vetti*, *adhīte*, *tasyedaṃ*, and so forth. (Kātantra 2.6.7)

"Rāga" [in this context] means "due to connection with color": it refers to saffron (*kausumbha*) or turmeric (*hāridra*), meaning that which is dyed by safflower or turmeric. How is it that the donkey's ears are called "ochre-colored" (*kāṣāya*) or the cock's feet "turmeric-colored" (*hāridra*)? It is because of the superimposition of those qualities [onto the objects].

The conjunction with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) occurs only with the moon; it is through that connection that time is denoted. However, the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed by the direct mention of the word "lunar mansion" itself. Thus, [we have] *pauṣam ahaḥ* ("the day of Puṣya") and *pauṣī rātriḥ* ("the night of Puṣya"), meaning a night joined with the moon in conjunction with Puṣya. In the case of expressions such as *kṛttikāsu*, *viśākhāsu*, *maghāsu*, and *bharaṇīṣu*, although they denote time, the suffix *aṇ* does not apply because of the optionality [of its usage]. For a collection is non-different from its substrata (*dharmī*), as in *vāyasam*, *kākam*, *bhaikṣam*, and *yauvatam*.

That which has Śiva as its deity is *śaiva*; likewise, there is an *aindra* oblation (*havis*) and an *aindra* mantra. One who knows or studies the *chandas* is a *chāndasa*; similarly, one is a *vaiyākaraṇa*.
That which belongs to a deer is *mārga* meat; likewise, there is *śaukara* [meat].

In this way, when a group is understood through the relationship between a word and its meaning—such as that which has "this" as its beginning—the suffix is applied: that which is perceived by the eye is *cākṣuṣa*, namely form (*rūpa*); likewise, sound is *śrāvaṇa*.
Flour ground on a grinding stone is *dārśada*;
mung beans crushed in a mortar are *audūkhalāḥ*.
A chariot carried by horses is an *āśva* chariot. A cart carried by four [oxen] is a *cātura* cart.
That which is seen on the fourteenth day is a *cāturdaśa* demon.

In this regard, the analysis (vigraha) should be made as "born there," "come from there," and so forth; this is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). By means of this [suffix], one forms words for: that with which one plays, that with which one is joined, that which one crosses, that which one traverses, that which one buys, that which is one's craft, that which is one's duty, that which is bought and so forth, and even that which is a weapon. (Kātantra 2.6.8)

The suffix *ikaṇ* occurs after words such as *krīta* ("bought"), *āyudha* ("weapon"), and others, according to their respective relationships—namely, when [the action] is performed with that (*tena dīvyati*), when mixed with that (*tena saṃsṛṣṭam*), when one crosses by means of that (*tena tarati*), or when one moves by means of that (*tena carati*)—due to the application of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*). For example: he plays with dice (*akṣair dīvyati*), thus *ākṣikaḥ*.
That which is mixed with curd (*dadhnā saṃsṛṣṭam*), thus *dādhikam*; likewise, *mārīcikam*.

He crosses by means of a cow's tail (*gopucchena tarati*), thus *gaupucchikaḥ*; likewise, *kāṇḍaplavikaḥ* [crosses] by means of a reed-raft over a river, and *āśvamedhikaḥ* [atones for] the murder of a Brahmin by means of the horse sacrifice.

One who moves about with a cart is a *śākaṭika*; likewise, one who moves about with a bell is a *ghaṇṭika*. One who moves about with ginger is a *śārṅgaverika*. From the occupation of selling betel leaves, one is a *tāmbūlika*; from the craft of playing the mṛdaṅga drum, one is a *mārdaṅgika*; similarly, one is a *pāṇavika* (drummer). From the duty of guarding a gate, one is a *dauvārika*; similarly, one is a *śaulkaśālika* (customs officer).
Purchased for two *śūrpa*s is *dviśaurpika*; likewise, [purchased for] a thousand is *sāhasrika*. Worthy of a *kārṣāpaṇa* is *kārṣāpaṇika*.
From the employment of the *tomara* weapon comes *taumarika*; likewise, *cākrika* [from the employment of the *cakrin*].

The fifth case (*pañcamī*) is also employed in relation to non-difference even with words such as *krīta* ("purchased"), and the mention of "manifestation of action" (*kriyāvirbhāva*) is for the sake of clarity: e.g., *kuddālena khanati* ("he digs with a spade") and *kauddālikaḥ* ("one who digs with a spade").

Similarly: *ojaḥsaho'mbhasā vartate*, as in *aujasikaḥ śūraḥ* ("a hero who acts with vigor"), *sāhasikaś cauraḥ* ("a thief who acts with rashness"), and *āmbhasiko matsyaḥ* ("a fish that lives in water"), and so forth. [The suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after the word *nau* when meaning "to be crossed," after *viṣa* when meaning "to be killed," and also after *tulā* when meaning "to be weighed."

In that regard, regarding the suffix *ya*: Kāt_2.6.9 states that the suffix *ya* occurs after a word ending in the third case (*tṛtīyāntāt*) in the sense of "to be crossed" (*tārya*), after a word ending in the third case meaning "poison" (*viṣāt*) in the sense of "to be killed" (*vadhye*), and after a word ending in the third case "by means of a balance" (*tulayā*) in the sense of "equal to" (*saṃmite*). Furthermore, the suffix *ya* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamyantāt*) in the sense of "suitable for" (*sādhu*). Examples: that which is to be crossed by boat is *nāvyam*; one who is to be killed by poison is *viṣyaḥ*; that which is equal by means of a balance is *tulyam*; one who is suitable for action is *karmaṇyaḥ*. Moreover, because of the explicit mention of the word "also" (*api ca*), we have: an elephant equal to a mountain is *giritulyaḥ*.

Others say that *tulya* means "similar" (*sadṛśa*). *Kuśala* is said to mean "skilled," "suitable," and "beneficial. However, in the sense of "beneficial," the suffix *-īya* is used according to Pāṇini 5.1.5 (Kāt_2,6.10): the suffix *-īya* occurs in the sense of being beneficial (*hita*). For example, one who is beneficial to calves is a *vatsīya* cowherd; likewise, one who is beneficial to horses is an *aśvīya*.

By means of the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*), the vowel *ā* is substituted for the initial vowels [of the following bases], and the suffix *vṛddhi* is applied; thereafter, the suffix *īya* occurs in the sense of "belonging to" (*śeṣe*). For example: *śālīyaḥ*, meaning "born in or belonging to a hall" (*śālāyāṃ bhavaḥ*); *aitikāyanīyāḥ*, meaning "these are the students of Aitikāyana"; likewise *aupagavīyāḥ*, and so on with others as well. Regarding the rule *yad ugavāditaḥ* (Kātantra 2.6.11): the suffix *yat* is applied after words ending in *u* and after the group beginning with *go* (*gavādi*) in the sense of "beneficial to" (*hite*). For example: *kṛkavākavyam*, meaning "milk beneficial to cocks" (*kṛkavākubhyo hitam payaḥ*); *vadhavyaḥ*, meaning "a region beneficial to women" (*vadhūbhyo hito deśaḥ*); *gavyam*, meaning "a forest beneficial to cows" (*gobhyo hitam vanam*); likewise, *haviṣyāḥ taṇḍulāḥ*, meaning "rice grains beneficial for oblation."
The rule of extension to the end of a compound (*tadanta-vidhi*) is intended in cases such as *sugavyam* and *atigavyam*.
Words beginning with *go*, *havis*, *aṣṭakā*, *barhis*, *medhā*, and *sruca* should also be understood accordingly.

When a word denoting a modification signifies its material cause (*prakṛti*), the suffix should be understood in the sense of "beneficial" (*hita*) as previously stated; for example, *aṅgārīyāṇi kāṣṭhāni* ("wood beneficial for charcoal") and *picavyaḥ kārpāsaḥ* ("cotton beneficial for a blanket").

The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). According to Pāṇini 5.1.117, "comparison" (*upamiti*) is the standard of comparison; the suffix *vati* occurs when there is the meaning of a standard of comparison. For example: "he behaves like a king" is *rājavat*;
"his conduct is like that of a Brahmin" is *brāhmaṇavat*; "there is a palace in Pāṭaliputra as in Mathurā" is *mathurāvat*.
He has conducted himself like a king; he is like a king. I see you as if you were a god; you are like a god.
He descends from his seat as if from a mountain; he is like a mountain.
"He gives wealth to Devadatta as to a Brahmin," [meaning] "like a Brahmin.
In this case too, the suffix *vat* must necessarily be understood by others as expressing "worthiness" (*tadarham*).
Even when there is equality in qualities, as in "Devadatta is fat like Devadatta" (*Devadattavat sthūlaḥ*).
Even from one devoid of qualities, as in the case of the blind or the dull-witted;

even when there is equality of substance, as in "Devadatta possesses cows" (*gomān devadattaḥ*) or "like Devadatta," because of the existence [of the quality], there must necessarily be equality of action everywhere.
This is the sense in the state of reality. (Kātantra 2.6.13)

The basis for the application of a word (*pravṛttinimitta*) is an entity (*bhāva*). When an entity is the meaning to be expressed, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are employed: the entity of a white cloth is "whiteness" (*śuklatā*), "the state of being white" (*śuklatvam*). The entity of the quality of whiteness, or the entity of the quality "white," is the universal of the quality "white"—namely, "whiteness" (*śuklatā*), "the state of being white" (*śuklatvam*). "Cowness" (*gotā*), "the state of being a cow" (*gotvam*) is the universal of the cow. Similarly, "cook-ness" (*pācakatvam*), "staff-bearer-ness" (*daṇḍitvam*), "horned-ness" (*viṣāṇitvam*), and "king's-man-ness" (*rājapuruṣatvam*) denote the state of being related to an action and so forth.
The state of being Devadatta, the state of being the moon, and the state of being the sun [are distinguished] by difference of condition (*avasthābheda*).

The state of being space (*ākāśatva*) is [distinguished] by difference of location (*pradeśabheda*); the state of being non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is [distinguished] by difference of relatum (*saṃbandhibheda*). "Nānātva" (manifoldness) is the state of being manifold (*nānā*); and this is what has been proclaimed [as *yaṇ*]. (Pāṇini 2.6.14)

When the abstract state (*bhāva*) is to be expressed, *yaṇ* is prescribed; by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), *tva* and *tal* are also included. Thus: the state of being dull (*jaḍa*) is *jāḍyam*, *jaḍatā*, or *jaḍatvam*.

The state of being a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*) is *brāhmaṇyam*, *brāhmaṇatā*, or *brāhmaṇatvam*. Similarly: *māṇavyam* (the state of being a descendant of Manu), *vāḍavyam* (the state of being a descendant of Vada).

The inclusion of the term *prakīrtita* (well-known) is for the sake of conforming to the observed usage (*lakṣya*); therefore, it is seen even after words other than those denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) or those beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, and even when the action itself [is the meaning]: *jaḍasya karma jāḍyam* (the action of a dull person is dullness), *brāhmaṇasya karma brāhmaṇyam* (the action of a Brāhmaṇa is Brāhmaṇahood).
[The suffixes] *-mantu* and *-vin* are added [after a word ending in *-mat*] in the sense of "this belongs to him" (*tad asyāsti*). (Kātantra 2.6.15)

From a word ending in the nominative case, the suffixes *mantu*, *vantu*, *vin*, *in*, and *it* are applied in the sense of "this belongs to him. For example: because he possesses cows (*gāvaḥ*), he is called *gomān*; likewise, *āyuṣmān*, *lakṣmīvān*, *kiṃvān*, *vidyutvān*, *payasvān*, *bhāsvān*, *karmavān*, *vṛkṣavān*, *mālāvān*, *tejasvī*, *payasvī*, *daṇḍī*, *māyī*, and *māyāvī*.
The word *iti* is used for the sake of indicating the intended meaning [of the examples].
[These suffixes are also applied] in the senses of abundance, censure, praise, constant connection, and excellence.
When there is a desire to express existence through association, these suffixes *mant* and so forth occur.

Likewise, [the suffix *vat* occurs] after a word ending in *m*, *p*, or *n*; after a word ending in *dh*; after a word ending in *ś* or *ṣ* (provided it does not end in *i* or *u*); after a word having *a* as its penultimate letter; and likewise after a word ending in *v*. 1–2.
From *māyā* [the suffix] *śīrṣa*, from *svarūpa* [the suffix] *ca*, from *vrīhi* [the suffix] *artha*, and from *svarūpa* [the suffix] *taḥ*;
just as in *vrīhiḥ* and *śālī*, [the suffix] *in* occurs after a word with more than one vowel. 3.
From *māyā*, *asmedha*, and *sraj*, the suffix *vin* may optionally occur due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "vibhāṣayā."
All these [suffixes] have been prescribed; however, the suffix *man* is desired after the remaining [bases].
(4) Indeed, the suffix *in* occurs only after words denoting diseases that affect living beings and are expressed as duals or in the negative form;
for example, one might be called *kaṭakavalayī* ("possessing bracelets and bangles") or *kuṣṭhī* ("afflicted with leprosy"), just like one who has a palate like a crow's (*kākatālukī*). (5)
But from its own constituent parts (*svāṅga*), it may occur according to usage, as in "possessing breasts and hair.

Who would [deny] that these [suffixes] always occur in their own sense? For example, one who has wind is called *vātakī*. (6) Similarly, there would be such a form as *atīsārakī*, and likewise *piśācakī* is recorded.
The word *piśāca* is used to denote one who is demented by dejection. (7) Furthermore, when age is implied, the suffix *-in* is indeed added to a numeral ending in *-an*;
for example, "the fifth child" refers to one who is five days or five months old. (8)
The suffix *in* alone should be applied after *sukha* and the others, and also after *bāhu*, *ūru*, and *bala*.
Thus, the examples are cited as: *sukhī*, *duḥkhī*, *alīkī*, *karuṇī*, *kṛpaṇī*, *halī*, *tṛprī*, *kṛcchrī*, *pratīpī*, *soḍhī*, *āśrī*, and *asrī*. 9.
*Bāhubalin*, *ūrubalin*, and likewise *sarvādin* (always eating everything) should be understood as ending in *-in*; *sarvabījī* and *sarvakeśī* are cited [as examples]. 10.
After words ending in *dharma*, *śīla*, or *varṇa*, the suffix *-in* alone is intended [to apply].

One who possesses the nature of a Brahmin, is virtuous in conduct, and is of Brahminical appearance is thus designated as a *brahmavarṇin*. (11) However, in the case of birth (*jāti*), the suffix *in* is applied after the words *hasta*, *danta*, and *kara*;
thus, one should know the terms *hastī*, *dantī*, and *karī*. After the word *varṇa*, the suffix *in* is applied when referring to a religious student (*brahmacārin*). (12)
On account of practicing celibacy (*brahmacaryā*), those of the [upper] classes may be Brāhmaṇas;
yet, even without celibacy, they may be Brāhmaṇas by virtue of their birth.
From the *puṣkara*, *utpala*, and *padma* [lotuses], and from the *naḍa*, *visatā*, and *māla* [reeds]. 13.
From *kapittha*, *kumuda*, *mṛṇāla*, *kardama*, and *payaḥ*;
from *śālūka* and *karīṣa*; and from *hiraṇya* when it refers to a place where [something] has grown—the suffix *-in-* is indeed intended, as in the example *puṣkariṇī*. 14–15.

After words ending in *man*, *mant*, and *vat*, only the suffix *ini* is desired when they function as proper names (*saṃjñā*), and this is for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) to prevent [other suffixes from applying], as in *dāminī* and *sominī*. Regarding the scope of *ini*, it should be stated that after a vowel (*ik*), it applies optionally, because of the aforementioned restrictive rules.

The suffix *ka* may optionally be used in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in "daṇḍika" for "daṇḍin. (17) The suffix *in* is optionally prescribed after the words *aṣṭakā*, *vīṇā*, *mekhalā*, *vaḍavā*, *śikhā*, *balākā*, and *patākā* when they function merely as proper names (*saṃjñāmātre*). (18)

Or from armor made of leather or hide, [there arise] the uprooting, the enthusiasm, the force, the unrestrained [state], the root, the leaf, the nest, the ascent, the exertion, the restraint, the exercise, and the descent. 19.
[Of these: vyāyāmāvarohāṇām.
Why would the wise not accept that these [suffixes] always have their own meaning? 20.
The same applies to others as well.
[The suffixes] *ḍa* and *mau* are used for the completion of a number (Kāt_2.6.16).

The suffixes *ḍa* and *mau* occur in the sense of completing a number (*pūraṇa*). Due to the governing rule of fixed application (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), the suffix *ma* occurs after a numeral that does not begin with *vā* (i.e., *viṃśati*, etc. and ends in *n*; otherwise, the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the remaining [numerals]. Examples: "That which completes eleven" is *ekādaśaḥ* (masculine/neuter) or *ekādaśī* (feminine). Likewise, *pañcamaḥ* (masculine/neuter) or *pañcamī* (feminine). Why "in the sense of completing a number"? Consider: "A jar that completes five or eleven water-carrying pots (*uṣṭrikā*). [The suffix] *tīya* occurs after the numeral two: *dvitīyaḥ*. (Kātantra 2.6.17)
The suffix *tīya* occurs after the word *dvi* in the sense of ordinal completion; [thus] the completer of two is *dvitīya*.

After *tri*, there is also the substitution of *tṛ*; [thus] the suffix *tīya* occurs after *tri* in the sense of ordinal completion, and there is the substitution of *tr* for it; the completer of three is *tṛtīya*.
*Antas tho ḍe rṣoḥ*. (Kāt. 2.6.19) When followed by *ḍe*, *th* occurs in place of *ra* and *ṣ*; for example, *caturṇām pūraṇaḥ* becomes *caturthaḥ*, and likewise *ṣaṣṭhaḥ*.
Because these are treated as augments (*āgama*), the *visarga* and the change to *ḍ* would not otherwise occur.
From *katipaya* and *kata*. Kāt_2.6.20: After *katipaya* and *kata*, the suffix *tha* occurs in the sense of a ordinal number; thus, *katipayathaḥ* and *katithaḥ*.
After *viṃśati* and other such words, the suffix *tamaṭ* [occurs]. Kāt_2.6.21.
The suffix *tamaṅ* occurs in the sense of completing a number such as twenty and so forth: the completer of twenty is *viṃśatitamaḥ*, *viṃśatitamī*; *triṃśattamaḥ*, *triṃśattamī*.
Because of the mention of "always" (*nityam*) in the subsequent rule, an option is obtained for [numbers] like twenty: *viṃśaḥ*, *triṃśaḥ*.
For numbers beginning with one hundred, however, it is always [the case]. (Kātantra 2.6.22)

The suffix *tamaṅ* is invariably applied after [numerals] beginning with *śata* in the sense of ordinal completion: *ekaśatatamaḥ*, *ekasahasratamaḥ*, *ekakoṭitamaḥ*. *Kātantra 2.6.23*: "After [numerals] beginning with *ṣaṣṭi*, provided they are not followed by another numeral. Here, *tatpara* means "following that"; the meaning is "after a numeral followed by another numeral. After [numerals] beginning with *ṣaṣṭi*, provided they are not followed by another numeral, the suffix *tamaṅ* is invariably applied in the sense of ordinal completion: *ṣaṣṭitamaḥ*, *saptatitamaḥ*, *aśītitamaḥ*, *navatitamaḥ*.
Why [is it said] "not having that as its primary referent"? [Examples are: *ekaṣaṣṭaḥ*, *ekasaptataḥ*.

Hereafter, those which will be taught are to be understood as case-designations (*vibhakti-saṃjñā*); they are traditionally held to follow after words other than *dvi* and so forth, as well as after pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and *bahu*. (Kātantra 2.6.24)

Because it is heard [in the grammatical tradition], the designation *vibhakti* applies only with respect to the functions of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*); therefore, in cases such as *yadā* or *kadā*, there is no lengthening before a voiced consonant.
Here, the word *bahu* denotes a number due to its association with pronouns.
In this context, *idam* becomes *ih*. (Kāt. 2.6.25)
In these [words] designated as case-endings (*vibhakti*), this substitution of *ikāra* occurs: *itaḥ*, *iha*, *idānīm*, *adhunā*.
Regarding *rathoḥ etet*: after *rat* and *thaḥ*, the forms *eta* and *it* respectively take the place of *idam*, as in *etarhi* and *ittham*.
But in those [cases], this [substitution] becomes *a*.
(Kāt_2.6.27) In those [suffixes] beginning with *t*, this [suffix] attains the state of being *a*; therefore, [the rule applies] here.
Why say "in those beginning with *t*"? [Consider: *etathā*.

*Kāt_2,6.28*: The suffix *tas* optionally occurs after a word ending in the fifth case that is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), provided it is not *dvi* or similar, or is *bahu*. For example: *sarvasmāt* → *sarvataḥ*; *tasmāt* → *tataḥ*; *bahubhyaḥ* → *bahutaḥ*.
Why does it say "not *dvi* or similar"? [Because] from *dvābhyām*, one says *bhavataḥ*.

Based on the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) that [the suffix] *tas* is used after words such as *ugan* and *vādita* due to their specific application, it should be stated that *tas* occurs even after non-pronouns (*asarvanāman*) when expressing a mere limit (*avadhi*), as in *grāmāt* and *grāmataḥ*.
However, it does not occur after the words *hā* and *gṛha* when expressing a limit, as in *yuṣmad dhīyate*, *sārthāddhīnaḥ*, and *parvatād avarohati*.
[The suffix] *tra* is used for the seventh case (*saptamī*). (Kātantra 2.6.29)

The suffix *tra* is optionally added to a word ending in the locative case that is a pronoun (except for *dvi* and others) or the word *bahu*: from *sarvasmin*, *sarvatra*; from *bahuṣu*, *bahutra*. Why "except for *dvi* and others"? [Because it does not apply to] *dvayoḥ*, *tvayi*, or *mayi*.

It should be stated that the suffix *tas* is added after words such as *ādi*: from *ādau*, *āditaḥ*; from *madhye*, *madhyataḥ*; from *ante*, *antataḥ*; from *pṛṣṭhe*, *pṛṣṭhataḥ*; from *mukhe*, *mukhataḥ*; from *pārśve*, *pārśvataḥ*.
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class).
[The rule] *idamo haḥ* (Kātantra 2.6.30) states that the suffix *ha* optionally occurs after the word *idam* when it ends in the locative case; thus, from *asmin*, we have *iha*.
From *kim*: After the word *kim* ending in the locative case, *ha* optionally occurs; as in *kasmin* or *kuha*. Others say this applies only in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
At *kva* and *ca*. [Kāt. 2.6.32] After the word *kim* ending in the locative case, *ad* is substituted, and *kva* is the substitute; thus, in *kasmin*, it becomes *kva*.
*tahoḥ kuḥ*. [Kāt. 2.6.33] After *tah* and *hoḥ*, *ku* is substituted.
When *takāra* and *hakāra* follow, what becomes of *kim*? It becomes *ku*: *kutaḥ*, *kuha*. Regarding the suffix *dā*:

after *kim*, *sarva*, *yad*, and *eka-anya* only, when expressing time. (Kāt_2.6.34) After these words used in the sense of time and ending in the locative case, the suffix *dā* is applied: in what time? *kadā*; likewise, *sarvadā*, *yadā*, *ekadā*, *anyadā*.

What is meant by "time"? It refers to every location. From the pronoun *idam* (this), when denoting time, the suffixes *rhi*, *adhunā*, and *dānīm* are applied. According to Pāṇini 5.3.17, these suffixes—*rhi*, *adhunā*, and *dānīm*—occur after the locative case of *idam* when it signifies time; thus: *etasmin kāle* = *etarhi*, *adhunā*, and *idānīm*.
The suffixes *dā* and *dānīm* are prescribed after the word *tad* when it denotes time.
(Kātantra 2.6.36) When *tad* refers to time and ends in the locative case, the suffixes *dā* and *dānīm* are prescribed; thus: *tasmin kāle*, *tadā*, and *tadānīm*.
The words beginning with *sadyas* are formed as irregular derivatives (*nipātyante*). (Kātantra 2.6.37)
On the same day: *sadyas*; here, the substitution of *sa* for *samāna* and the suffix *dyas* are subsequent rules (*paravidhi*).
On another day: *paredyavi*; here, *edyavi* is substituted for the initial *para*. On this day: *adya*; here, the substitution of *ad* for *idam* and the suffix *dya* are subsequent rules.
The suffixes *para* and *udāra* are substituted for *parut* and *parāri*, respectively, when referring to previous years.
For this year, the suffix *sama* is added to *idam* with the replacement of its final vowel by *siṇ*.
For the previous day, the suffix *edyus* is added to *pūrva* and similar words; thus, one says *pūrvedyuḥ*, and likewise *aparedyuḥ*.

[The suffix *rhi* is optionally applied after the following words when they do not refer to the immediate past (*anadyatana*): *adharedyus*, *uttaredyus*, *anyedyus*, *anyataredyus*, *itaredyus*, *ubhayedyus*, and *ubhayād dyus*.

[The suffix *dā* is applied] after *kim*, *anyat*, *yat*, and *tat*, provided they do not refer to the immediate past: *karhi* (at what time?), *kadā*, *anyarhi*, *anyadā*, *yarhi*, *yadā*, *tarhi*, *tadā*; this applies even when referring to the immediate past.
In the same manner, *purastāt* and the others are also to be understood accordingly.

Regarding the suffix *thā* when expressing a manner (*prakāra*): Pāṇini 5.3.23 states that the suffix *thā* occurs after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) other than *dvi* and so forth, when expressing a manner. A manner is that which differentiates a general category. [Examples are: *sarveṇa prakāreṇa* (in every way) becomes *sarvathā*; likewise, *yathā* and *tathā*.
It should be understood that this suffix is applied from all case endings according to the requirements of the sentence meaning.

Or [the suffix] *thā* may be used in the plural; by that, in the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*) of a number, the suffix *dhā* is applied: *ekadhā*, *dvidhā*, *tridhā*, *caturdhā*, *pañcadhā*, *saptadhā*.
After the words *dvi* and *tri*, the suffixes *dhamuṇ* and *edhā* are also applied: *dvaidham*, *dvedhā*; *traidham*, *tredhā*.
After the word *eka*, the suffix *dhyamuṇ* is optionally applied: *aikadhyam*, *ekadhā*.

The suffix *thamu* should be applied after the words *idam* and *kim*. (Kāt_2.6.39) After *idam* and *kim*, when expressing a manner, the suffix *thamu* is applied: "in this manner" is *ittham*; "by what manner? is *katham*.
And the suffixes *tamap* and others [are applied] after a verb. (Kāt_2.6.40)

The suffixes *tama* and so forth are prescribed as irregular forms (*nipātana*) after nouns and verbs; a verb is that in which action is predominant. Thus: *āḍhyataraḥ*, *āḍhyatamaḥ*—these express one who is preeminent among the wealthy, because the scope of an irregular prescription is restricted to what is intended. Likewise: *pacatitarām*, *pacatitamām*; *kintarām*, *kintamām*; *pūrvāhṇetarām*, *pūrvāhṇetamām*; *uccaistarām*, *uccaistamām*. The suffixes *tarām* and *tamām* follow verbs, the interrogative pronoun *kim*, monosyllabic words ending in *ī*, and indeclinables, provided they function to express the excellence of an action or a quality.
Similarly, the suffixes *iṣṭha* and *īyas* optionally follow a word expressing a quality (*guṇa*).
*paṭiṣṭhaḥ*, *paṭīyān*, *paṭutaraḥ*, *paṭutamaḥ*. The suffix *rūpa* is used in the sense of excellence (*prakarṣe*). Examples:
*prakṛṣṭaṃ pacati* (he cooks excellently) becomes *pacatirūpam*; *prakṛṣṭo vaiyākaraṇaḥ* (an excellent grammarian) becomes *vaiyākaraṇarūpaḥ*.
The suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are used in the sense of "slightly incomplete.

Examples: *paṭukalpaḥ* (almost clever), *paṭudeśyaḥ* (nearly clever), *paṭudeśīyaḥ* (somewhat clever); *pacatikalpam* (cooking poorly), *pacatideśyam*, *pacatideśīyam*. The suffix *pāśa* is added to a noun itself when it denotes contemptible conduct.
A contemptible grammarian is called a *vaiyākaraṇapāśaḥ*.
The suffix *taṭ* is applied to express a former state:
one who was formerly wealthy is called an *āḍhyacaraḥ* (masculine) or *āḍhyacarī* (feminine).
The suffix *rūpya* (and also *cara*) is added after a word ending in the sixth case when something previously existing is to be expressed. For example:
*devadattasya bhūtapūrvo gauḥ* ("Devadatta’s former cow") becomes *devadattarūpyaḥ* or *devadattacaraḥ*.
When a blessing is implied, the suffix *śas* is optionally added after a word denoting an agent (*kāraka*) that signifies "much" or "little."
"Give much," "give many times," "give thus abundantly," "give abundantly many times," "give in small measure," "give in little measure.
[The suffix -śas is used] with numerals and words meaning "one" when expressing repetition (*vīpsā*).
"Give two by two," "give in twos"; likewise, "give in *kārṣāpaṇas*," "in *kuḍavas*," "in *pādas*."
The suffix *vat* is added after words meaning "how many" (*kati*) and "group" (*gaṇa*).
[Examples: *katiśaḥ*, *gaṇaśaḥ*, *tāvacchaḥ*.
After a numeral denoting a number of times, the suffix *kṛtvas* is added.
He eats five times: *pañcakṛtvaḥ*, *katikṛtvaḥ*, *gaṇakṛtvaḥ*, *tāvatkṛtvaḥ*; he eats a hundred times: *śatakṛtvaḥ*, or *śataṃ vārān bhuṅkte*, or *śataṃ vārāṇāṃ bhuṅkte*.
After the word *bahu* (many), when there is no remoteness [of time], the suffix *dhā* is also applied:
*bahūn vārān bhuṅkte*, *bahudhā divasasya*, or *bahukṛtvaḥ*.
The suffix *suc* is added after the words *dvi*, *tri*, and *catur*. [Examples:
he eats twice, *dvir bhuṅkte*; he eats thrice, *trir bhuṅkte*; he eats four times, *catur bhuṅkte*.
[The suffix] *mayaṭ* is added when the context concerns the material from which something is made.

When *mayaṭ* is used for food or clothing, it does not exclude *aṇ* when applied to a modification or a part of the material substance. For example: *annaprastutaṃ*, *annamayaṃ*, and likewise *yavāgūmayī*. [Examples of modifications: *aśmamayaṃ*, *bhasmamayaṃ*, *suvarṇamayaṃ*.
However, regarding food and clothing, [examples include] *maudgaḥ sūpaḥ* (bean soup) and *kārpāsam ācchādanaṃ* (cotton garment); here, *mayaṭ* does not exclude *aṇ*.
[The suffix *śas* is applied] always after a word consisting of a single vowel.
[The suffix *mayaṭ* is applied] to denote that which consists of speech (*vāṅmaya*), that which consists of skin (*tvaṅmaya*), or that which consists of clay (*mṛnmaya*).

When expressing the transformation of something into what it was not previously, the suffix *cvi* is applied after a word denoting the material undergoing change, provided that the verbs *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as* follow.
He makes what is not white white; he whitens it.
That which was not white becomes white; it whitens; it may become white.
[The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied] after the words *aru*, *manas*, *cakṣus*, *cetas*, *rahas*, and *rajas*.

This rule applies only after [stems ending in] *sa* that have been elided, because a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) has its scope restricted to what is desired; for example: *anaruḥ aruḥ karoti* (one who was not wounded makes himself wounded), *arūkaroti*, and so forth.
Regarding the senses of "complete pervasion" (*abhivyāpti*) and "becoming" (*saṃpatti*), the suffix *sāti* is optionally used:
*varṣāsu lavaṇam udakam saṃpadyate* (in the rainy season, salt becomes water), *udakasāt saṃpadyate*, *udakasāt karoti*, *udakasāt bhavati*, *udakasāt syāt*.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case when it means "to come under the control of" (*āyatta*) its owner.
For example: *rājāyattaṃ karoti*, *rājasātkaroti*, *rājasādbhavati*, *rājasātsyāt*, *rājasātsaṃpadyate*.
Furthermore, the suffix *tra* is also applied in the sense of "that which is to be given."

One performs an offering for the god (*devāya deyaṃ karoti*), one acts toward the god (*devatrā karoti*), one becomes [the god] (*devatrā bhavati*), one may be [the god] (*devatrā syāt*), or one attains the state of being the god (*devatrā saṃpadyate*); other cases are likewise treated.
After an unmanifested imitation sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) consisting of more than one vowel, provided it is not followed by *iti*, the suffix *ḍāc* is added:
*paṭat paṭat karoti* (he makes the sound "paṭat"), *paṭapaṭākaroti*, *paṭapaṭābhavati*, *paṭapaṭāsaṃpadyate*, *paṭapaṭāsyāt*.
From the words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *śamba*, and *bīja* [as first members], when combined with the verb *kṛ* in the sense of agriculture, [the suffix *aṅ* is applied]:
*dvitīyākaroti*, *tṛtīyākaroti*, *śambākaroti*, *bījākaroti*.
[This applies] after a numeral or a word expressing quality (*guṇa*).
He makes the field twofold; he makes the field threefold.
"Samayā" means for the sake of passing time; thus, "samayākaroti."
With *sapatra* and *niṣpatra*, [the suffix *ṇic* is used] in the sense of causing extreme pain:
*sapatrākaroti* and *niṣpatrākaroti* [meaning] he pierces a deer through and through.
With *niṣkula*, [it is used] in the sense of eviscerating.
He husks the pomegranate.
With *priya* and *sukha*, [the suffix *kṛt* is used] in the sense of favoring:
he makes [him] dear (*priyākaroti*), he makes [him] happy (*sukhākaroti*).
In opposition to suffering (*duḥkha*): "it causes suffering" (*duḥkhākaroti*). In relation to a stake (*śūla*): "it cooks" (*pāka*).
He cooks meat on a spit; he impales it on a spit. Regarding "satyāt" as meaning "not an oath":
he verifies the merchant's goods by means of truth.
In the case of *vapana* (shaving), [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *madrabhadra*.
One says *madrākaroti*, *bhadrākaroti*. Alternatively, words such as *rājan* ending in a compound possess the property of not having a final vowel *a* (*adantatā*). (Kāśikāvṛtti 2.6.41)

Alternatively, words such as *rājan* and others occurring at the end of a compound are irregularly treated (*nipātana*) as not ending in *-t*; or the analysis may be: "those for which the suffix *ap* [forming the feminine] ends in *-a*. Since even a constituent part of a constituent is a constituent of the compound itself, by that [rule], *uparājam*, *adhyātmam* [are formed]; from an *avyayībhāva* compound, the case endings take the substitute *am*. *Dvipurī*, *tripurī*: because [the compounds] are *dvigu*s beginning with *nadī*, the suffix *ī* is applied. *Sraktvacinī*: the suffix *in* is applied according to the rule "after a *dvandva*, a word denoting a disease, or a word expressing censure" (*dvandvaninditarogebhyaḥ*). Other examples are to be understood in the same way.
Having prostrated before the lotus feet of Rudra, Hari, Bhavānī, Vāṇī, and Gaṇeśa,
Ratneśvaracakravartin composes this work.
For the benefit of those studying the usage of *rājan* and other such words:
*rājann ahan sakhi*.

(1) The rule previously stated will now be explained specifically for the *tatpuruṣa* compound; the meaning is that these words—*rājan* and others—occur as final members in a *tatpuruṣa*, and by virtue of belonging to the *rājan*-group, they take the form ending in *-an*. Examples: *mahārājaḥ*, *paramāhaḥ*, *dvyahaḥ*, *vibudhasakhaḥ*.

What is the purpose of the term *tatpuruṣa* [in this rule]? [Examples where it does not apply: *śobhanarājā magadhaḥ* (the Magadhan king is excellent), *dīrghāho nidāghaḥ* (the summer is long), *vāyusakhā rājā* (the king is a friend of the wind). *gaur ataddhitābhidheye*: In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the word *go-* becomes *gava-* when it is not denoting a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Excluding cases where a *taddhita* suffix is to be applied, *go-* becomes *rājādi* (i.e., *gava-*) in a *tatpuruṣa*: *rājagavaḥ*, *paramagavaḥ*.
Why is it said "not denoting a secondary derivative (taddhita)"? [Consider] *pañcaguḥ* ("one who has five cows"), as opposed to *citraguḥ* ("one who has brindled cows").

The word *uraḥ* is for the sake of expressing the primary object. 3. The word *uraḥ*, when preceded by *rājā* and others, expresses the primary object; for example, *aśvorasam* ("the preeminent among horses") and *hastyurasam* ("the preeminent among elephants"). The meaning is: "the foremost among horses" and "the foremost among elephants."
What is meant by "for the sake of the primary meaning"? For example, *aśvoraḥ*, which means "the chest of horses.

[The rule] *anas-aśman-ayas-saras-jāti-saṃjñayoḥ* [states]: these four, beginning with *rāja*, occur when referring to a genus (*jāti*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*). When it is a genus, as in *upagatam anaḥ* ("a cart that has arrived"), it becomes *upānasam*; this refers to the genus.
Mahānasa is a proper name (saṃjñā).
Amṛtāśman is a genus (jāti).
Kṛśāśman is a proper name (saṃjñā).
Iron ball: birth.
Copper: perception.
Frog-pool: birth.
*jalasarasam* is an illustration of *saṃjñā*.
Why [is it said] "of these two"? [To show that it does not apply] in cases such as *bṛhadana*, etc.
[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *grāma* and *kuṭa* when followed by *takṣan*. 5.
From these two [prefixes], a carpenter becomes a king or the like: *grāmatakṣaḥ* (village carpenter), *kauṭatakṣaḥ* (secret carpenter).
Why "from these two"? [To show that] *rājatakṣā* (king-carpenter) is not included. After the root *at*, [the suffix *kan* is applied] when *śvan* follows. 6.
*Atiśvaḥ* as a king and so forth means "exceedingly swift"; *atiśvo varāhaḥ* means "swift," that is, possessing great speed.
*Atiśvaḥ sevakaḥ* means "a devoted servant," that is, one who is well-attached to his master.
*Atiśvī sevā* means "lowly service," that is, inferior service.

"From an upamāna [compound], when it does not refer to a living being. 7. When there is an upamāna compound whose object is a non-living being, that [first member] becomes *rājādi* (belonging to the *rājan* class): *ākarṣaḥ śveva* → *ākarṣaśvaḥ* ("a gambling-stake like a dog"); *phalakaḥ śveva* → *phalakaśvaḥ* ("a wooden board like a dog").

What is the purpose of the restriction "not pertaining to a living being" (*aprāṇini*)? [Consider: *vyāghraḥ śveva* (a tiger like a dog), resulting in *vyāghraśvaḥ*. And after [the words] *mṛga*, *pūrva*, *uttara*, and these [others], the word *sakthi* becomes a member of the *rājādi* group when preceded by a standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus: *mṛgasaktham*, *pūrvasaktham*, *uttarasaktham*, and *phalakasaktham*.
In a *dvigu* compound, when it does not have the sense of a *taddhita* suffix, the word *nau-* [becomes] *rājādi*.

9. Excluding the sense of a *taddhita* suffix, when it occurs as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*) or in a collective (*samāhāra*), the *nau-* belonging to a *dvigu* becomes *rājādi*: *dvināvaṃ dhanaṃ*, *pañcanāvaṃ dhanaṃ*.
Why "excluding the sense of a *taddhita* suffix"? [Consider: *pañcanauḥ*.
Why say "of a *dvigu*"? [Consider] *paramanauḥ*.
And [the rule applies] after *ardha*: 10.
A word beginning with *nau*, such as *rājan*, follows even after the word *ardha*; [thus] *ardhanāvam*.
Because the gender of a word is based on common usage (*lokāśrayatva*), the neuter gender alone [applies] here.
Alternatively, *khārī* [is used]. 11.

After the word *ardha*, when it does not have the sense of a *taddhita* suffix, the *khārī* following a *dvigu* compound optionally belongs to the *rājādi* group; thus, one says either *ardhakhāram* or *ardhakhārī*. Due to the force of the specific rule [of the *rājādi* list], there is no feminine gender.

*dvikhāradhana*, *dvikhārī*: because the feminine suffix of a *dvigu* compound is elided when it does not have the sense of a secondary derivative (*ataddhitārthe*), there is no exclusion [of the feminine form]. *pañcabhiḥ khārībhiḥ krītaḥ* (bought for five *khārīs*) results in *pañcakhāraḥ*. *dvitribhyām añjaliḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.106): the word *añjali* following these two [words, *dvi* and *tri*,] optionally belongs to the *rājādi* group. Thus, *dvyañjalam* or *dvyañjali*, *tryañjalam* or *tryañjali*; *dvyañjalapriyaḥ* or *dvyañjalipriyaḥ*, *tryañjalapriyaḥ* or *tryañjalipriyaḥ*.
Others do not desire [the suffix] when the subsequent member expresses a meaning other than a secondary derivative (*ataddhitārtha*).
Why say "when it is a *dvigu* compound expressing a meaning other than a secondary derivative"? [Consider: *dvyañjaliḥ*, *tryañjaliḥ*.
From a country name, O Brahmin. 13.

After a word denoting a country (*janapada*), the suffix *brahman* occurs before [the word] *rājan* and so forth; for example, *avantibrahmā*, meaning "a Brahmin among the Avantis. Or it does not occur, because of the mention of the alternative (*vā*) in the subsequent rule. [The suffix *brahman*] is optionally used after the words *ku-* and *mahat*: 14.

With these two [prefixes], O Brahmin, [the word] *brahman* becomes *rājādi* (belonging to the *rājan* class), or it denotes a contemptible Brahmin: *kubrahmaḥ*, *kubrahmā*, *mahābrahmaḥ*, *mahābrahmā*.
Why "with these two"? [To exclude cases such as: *paramabrahmā*. When femininity is possible among those mentioned, they should be regarded as belonging to the *nadādi* group. 15.

If these words ending in the suffix *at* denote a feminine, they should be regarded as belonging to the *nadādi* group; that is to say, they take the suffix *ī*. For example: *atikrāntā rājānam* (one who has surpassed the king) becomes *atirājī*, and so forth.
Why is the word "possible" (*saṃbhava*) used? [To exclude cases where it is not possible, such as] *ardhanāvam* (half a boat) and *ardhakhāram* (half a khāra measure).
[The rule continues: *aṅguli* [takes the suffix *ī*] after a numeral or an indeclinable. 16.

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has a numeral or an indeclinable as its first member. A word beginning with a numeral or an indeclinable, such as *aṅguli*, belongs to the *rājādi* group. The aggregate of two fingers is *dvyaṅgulam*. That wood whose measure is two fingers is *dvyaṅgulaṃ dāru*.

This is a *dvigu* compound when the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning is to be expressed; therefore, the suffixes *dvayasaC*, *daghnaC*, and *mātraC* prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.2.37] for denoting measure do not occur, because the meaning has already been expressed [by the compound], just as in: "that which has a finger as its measure" (*aṅguliḥ pramāṇam asya*), resulting in *aṅgulidvayasam*, *aṅgulidaghnam*, or *aṅgulimātram*.

[The suffix] *aC* is applied after *avyaya*, *ati*, and *niraṅgula*. Furthermore, the word *rātri* becomes [a member of the] *rājādi* group when following *ahan*, *sarva*, a word denoting a part (*ekadeśa*), a numeral (*saṃkhyāta*), *puṇya*, *varṣa*, *dīrgha*, and so forth. (17) After these—namely, numerals, indeclinables (*avyaya*), and the rest—the word *rātri* belongs to the *rājādi* class; for example: *ahorātraḥ*, *sarvarātraḥ*.

*Pūrvarātraḥ* (the first part of the night) and *apararātraḥ* (the latter part of the night) form a *karmadhāraya* compound because the words *pūrva* and so on denote a single part when they refer to a portion [of a whole]. In other cases, *pūrvarātriḥ* means "a night that has passed. Examples include *saṃkhyātarātraḥ*, *puṇyarātraḥ*, *varṣārātraḥ*, and *dīrgharātraḥ*.
Furthermore, compounds beginning with numerals or indeclinables (*avyaya*) are also formed: *dvirātram* (two nights) and *trirātram* (three nights).
In these cases, the elision of the *n* of *ahar* is not observed, as in *pūrvāhṇa* and so forth.
Alternatively, after a numeral, there is the form *saṃkhyātāhnaḥ* or *saṃkhyātāhaḥ*.
In a collective *dvigu* compound, there is elision of the *n*: *dvyahaḥ*, *tryahaḥ*.
The rule previously stated applies only to the *tatpuruṣa* compound. 18.

It should be understood that the rule beginning with "rājā," "ahan," and "sakhi" applies only when [the word] becomes a *rājādi* (a member of the *rājādi* group) within a *tatpuruṣa* compound; therefore, it does not apply in *bahuvrīhi* compounds and the like. For example: *indraḥ sakhy asya* → *indrasakhaḥ*;
*upasa-khi*, *rājāha-sakhāyaḥ*, and so forth.
*Panthyapprah*. 19. These words, beginning with *rājan*, occur only when they are members of a compound: for example, "that which is both thick and a path" is *sthūlapathaḥ*;
"a lake where the waters are pure" is *vimalāpaṃ saraḥ*; and "the forehead is like a city" is *lalāṭapūram*.

The word *dhur* [is treated as belonging to the *rājādi* group] except when it is connected with *akṣa*. 20. With the exception of that which is related to *akṣa*, the word *dhur* belongs to the *rājādi* class: *rājadhurā*, *mahādhurā*. Why "except when connected with *akṣa*"? [Because in those cases it does not belong to the *rājādi* class: *akṣadhūḥ*, *dṛḍhadhūr akṣaḥ*.

The word *ṛc* becomes [a neuter] *rājādi* compound when it signifies a whole, as in *ardharcaḥ* (half-verse) and *saptarcaḥ* (seven verses). It also forms a *nañ-bahuvrīhi* and other compounds with words beginning in *bahu* when referring to a student (*māṇavaka*) or a Vedic school (*caraṇa*). 22.

The particle *ca* signifies mere conjunction (*samuccaya*). The word *ṛc*, when preceded by *nañ*, *bahu*, and so forth, becomes a member of the *rājādi* group [and thus takes the suffix *ka*]. This applies to the two senses of "Māṇavaka" and "Caraṇa": *anṛco māṇavakaḥ* ("a Māṇavaka who has no *ṛc*s") and *bahvṛcaś caraṇaḥ* ("the Caraṇa school of the *Bahvṛcas*"). Why specify "to these two"? [Consider: *anṛkkaṃ sāma* ("a Sāman that does not contain *ṛc*s") and *bahvṛkkaṃ sūktam* ("a hymn containing many *ṛc*s"); here the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *śeṣād vā*. [The rule continues: *pratyanvavebhyaḥ sāmalomanī* (Pāṇini 5.4.75).

*Vṛddhi* occurs at the beginning before a suffix with the *ṣaṇ* marker.

Now, the *parasmaipada* endings. [Kāt 3.1.1] Now, the immediately following suffixes beginning with *ti* and ending with *syāmaḥ* bear the technical designation *parasmaipada*. Since it has been stated that "the nine subsequent ones are *ātmanepada*," this precludes [the possibility of more], and thus there are exactly nine case-endings (*vacana*) for all the tenses and moods (*vibhakti*).

They are called *vibhaktis* (case-endings) because they divide the meaning (*arthasya vibhañjanāt*). They are: *ti*, *tas*, *anti*; *si*, *thas*, *tha*; *mi*, *vas*, *mas*. This applies everywhere. These are the instances of the *parasmaipada* (active voice), such as the rule: "The *parasmaipada* occurs for the agent after a root other than those [specified]" (*śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam*, Kāt. 3.2.47). Next, there are nine subsequent ones for the *ātmanepada*. According to Kāt. 3.1.2, the next nine verbal endings are designated as *ātmanepada*; it is understood that these are the "forms" (*padāni*).

*te*, *āte*, *ante*; *se*, *āthe*, *dhve*; *e*, *vahe*, *mahe*—thus it is everywhere.
