The rules concerning the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) include such statements as: "The middle endings are used for the impersonal (*bhāva*) and passive (*karman*) voices" [Kāt. 3.2.40]. There are three of each: first, middle, and last (third, second, and first persons). [Kāt. 3.1.3]

Of the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings, there are three forms each designated as first (*prathama*), middle (*madhyama*), and last (*uttama*) respectively: *ti*, *tas*, *anti* constitute the first; *si*, *thas*, *tha* constitute the middle; and *mi*, *vas*, *mas* constitute the last.
*te*, *āte*, *ante*—this is the first person; *se*, *āthe*, *dhve*—this is the middle person; *e*, *vahe*, *mahe*—this is the last person; thus it is everywhere.

The rules for the application of *saṃjñās* (technical designations) include: "When *nāman* [the first person pronoun] is employed, the first person [is used]; when *yuṣmad* [the second person pronoun], the middle person; when *asmad* [the first person pronoun], the highest person" [Kāt. 3.1.5–7], and so forth. Regarding simultaneous expression: "In the case of simultaneous expression, the highest among the persons [prevails]. [Kāt. 3.1.4] "Simultaneous" (*yugapat*) means at one and the same time. When expressing the time of a single action through simultaneous expression, that which is the highest among the persons [of the three] occurs. For example: *sa ca tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāmaḥ* ("He, you, and I are cooking"), *sa ca tvaṃ cāhaṃ cāpākṣma* ("He, you, and I cooked"), and *sa ca tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pakṣyāmaḥ* ("He, you, and I shall cook").
The mention of "number" (vacana) is not restrictive; thus, one says *sa ca tvaṃ ca pacathaḥ* ("he and you two cook") and *tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāvaḥ* ("you and I cook").

Why specify "simultaneous number"? [To exclude cases like] *sa pacati*, *tvaṃ pakṣyasi*, *aham apākṣam* ("he cooks, you will cook, I cooked"), where the times differ, so that the form *vayam apākṣma* ("we cooked") does not occur.

The inclusion of the word "number" is to prevent it from applying to simultaneous instances such as *sa pacati*, *tvaṃ pacasi*, *ahaṃ pacāmi* ("he cooks, you cook, I cook"), which would otherwise result [in the incorrect application of the plural].
This is a governing rule (*paribhāṣā*) applicable when there is either non-occurrence or an alternative case.

Even when a noun (*nāman*) is employed, the first person [is used]. (Kāt. 3.1.5) Whether a noun is employed or not employed, the first person occurs: *sa pacati* (he cooks), *tau pacataḥ* (the two cook), *te pacanti* (they cook); *sa pacate*, *tau pacete*, *te pacante*. Likewise: *pacyate ghaṭaḥ* (the pot is cooked), *pacyete ghaṭau* (two pots are cooked), *pacyante ghaṭāḥ* (the pots are cooked).
Even when not employed [as a word], [the verb retains its number]: *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*; thus it is everywhere.

Why is the mention of "being employed" (*prayujyamāna*) made? So that [the rule] may apply when [the pronoun] is connected with a verbal root; for example, in *tena devadattena hanyase tvam* ("by that Devadatta you are being struck"), the middle voice (*madhyama*) occurs because of the connection with *yusmad* (the second person).
[The rule states: "In the case of *yusmad*, the middle voice. (Kātantra 3.1.6)
When *yuṣmad* is employed, whether it is actually expressed or not, the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) occurs: *tvaṃ pacasi*, *yuvāṃ pacathaḥ*, *yūyaṃ pacatha*.
Even when it is not expressed: *pacasi*, *pacathaḥ*, *pacatha*; thus it is everywhere. Why is the word "employed" (*prayujyamāna*) mentioned? [To exclude cases such as: *tvayā pacyate odanaḥ*.

The first person [is used] when *asmad* [is present]. (Kāt. 3.1.7) When *asmad* is employed, or even when it is not employed, the first person is used: *ahaṃ pacāmi* (I cook), *āvāṃ pacāvaḥ* (we two cook), *vayaṃ pacāmaḥ* (we cook).
Even when it is not employed: *pacāmi*, *pacāvaḥ*, *pacāmaḥ*; thus it is in all cases.

It must necessarily be that *atvam* becomes *tvam*, *anaham* becomes *aham*, *tvadbhavati*, and *madbhavati*, because the bases *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are secondary (*gauṇa*) [in those forms]; however, the substitutes *tvad* and *mad* rely merely on the word-forms themselves.

In examples such as "Come, I think you will go by chariot" (*ehi manye rathena yāsyasi*) and "Your father has gone" (*yātas te pitā*), the second and first persons (*madhyama* and *uttama*) apply only within their own proper domain.
*adāb dādhau dā*. (Pāṇini 1.4.36) With the exception of *dāp* and *daip*, these two roots *dā* and *dhā* receive the technical designation *dā*. [Examples: *dīyate*, *dhīyate*.

Why say *adāb*? [Counter-examples: *dāyante vrīhayaḥ* ("the rice grains are given"), *nidāyante bhājanāni* ("the vessels are bound"). This letter *p* is mentioned in the list [of exceptions] solely for the purpose of exclusion.

A *dhātu* (verbal root) is that which has action as its being (*kriyābhāva*). According to Pāṇini 3.1.9, any word that brings about or expresses action receives the designation *dhātu*. Examples include: *bhavati*, *atti*, *juhoti*, *dīvyati*, *sunoti*, *tudati*, *ruṇaddhi*, *tanoti*, *krīṇāti*, and *corayati*.

Action (*kriyā*) is so called because it is "being done" (*kriyate*); it is defined as that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and it consists precisely of parts arranged in a temporal sequence of before and after.

How then [is it]? There is; the palace perishes, whitens, joins, or inheres; existence is permanence, non-existence is destruction; whiteness and conjunction are also qualities, and inherence is also a distinct entity. This is true: for here, everything whose arising depends upon a means of accomplishment (sādhana) appears as an action (*kriyā*) because it is established through dependence on that [means]. This is due to the fact that the linguistic usage of "action" and "agent" is based on states of cognition. Thus, it is like [the word] *gati* [being used] for a part of the face, or *vidhi* for a part of a syllogism; likewise, "the sprout is born."
Thus, "birth" (janman) means simply manifestation; or alternatively, it is born—that is, it is specifically perceived—and therefore the sprout possesses the status of an agent. As it has been said:
"Whether already established or not yet established, that which is perceived as something to be accomplished is designated as 'action' (kriyā), because its nature consists of a sequential process."

Examples include *dhātupradeśāḥ* and *dhātoś ca hetau* (Kāt. 3.2.10), and so forth. Regarding the word *kāle*: in Kāt. 3.1.10, the word *kāle* ending in the locative case is repeated; it should be understood as being the governing term (*adhikṛta*). Consequently, [the suffixes prescribed by that rule] would not apply when the action is expressed as a means (*sādhana*) in the past or future tenses, as in: *ayaṃ Devadatto grāmaṃ gataḥ* (this Devadatta has gone to the village) and *gamiṣyati* (he will go); *Rāmo vanaṃ agacchat* (Rāma went to the forest); and *Baliḥ indro bhaviṣyati* (Bali will become Indra).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "present" and so forth? This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*) intended to resolve the doubt as to whether these terms qualify the verbal root (*dhātu*) or the substance (*dravya*). Time is eternal and all-pervading; though it is one and like unto space, it is divided by its connection with actions that have occurred, are occurring, or will occur, and it resides within substances.

"Presently" (*saṃprati*) means the present. According to Pāṇini 3.2.123, the present tense suffix (*vartamānā vibhaktiḥ*) occurs when the time is present, as in *pacati* (he cooks) or *yajate* (he sacrifices).
Time is qualified by its own designation alone.
What is the purpose of [the word] *saṃprati*? [Examples: "The mountains stood," "the mountains will stand.
[The rule applies] with the past tense marker *sma*. (Pāṇini 3.2.12)

When used in conjunction with the word *sma*, a verb form occurs in the present tense even when referring to past time; for example: *dahati sma tripuraṃ Haraḥ* ("Hara was burning Tripura") and *iti sma janaḥ kathayati* ("thus people used to say"). This [present tense] supersedes those [verb forms] whose scope is the past. [This is the rule for] the *parokṣā* (periphrastic past). Kātantra 3.1.13.

In the past tense, the remote (parokṣā) case-ending occurs, as in: "Vāsudeva indeed slew Kaṃsa," or "Devadatta made a mat. And [the endings] characterized by the past instrument (bhūtakaraṇavatyaḥ). According to Pāṇini 3.2.114, those [tenses] which possess the past as their instrument (karaṇa)—that is, by process of elimination, only the perfect (hyastanī), the recent past (adyatanī), and the conditional (kriyātipatti)—are conventionally known as the three case-endings characterized by the past instrument. These three case-endings occur in the past tense: *akarot*, *akārṣīt*, and *akariṣyat*.
The future tense, the benedictive, and the periphrastic future (śvastanī) occur in the sense of the future. (Kāt.

3.1.15) In the future time, three tenses—the future, the benedictive, and the periphrastic future—occur: *kaṭaṃ kariṣyati* ("he will make a mat"), *śakraṃ vadhyāt* ("may he slay Śakra"), *odanaṃ bhoktā* ("he is about to eat rice").
Their specific temporal application is determined by their own technical names. (Kāt. 3.1.16)

The specific distinction of time—such as the present and so forth—should be understood through their respective designations. Thus, in the present time, the [suffix] *vartamānā* occurs; "it exists" (*vartate*) is "present" (*vartamāna*). This refers to an action that has begun but is not yet completed. Examples include: "He does not eat meat," "The boys are playing here," "The mountains stand," "When did you arrive? "I am coming right now," "When will you go? "I am going right now. In the past time that is beyond the range of perception, the term *parokṣā* applies; "beyond the senses" (*akṣāṇāṃ param*) means *parokṣam*, which signifies being outside the domain of the sense organs.

"How did I sleep? What did I murmur? How did I wander while intoxicated?"—due to the distraction of the mind, one denies even what is directly perceived, thinking, "I did not go to Kaliṅga," out of fear of the fault of having gone there.

When something is beyond the senses yet known by the world, because it is capable of being seen by the speaker, there is a non-intention to express that which is beyond the senses; for instance, even though [the breasts] exist, one says "she has no breasts" (*anudarā kanyā*), and likewise, even though [the sacrifice] was performed, one says "he sacrificed" (*ayajat*, *iyāja*) when there is a non-intention to express its actual occurrence.

The *hyastanī* [suffix] applies to the past time of yesterday; "yesterday" (*hyastana*) refers to the time belonging to yesterday. When there is a mixture, such as "we ate either today or yesterday," the *adyatanī* [suffix] is used because of the proximity [of the two times]. The *adyatanī* applies to the immediate past; "today" (*adyatana*) refers to that which belongs to today. Regarding the day: it extends from the proper time of rising until the proper time of retiring, or, according to common worldly usage, it consists of both halves of the night.

"How did I spend the entire night there while awake?"—because the night lacks light, one perceives that time as being like the present; thus, one who has slept for even a moment, knowing it was not the present day, says, "I stayed there. In the expressions "We went to the cowherd villages" (*agamāma ghoṣān*) and "We drank milk" (*apāma payaḥ*), there is simply no intention to express the past of yesterday (*hyastana*). According to the view held here, the *hyastanī* (past tense marker) occurs when the "yesterday" refers to the meaning of the individual word (*padārtha*), and not when it refers to the meaning of the sentence as a whole (*vākyārtha*). Thus, one would say, "Yesterday we went to the cowherd villages" (*hyo 'gamāma ghoṣān*).

Regarding the rule "in the case of the non-occurrence of an action (kriyātipatti), [the conditional suffix is used] in the past time": if he had obtained fuel, he would have cooked rice. When there is a non-occurrence in the future, the future suffix (*bhaviṣyantī*) is indeed used.

In the future time, the future suffix is employed because the future time is specified by the future tense itself; thus, even when one says "he will go today or tomorrow," it supersedes the suffix for the next day (*śvastanī*). When associated with a benediction (*āśis*), the future time takes the benedictory suffix (*āśīḥ*); a benediction is the manifestation of obtaining a desired object not yet arrived. By implication, it has the future as its domain; the specific prescription of the benedictory suffix for the future is for the sake of easy comprehension.

The time that is to come is *śvastana*; and since it is, by implication, something yet to happen (*bhaviṣyan*), its designation as "future" is for the sake of general understanding, as seen from the grammatical derivation of words such as *śvo gamiṣyati* ("he will go tomorrow") and *māsena gami�ṣyati* ("he will go in a month"). Because a term based on its literal meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) is generally applicable, [the rule] might otherwise lead to confusion; therefore, this is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule). And [this is established] from usage. (Kātantra 3.1.17)

"Prayoga" means application (*prayujyate iti prayogaḥ*). From this application, the specific nature of the time limit (*avadhi*) is to be understood; that is to say, when there is a connection with another word, as in "he goes after he has eaten," a future state is implied. However, when there is an intention to express the future (*bhaviṣyantī*), the word *yāvat* is simply not used at all. In examples such as "Study, O boy, before the lightning flashes" (*purā vidyotate vidyut*) or "Make the mat quickly, before you go to the village," the proximity to the present (*vartamānasāmīpya*) is included by that very [usage]. Since the future is understood from the word *purā*, its status as the present may then be [figuratively] attributed to it.

When used in conjunction with *kadā* or *karhi*, the present, future, and periphrastic future (*śvastanī*) tenses occur: *kadā bhuṅkte*, *kadā bhokṣyate*, *kadā bhoktā*; *karhi bhuṅkte*, *karhi bhokṣyate*, *karhi bhoktā*.
The future (*bhaviṣyat*), the remote past (*parokṣā*), and others also occur: *kadā bubhuje*, *kadā bhuktaḥ*, *kadā bhuktavān*.

Likewise, when there is the use of an interrogative pronoun (*kim*) ending in the comparative suffix *-tara* or the superlative suffix *-tama*, and a desire for gain (*lipsā*) is implied—whether in the future tense or in a general sense—the following occurs: "Which among you gives, will give, or is a giver of alms? (*ko bhavatāṃ bhikṣāṃ dadāti dāsyati dātā vā*), or "Which one among you gives, will give, or is a giver of alms? (*kataro bhavatāṃ katamo bhavatāṃ bhikṣāṃ dadāti dāsyati dātā vā*).
Forms prescribed for the past tense are also seen, such as: "Which among you went to Pāṭaliputra? (*ko bhavatāṃ pāṭaliputram agacchat*) or "went" (*agamat*).

Likewise, even when the accomplishment [of the action] is desired, there are such forms as: "He who gives you alms, will give you alms, or has given you alms, goes to, will go to, or has gone to the heavenly world"; and "He who did not give you alms went to the heavenly world. Other examples should be understood in the same way. The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of permission (*anumati*). Permission is the authorization of one who wishes to act; and that [permission] pertains only to the present or the future. When there is permission, the fifth case ending occurs after a verb in the present tense, as in: *evaṃ kuru* ("Do thus"), *kaṭaṃ kuru* ("Make a mat"), *tṛṣṇāṃ chinddhi* ("Cut off craving"), *bhaja kṣamām* ("Cultivate forbearance"), *kuru dayām* ("Practice compassion").

And [the fifth case ending occurs] after a verbal root expressing justification (*samarthanā*) or benediction (*āśis*). (Kātyāyana 3.1.19) Justification is the determination of a thing that cannot be accomplished by others; benediction is the wishing for a desired object. After a verbal root expressing justification or benediction, the fifth case ending occurs. For example: *parvatam apy utpāṭayāni* ("I shall even uproot the mountain"), *samudram api śoṣayāṇi* ("I shall even dry up the ocean"). Someone says, "The ocean cannot be dried up," and he replies, "I shall even dry up the ocean. Thus, he justifies his own conviction.

And in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), as in "May you live," "May you rejoice," or "He might even split a mountain with his head," and "He might even sprinkle a thousand roots"—here the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*), and it is established that the word *api* is employed here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). Now, one might object: "Is not the wishing for what is desired also simply a form of petition (*prārthanā*)? True; however, this statement is intended so that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) should not be superseded by the benedictory case-ending. Furthermore, the seventh case is also used in the sense of injunction and so forth. (Kātantra 3.1.20)

The seventh (saptamī) and fifth (pañcamī) case endings occur after a verbal root when it denotes an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth. An injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely the making known of what was previously unknown: "one should make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuryāt*), or "may you make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ karotu bhavān*). Where there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in refusing [the request], that is an invitation (*nimantraṇa*): "one should eat here" (*iha bhuñjīta*), or "may you eat here" (*iha bhuṅktāṃ bhavān*). Where there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) in refusing, that is a polite request (*āmantraṇa*): "one may sit here" (*ihāsīta*), or "may you sit here" (*ihāstāṃ bhavān*). A solicitation (*adhyeṣaṇa*) is an activity preceded by respect: "one should teach the boy" (*māṇavakam adhyāpayet*), or "may you teach [him]" (*adhyāpayatu bhavān*).

Inquiry (*nirūpaṇā*) is a question: "O sir, what indeed should I study—grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) or Vedic meter (*chandas*)? O sir, what indeed should I study—grammar or Vedic meter? Entreaty (*yācñā*) is a request: "May I receive alms; give me alms.

It is the opinion that the seventh and fifth case endings may also be used for the senses of "command" (*praiṣya*) and "proper time" (*prāptakāla*): "You have been commanded: you should go to the village; go to the village," or "The time has come for you to make a mat: one should make a mat; may your honor make a mat."

How should one perform? One should invite (*nimantrayet*), address (*āmantrayet*), command (*adhīcchet*), inquire (*saṃpṛcchet*), or request (*prārthayet*). This is because those two [suffixes] are prescribed for the injunctive (*vidhi*) and other such forms within the category of verbal activity (*kṛtya*). However, when the sense of the verbal root does not involve something to be performed, then forms such as *vidadhāti* (he performs) are established. In the case of the intensive repetition of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), the second person singular ending is used for all tenses from the fifth [case-ending] onwards. (Kātantra 3.1.21)

The intensive repetition (*samabhihāra*) of an action means either frequency or intensity. When an action is expressed with intensive repetition, the fifth person singular middle ending is used for all tenses of the verb. For example: *lunīhi lunīhi* (cut, cut!)—thus he cuts; *lunītaḥ*, *lunanti*; *lunāsi*, *lunīthaḥ*, *lunītha*; *lunāmi*, *lunīvaḥ*, *lunīmaḥ*. Also: *alunāt*, *laviṣyati*. Likewise: *adhīṣvādhīṣva* (study, study!)—thus he studies; *adhyaita*, *adhyeṣyate*.

Because of the statement "at all times of action," no specific number is understood; thus, there is no subsequent application (*anuprayoga*). This is for the sake of ease, [meaning] that by means of that very root and that same factor of action (*kāraka*) due to proximity. Otherwise, this would be established by the intention that he is so hurried that while instigating others, he himself performs the action—as in: "Mow, mow! You are mowing," or "Study, study! You are studying."

Likewise, "he wanders through the frying pan," "he wanders through the monastery," "he wanders through the sword," and "he wanders through the covering of the vessel"—these are the intended meanings of such expressions as "he wanders.
Regarding the rule *mā-yoge 'dyatanī* (Kātantra 3.1.22):
when used in conjunction with the word *mā*, the *adyatanī* (imperfect) tense occurs after a verbal root; for example, *mā kārṣīt* ("may he not do") and *mā bhavān apākṣīt* ("may you not cook").
"How might it not be? May he not commit that sin"—this is because of the inclusion of the term *niranubandha* (without an indicatory letter).

Some say that [the prohibition] "it shall not apply when used in conjunction with an *anubandha*" means this is an exception (*bādhaka*) to those [rules] whose scope concerns the present and the future.

In connection with *mā sma*, the aorist (*hyastanī*) [is used]. (Kātyāyana Vārttika 3.1.23) When joined with the word *mā sma*, the aorist occurs after a verbal root; because of the word "and" (*ca*), the perfect (*adyatanī*) also occurs: *mā sma karot* and *mā sma kārṣīt*.
Some also desire [the use of the aorist] when the words are separated: *sma mā karot*.
Because of the separate rule, it would not apply when only *mā* is present. [The suffixes] for the present tense are: *ti*, *tas*, *anti*; *si*, *thas*, *tha*; *mi*, *vas*, *mas*. (Pāṇini 3.4.78)

*te*, *āte*, *ante*; *se*, *āthe*, *dhve*; *e*, *vahe*, *mahe*. These verbal endings are designated as "present" (*vartamāna*). The rules governing the present tense (*vartamānapradeśāḥ*) include such statements as "the present is used for what is occurring at this very moment" (*saṃprati vartamānā*) and so forth.
The seventh [person]. *Kāt_3.1.25*: *yāt*, *yātām*, *yus*; *yās*, *yātam*, *yāta*; *yām*, *yāva*, *yāma*. *īta*, *īyātām*, *īran*; *īthās*, *īyāthām*, *īdhvam*; *īya*, *īvahi*, *īmahi*.
These words are designated as the seventh case (saptamī).
The sections concerning the seventh case include such rules as "the seventh case is also used in the sense of injunction and so forth" (vidhyādiṣu saptamī ca, Kāt 3.1.20), and others.
The fifth case (pañcamī) is treated at Kāt 3.1.26.
*tu*, *tam*, *ta*; *āni*, *āva*, *āma*;
*tām*, *ātām*, *antām*; *sva*, *āthām*, *dhvam*; *ai*, *āvahai*, *āmahai*—these suffixes are designated as the fifth (pañcamī).

The fifth case endings (*pañcamī-pradeśāḥ*) are those beginning with *pañcamy anumatau* (Kāt 3.1.18). The past tense (*hyastanī*) [endings] are *di*, *tām*, *an*; *si*, *tam*, *ta*; *am*, *va*, *ma*. (Kāt 3.1.27)

*t*, *ātām*, *anta*; *thās*, *āthām*, *dhvam*; *i*, *vahi*, *mahi*—these verbal endings are designated as *hyastanī*. The rules governing the *hyastanī* include such statements as "the *hyastanī* is used in conjunction with *mā sma*" (Kāt. 3.1.23), and so forth.
In the same way, the *adyatanī* [tense] occurs. [Kāt 3.1.28] It is exactly like this: the *adyatanī* [tense] occurs.
The references to the *adyatanī* include such rules as "the *adyatanī* [is used] in conjunction with *mā*" (Kāt 3.1.22), and so forth.
The *parokṣā* (perfect tense) endings are:
*aṭ*, *atus*, *us*; *thal*, *athus*, *a*; *aṭ*, *va*, *ma*; *e*, *āte*, *ire*; *se*, *āthe*, *dhve*; *e*, *vahe*, *mahe*.
These verbal suffixes are designated as *parokṣā*.
Examples of the application of *parokṣā* include [Kāt 3.1.13]: "The *parokṣā* [is used for the past not witnessed by the speaker]," and so forth.
[Kāt 3.1.30]: "The *śvastanī* [is used for the future]."
*tā*, *tārau*, *tāras*; *tāsi*, *tāsthas*, *tāstha*; *tāsmi*, *tāsvas*, *tāsmas*.
*tā*, *tārau*, *tāras*; *tāse*, *tāsāthe*, *tādhve*; *tāhe*, *tāsvahe*, *tāsmahe*.
These verbal endings are designated as *śvastanī* (the periphrastic future).
The *śvastanī* (periphrastic future) forms include such examples as "bhaviṣyati," "bhaviṣyantī," "āśīḥ-śvastanyau" (the benedictive and the periphrastic future), and so forth.
Regarding the benedictive (*āśīḥ*): according to Kāt.
3.1.31, the endings are *yāt*, *yāstām*, *yāsuḥ*; *yās*, *yāstam*, *yāsta*; *yāsam*, *yāsva*, *yāsma*.
*sīṣṭa*, *sīyāstām*, *sīran*; *sīṣṭhās*, *sīyāsthām*, *sīdhvam*; *sīya*, *sīvahi*, *sīmahi*.
These verbal endings are designated as *āśis* (benedictive).
Applications of the term *āśis* include [rules] such as *āśiṣi ca parasmai* [Kāt. 3.5.22], and so forth.
The suffixes beginning with *ti* that follow a verbal root (*dhātu*) and are combined with *sy-* shall be designated as *bhaviṣyantī*.
[Thus: *syati*, *syatas*, *syanti*; *syasi*, *syathas*, *syatha*; *syāmi*, *syāvas*, *syāmas*.
[In the middle voice: *syate*, *syete*, *syante*; *syase*, *syethe*, *syadhve*; *sye*, *syāvahe*, *syāmahe*.
The *bhaviṣyantī* (future) suffixes are those beginning with *bhaviṣyati*, as well as *bhaviṣyati*, *bhaviṣyantī*, *āśīḥ* (benedictive), and *śvastanya* (periphrastic future), and so forth.

The suffixes beginning with *dy* are the *kriyātipatti* (conditional). According to Kāt. 3.1.33, the suffixes beginning with *dy* that follow a verbal root and are joined with *sy* are designated as *kriyātipatti*. They are: *syat*, *syatām*, *syan*; *syas*, *syatam*, *syata*; *syam*, *syāva*, *syāma*.
*syāt*, *syetām*, *syanta*; *syathās*, *syethām*, *syadhvam*; *sye*, *syāvahi*, *syāmahi*.

The points concerning the conditional mood (*kriyātipatti*) include such rules as "the augment *aṭ* is placed at the beginning of the verbal root in the past tense (*hyastanī*), the present tense (*adyatanī*), and the conditional (*kriyātipatti*)" (Kāt.
3.8.16). These technical terms, established by the ancient masters, are explained here according to their literal meaning.
"Six, beginning with the first, are *sārvadhātuka*. (Kāt.

3.1.34). Of the six case-endings (*vibhakti*), the first—namely the present (*vartamāna*), the seventh (*saptamī*), the fifth (*pañcamī*), and the past (*hyastanī*)—bear the designation *sārvadhātuka*.
Instances of the term *sārvadhātuka* include rules such as "for the roots of the *juhotyādi* class, [the substitution of *guṇa* occurs] before a *sārvadhātuka*" (Kāt. 3.3.8), and so forth.

Thus, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi, the first quarter has been explained and is completed. **The suffix (*pratyaya*) follows.** (Kāt_3.2.1) That by which a meaning is understood is conventionally known as a *pratyaya* (suffix). Just as that from which [the word] is first produced is called the *prakṛti* (base), so too the suffix should be understood as following the base. Examples: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *aśvakaḥ*, *yāvakaḥ*, *khaṭvā*, *aupagavaḥ*, *jugupsate*, *gopāyati*, *kartā*, *kartavyaḥ*.
Since there would otherwise be no restriction, this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) serves as a supplement to the injunction.

*Kāt_3.2.2*: "The suffix *san* follows the roots *gup*, *tij*, and *kit* in their own sense (*svārthe*). Examples: *jugupsate mām* ("he feels aversion toward me"), *titikṣate tapas tāpasaḥ* ("the ascetic endures the penance"), *vicikitsati me manaḥ* ("my mind hesitates"), *cikitsaty āturam vaidyaḥ* ("the physician treats the patient"), *ripuṃ cikitsati* ("he treats the enemy"), *cikitsyāni kṣetre tṛṇāni* ("the weeds in the field must be treated [removed]").
The suffix *saN* is prescribed after the root *gup* in the sense of reproach, and likewise after *tij* in the sense of destruction;
it is also prescribed after *kit* in the sense of doubt and remedy.
Why is the vowel *a* pronounced [in the rule]? For the purpose of reduplication according to [Kātantra 3.3.2], "of the second [root] beginning with a vowel"; by that, one says *arthān pratīṣiṣati*.
*Pāṇini 7.4.54*: "After the roots *māna* and others, the suffix *saN* occurs in the sense of the root itself (*svārtha*), and there is lengthening of the vowel of their reduplicated syllable.
After *māna* and the following roots, *saN* follows in its own meaning; furthermore, the vowel of their reduplicated syllable becomes long: *mīmāṃsate*, *bībhatsate*, *dīdāṃsate*, *śīśāṃsate*.
Regarding modifications of the reduplicated syllable, an exception does not supersede the general rule.

How is *avadānam* [derived]? It is established by adding the suffix *yuṭ* to the roots *dyati* and *śyati*. [The form] *mānaḥ* is derived from the root belonging to the *cur*-class, as in *mānayati*. Both *dān* and *śān* take the suffix *kit* and are conjugated in the *parasmaipada*.

"Or, after a verbal root ending in *tum*, provided that it has the same agent as the verb *icchanti* (to wish), the suffix *san* follows. (*Kātantra* 3.2.4). The analysis of the compound is "that which has a *tum*-ending [root]. Thus, *san* occurs after a verbal root ending in *tum* when it does not have a different agent from *icchanti*. For example: *kartum icchati* ("he wishes to do") becomes *cikīrṣati*; *bhoktum icchati* ("he wishes to eat") becomes *bubhukṣate*.

Because the meaning of *iṣ* ("to wish") is already expressed by *san*, the root *iṣ* is not used. Some say that this applies only to the domain of *tum*-infinitives, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) *sani cāniṭi* (*Kātantra* 3.5.7).

What is the purpose of the phrase "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [Consider: *prācikīrṣat*. What is the purpose of the phrase "from that which ends in the suffix -tum" (*tumantāt*)? [Consider: *bhojanam icchati*.
Since the rule is already established by the condition "when there is a desire" (*icchāyām*), the addition of "having the same agent" (*ekakartṛkāt*) is for the sake of clarity.

The suffix *san* does not occur after a verb ending in *icchā* (desire), because of the contradiction of an action [acting] upon itself. How then can one say "the riverbank wishes to fall" (*pipatiṣati*) or "the dog wishes to die" (*mumūrṣati*)? The view is that as with the sentence, so too here it is due to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
After a nominal stem (*nāman*), the suffix *yin* is used when expressing the desire of the self. (Pāṇini 3.1.8)

When there is a desire for oneself (*ātman*) regarding a noun, the suffix *yin* occurs after that noun; for example, *putram icchati* (he desires a son) becomes *putrīyati*, and likewise *ghaṭīyati*. Here, the word *ātman* is used specifically in the sense of "one's own" (*adhyātma*), intended for the ease of those of dull intellect. This is because [otherwise] there would be a state of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*): one might say "he desires the brother's son" (*bhrātuḥ putram icchati*), "he desires a great son" (*mahāntaṃ putram icchati*), or "he desires his own son" (*ātmanaḥ putram icchati*). However, since the meaning is properly restricted by the context, we have *bhrātṛputrīyati* (he desires a brother's son). Because the connection with the noun is through the act of desiring, the suffix would not apply to an intransitive case such as *dātreṇecchati* (he desires with a sickle), because that would involve a state of dependence.

Because it is a rule established by specific restriction (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*), [the suffix] would not occur after words ending in *m* or after indeclinables (*avyaya*); for example, *kim icchati* ("what does he desire? and *svar icchati* ("he desires heaven"). And [the suffix] *kāmya*:

According to Kāt_3.2.6, the suffix *kāmya* follows a nominal stem (*nāman*) in the sense of "desiring for oneself. Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, the suffix *yiṅ* also occurs. This [mention of *kāmya*] is solely for the sake of what follows, so that the immediately preceding suffix *kāmya* (from 3.2.5) might not apply here; for example: *putram icchati* ("he desires a son") becomes *putrakāmyati*; *idam icchati* ("he desires this") becomes *idaṃkāmyati*; *svaḥ icchati* ("he desires heaven") becomes *svaḥkāmyati*.

*Upamānād ācāre* (Pāṇini 3.1.10): After a word denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffix *kyac* (*yin*) occurs when the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra*) is to be expressed. For example: *putrīyati māṇavakam* ("he behaves toward the boy as if he were a son"). Since the accusative case is not used for the boy (*māṇavaka*) because its meaning is already expressed [by the suffix], it follows that the suffix may also occur after a word denoting a locus (*ādhāra*), because it is independent [of other factors]. For example: *kuṭīyati prāsāde* ("he behaves in the palace as if he were in a hut").

*Kartur āyiḥ salopaś ca* (Kātantra 3.2.8): After a noun that is the name of the agent used as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), the suffix *āyi* is added when the sense of "acting like" (*ācāra*) is to be expressed, and there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of the *s* [of the suffix], as far as possible. For example: he acts like a hawk (*śyena*)—*śyenāyate*; likewise, *sārasāyate*, *ojāyate*, *apsarāyate*, *payāyate*, *payasyate*. Because the word *vā* has the sense of "desired" (*iṣṭa*), there is also the elision of *āyi*: he acts like a donkey (*gardabha*)—*gardabhati*; it is held that *aśvatī* [is formed in the same way].

How does one conjugate *galbhate*, *klīvate*, and *hoḍate*? These are ātmanepada roots; because they end in a suffix, the addition of *ām* is indeed desired. After *ojas*, *apsaras*, and *payas*, [the suffix *ām*] is applied invariably, whereas after *payas* it is optional. Furthermore, the elision of the *āy* suffix should be understood as occurring in cases such as *na cāśvo gardabhaḥ*.

Likewise, according to the rule *cvyarthe bhṛśādes tasor lopaś ca*, when the sense of becoming something else (the meaning of the suffix *cvi*) is intended, there is elision of the suffixes *t* and *as*. Thus: that which was not intense (*abhṛśaḥ*) becomes intense (*bhṛśaḥ*), [expressed as] *bhṛśāyate*; similarly, *unmanāyate* and *durmanāyate*.
*Vehat* [becomes] *vehāyate*. *Śaśvat* [becomes] *śaśvāyate*.

Because of the mention of the word *vā* (optionally), the suffix *cv-* also applies: *bhṛśībhavati*. That which was not intense (*abhṛśa*) becomes intense (*bhṛśa*); it acts as if it were intense. It is held that there is non-difference from the object due to similarity; this is the desired rule for the elision of *t*. Likewise, after words such as *paṭa* and *lohita*, the suffix *cv-* is used in the sense of becoming that [which it was not before]: *paṭapaṭāyati*, *paṭapaṭāyate*; *lohitāyati*, *lohitāyate*. Their inclusion among the roots beginning with *yaj* is desired. [Examples: *kaṣṭāya karmaṇe krāmati* (he exerts himself toward a difficult task), *kaṣṭāyate*; likewise, *pāpāyate*, *kakṣāyate*, *satrāyate*, *gahanāyate*.
It does not occur except for evil activities; it undergoes painful austerity.

"The cow chews the cud" (*romanthaṃ vartayati*, *romanthāyate gauḥ*); here there would be no [application] if there were merely the movement of the jaw, as in "the insect chews the cud" (*kīṭo romanthaṃ vartayati*).
"He emits vapor" (*bāṣpam udvamati*, *bāṣpāyate*); likewise, *uṣmāyate* ("he emits heat") and *phenāyate* ("he emits foam").
One experiences pleasure and so forth; one feels pleasure (*sukhaṃ vedayate*), one becomes happy (*sukhāyate*), and likewise one suffers (*duḥkhāyate*).
One produces sound and so forth; one makes a sound (*śabdaṃ karoti*), one sounds (*śabdāyate*), and likewise one acts with enmity (*vairāyate*) or quarrels (*kalahāyate*).

As for *namas*, *tapas*, and *varivas*: one pays homage (*namaskaroti*), one honors the gods (*namasyati devān*); likewise, one torments enemies (*tapasyati śatrūn*) or honors teachers (*varivasyati gurūn*).

*Citri* is used in the sense of wonder; it causes wonder, as in *citrīyate*. From the *kaṇḍvādi* group, the suffix *yan* is applied: from *kaṇḍūñ*, one performs scratching, as in *kaṇḍūyati* or *kaṇḍūyate*.

*Mahīṅ*, meaning "to become great," as in *mahīyate*, and others of this kind should also be understood accordingly. All of this is established either by the word *vā* (or) or by the sense of *bahulam* (variously).

The suffix *kāritam* occurs in the sense of a verbal root (*dhātvarthe*). According to Pāṇini 3.2.9, when a noun denoting an action is used in the sense of a verbal root, the suffix *in* follows it; that [suffix] is designated as *kāritam*. For example: he takes hold of the plough (*halim*) or the spade (*kalim*), thus *halayati*, *kalayati*; likewise, *kṛtayati*, *varṇayati*, *tvacayati*.
He threshes the chaff (*tūstāni*), thus *vitūstayati*.
He covers with a garment; he clothes.
He arms with armor; he armors.
He sprinkles with powders; he dusts.

He does that; he speaks of that. He makes [someone] bald, *muṇḍayati*; likewise, he mixes, *miśrayati*; he smoothes, *ślakṣṇayati*; he seasons with salt, *lavaṇayati*; he threads with a string, *sūtrayati*. "He observes a milk-vow," *payo vratayati*, is understood to mean "he eats milk"; "he observes the food-vow of a Śūdra," *vṛṣalānnaṃ vratayati*, means "he eats [the food of a Śūdra]. He speaks the truth, *satyāpayati*; likewise, he makes it meaningful, *arthāpayati*; he causes [them] to know the Vedas, *vedāpayati*.

It expresses "dear," it causes to reach, and it includes the prefix *ā*. By means of that [suffix], one says: *atikrāmati* (he overcomes), *hastinātikrāmati* (he overcomes with an elephant), *atihastayati* (he surpasses by means of an elephant).

When used in the sense of the agent or the instrument: *vīṇayopagāyati* (he sings along with a lute), *upavīṇayati* (he plays the lute for someone); *tūlair avakuṣṇāti* (he winnows with cotton), *avatūlayati* (he winnows with cotton); *ślokair upastauti* (he praises with verses), *upaślokayati* (he praises with verses); *senayābhiyāti* (he marches against with an army), *abhiṣeṇayati* (he marches against with an army).
Sometimes, in the sense of seeing, one sees a form and examines it; this is a frequent illustration.
Likewise, in the sense of throwing away (*nirasana*), from the root *inaṅ*: one throws away the hands, *hastayate*;
one throws away the feet, *pādayate*.
In this way, he raises his tail: *utpucchayate* the cow.
He swings his tail around: *paripucchayate*. Likewise, the merchant gathers his wares together: *saṃbhāṇḍayate*. The monk cleanses or puts on his robe: *saṃcīvarayate*.
This much may also be inferred from the words of the authors of the *Gaṇapāṭha*.
Regarding the rule *dhātoś ca hetau* (Kātantra 3.2.10):

by the word "cause" (*hetu*), the activity of the causal agent (*hetukartṛvyāpāra*) is understood by implication. Others [interpret it as] the cause of the root-meaning. If a suffix follows a root that denotes the activity of a causal agent, that suffix is designated as *kārita*; for example, one who employs another to act is expressed as *kārayati* ("he causes to do").

One employs another who is cooking, as in *pācayati* ("he causes to cook"). Likewise, one causes alms to be stayed for, as in *bhikṣāṃ vāsayati*; or one causes cow-dung fuel to teach, as in *kārīṣo 'dhyāpayati*.

Similarly, a narrator causes Kaṃsa to be killed, as in *kathakaḥ kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*, or causes Sītā to be abducted, as in *sītāṃ hārayati*, or causes the king to come, as in *rājānam āgamayati*; and likewise, there is the worldly intention of speech: "What is the use of going? Kaṃsa has already been killed."

Likewise, it causes the night to pass away; the root *vas* preceded by the prefix *vi-* signifies transgression. Why [is the condition] "ujjayi" stated? [Because in cases such as: *ārabhate*, *ālabhate*, *rebhe*, *lebhe*.
[Furthermore,] after the roots *hu* and *dhuḍ*, the substitute *dhi* takes the place of *hi*. (Kātantra 3.5.35)
After *hudh* and *duh*, the substitute *dhi* occurs in place of *hi*. Thus: *juhudhi*, *cakāddhi*, *bhinddhi*, *chinddhi*.
[In the forms] *bhinttāt* and *chinttāt*, *tāt* is substituted because it is subsequent [to the rule for *dhi*].
[In the forms] *bhinddhaki* and *chinddhaki*, *ak* is applied subsequently.

How is it that *rudihi* and *svapihi* are formed? Because of the designation *seṭ*. Regarding the root *as*: by Pāṇini 3.1.36, *dhī* replaces the *hi* following *as*, as in *asa* and *edhi*. This rule is stated because [the substitution of] *etva* [to *e*] occurs due to its being obligatory (*nitya*) and internal (*antaraṅga*).
And from *śās*. According to Kāt_3.5.37, *dhī* replaces the *hi* following *śās*, and *śās* becomes *śā*; thus, *śādhi*.
By the rule *ac ca*, the substitution of *it* would occur [after the root vowel].
*lopo 'bhyastād antinaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.112): After an abhyasta (repeated) root, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *n* of the suffix *anti*. For example: *dadati*, *dadatu*, *jāgrati*, *jāgratu*.
This is repeated because the elision of *n* was previously established as a rule to be proven.
And [the *n*] of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) following a root that does not end in *a*.

(Pāṇini 6.4.107) In the middle voice, the *n* of the root *ant-* is elided when it follows a suffix that does not end in *a*. For example: *kurvate*, *kurvatām*; *lunate*, *lunatām*; *vyatilāte*, *vyatilātām*. Why "not ending in *a*"? Consider: *pacante*, *pacyante*.
The initial [sound] of *anta* following *śī* becomes *ri*. (Kāt.
3.5.40) The initial sound of *anta* that follows *śī* becomes *ri*: *śerate*, *śeratām*, *aśerata*.
The mention of *anti* is so that *ri* does not become the initial [sound] of *antī*.
Or rather, it should be stated that [the substitution] occurs for *saṃvidate* and *saṃvidrate*.
By Pāṇini 6.4.114 (*ākārād aṭ au*), the *au* replaces the *aṭ* augment following an *ā* vowel;
thus, *papau*, *tasthau*.

In the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the suffixes *tuhi*, *oḥ*, *tāt*, and *a* (forming *tvam*) should be stated [as substitutes for the imperative endings]. Examples: *jīvatu*, *jīvatāt*, *jīva tvam*; *nandatu*, *nandatāt*, *nanda tvam*; *chinttāt*, *kurutāt*.
The letter *ṇ* [in the suffix *ṇal*] is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution.
[The rule] "for a root ending in *ṛ*, there is *īr* before a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*" applies here. (Kāśikā 3.1.42)
When a root ending in *ṛ* is heard as the substituend, the closest internal substitute *ī* (<*i*) occurs before a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*, as in *cikīrṣati*, *jihīrṣati*, and *titīrṣati*.
Why specify "ending in *ṛ*" (*ṛdanta*)? Consider *cakratuḥ*.
Due to the technical indication in the rule *kīrtīṣoḥ ktiś ca* [Kāt. 4.5.86], we have *kīrtayati*.
The following has not yet been commented upon:

*ur oṣṭhyopadhasya ca* (Kāt. 3.5.43). When a suffix beginning with a vowel follows a root ending in *ṛ* that has a labial (*oṣṭhya*) as its penultimate letter, *uṛ* is substituted [for *ṛ*] before a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*. Examples: *pupūrṣati*, *mumūrṣati*, *bubhūrṣati*, *bobhūryate*.
[The substitution occurs] even after a dental or labial [consonant]: *prāvuvūrṣati*, *saṃvuvūrṣati*.
Why [is it specified] "of a root having a labial as its penultimate"? [Consider: the root *ṛ* in the sense of "motion," as in *samīrṇaḥ*.
[The rule] *ini asamānalopopadhāyā hrasvaś caṇi* (Kāt. 3.5.44) [applies].

A short vowel is substituted for the penultimate (upadhā) of a root that does not undergo a single (samāna) elision, when followed by the suffix *ini* which itself is followed by *caṅ*. Examples: *acīkarat*, *ajījapat*, *alīlavat*.

The mention of *in* is intended to refer to *in* in general; therefore, in the case of "he caused one who had played [the lute] to play," as in *avīvadad vīṇāṃ parivādakena*, there is indeed no single elision.
Why specify "of a root whose penultimate does not undergo a single elision"? Consider: *asasāmat*.
What is the purpose of the condition "after a penultimate vowel" (*upadhāyāḥ*)? [Consider: *acakāṅkṣat*.

How about *gonāvam ākhyātavān* (he called it a cow-boat) and *ajugonat* (he did not diminish)? [The answer is: because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the long vowel *au*. [This is negated by the rule: "Not for roots with indicatory letters (*anubandha*) such as *śās* and *ṛ*. (Kātantra 3.5.45).

For roots marked with the indicatory vowel *ṛ*, including the root *śās*, there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel before the suffix *ini* when followed by *caṇ*. Examples: *aśaśāsat*, *aḍuḍhaukat*.
Why specify "*śās*" [in the rule]? Consider *āṅaḥ śāsa icchāyām* (the root *śās* preceded by *āṅ* in the sense of desire): *āśīśasat*.
The inclusion of *oṇ* as having the indicatory vowel *ṛ* is for the purpose of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*).
Even the reduplication is superseded by the shortening [of the vowel]; therefore: *mā bhavān aṭiṭat*.

For the roots *bhrājṛ*, *bhrāsṛ*, and *bhāsṛ*, the indicatory letter *ṛ* is not taken into account: *abibhrajat* from *bhrāj*, *abibhrasat* from *bhrās*, and *abībhasat* from *bhās*. Likewise: *adīdipat* from *dīp*, *ajījivat* from *jīv*, *amīmilat* from *mīl*, *apīpiḍat* from *pīḍ*, *acīkaṇat* from *kaṇ*, *avīvaṇat* from *vaṇ*, *abībhaṇat* from *bhaṇ*, *aśīśraṇat* from *śraṇ*, *ajīhiṭhat* from *heṭh*, and *alūlupat* from *lup*.

He caused it to shine; *bhrājanam*, *bhrājam*, he caused that to shine, *ababhrājat*. Because there is elision of the same [portion], it need not be stated that "for *bhrāj* and others, optionally" applies. There is elision of the penultimate vowel of *pibati*, and the substitute *īC* occurs for the reduplication. (Kāśikā 3.1.46): Elision of the penultimate vowel of *pibati* occurs, and *īC* occurs for the reduplication, when followed by *ini* which itself is followed by *caṇ*; thus, *apīpyat*.
Why [is the root] *pibati* mentioned? [In the case of] *pai* (to swell) and *ovai*, we have *apīpayat*.
[In the case of] *pā* in the sense of "protecting," we have *apīpalat*.
[The rule applies] after *tiṣṭhati*. (Kāt. 3.5.47)

In this context, the short *i* of the reduplicated syllable [is substituted]; the penultimate vowel of the root *sthā* becomes *i* when followed by an affix beginning with *n* that has *caṇ* as its subsequent element, as in *atiṣṭhipat*.

Or, according to Kāt_3.5.48, the penultimate vowel of the root *ghrā* optionally becomes *i* when followed by an affix beginning with *n* that has *caṇ* as its subsequent element, as in *ajighripat* or *ajighrapat*.

How is it that *avīvṛdhat*, *avavardhat*, *amīmṛjat*, *amamārjat*, *acīkḷpat*, *acakalpat*, *acīkṛtat*, and *acikīrtat* are formed? Because the rule regarding the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṛ* in the case of the suffix *caṇ* is conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), and because the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule *kīrtīṣoḥ ktiś ca* [Kāt 4.5.86] is not universally valid (*anitya*). Thus ends the fifth section (*pāda*) on verbs in the *Daurgasiṃhī-vṛtti*. [Now begins: "The elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the penultimate consonant) occurs before a suffix that lacks a *guṇa*-strengthening vowel and does not have *i* as its *anubandha*. [Kāt 3.6.1]

For roots that do not have *it* as an indicatory letter (*anidanubandha*), there is elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the penultimate nasal) when followed by a suffix that does not possess a *guṇa*-strengthening vowel. Examples: *śrasyate*, *dhvasyate*, *naṣṭaḥ*, *naṣṭavān*. Why specify "for roots that do not have *it* as an indicatory letter"? [Consider] *śaṅkyate* and *vaṅkyate*. Precisely because of this exclusion, there is no such elision for roots with an *it* indicatory letter. Consequently, in the case of *vṛṃhaṇam*, since it ends in a vowel, there would be the substitution of *n* for *m*; however, because that which is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*), [the rule does not apply].
The forms *laṅgika* and *kampya* would occur in the sense of affliction (*upatāpa*) and bodily transformation (*śarīravikāra*), as in *vilagitaḥ* and *vikapitaḥ*.

For the roots beginning with *tṛph* and ending with *śunph*, the suffix *ani* is applied and the nasal is not elided; thus, from *tṛpha* and *tṛnpha* in the sense of satisfaction (*tṛpti*), we have *tṛmphati*, and so forth. This also applies after the suffix *na*, which is a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*). (Kātantra 3.6.2)

The conjunction with the letter *ca* serves to include both those roots having *i* as an indicatory vowel (*idanubandha*) and those not having *i* as an indicatory vowel (*anidanubandha*). The general rule is that "before a suffix marked with *P* or *K*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. For roots having *i* as an indicatory vowel and for those not having *i* as an indicatory vowel, when the suffix is one that causes *guṇa* (i.e., marked with *P* or *K*), and also after the root *naś*, the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal augment) is elided. Examples: *bhanakti*, *bhaṅktaḥ*, *bhañjanti*; *hinasti*, *hiṃstaḥ*, *hiṃsanti*.
Furthermore, in the *parokṣā* (perfect tense), the *anuṣaṅga* is elided after the roots *indh*, *śranth*, *granth*, and *dambh* before a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*. (Kātantra 3.6.3)

In the *parokṣā* (perfect tense), the suffix *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal consonant) of roots beginning with *indh* is elided when followed by a suffix that does not contain the augment *guṇa*. Thus: *samīdhe*, *samīdhāte*, *samīdhire*; because of the specific rule, there is no *ām* [augment]. *śrethtuḥ*, *grethatuḥ*, *debhatuḥ*.
By the restrictive rule "only for *indh* and its congeners," [there is no elision] in *śaśraṃse* and *babhañjatuḥ*.
For the roots *danśi*, *sanji*, *svanji*, and *ranji*, [the *anuṣaṅga* is elided] before *ani*. (Kātantra 3.6.4)

In the case of roots such as *danś*, when there is no *vikaraṇa* suffix, the elision (*lopa*) of the *anuṣaṅga* occurs: *daśati*, *sajati*, *pariṣvajate*, *rajati*. How is it that [the form] *pariṣvajete* is formed? Because [the substitution of *ś* for *s*] is internal (*antaraṅga*) and because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
This is because of the grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) "√*danś* biting," [which implies that the root is *daṃś*]; thus, the noun form is *daśanam*.
How is it broken? It is analyzed (*abhāji*). Since the root *bhaj* is used here in the sense of "breaking" (*bhañjane*) as well, the following rule applies:
"In the presence of the suffixes *in*, *ic*, and *aṭ*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel and *vṛddhi* for those [roots] ending in a *nāmin* vowel. (Kātantra 3.6.5).

When these suffixes—*in*, *ic*, or *aṭ*—follow, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the root, and *vṛddhi* occurs for those [roots] whose penultimate is a *nāmin* vowel. Examples: *pācayati*, *apāci*, *papāca*; *lāvayati*, *alāvi*, *lulāva*; *nāyayati*, *anāyi*, *nināya*; *kārayati*, *akāri*, *cakāra*.

What is the purpose of the phrase "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [It is to exclude cases such as: *tvacayati*. How then is it that one has described [the root] *paṭu* as having undergone reduplication in *apīpaṭat*? [The answer is: when there is *vṛddhi*, there is the elision of the diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*). Since the root contains a *nāmin* vowel, once the *guṇa* substitution has occurred, the lengthening of the *upadhā* is established. The mention of *nāmin* is solely for the sake of indicating the grammatical gender, or else the plural number is used for the sake of generalization.

How is it that there is no *acakalat* or *ajahalat*? Because the rule for *vṛddhi* is non-obligatory when preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvakatvāt*), the treatment as if it were a *san*-stem (*sanvadbhāvaḥ*) does not apply due to the elision of the same vowel (*samānalopatvāt*). Likewise, in the case of the first person plural ending *-āma* (the *uttama*), there is an option: *ahaṃ papaca*, *ahaṃ papāca*; *ahaṃ ninaya*, *ahaṃ nināya*; *ahaṃ lulava*, *ahaṃ lulāva*; *ahaṃ cakara*, *ahaṃ cakāra*. [This applies] to roots ending in vowels in the *parasmaipada* when followed by the *sic* suffix. (Kātantra 3.6.6)

When the *sic* affix follows in the *parasmaipada*, a vowel-ending root undergoes *vṛddhi* substitution, but only if it is a *nāmin* (a vowel other than *a*). Examples: *arāvīt*, *alāvīt*, *acaiaṣīt*, *anaiṣīt*. The mention of "ending in a vowel" (*svarānta*) is for the purpose of the original instruction (*upadeśa*); therefore, [the rule applies] in cases such as *udavoḍhām*. Why specify "*sic*" [in the rule]? Observe: *navāva*.
What is the meaning of "from another" (parasmāt)? [As in: *acyoṣṭa*.
Or, after the root *ūrṇu*, [the suffix *sic* is optionally used]: *praurṇāvīt*, *praurṇavīt*.
[This applies] to those roots ending in consonants that lack the augment *iṭ*. (Kāt. 3.6.7)

When *sic* follows in the *parasmaipada*, there is *vṛddhi* of the *nāmin* vowel of *aniṭ* roots ending in a consonant, and this occurs only for the *upadhā* [vowel]: *abhaitsīt*, *arautsīt*, *atārpsīt*.
Why "of *aniṭ* roots"? [Observe: *akoṣīt*.
And for this [root], there is lengthening: Kāt_3,6.8.

When *sic* follows in the *parasmaipada*, there is lengthening of the vowel of roots ending in a consonant that are *aniṭ*, as well as [the lengthening] of the vowel of *vada*, *vraja*, and roots ending in *r* or *l*: *apākṣīt*.
Because of the separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*), [it applies to] *abhāṅkṣīt*. [This applies to] *vada*, *vraja*, and those ending in *r* or *l*. (Kātantra 3.6.9)

When *sic* follows in the *parasmaipada*, there is lengthening of the vowel for the roots *vad*, *vraj*, and those ending in *ra* or *la*. Thus: *avādīt*, *avrājīt*, *acārīt*, *acālīt*. How is it that we have *avabhrīt* and *aśvallīt*? It is because the vowel *a* does not end in *ra* or *la*. According to the rule "for roots beginning with a consonant that take *iṭ*, and for those with *an* or *it* as indicatory letters, and for *mī*, *han*, *kṣaṇ*, and *śvas*, [the substitution of *iṭ*] is optional," we have *araṇīt* or *arāṇīt*.
And of *edanubandha* and so forth: from *kage*, *akagit*;
from *graha*, *agrahīt*; from *ṭuvama*, *avamīt*;
from *vyaya*, *avyayīt*.
*kṣaṇa*, *akṣaṇīt*;
*śvasa*, *aśvasīt*.
This is because the rule "of those that do not take *iṭ*" (*aniṭām*), being indicated by the negative particle *nañ*, is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
*Śvij* and *jāgṛ* undergo *guṇa* substitution. According to Kātantra 3.6.10, when the *sic* suffix follows in the *parasmaipada*, *guṇa* occurs for *śvij* and *jāgṛ*: *aśvayīt*, *ajāgarīt*.
This is an exception to the rule regarding *vṛddhi*.
*Kāt_3.6.11*: Before the suffix *aṇ*, there is *guṇa* substitution for the roots *ṛ* and *sṛ*. Thus, [we have] *mā bhavān arat* (do not go) and *asarat* (he went).
How is it that we have *ajarat* (he grew old) and *adarśat* (he saw)? Because the vowel *ṛ* is used here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the root *jāgarti* when followed by a causative suffix: Kāt_3.6.12 states that when a causative suffix follows the root *jāgarti*, guṇa substitution occurs; thus, *jāgarayati*.
Regarding the suffix *ya* in the sense of the benedictive (*āśis*) and in the formation of denominatives (*yaṅ*): Kāt_3.6.13.

When *ya* follows the root *jāgarti*, except in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), *guṇa* substitution occurs: *jāgaryate*, *jāgaryāt*. Why is it said "when *ya* follows"? [Consider] *jāgariṣīṣṭa*; here, by the rule *iḍ vejvac ca*, there would be *vṛddhi*. [This applies] in the *parokṣā* (perfect) when there is no *guṇa*. (Kāt. 3.6.14)
In the *parokṣā* (perfect) tense, a *guṇa* substitution occurs for the root *jāgarti* when it is followed by an affix that does not cause *guṇa*. Thus: *jajāgaratuḥ*, *jajāgaruḥ*.
Why "when there is no *guṇa*" (*aguṇe*)? [Observe: *jajāgāra*. [The rule] also applies to roots beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in *ṛ*: Pāṇini 3.1.5.15.

In the *parokṣā* (perfect) tense, when followed by a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*, a *guṇa* substitute occurs for a verbal root beginning with a conjunct consonant and for roots ending in *ṛ*. [Examples: *sasmaratuḥ*, *sasmaruḥ*.

How is it that we have *saṃcaskaratuḥ* and *saṃcaskaruḥ*? This rule is non-eternal (*anitya*), according to the principle that "what is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to what is internal (*antaraṅga*). And [the *guṇa* applies] to roots ending in *ṛ*. (Kātantra 3.6.16)

In the periphrastic future (*parokṣā*), a *guṇa* substitution occurs for roots ending in *ṛ* when no other *guṇa* is applied: *teratuḥ*, *teruḥ*; *viśaśaratuḥ*, *viśaśaruḥ*; *vidadaratuḥ*, *vidadaruḥ*; *nipaparatuḥ*, *nipaparuḥ*.

How is it that we have *viśaśratuḥ*, *viśaśruḥ*, *vidadratūḥ*, *vidadruḥ*, *nipapratuḥ*, *nipapruḥ*? [The answer is: in the sense of the roots *śṝ*, *dṝ*, and *pṝ*, the forms *śrā*, *drā*, and *prā* are also employed.
*Kāt_3.6.17*: For the root *ṛcch*, the substitute *ṛt* is applied.

The repetition [of the word *guṇa*] is for the purpose of specifying the scope: in place of *ṛcch*, after the root *ṛ*, in the *parokṣā* (perfect) tense, both when a *guṇin* follows and when no *guṇin* follows, a *guṇa* occurs. Thus: *ānarcha*, *ānarchatuḥ*, *ānarchuḥ*.

How is it that [the form] *āratuḥ* is formed? Because the rule is obligatory, or because the cause [for the application of the previous rule] is absent, there is no obstruction to the augment (*āgama*).
[The rule] *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke* [Kātantra 3.6.18 applies].

In the presence of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that does not have *guṇa*, *guṇa* occurs for the root *śī*; because it consists of a single vowel, [the rule] applies at the end of the syllable: *śete*, *śayīta*, *śetām*, *aśeta*.
Below follows the uncorrected translation: *ay īr ye*. Kāt_3,6.19.
The vowel *ī* of the root *śīṅ* becomes *ay* when followed by the suffix *ye*: *śayyate*, *adhiśayya gataḥ*.
How is it that [the forms] *samuhyate* and *samuhya gataḥ* occur, given that the root *vah* has the meaning of *ūh*?

Because of the statement [in the grammatical tradition], the substitution of *ay* for *ūh* occurs only after a prefix before a suffix beginning with *y* that lacks *guṇa*; therefore, the shortening [of the penultimate vowel] need not be explicitly stated.
*Kāt_3,6.20:* For roots ending in *ā*, when *ic* follows, *āy* is substituted for the specified *ā*.
Examples: *asthāyi*, *adāyi*, *dāyiṣyate*, *adāyiṣata*, *dāyiṣīṣṭa*, *dāyitā*; and [the rule] *iḍvejvacca*.
*Kāt_3,6.21:* For the roots *śā* (to sharpen), *chā* (to cut), *sā* (to bind), *hvā* (to call), *vyā* (to pervade), and *vep* (to tremble), *in* is substituted [for the suffix *ya*].

The suffix *ini* follows the roots *śā*, *chā*, *sā*, *hveñ*, *vyeñ*, *veñ*, and *pā* (in the sense of drinking), as well as *pai* (ovai) and those ending in *ā*. Thus: *śā* becomes *śāyayati*; *chā* becomes *chāyayati*; *sā* becomes *sāyayati*; *hveñ* becomes *hvāyayati*; *vyeñ* becomes *saṃvyāyayati*; *veñ* becomes *vāyayati*; and *pā* (to drink) and *pai* (ovai) become *pāyayati*. According to Kātantra 3.6.22: For the roots *ṛ*, *hrī*, *vlī*, *rī*, *lū*, *yī*, *kṣmāy*, and those ending in long *ā*, the final vowel is replaced by *p*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the penultimate vowel, and *guṇa* substitution occurs for the *nāmin* vowels.

When the suffix *ini* follows, the letter *p* becomes the final element of roots beginning with *arti* and those ending in *ā*; there is elision of *y* as applicable, and for roots with changeable vowels (*nāmin*), *guṇa* substitution occurs. By the rule *tipā dhātur eva nirdiśyate*, the verbal root itself is indicated [by the tip]: *arpayati*, *hrepayati*, *blepayati*; from *rī* in the sense of "scattering" or *rīṅ* in the sense of "hearing," *repayati*; *knopayati*, *kṣmāpayati*, *sthāpayati*, *krāpayati*, *adhyāpayati*. *Kāt_3.6.23*: For the root *pāti*, *l* is the final element when *ini* follows. Thus, *pālayati*. Since *pala* also exists in the cur-ādi class in the sense of "protection," there is the statement that *āyi* should be added to *pāti*.

Furthermore, there may be the inclusion of the final letter or its replacement. According to *Kātantra* 3.6.24: "In the case of the roots *dhūñ* and *prī*, when the suffix *ini* follows, the letter *n* becomes the final [augment]. Thus: *dhūnayati*, *prīṇayati*.

Why [is it specified] "of *dhūñ* and *prīṇāti*"? [Consider: *dhū* in the sense of shaking (*vidhūnana*), as in *vidhāvayati*; *prīṅ* in the sense of delighting (*prīti*), as in *prāyayati*. [In the case of] *ghṛtaṃ vilīnayati*, the suffix *in* is applied in the sense of "making melted" (*vilīnaṃ karoti*). However, [one does not say] *ghṛtaṃ vilālayati*; for although *lalate* is a form [derived from *lī*], the root *lī* has no application in the causative when meaning "the liquefaction of oiliness," because such usage is not expressed [by the grammatical system]. In the phrase *pakṣeṇopavājayati*, the form is *vajate*; however, the root *vā* has no application in the causative when meaning "trembling."

The roots *satyā*, *arthā*, and *vedā* have the suffix *-āp* added to them specifically in the *curādi* (tenth) class: *satyāpayati*, *arthāpayati*, and *vedāpayati*. How is it that [one forms] *kārāpayati*, *varṇāpayati*, and *śabdāpayati*? [The answer is: the root *āp* has the form *āp*; from this comes *kārāpaḥ* [meaning] "the act of making (*kāra*)"; one who performs that is *kārāpaḥ*, and thus [the denominative] *kārāpayati* is formed with the suffix *-in*. [This applies] when it is appropriate for the cause (*hetu*). Or, it should be stated as an alternative. There is the substitution of *sphā* for the root *sphāyi*. (Kātantra 3.6.25)

When the suffix *ini* follows, the substitute *sphā* occurs for the root *sphāy*; thus, one forms *sphāvayati*. The mention of a "substitute" (*ādeśa*) implies that there would otherwise be an augment (*āgama*). For the root *śad*, when not meaning "to go," the substitute *ta* occurs when *ini* follows (Kātantra 3.6.26):
for the root *śad* in the sense of non-motion, *ta* is the substitute when *ini* follows; as in *phalāni śātayati* ("he causes the fruits to fall").

What is the meaning of "agatau" (not in the sense of going)? [Examples: *gāḥ śādayati*, which means "he causes the cows to eat. Regarding the sense of *ruh* (to grow), there is the suffix *ṇic*: *vrīhīn ropayati*, "he causes the rice to grow," or "the elephant makes the mahout mount his body. For the root *han* (to kill), there is the suffix *ta*. (Kāśikā 3.1.27)
In the case of the root *han*, when followed by the suffix *ini*, the final letter becomes *gh*. Thus, *ghātayati*.
The repetition of the word "that" (*tat*) is for the purpose of including the sense of motion; therefore, in *śasyād gāṃ ghātayati*, the meaning is "he causes the cow to go to the field.
By the rule *hasya hanter ghir ini coḥ* (Kātantra 3.6.28), the *h* of *han* becomes *gh* before the suffix *ini*.
The substitution of *gh* occurs for the root *han* when followed by the suffixes *cha* and *ṅi*; thus, *ghātayati* and *aghāni*.
The term *han* is mentioned again as a qualifier for the root ending in *han*, [to indicate that the rule applies even] when the penultimate vowel is elided; [this is stated in] Kātantra 3.6.29.
In the case of a root with a lost penultimate vowel, the *ha* becomes *gha*; thus, *ghnanti*, *āghnate*.
Why "with a lost penultimate vowel"? [To exclude cases such as] *kleśāpahaḥ*, *tamopahaḥ*.
And [the substitution occurs] after a reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). (Kātantra 3.6.30)

Due to reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the *ha* of the root *han* becomes *gh*; as in *jaghāna*. Why specify "due to reduplication of *han*"? [Consider: *jihananīyiṣati*, meaning "he desires to wish to kill" (*hananīyitum icchati*). It should be stated that this applies to the root *hi* when not followed by *caṇ*; as in *jighīṣati*, and *prajighāyayiṣati*, meaning "he desires to cause to strike away" (*prahāyayitum icchati*).
From the statement "it is not to be reduplicated," [we have] *prājīhayat*.
Regarding the rule *jer giḥ sanparokṣayoḥ* (Kāt. 3.6.31):
for the root *ji*, the substitution of *gi* occurs in the *san* (desiderative) and *parokṣa* (periphrastic/perfect) [suffixes]; thus, *jigīṣati* and *jigāya*, *vijigye*.
Because *jināti* is irregular (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*), [we have] *jijyatuḥ*.

Or, by *ceḥ ki vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.63): after the root *ci*, the augment *k* optionally occurs before the desiderative suffix (*san*) and the periphrastic past (*parokṣa*). Thus: *cikīṣati*, *cicīṣati*; *cikāya*, *cicāya*; *cikye*, *cicye*.
Regarding the statement that *jñā* is *parasmaipada*, [it is said]:
"The elision of the *ṣaṇ* [suffix] occurs before a vowel, except in the plural. (Kāt.
3.6.33) The letter *a* of the *ṣaṇ* suffix is elided before a vowel when not in the plural: *adhukṣātām*, *adhukṣāthām*, *adhukṣi*.
What is meant by "a vowel"? *adhukṣat*. What is meant by "non-plurality"? *adhukṣanta*; [in this case], because it ends in the vowel *a*, the elision of *n* would not occur.
[The rule applies] to the root *daridrāti* before an affix other than a sārvadhātuka. (Kāśikā 6.4.114)

Only the root *tip* (the verbal suffix) is specified; for the root *daridrā*, there is elision of the final [phoneme] before any non-sārvadhātuka suffix. Thus: *daridrayati*, *adaridri*, *daridro vartate*, *daridryate*, *daridryāt*. How is *daridreyam* formed? By the rule *ātkhanoricca* [Kāt 4.2.12], which states that the vowel *i* replaces the final [of *daridrā*] before the suffixes *yus* and *vas* when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant (*aniṭ*) or the desiderative (*san*), this would not apply due to the subsequent rule [*paratvāt*]. However, by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) interpretation, it does apply. Examples: *daridrāṇam*, *dridrāyakaḥ*, *didaridrāsakaḥ*. [The rule] *vraścimasjor dhuṭi* [Kāt 3.6.35 applies next].

When a *dhuṭ* consonant follows, there is elision of the final [consonant] of the roots *vraśc* and *masj*. Thus: *vraṣṭā*, *vrakṣyati*; *maṅktā*, *maṅkṣyati*. Because the insertion of *n* (*nāgama*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), the third sound (*ṭ*) replaces *s* first, and only afterwards does the elision take place. Why "when a *dhuṭ* follows"? Observe: *vṛścyate*.
[The rule *yaṇy okārasya* (Kāt. 3.6.36) applies.]

The elision of the vowel *o* occurs in a verbal root when followed by the suffix *yan*, as in *dyati* and *syati*. Why specify "*yan*" [as opposed to *yani*]? [To exclude cases such as] *upoyate*; a substitute conditioned by a subsequent element remains the same as the original with respect to what precedes it. [Furthermore, the elision of *o* occurs] for the vowel *ā* before the suffix *usi*. (Pāṇini 6.4.111–112)
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs after a verbal root when followed by the suffix *usi*, as in *udaguḥ* and *aduḥ*;
and also [after a root ending in] a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), as in *aruḥ* and *aluḥ*. (Kāt. 3.6.38)
The elision of the vowel *ā* occurs in a verbal root when followed by a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), as in *vyatire* and *vyatile*.

Regarding the root *as-* (to be) with the nominative singular suffix *su*: according to Pāṇini 6.4.111 (*aster bhūḥ*), when *su* follows, there is elision of the final [element] of *as-*, resulting in *asi*.
How is it that [the substitution of] *āś* occurs? Because it is based on the characteristic [of the sound].

In the forms *ādhvam* and *āśādhvam*, although the third person suffix is present, there is no difference in the pronunciation of *dhva*. The substitution of *ha* should be stated when *e* follows; as in *vyatihe*.
How is this desired? Because the nature of the verbal roots is indicated by the *tip* suffix. According to Kātantra 3.6.40:

"In this context concerning verbal roots, when the vowel *a* is followed by the vowels *a* or a diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*), those two [sounds]—the *a* and the diphthong—become the phonemes [replacing the original *a*], respectively; and when those two serve as the cause [of the substitution], their elision occurs. Examples: *cikīrṣati*, *dīvyanti*, *pacyante*, *pace*.
What does "asya" (of this) mean? It means "yānti" (they go).
What is the purpose of the condition "asandhyakṣarayoh" (when there are no diphthongs)? [Consider] "pacati" (he cooks).

Since the elision of "asya" is already established by the rule "asya lopaḥ," why is it stated as "tau tallopaś ca"? [Consider] "pacyante" (they are cooked); [the rule is necessary] so that the elision of the *n* (nalopa) does not occur.

*Kāt_3.6.41*: In the case of *dīdhī* and *vevī*, there is elision of the final vowel when followed by an *i*-vowel or the letter *y*. Thus: *ādīdhitā*, *āvevitā*; *ādīdhīta*, *āvevīta*; *ādīdhyate*, *āvevyate*.
It is not here according to the respective order [of the rules], because each root undergoes reduplication individually.
[The suffix] *āyi* is [added after a verbal base] ending in a vowel or a consonant.
According to Pāṇini 3.1.42, there is elision of the initial [vowel] of *āyi* when it follows a base ending in a vowel or a consonant: *agnīyate*, *raiyate*, *viduṣyate*, *anuḍuhyate*.
In the case of "he acts like a Brāhmaṇī," because [the rule for] masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) is permanent, [the feminine suffix is replaced], resulting in *brāhmaṇāyate*.

The mention of the suffix *ni* is for the purpose of [defining] the characteristic of the *saṃnipāta* (conjunction). [Kātantra 3.6.43]: "In the case of the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel that is not *aṇ* and does not undergo *guṇa*. In the case of the roots beginning with *gam*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel other than *aṇ* and which does not undergo *guṇa*, elision occurs: *jagmatuḥ*, *jagmuḥ*; *jaghnatuḥ*, *jaghnuḥ*; from *jan* (to be born), *jana*, [the form is] *jajñe*; *cakhnatuḥ*, *cakhnuḥ*; *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "before a vowel-initial [suffix]" (*svarādau*)? Consider *gamyate*. What is the purpose of [specifying] "not before a non-ṇatva vowel" (*anaṇi*)? Consider *agamat* and *aghasat*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "when there is no guṇa" (*aguṇe*)? Consider *gamiṣyati*.
Kāritalopa (Kāt. 3.6.44):

When a suffix other than *ām*, *iṭ*, or a *vikaraṇa* follows, there is elision of the *kārita* [suffix]. Examples: *acīkarat*, *acīkamata*, *ararakṣat*, *kāryate*, *kāraṇā*, *udapādi*. This supersedes rules such as those concerning *yatva* (the change of *r* to *ri*). Why does it say "other than *ām*, *iṭ*, or a *vikaraṇa*"? Consider: *kārayāmāsa*, *kārayitā*, *kārayati*, *ahaṃ kāraye*. Because of that state (*tadbhāva*) and because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution takes place.
In the case of a patronymic suffix preceded by a vowel, [the substitution of] *yin* or *āyiṣ* occurs before the suffixes *yat* and *cha*. (Kāśikā 3.1.64)

The two suffixes *yin* and *āyi* are plural forms for the sake of including the entire group; the vowel *a* in *yasya* is for the purpose of pronunciation. When there is elision (*lopa*) of the vowel preceding [the final consonant] of that which is related to a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix denoting offspring—provided it is not preceded by a vowel—in the case of *yin*, *āyi*, *taddhita* suffixes, as well as in the case of *svar*, *cvī*, and feminine forms (*strīkāra*), [the following examples apply]: *gārgīyati*, *gārgīyate*. Because the word *gārgya* is derived from the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) as "one who is proficient in the Garga lineage," there is no difference [between the base and the derivative]. In the case of *kuru*, the substitute *na* is applied, and since the word is conventional (*rūḍha*) and denotes offspring in general, the suffix *ṇya* is added according to the *gargādi* class: *kauravyasyāpatyam* ("the offspring of Kauravya") results in *kauraviḥ* (with the suffix *in*). Similarly, *naiṣādiḥ*. [The suffix *cha* is applied: *gārgyasyāyaṃ* ("belonging to Gārgya") results in *gārgīyaḥ*; [and] *gārgāṇām* ("of the Gargas").

The suffix *akaṇ* is applied to denote a collection, as in *gārgakam*. How then is *rājanyakam* formed? [It is because] "that which is produced by a group (*gaṇa*) is not fixed"; thus it would be *gārgī* when referring to a female group. Why does the rule specify "not after *āt* and a vowel"? Consider *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*. The reading "after *yin*, *āyī*, etc. is more logical, because secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) primarily express a class (*ākṛti*); for instance, we see both *saumī* and *ṛk* used in the sense of "this verse has Soma as its deity."
What is the purpose of the rule "not preceded by a vowel" (*asvarapūrvasya*)? [Consider: *ātreyīyati*, *ātreyāyate*, *ātreyīsyāt*, and *ātreyī* (a woman).
[Also: the substitution of *ya* for the final *s* of *matsya* before the feminine suffix *ī* and before the suffix *īya*;
and the elision of the final *y* of *tiṣya* and *puṣya* when denoting a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), due to their separation from the following vowel.

*matsī* [is derived from *matsya* with the suffix *ṅīp*]. *Āgastya* is the descendant of Agastya, hence the suffix *aṇ*; *āgastīya* is that which belongs to Āgastya; *āgastī* is that which pertains to Āgastya. *Saurya* is that which belongs to Sūrya; *saurīya* is that which arises there (in the sun); *sauro dik* is the direction belonging to Sūrya. *Taiṣamah* is the day of Taiṣa; *taiṣī* is the night of Taiṣa. *Pauṣamah* is the day of Pauṣa; *pauṣī* is the night of Pauṣa. The mention of *gaṇa* separately [from the previous rule] is for the sake of subsequent rules. *Nalopaś ca* (Kātantra 3.6.46): "The elision of *na*" refers to the rule (*yoga*) by which the letter *n* is dropped. By implication, only the elision of *n* should be applied in the case of the suffixes *yin* and *āyy*. Thus: *viduṣyati*, *viduṣyate*; likewise, *rājīyati*, *pathīyati*.
The suffix *yat* also occurs after roots ending in long *ī*.
What is the restriction? It also occurs after roots ending in *ī* such as *dīv* (to play), as in *dīvyati*.
How then do we derive *caturyati*, *anuḍuhyati*, *gīryati*, and *dhūryati*? The restriction applies because it depends on the specific verbal roots.
In *sarpiṣyati* and *dhanuṣyati*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* must indeed occur.

[Regarding the form] *gomatyati*: this is derived with the suffix *kvip*. How then do we get *gomān*, *pacan*, and *pumān*? Because the elision of a suffix (*pratyaya-lopa*) is not invariably permanent, [the rule] applies only to those ending in *ud-anubandha*, as well as to the suffix *śatṛ* and the word *puṃs*. [The rule] "after a consonant, before *di* and *si*" (Kātantra 3.6.47).

There is elision of the *i* and *s* of the suffixes *di* and *si* after a verbal root that ends in a consonant; for example, *adhok* and *aleṭ*. How [is it that there is no elision] in *haṃsi*? Because of association (*sāhacarya*).
[The rule] *yasyānan-ani* (Pāṇini 6.4.48) [applies].

In the rule *yasya*, the vowel *a* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*). When a consonant is followed by a verbal root, there is elision (*lopa*) of the *ya* [of the suffix] when the suffix *anani* follows; e.g., *bebhiditā*. One who desires or acts like a grinding stone (*dṛṣad*): *dṛśaditā*. The verbal root *bhiṣaj* is included in the *kaṇḍūyādi* group; e.g., *bhiṣajitā*.

Some do not accept [the substitution] for *yin* and *āyy*. Therefore, because both [roots] possess the status of a valid measure (*pramāṇa*), there is no fault regarding forms such as *mavyitā*, *sūrkṣyitā*, and *īrṣyitā*, whether due to the statement of elision (*lopa*) to be mentioned later [regarding the suffix *ktvā*], or due to the reading of two *y*-sounds.

Why is it said "after a consonant" (*vyañjanāt*)? [Consider: *lolūyitā*. When the suffix *in* is elided and *y* is substituted [for the final vowel], we have *momūtritā* and *śāśayitā*. Why is it said "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [Consider: *pacyate*.
What is *anan*? As in *pāpacyate*. And there is its elision. According to Kāt. 3.6.49, the elision of the vowel *a* of a verbal root occurs when the suffix *anan* follows, as in *cikīrṣitā*.
*Kusubham* becomes *magadham*; [the forms] *kusubhitā* and *magadhitā*.

Even when the locative case is used for the object, [the suffixes] *kaṇḍūḥ*, *lolūḥ*, and *yāyāvaraḥ* [are formed]; and when there is elision (*lopa*) of that [suffix], there should be elision of the *y*.
[This applies] after the root *sic* when followed by the letter *dh*. (Kātantra 3.6.50)
The *s* is elided when followed by the letter *dh*. [Examples: *alaviḍhvam*, *acyoḍhvam*.
This is because even though the third letter (*ḍh*) occurs in place of *s* in the form *ayandhvam*, there is no difference in the pronunciation of *dh*.
And [there is elision] of a *dhuṭ* [consonant] before a *dhuṭ* [consonant]. (Kātantra 3.6.51)

There is elision of the suffix *sic* following a consonant (*dhuṭ*) when another consonant (*dhuṭ*) follows; as in *abhitta* and *abhitthāḥ*. Why "following a consonant" (*dhuṭaḥ*)? Consider *amaṃsta*. Why "when another consonant follows" (*dhuṭi*)? Consider *abhitsātām*.
*Kāt_3.6.52*: After a short vowel, there is elision of *sic* when it is *aniṭ*, provided a *dhuṭ* sound follows. Examples: *akṛta*, *akṛthāḥ*, *samasthita*, *āhata*.
Why "after a short vowel"? [Consider: *acyoṣṭa*.
The phrase "or after [a root] other than one ending in *iṭ*" is for the sake of ease; by this, we have *avāriṣṭām* and *vyadyotiṣṭa*.
Regarding the rule *iṭaś ceṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.65):
there is elision of the *s-* of *sic* when it follows an augment *iṭ* and is followed by another *īṭ*; thus, *alāvīt* and *akoṣīt*.
What is the purpose of [the condition] "when *iṭ* follows"? [Example: *abhaitsīt*. What is the purpose of [the condition] "when *īṭ* follows"? [Example: *akāniṣam*.
[The rule] *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* [Pāṇini 8.2.29 applies]. *Kātantra* 3.6.54.

The *s* and *k* of a verbal root (*dhātu*) that begins with a conjunct consonant are elided when followed by a *dhūṭ* suffix at the end of a word; as in *āripsate*, *ālipsate*, *ācaṣṭe*, *bhraṣṭā*, and *bhrakṣyati*.
[The *k* is elided] in *tvakṣu* and *tvaṣṭiḥ*; there is no *iṭ* augment before the suffix *ktin*.
The phrase "at the end" (*ante*) is for the sake of subsequent rules; some say that even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), there is a form with the elision of the *yaṅ* suffix, as in *abābhraṭ*.
What is the purpose of the word *skor*? [Examples: *akārṣṭām*, *amārṭ*. What is the purpose of the phrase *dhuṭy-ante*? [Examples: *bhṛjjate*, *ācakṣmahe*.
[The rule] *cavargasya kir asavarṇe* (Kāt. 3.6.55) [applies].
The *k* substitute occurs for the *ca*-class (palatals) when followed by a non-homogeneous *dhuṭ* sound or at the end of a word. Examples:
*vaktā*, *yoktā*, *anenek*, *avevek*. Why "non-homogeneous"? [Observe: *uñchati*, *ujjhati*.
*Ho ḍhaḥ*. (Kāt_3,6.56) The *hakāra* of a verbal root becomes *ḍha* before a *dhuṭ* suffix and at the end of a word: *leḍhā*, *lekṣyati*, *aleṭ*.
*Dāder ghaḥ*. (Kāt_3,6.57) [The *hakāra*] of a root beginning with *da* becomes *gha*.

In place of *h* that is a constituent part of a verbal root beginning with *d*, there occurs *gh* before an affix marked with *ḍh* or at the end of a word; thus, *adhokṣyat* and *adhok*. How [is it explained] in the case of *dogdhā*? It is by virtue of the principle that "the beginning and the end behave as if they were the whole. [Furthermore,] in place of the *h* of the root *nah*, there occurs *dh*; thus, *naddham*. (Pāṇini 8.2.34–36)
The letter *ṣ* becomes *dh* when followed by a *dhuṭ* sound, at the end of a word, or after a vowel: *naddhā*, *natsyati*, *anānat*. *Kāt_3.6.59*:
