For the roots beginning with *bhṛj*, the final letter becomes *ṣ* when followed by a *dhuṭ* sound or at the end of a word: *bhraṣṭā*, *bhrakṣyati*; *sraṣṭā*, *srakṣyati*; *mārṣṭā*, *amārṣṭa*, *mārṣyati*; *yaj* → *yaṣṭā*; *rājṛ* → *rāṣṭiḥ*; *bhrājṛ* → *bhrāṣṭiḥ*.

The root *bhrasj* is here used as an illustration for *bhṛj*; because the irregularity (*nipātana*) is intended to apply specifically to that case, there is optionally [the substitution of *ṛ*] elsewhere than in the case of *saṃprasāraṇa*. Thus: *bhraṣṭā*, *bharṣṭā*; *bhrājanam*, *bharjanam*, *bharjanam*.
But when *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs, it is *bhṛjjati*, *bhṛjjate*.
[And the same applies to] *cha* and *śa*: *Kāt_3.6.60*.
The sound *ṣ* occurs in place of *cha* before a *dhut* consonant or at the end of a word: *praṣṭā*, *prakṣyati*, *kroṣṭā*, *krokṣyati*, *acokroṭ*.
There is an alternative reading [of the rule] because of the absence of a specific cause.
A word that has been mentioned with a masculine form is treated like the masculine when followed by the suffixes *āya* and *ī*: Kāt_3.6.61.

That which has been stated as masculine becomes like the masculine when followed by *āy* (the suffix of the denominative verb). For example: *brāhmaṇīvācarati* [she behaves like a Brāhmaṇī] becomes *brāhmaṇāyate*; *śyenī* [a female hawk] becomes *śyetāyate*; *hariṇī* [a female deer] becomes *haritāyate*; *enī* [a spotted cow] becomes *etāyate*; *lohinī* [a red cow] becomes *lohitāyate*. According to the rule *nadādau*, the *t* of these words—*śyeta*, *eta*, *harita*, and *lohita*—is replaced by *na*. However, this does not apply in the sense of the *cv*-suffix because of its secondary (*gauṇa*) nature; thus, according to others, *alohinī lohinī bhavati* [that which was not red becomes red] results in *lohinīyate*. The term *puṃvat* ("like the masculine") means "a woman is like a man," which is established by common worldly usage. In this context, by the force of the governing heading (*adhikāra*), even the non-primary neuter is treated as "like the masculine"; therefore, *atinūyate* [he behaves excessively like a man].

The term *pumān* (man) is used here because it has been spoken in that sense according to the rules of compound formation (*samāsa*). [Thus] one acts like a *droṇa*. How is it that one says *śvaśrūyate*? Because of the irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the word for mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*) ends in a long vowel (*ūṅ*). One’s being a mother-in-law is not merely the state of being a relative (*āptībhāvatva*), but rather a specific conventional meaning (*rūḍha*).
How is it that rice is said to "conceive" (*garbhīyate*)? It is by intending to express the mere fact of its being contained within.

*Ād ātāmāthām āder iḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.4.106) After an *a*-vowel, the initial sound of the suffixes *ātām* and *āthām* becomes *i*. For example: *pacetām*, *pacethām*. Why is it said "after an *a*-vowel"? [Consider: *vyatyapātām*.
Regarding *āte* and *āthe*: according to Pāṇini 7.1.6, the initial vowel of these two suffixes (*āte* and *āthe*) becomes *i* when they follow an *a*-vowel; thus, *pacete* and *pacethe*.

Because the rule is stated using the unmodified forms (*avikṛtanirdeśāt*), there is no modification in the accent (*svara*). This phrase "and so forth" (*iti caivamprakāre*) is to be understood as applying here as well; therefore, in the case of *pacāvahe āvām*, there shall be no modification of the accent.

Regarding the word *yā* [in the sense] of the seventh case: according to Kāt_3.6.64, the vowel *i* (ir) is substituted for the word *yā* following an *a*-vowel in the seventh case; as in *paceḥ*, *pacetām*, *paceyuḥ*. Why "following an *a*-vowel"? [Consider: *adyāt*.
*yāmyusor iyamiyusau* (Kāt_3.6.65). After the vowel *a*, the suffixes *yām* and *yus* become *iyam* and *iyus* respectively; for example, *paceyam* and *paceyuḥ*.
How is it that [the forms] *āha*, *āhatuḥ*, *āhuḥ*, *āttha*, and *āhathuḥ* occur? [They occur] because in the five roots beginning with *brū*, these are optionally treated as substitutes (*nipāta*).
Likewise, from the root *vid*, [the forms are]: *vidanti* (in the nine cases), *veda*, *vidatuḥ*, *viduḥ*, *vettha*, *vidathuḥ*, *vida*, *veda*, *vidva*, *vidma*.
According to Kāt. 3.6.66, there is lengthening for *śam* and others before *yan*:
there is lengthening for *śam* and others when *yan* follows; thus, *śāmyati*, *dāmyati*.

The group beginning with *śam* and ending with *mad*. Why [is the rule] "yan" mentioned? [To show that it does not apply here: *śamyate*. *Kāt_3.6.67*: For these roots—*ṣṭhivu*, *klam*, and *ācam*—a long vowel occurs before the suffix *ani*: *ṣṭhīvati*, *klāmati*, *ācāmati*.
What is the purpose of the particle *āṅ*? [Examples: *vicamati*, *camati*.
Regarding the rule *kramaḥ parasmai* (Kāt.
3.6.68): the root *kram* undergoes vowel lengthening before a suffix marked with *ṅ* when it is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*; thus, *krāmati*.

How is it that *krāma* [is formed]? Because of the elision of *her*. Why [specify] "from what follows" (*parasmāt*)? [To exclude cases such as] *parākramate* and *upakramate*. [The suffix] *cha* is applied to the root *gam* when it is about to be used [in the future]. (Pāṇini 3.1.69)
The general rule applies; for these [roots], *cha* is substituted for the final [consonant] when followed by the suffix *ani*: *gacchati*, *saṃgacchate*, *icchati*, *yacchati*, *āyacchate*.
For the root *pā*, *piba* is substituted when followed by the suffix *ani*: *pibati*. (Kāt. 3.6.70)
In the case of *adanta* (ending in a vowel) or when *ani* follows a verbal root ending in *ū*, what [is the result]? *pai* becomes *ovai*; *pāyati*. *ghra* becomes *jighra*:
according to Pāṇini 3.1.67, when *ani* follows the root *ghrā*, the substitution *jighra* occurs; thus, *jighrati*.
*dhma* becomes *dham*. According to Kāt 3.6.72, the substitution of *dham* occurs for the root *dhmā* when followed by the suffix *ani*; thus, *dhamati*.
*stha* becomes *tiṣṭha*. According to Kāt 3.6.73.
When the suffix *ani* follows the verbal root *sthā*, it undergoes the substitution *tiṣṭhā*; thus, *tiṣṭhati*.
When the suffix *ani* follows the verbal root *mnā*, it undergoes the substitution *manā*; thus, *manati*.
*dāṇ* becomes *yaccha*. (Kāt 3.6.75) When the suffix *ani* follows the root *dāṇ*, the substitution *yaccha* occurs; [thus] *yacchati*. *dṛś* becomes *paśya*. (Kāt 3.6.76)
When the suffix *ani* follows, the substitute *paśya* occurs for the root *dṛś*; thus, *paśyati*.
For the root *ṛ*, the substitute *ṛccha* occurs; thus, *ṛcchati*.
(Kātantra 3.6.77) When the suffix *ani* follows, the substitute *ṛccha* occurs for the root *ṛ*; thus, *ṛcchati*.

The [term] *tivr* is for the purpose of specification alone. Regarding the root *sṛ*: according to Pāṇini 6.4.122 (*sarteḥ* Kāt_3.6.78), when the suffix *ani* follows, the substitute *dhāv* occurs for *sṛ*; thus, *dhāvati*.
But surely the root *dhāv* exists in the sense of "going" as well as in the sense of "running," according to the rule stating that it should be used [in both]; thus, he follows his beloved.
Regarding the root *śad*, there is the substitution of *śīy*:
by the rule *Kāt_3.6.79*, when *ani* follows, the substitute *śīy* occurs for *śad*; thus, *śīyate*.
Regarding the root *sad*: [Kātantra 3.6.80] the substitution of *sīd* occurs for *sad* when followed by the suffix *an*; thus, *sīdati*.
Regarding the root *jan*: [Kātantra 3.6.81] [the substitution of *jā* occurs] before a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).

In place of the verbal root *jan*, the substitute *jā* occurs before a vikaraṇa; thus, from *janī*, we have *jāyate*. However, when the *yaṇ* [substitution] applies, it may optionally become *ya*; thus, *jāyate* or *janyate*. The same applies to the root *jñā*. (Kātantra 3.6.82)

And when the *jñā* root undergoes a verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*), the substitution of *jā* occurs, as in *jānāti*. According to Pāṇini 3.1.73, "pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ," a short vowel is substituted for the roots beginning with *pū* when a verbal suffix follows; thus, *punāti* and *lunāti*.
Because of this [rule], the term *vṛt* is used to exclude roots such as *lvī* and others that begin with *l*.
However, *pūṅ* becomes *pavate* and *mūṅ* becomes *mavate*.
Furthermore, there is *vṛddhi* before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant when it possesses *guṇa*. (Kāśikāvṛtti 3.1.84)

A *vṛddhi* substitute occurs for the *u*-vowel of a verbal root (*dhātu*) when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant that possesses *guṇa*. Thus: *rauti*, *rauṣi*, *raumi*; likewise, *nauti*, *stauti*. How is it so in the case of *juhoti* and *juhotiḥ*? Because of the specific grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*). Why [is there] the mention of "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [To exclude cases such as: *sunoti*, *tanoti*.

There is *guṇa* substitution for the root *ūrṇu*. According to Kāt_3,6.85, it is understood here through the connection with the subsequent rule (*parayogena*): when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant that undergoes *guṇa*, there is optionally *guṇa* substitution for the root *ūrṇu*; thus, *prorṇoti* or *prorṇauti*.
And [this applies] also in the past tense (*hyastanyām*). Kāt_3,6.86.

In the case of the root *ūrṇoti*, when followed by a consonant-initial suffix that undergoes *guṇa* substitution, as well as in the past tense (*hyastanī*), the *guṇa* substitution occurs invariably; thus, *praurṇot* and *praurṇoḥ*.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; therefore, there may optionally be the augment *iṭ*, resulting in *prorṇavitā* or *prorṇuvitā*.
Furthermore, forms such as *praurṇāvīt* or *praurṇuvīt* may also occur.

The augment *iṭ* follows the suffix of the root *tṛh*. Because it is the subject under discussion, "sārvadhātuka" is understood [from the previous rule]. The augment *iṭ* occurs after the suffix of the root *tṛh*, before a sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant that undergoes *guṇa* substitution: *tṛṇeḍhi*, *tṛṇekṣi*, *tṛṇehmi*.
For the root *brū*, the augment *īṭ* is prescribed before the suffix of speech (*vacanādi*). (Kāt. 3.6.87–88)
The root *brū* becomes *īḍ* when followed by a sārvadhātuka affix beginning with a consonant that possesses *guṇa*; thus, *bravīti*, *bravītu*, *abravīt*.
According to some, this also applies after the *carkarīta* (intensive) formation: *bobhavīti* or *bobhoti*.
[In the case of] *as*, [the substitute *bhū* occurs] before *di* and *si*. (Kātantra 3.6.89)
The augment *īṭ* is applied to the beginning of the endings of the second person plural (*di*) and third person singular (*si*) following the root *ās*; thus, *āsīt* and *āsīḥ*.
However, because of their association [with the present tense], it does not apply to *asi* (the second person singular present).
Because the form of the root is indicated by the suffix *tip*, [the augment does not apply there either]; thus, *abhūt*.
Regarding *sic*: According to Pāṇini 3.1.44 (*sicaḥ*), the augment *īṭ* is applied to the beginning of the suffixes *di* and *si* following *sic*; thus, *akārṣīt* and *akārṣīḥ*.
Some maintain that the rule for augments is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), [but one should say] "do not fear."
Kāt_3,6.91: After the roots beginning with *rud*, the augment *īṭ* is applied to the initial of the suffixes *di* (the second person singular) and *si* (the third person singular).

Examples: *arodīt*, *arodīḥ*; *asvapīt*, *asvapīḥ*; *aśvasīt*, *aśvasīḥ*; *aprāṇīt*, *aprāṇīḥ*; *ajakṣīt*, *ajakṣīḥ*. These five are the roots beginning with *rud*. Kāt_3,6.92: [The augment] *aṭ* is added after the root *ad*.
The augment *aṭ* is placed before the beginning of the second person endings of the two [moods] (the imperative and the injunctive), as in *ādat* and *ādaḥ*.
According to some, it is also applied to roots beginning with *rud*, as in *arodat* and *arodaḥ*.
When *s* follows [the root-final consonant], it is replaced by *t* before a non-sārvadhātuka suffix ending in *se*. (Kāt. 3.6.93)

The *takāra* (t) is substituted for the root-final *s* in the domain of non-ārdhadhātuka suffixes; thus, *jighatsati* and *vatsyati*. Why "in the domain of non-ārdhadhātuka"? [Observe: *vasse* (second person singular imperative). In the case of the root *vac*, when followed by an *aṇ* suffix, the *o* is substituted for the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). (Kātantra 3.6.94)
The *upadhā* vowel of the root *vac* becomes *o* when followed by an *aṇ* suffix; thus, *avocat*, *avocaḥ*.
How is [the form] *pustakavācaḥ* [justified]? Because of the qualification "not being an *asārvadhātuka*" [suffix]; the same applies in subsequent cases.
For the root *as*, the final [element] is *stha*; [Kātantra 3.6.95].
The [substitute] *as* occurs in place of *asyati* when it is internal, provided that an *aṇ* follows; for example, *apāsthat*.
For *pateḥ*, there is *paptiḥ*: according to Pāṇini 6.4.125, *papti* occurs in place of *pati* when an *aṇ* follows; for example, *apaptat*.
It should be stated that [the substitution occurs] after *śvi*: *aśvat*.
Regarding *kṛp*, *r* becomes *l*: Kāt_3.6.97 states that the *repha* (the letter *r*) of *kṛp* becomes *lakāra* (the letter *l*); thus: *kalptā*, *kalpayati*, *kalpaḥ*.

How is this established? Regarding the rule "kḷptaḥ," one might say that the hearing of *l* is prescribed in place of the hearing of *r*. However, here, when the *l*-sound residing in the *ḷ*-vowel arises from the *r*-sound residing in the *ṛ*-vowel—which is not of the nature of the vowel *a*—it would have to be the *ḷ*-vowel itself, because it is non-different [from the original] due to being the closest analogue (*antaratamya*).

How then is the word *kṛpā* formed? It is so because it is derived through grammatical rules (*lākṣaṇikatvāt*); for words such as *kṛpaṇa* are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes. And [the form *cikīrṣati*] is derived from the root *gṛ* in the intensive (*cekrīyita*) form. (Kātantra 3.6.98)

In the word *girate*, the letter *ra* becomes *la* when followed by the suffix *cekrīyate* (the intensive marker), as in *nijegilyate*, meaning "he swallows contemptuously. Alternatively, before a vowel, [the substitution is optional]. According to Kāt.
3.6.99, the *ra* of *girate* optionally becomes *la* before a following vowel: *girati* or *gilati*; [the nouns] *nigaraṇam* or *nigalanam*.

The form *inaḥ* is derived from the root *nigālyate*, due to the application of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*. The word *galaḥ* refers to a limb of a living being, whereas *garaḥ* refers to poison. Words such as *kapirikā* and others are established through common usage: *kapirikā*, *kapilikā*, *rohiṇī*, *lohiṇī*, *roma*, *loma*, *paryaṅkaḥ*, *palyaṅkaḥ*, *parighaḥ*, *palighaḥ*, *pariyogaḥ*, *paliyogaḥ*, *cūḍā*, *cūlā*, *vaḍabhī*, *valabhī*, *jaḍam*, *jalam*, *jaḍadhiḥ*, *jaladhiḥ*; for *ḍa* and *la* are treated as identical.
Likewise, when there is a prefix (*upasarga*), as in *parāyate*, *palāyate*.
After *ni-* and *dur-*, it may optionally occur: *nirayaṇam* or *nilayanam*; *durayaṇam* or *dulayanam*.
It is not desired when [the prefix] is very remote, as in *pratyayate*.

In the presence of *sa* and *dhva*, a root beginning with a third-class consonant and ending in *gh*, *ḍh*, *dh*, or *bh* undergoes the substitution of a fourth-class consonant at its beginning. (Kāśikā 3.6.100) A constituent part of a root beginning with a third-class consonant and ending in *gh*, *ḍh*, *dh*, or *bh* becomes a fourth-class consonant by virtue of proximity (*āntaratamya*), when followed by *sa* or *dhva*. Examples include: *dudhukṣati*, *adhugdhvam*, *aghukṣata*, *aghūdhvam*, *bubhutsate*, *abhuddhvam*, *dhīpsati*, *bhotsyate*, *nighokṣyate*; these follow from the principle of "treating the initial as the final" (*ādyantavadbhāva*). Why specify "in the presence of *sa* and *dhva*"? [Observe: *didambhiṣati*, *dugdhaḥ*, *dugdhavān*.

The repetition of the word *dhātu* here is for the sake of clarity. [Kātantra 3.6.101 states: "When *di* and *si* are elided, the third letter onwards of a verbal root ending in *gh*, *ḍh*, *dh*, or *bh*, as well as the first letter, undergoes substitution by the fourth letter. This occurs when *di* and *si* are elided, as in *adhok*, *ajoghoṭ*, and *abobhīt*.

Why [is it specified] "of a *dasyu*"? [Consider: *adhugdhāḥ*; because this depends on the phoneme (*varṇāśrayatvāt*), there is no application of the rule concerning the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇa*).

And [the rule applies] to *dadhāti* after *t* and *th*, as well as in *sadhva*. (Kātantra 3.6.102): For the root *dadhāti*, when it ends in *dh*, the fourth letter [the retroflex *dh*] is substituted for the initial [dental *d*], when *t* and *th* follow, as well as in *sadhva*: *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*, *dhatse*, *dhaddhve*.
Why [is it specified] "of that which ends in a dh"? [Examples: *dadhāti*, *dadhāsi*.
Thus ends the sixth quarter on verbal conjugation in the commentary by Daurgasimhi.
[Sūtra: The augment *iṭ* is added to the beginning of an *asārvadhātuka* suffix that begins with a consonant and does not begin with the letter *y*. (Kāt_3.7.1)

The augment *iṭ* is added to the beginning of an *asārvadhātuka* suffix prescribed after a verbal root (*dhātu*), provided that the suffix begins with a consonant and does not begin with the letter *y*. Examples: *bhavitā*, *bhaviṣyati*, *bhavitavyam*. The repetition of the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of including those *asārvadhātuka* suffixes that depend upon the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a root; thus, it applies to forms such as *gṛhṇāti*, *vṛṇoti*, *jugupsate*, and *mīmāṃsate*. Why specify "of an *asārvadhātuka* [suffix]"? Consider *śete* and *vetti*. (In these cases, the suffixes are *sārvadhātuka*.)

The letter *ṭ* serves a specific purpose in rules such as *ṭakāra iṭi ca* (Kāt. 3.4.28). Why is it said "beginning with a consonant"? [Consider: *babhūva*. Why is it said "not beginning with the vowel *a*"? [Consider: *bhūyāt*.

Regarding *snū* and *krami* in the context of the *parasmaipada*: according to Pāṇini 7.2.36 (*snukramibhyāṃ parasmaipade*), an augment *iṭ* is added to the beginning of a consonant-initial *asārvadhātuka* suffix that does not begin with *yak*, following those two roots (*snū* and *krami*) when they occur in the domain of the *parasmaipada*. Examples: *prasnavitā*, *prasnaviṣyati*; *kramitā*, *kramiṣyati*; *cikramiṣati*.

Because of the restriction "only in the domain of the *parasmaipada*," [the augment does not apply in the *ātmanepada*]: *vyatisnoṣyate*, *pracikraṃsate*, *upacikraṃsate*. Furthermore, *krami* follows *pra* and *upa* as a verb belonging to the *rucādi* group when expressing the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*).
The suffix *iṭ* [is applied] because the objects [of the two roots] are not identical: one must ask (*prasnavitavyam*) and the other must proceed (*prakramitavyam*).

How is it that [the forms] *prakrāntā* and *upakrāntā* [are formed]? There is a prohibition of *iṭ* for the root *kram*, which has the *ātmanepada* as its scope, when used in the active voice (*kartari*) with a *kṛt* suffix. [In the case of *prasnavitrīyate*: "he acts like one who asks" (*prasnavitrīyate*); here, the suffix *āyi* is *ātmanepadi*.

*rudādeḥ sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 7.2.76). After the verbal root *rud* and the others of that class, when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant and not having the letter *y*, the augment *iṭ* is placed at the beginning. Thus: *roditi*, *ruditaḥ*; *svapiti*, *svapitaḥ*; *śvasiti*, *śvasitaḥ*; *prāṇiti*, *prāṇitaḥ*; *jakṣiti*, *jakṣitaḥ*.
As for the form *rudyate*, since there is the substitution of *ra* [for the *ru* of the root], it ought to become *ryaṇ* [by the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*].
*roditi*, *svapiti*, *śvasiti*, *prāṇiti*, and *jakṣiti* should be known as the five-membered class beginning with *rud*. (Kāt.
3.7.4) *īśaḥ* [is also included]. *se*. (Kāt. 3.7.4)
The augment *iṭ* is placed at the beginning of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix that begins with *s*. Thus: *īśiṣe*, *īśiṣva*.
[Also] after *īḍ* and *jan*, and before *sadhve*: Kāt_3.7.5.

After *īḍ* and *jan*, the augment *iṭ* is placed at the beginning of a following *sārvadhātuka* suffix that begins with *s*. Thus: *īḍiṣe*, *īḍiṣva*, *īḍidhve*, *īḍidhvam*; *vyatijajñiṣe*, *vyatijajñdhve*, *vyatijñidhvam*.
In the case of *jana* (the root √jan), [the substitution of *śnā* for *śap*] does not apply because it is separated by *janī*.
Since *sadhve* is also recited in the rule, the word *īśi* is drawn forward by the particle *ca*; thus we have *īśidhve* and *īśidhvam*.
[The suffix *se* is substituted for the final vowel of the root] *gam* when followed by a Parasmaipada ending. (Kātantra 3.7.6)
The augment *iṭ* is applied after that *gam* which belongs to the *parasmaipada*; for example: *gamiṣyate*, *jigamiṣati*, *adhijigamiṣa tvam*, *jigamiṣā*, *jigamiṣuḥ*, *jigamiṣitavyam*.
Why specify "of the *parasmaipada*"? [To exclude cases such as: *adhijigāṃsate*, *saṃgaṃsīṣṭa*.
Some divide the rule and desire the *iṭ* even in the *ātmanepada*; according to their opinion, there are forms such as *saṃjigamiṣuḥ* and *adhijigamiṣitavyam*.
Some say that *aniṅgama* means "one who has accomplished [his goal]," while others say it means "one who desires to learn.

*Kāt_3.7.7*: After the root *han* and after a root ending in *ṛ*, the augment *iṭ* is added at the beginning of the suffix *sya*. Thus: *haniṣyati*, *haniṣyamāṇaḥ*; *kariṣyati*, *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*; *svariṣyati*, *svariṣyamāṇaḥ*; *asvariṣyat*.
Regarding *añjeḥ sici* (Pāṇini 7.2.71): after the root *añj*, the augment *iṭ* is applied at the beginning of the suffix *sic*. Thus, we have *āñjīt* and *āñjiṣṭām*.
Since the root has an *u*-indicatory letter (*ud-anubandha*), an option would otherwise apply; this rule is stated to ensure the augment is obligatory.

*Kāt_3.7.9*: After the roots *stu*, *sudhū*, and *bhyaḥ* (the root *dhāv*), when followed by the *sic* suffix in the *parasmaipada* voice, the augment *iṭ* is inserted at the beginning. Examples: *prāstāvīt*, *prāsāvīt*, *prādhāvīt*. Why "in the *parasmaipada*"? [Observe: *prāstoṣṭa*, *prāsoṣṭa*, *prādhoṣṭa*.
The root *dhūñ* also means "to shake"; [its aorist form is] *adhāvīt*.

According to Pāṇini 3.1.45 (*yamiraminamyādantānāṃ sir antaś ca*), for these roots ending in long *ā*—namely *yami*, *rami*, *nami*, and those ending in long *ā*—the augment *iṭ* is added to the beginning of the *sic* suffix when used with the *parasmaipada* endings, and *sic* itself becomes the final element [of the stem].

Thus: *ayaṃsīt*, *vyaraṃsīt*, *anaṃsīt*, *ayāsīt*, *ayāsiṣṭām*, *amlāsīt*, *amlāsiṣṭām*, *adaridrāsīt*, *adaridrāsiṣṭām*. Because of the mention of the word "final" (*anta*) in the rule, there is no elision of the vowel *ā* in the root *daridrāti*.

How is it that *adaridrīt* and *adaridriṣṭām* are formed? Because the augment (*āgama*) is not mandatory, there is an optionality. According to Pāṇini 7.2.74 (*smiṅpūṅranjvaśūkṝgṝdṛdhṛpracchāṃ sani*), when the desiderative suffix (*san*) follows these roots, the augment *iṭ* is placed at the beginning: for *smiṅ*, it becomes *sismayiṣate*.
*pūṅ*: *pipaviṣate*; *pūñ-stu*: *pupūṣati*. *ṛ*: *aririṣati*. *añj-ṛ*: *añjijiṣati*.
aśū, aśiśiṣate;
kṝ, cikariṣati;
gṝ, jigariṣati.
*dr̥ś* (to see): *didarśiṣate*. *dhṛṅ* (to stand firm): *didhariṣate*.
*pracch* (to ask): *pipr̥cchiṣati*.

The roots *kṝ*, *gṝ*, and *dhṛ* belonging to the *tudādi* class, as well as *kṝñ* in the sense of "injury," [form their desiderative bases as follows]: from *kṝ* (to injure), *cikariṣati*; from *kṝ* (to wish), *cikīrṣati*.
From *gṝ* (to sound), *jigariṣati* and *jigīrṣati*.
From *dhṛñ* (to hold), *didhariṣati* and *didhīrṣati*.
Because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for *kṝ* and *gṝ* possesses conceptual differentiation (*savikalpatva*), [the rule] would indeed apply to other roots ending in *ṝ*.

How is it that we have *prāvuvūrṣate*, *prāvivariṣate*, *saṃvuvūrṣati*, and *saṃvivariṣati*? It is because the mention of *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ* with the negative particle (*nañ*) indicates that [the rule] is not universal. For the roots *ṝ*, *vṛṅ*, and *vṛñ*, there may optionally be [the substitution of *iṭ*] before the suffix *san*, as well as before the *ātmanepada* endings, the *sic* aorist, and the benedictive (*āśis*).
The augment *suṭ* should be stated as being optionally applied to the vowel following a conjunct consonant; it is not established because it is external.
Thus: *tṝ*—*atariṣṭa*, *avṛta*, *variṣīṣṭa*, *vṛṣīṣṭa*.
*vṛ*—*avariṣṭa*, *avṛta*, *variṣīṣṭa*, *vṛṣīṣṭa*.

*dhvṛ*: *adhvariṣṭa*, *adhvṛta*, *dhvariṣīṣṭa*, *dhvṛṣīṣṭa*. *samskṛta*, *saṃskṛṣīṣṭa*; "that which is external is unestablished [in the presence of] that which is internal. The long vowel for *iṭ* occurs after *grah* except in the periphrastic future (*aparokṣā*). (Kāt_3.7.12)

The vowel of the root *grah* becomes long before a following *iṭ*, but not in the *parokṣā* (perfect tense); thus, [the forms] *gṛhītā* and *agrahīt* [are derived]. Because of the presence of *iṭ*, there would be the elision of *sic*, and for this [root], the lengthening would not occur.
How then [are the forms] *grāhitā* and *grāhiṣyate* [formed]? [They are formed] because the *iṭ* beginning with *ij* is not explicitly heard [as part of the suffix].
What is the purpose of the condition "in the non-perceptual (aparokṣā)"? [Consider: *jagṛhiva*, *jagṛhima*.

By the rule "the long vowel of *ṝ*, *vṛ*, and *vṛñ* does not occur in the non-perceptual or the benedictive (*āśis*), nor after *iṭ*," and by the splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "it is not taught [to occur] in the *sic* of the parasmaipada," [the long vowel is excluded].

*tṝ*: *taritā*, *tarītā*. *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*: *varitā*, *varītā*. But in the sense of "avoiding" (*varjana*), [the forms are] *viśaśariva*, *viśaśarima*, *vavaritha*; [in the benedictive: *tariṣīṣṭa*, *variṣīṣṭa*; [in the aorist: *atāriṣṭām*, *avāriṣṭām*.
A non-ṅit sārvadhātuka suffix following a root ending in *ā* that consists of a single syllable is *aniṭ*.
(Kāśikā 3.7.13) After a root consisting of a single syllable and ending in the vowel *ā*, a non-sārvadhātuka suffix is *aniṭ*; for example: *dātā*, *dāsyati*, *dātavyam*.
Why specify "consisting of a single syllable"? [Consider: *daridritā*.

The augment *iṭ* shall not be applied after roots beginning with *vṛt* when the *ātmanepada* endings are used, nor before the suffix *sya*, nor before the suffix *san*, nor in the periphrastic future (*śvastanī*). Furthermore, it is never applied to *kṛp* in those cases, nor to roots beginning with *kṛt* before the suffix *sa* (the desiderative marker) when followed by *asic*. For example: from *vṛt*, we have *vartsyati* (he will turn) and *vivṛtsati* (he wishes to turn).
vṛdhu: vartsyati, vivṛtsati. śṛdhu: śartsyati, śiśṛtsati. syandū: syantsyati, sasyantsati.

From the root *kṛp* (to be fit): *kalpsyati*, *cikḷpsati*, *kalptāsi*; for *kṛp*, there is optionally the status of belonging to the *rucādi* group in the periphrastic future (*śvastanī*). From *kṛtī* (to cut): *kartsyati*, *kartiṣyati*.
Likewise from *cṛtī* in the sense of injury: *cartsyati*, *cartiṣyati*.
uchṛdir: chartsyati, chardiṣyati; utṛdir: tartsyati, tardiṣyati;
nṛtī: nartsyati, nartiṣyati.
What is the meaning of *asicīt*? It means *akartīt*. [The rule] states:

*ivarṇād aśviśriḍīṅśīṅaḥ* (Kāt. 3.7.14). An *asārvadhātuka* suffix following a monosyllabic root ending in an *i*-vowel—excluding the roots *śvi*, *śri*, *ḍīṅ*, and *śīṅ*—is *aniṭ* (lacks the augment *iṭ*). For example: *cetā*, *ceṣyati*; *netā*, *neṣyate*.

Why [specify] *aśvi-śri-ḍīṅ-śīṅ*? [Because otherwise the rule would apply to: *śvi*—*śvayitā*; *śri*—*śrayitā*; *ḍīṅ*—*ḍayitā*; *śīṅ*—*śayitā*. Why [specify] *ekasvarāt* ("from a monosyllabic root")? [Because otherwise it would apply to: *ādīdhitā*, *āvevitā*. [The suffix *tṛc* follows roots ending in] *u*, except for *yū*, *ru*, *ṇu*, *snū*, *kṣū*, and *kṣṇu*. (Kātantra 3.7.15)

An *asārvadhātuka* suffix that does not take the augment *iṭ* follows a verbal root ending in the vowel *u*, consisting of a single syllable, provided it is not one of the roots *yu*, *ṛ*, *ṇu*, *snū*, *kṣu*, or *kṣṇu*. For example: *hotā*, *stotā*.
Why specify "not *yu*, *ṛ*, *ṇu*, *snū*, *kṣu*, or *kṣṇu*"? Consider: *yavitā*, *ravitā*, *navitā*, *snavitā*, *kṣavitā*, *kṣṇavitā*.
Why specify "ending in *u*"? Consider: *lavitā*.
What is the purpose of the condition "from a monosyllabic root"? [Consider: *prorṇavitā*.
[The rule] *ṛto ’vṛṅvṛñaḥ* (Kātantra 3.7.16) states:
after a monosyllabic root ending in *ṛ*, excluding the roots *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, a non-sārvadhātuka suffix is without the augment *iṭ*; for example, *kartā*, *hartā*.
Why [is it specified] "from the roots vṛ and vṛñ"? [Consider] *varitā*.
Why [is it specified] "after the vowel ṛ"? [Consider] *kṝ* (to scatter), [as in] *karitā*.
Why [is it specified] "from a monosyllabic root"? [Consider] *jāgaritā*.

After the root *śak*, following a *kā* vowel, there is no augment *iṭ*. (Kāt 3.7.17) After the roots *śak* (*śakḷ*), *pac*, *vac*, *sic*, *ric*, *ric*, and *muc*, there is also no augment *iṭ*. (Kāt 3.7.18) *śaktā*, *śakṣyati*.
*pac*, *vac*, *sic*, *ric*, *ric*, *muc*, and [the others]. (Kāt 3.7.18)
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these five roots: *ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking (*pāke*), or *paca* in the sense of making manifest (*vyaktīkaraṇe*); [the agentive noun] is *paktā*.
[From] *vac* or *vaci*, [the agentive noun is] *vaktā*.
[From] *sica*, [the agentive noun is] *sektā*.
The suffix *Kta* is applied after the roots *ric* (to leave) and *muc* (to release), provided that *cha* follows [the root] in the case of *pracch*. Kāt_3.7.19.

After a root ending in a consonant (*śānta*), the suffix *aniṭ* occurs: *praṣṭā*, *prakṣyati*. [The suffix *aniṭ* occurs] after *yuj*, *ruj*, *rañj*, *bhuj*, *bhañj*, *sañj*, *tyaj*, *hrasj*, *yaj*, *masj*, *sṛj*, *nij*, *vij*, and *svañj*. (Kāśikā 3.1.20) After these fifteen roots, the suffix *aniṭ* occurs; for example, from *yujir* (to join), *yoktā*.
ruj, roktṛ; rañj, raṅktṛ;
bhuj, bhoktṛ.
bhaja, bhaktā; bhanja, bhaṅktā;
sanja, saṅktā.
tyaja, tyaktā;
bhrasja, bhraṣṭā;
yaja, yaṣṭā.
ṭumasj, one who bathes; sṛj, one who emits;
nijir, one who cleanses.
The suffix *tṛc* is applied after the roots *vijir*, *vektṛ*, but not after *ovijī*, due to the strength of the indicatory vowel *ī*.
After *svañj*, it is *svaṅktṛ*.

[The suffix *tṛc*] is applied after the roots *ad*, *tud*, *nud*, *kṣud*, *svid*, *vidyati*, *vidyati*, *vindati*, *vinakti*, *chid*, *bhid*, *had*, *śad*, *sad*, *pad*, *skand*, and *khid*; this is according to Kātyāyana 3.7.21.
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these sixteen roots:
*ada*, *attā*; *tuda*, *tottā*.
nuda, nottā;
kṣudir, kṣottā; svida, svettā.
*vida* in the sense of existence (*sattā*), *vidḷ* in the sense of obtaining (*lābha*), or *vida* in the sense of discerning (*vicāra*): [the agent is] *vettā*.
*chidir*: *chettā*. *bhidir*: *bhettā*.
*hadá*, *hattá*; *śadlá*, *śattá*;
*padá*, *pattá*.
*skandir*, *skanttā*; *khida* in the sense of dejection (*dainya*) or obstruction (*parighāta*), *khettā*;
after the roots *rādhi*, *rudhi*, *krudhi*, *kṣudhi*, *bandhi*, *śudhi*, *sidhyati*, *budhyati*, *yudhi*, *vyadhi*, and *sādhi*, [the suffix] *dhak* [is applied]. (Kāt_3.7.22)
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these eleven [roots]:
*rādha*, *rāddhā*;
*rudhir*, *roddhā*.
krudha, kroddhā;
kṣudha, kṣoddhā;
bandha, banddhā.
śudha, śoddhā;
sidha, seddhā; budha in the sense of understanding, boddhā.
*yudh*, *yoddhṛ*;
*sādh*, *sāddhṛ*.
[The suffix] *nāt* follows the root *han* when it is preceded by *manya*. (Pāṇini 3.2.23)
After these two [roots], the suffix *ani* is applied: from *han*, *hantā*;
from *man* (in the sense of knowing), *mantā*.
How is it that [the form] *avadhīt* occurs? This [root] does not end in *n*.

Kāśikāvṛtti 3.1.24: After the eleven roots *āp*, *pi*, *piṣ*, *svap*, *vapi*, *śap*, *chup*, *kṣip*, *lip*, *lup*, and *sṛp*, the suffix *an* (forming the past passive participle) is applied without the augment *iṭ*.
From *āpḷ*: *āpta*.
*Tapta* means heated by heat, smoke, or distress, or heated by power;
[from the root] *tipṛ*, it is *teptā*;
[from the root] *ñisvapa*, it is *svaptā*.
ḍuvapa, vaptā;
śapa, śaptā;
chupa, choptā.
*kṣip*, *kṣeptṛ*; *lip*, *leptṛ*; *lup*, *loptṛ*.
The root *sṛp* [forms] *sarptā*.

How then [is it that] *tarptā* and *darptā* [are formed]? Because they belong to the *radhādi* group, the augment *iṭ* is optional. [The augment *iṭ* is applied] after the roots *yabh*, *rabh*, and *labh*, according to Kātantra 3.7.25.
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these three: *yabdha*, *rabdha*, and *labdha*.
According to Kātantra 3.7.26, *yam*, *ram*, *nam*, and *gam* take *māt*:
the suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these four, namely *yantṛ*, *rantṛ*, *nantṛ*, and *gantṛ*.
*Kāt_3.7.27*: After these ten roots—*riś*, *ruś*, *kruś*, *liś*, *viś*, *diś*, *dṛś*, *spṛś*, *mṛś*, and *daṃś*—the suffix *niṭ* does not occur.
*Riś* and *ruś* mean "to injure": [the agentive forms] *reṣṭā* and *roṣṭā*.
*krūśa*, *kroṣṭā*;
*liśa*, *leṣṭā*;
*viśa*, *veṣṭā*.
diś, deṣṭṛ; dṛś, draṣṭṛ;
spṛś, spraṣṭṛ.
After the roots *mṛś*, *danś*,
and those ending in the sibilant *ṣ*—
namely *dviṣ*, *puṣ*, *tṛṣ*, *śliṣ*, *tviṣ*, *piṣ*, *viṣ*, *śiṣ*, *śuṣ*, *tuṣ*, and *duṣ*— [the suffix *kta* takes the substitute *ṣṭhā*]. (Kātantra 3.7.28)
The suffix *ani* occurs after these eleven roots.
From *dviṣ*: *dveṣṭā*. From *puṣ*: *poṣṭā*.
He plows or causes to plow; he will plow.
He clings; he will cling. He flashes; he will flash.
piṣḷ, peṣṭā;
viṣḷ, veṣṭā;
śiṣḷ, śeṣṭā.
The suffix *sāt* is applied after the roots *śuṣ*,
*duṣ*,
and *vasati-ghas*. (Kātantra 3.7.29)
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these two [roots]: *vastā* and *jighatsati*.
This is not [the case] for *dānta*.
[The suffix *aniṭ* occurs] after *dah*, *dihi*, *duh*, *mihi*, *rihi*, *ruhi*, *lihi*, *luhi*, *nahi*, and *vahi*, when followed by *vā*. (Kātantra 3.7.30)
The suffix *aniṭ* occurs after these ten roots:
*daha*, *dagdhā*; *diha*, *degdhā*.
duh, dogdhā;
miha, meḍhā;
riha, reḍhā.
ruha, roḍhā; liha, leḍhā;
luha, loḍhā.
*naḍ*, *naddhā*;
*vah*, *voḍhā*. Some do not read *rihi* and *luhi* at all as roots listed in the *sūtra*.
Regarding the roots *grah* and *guh* with the suffix *san*: according to Kāśikā 3.7.31, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after *grah* and *guh* when followed by *san*.
Thus, from *grah*, we have *jighṛkṣati*;
from *guhū*, we have *jughuksati*.

And [the suffix] *iṭ* does not occur after a verbal root ending in an *u*-vowel. (Kāśikā 3.1.35) The mention of the "vowel" (*varṇa*) is for the sake of including the roots *ru*, *nu*, *snū*, *kṣū*, and *kṣṇū*.
Thus: *rurūṣati*, *nunūṣati*, *susnūṣati*, *cukṣūṣati*, *cukṣṇūṣati*, *lulūṣati*, *pupūṣati*.

Kāt_3.7.33: For these roots—those ending in *i*, as well as *bhrajj*, *danbhu*, *śri*, *ūrṇu*, *bhṛ*, *jñapi*, *san*, *tan*, *pat*, and *daridrā*—the augment *iṭ* is optionally not applied before the suffix *san*. [Examples: *ivanta*:
*dideviṣati*, *dudyūṣati*.
From *ṛdh*: *ardidhiṣati*, *īrtsati*.
From *bhrasj*: *bibhrajjiṣati*, *bibhrakṣati*.
From *danbhu*: *didambhiṣati*, *dhitsati*, *dhopsati*.
From the root *śri*: *śiśrayiṣati*, *śiśrīṣati*.
From *yu*: *yiyaviṣati*, *yuyūṣati*. From *ūrṇu*: *prorṇunaviṣati*, *prorṇunūṣati*.
*bhara*, *bibhariṣati*, *bubhūrṣati*; *jñapi*, *jijñapiṣati*, *jñīpsati*; *sanu*, *sisaniṣati*, *siṣāsati*.
*tanu*: *titaniṣati*, *titāṃsati*; *patḷ*: *pipatiṣati*, *pitsati*;
*daridrā*: *didaridriṣati*, *didaridrāsati*.
For the roots *bhrasj*, *bhṛ*, and *yū*, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) where [the rule] was not previously applicable.

For the root *bhū*, when there is elision (*luk*) of the *sij* suffix: Kāt_3.7.34 states that when there is elision of the *sij* suffix after the root *bhū*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur; thus: *abhūt*, *abhūtām*.
Why is it stated "after *sij* and *luk*"? [Example: *vyatyabhaviṣṭa*.

[The rule] "only after *sṛ*, *vṛ*, *bhṛ*, *snū*, *dru*, *su*, and *śvi* in the periphrastic future (*parokṣā*)" (Kāt. 3.7.35) means that the augment *iṭ* does not occur after these roots specifically in the periphrastic future (*parokṣā*). [Examples: from *sṛ*: *sasṛva*; from *vṛñ* and *vṛṅ*: *vavṛvahe*, *vavṛmahe*.
From the roots *ḍubhṛñ* or *bhṛñ*, *babhṛva*;
from *ṣṭuñ*, *tuṣṭuva*;
from *dru*, *dudruva*.
*sru*, *susruva*;

*śru*, *śuśruva*. Why "from these [roots] only"? [Consider] *peciva*, *śekiva*, *dadiva*, *rarandhiva*, *neśiva*. Because they belong to the *radhādi* group, the optional [substitution of *na* for *ta*] is also set aside; some say that because it is subsequent, there is an option, as in *rarandhiva* and *redhva*.
After a root ending in *ṛ*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before the suffix *thal*. For example: *dadhartha*, *jahartha*.
Why specify "before *thal*"? [Observe: *jahriva*, *jahrima*.
Why does it say "from those ending in ṛ"? [Consider] the root *stṝñ*: *tastaritha*.
For roots ending in vowels that are invariably *ātmanepada*, as well as for *sṛj* and *dṛś*, there is optionally *iṭ* in the suffix *thali*;
however, if they are invariably *aniṭ* in the suffix *tṛc*, then for *vṛ*, *vye*, and *ad*, *iṭ* is obligatory in *thali*.
papaktha, pecitha. papātha, papitha. cicetha, cicayitha.
*Sasraṣṭha*, *sasarjitha*;
*dadraṣṭha*, *dadarśitha*.
Because of the specific qualification "that which contains the vowel *a* [in the root] and is invariably *aniṭ*," the substitute *ghaslṛ* is applied for the root *ad*, resulting in *jaghasitha*.
[The substitution of] *ve* occurs for [the root] *vye* in the perfect tense (*uvāya*, *uvayitha*).
Because the root *añj* has the marker *vikalpet* (indicating optional application), [the forms] *ānañjitha*, *vavaritha*, *āritha*, and *vivyayitha* are formed; [likewise] *āditha*.
[This applies] to the root *kṛ* when it is not preceded by the augment *suṭ*. (Kāt. 3.7.37)

The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *kṛñ* when it is not preceded by *asuṭ*, in the *parokṣā* (perfect) tense and in the suffix *thal*; for example: *cakṛva*, *cakṛma*, *cakartha*. Why specify "when not preceded by *asuṭ*" in the case of *iṭ*? [Consider: *saṃcaskariva*, *saṃcaskarima*, *saṃcaskaritha*.

Furthermore, [the augment *iṭ* is not applied] in the future (*syas*), the conditional (*sic*), the benedictive (*āśīḥ*), and the periphrastic future (*śvastanī*), when they have a passive or impersonal sense.
It should be stated that [the suffix] iṭ is applied after roots ending in s, r, h, ṇ, and those with a penultimate vowel (a), as well as after √dṛś.
Thus: ceṣyate, cāyiṣyate; dāsyate, dāyiṣyate. Likewise: aceṣyata, acāyiṣyata.
adāsyata, adāyiṣyata; haniṣyate, ghāniṣyate, ahaniṣyata, aghāniṣyata;
grahīṣyate, grāhiṣyate, agrahīṣyata, agrāhiṣyata.
*drakṣyate*, *darśiṣyate*, *adrakṣyata*, *adarśiṣyata*. Also before *sic*:
*aceṣātām*, *acāyiṣātām*.
avadhiṣātām, aghāniṣātām;
agrahīṣātām, agrāhiṣātām;
adṛkṣātām, adarśiṣātām.
And in the sense of benediction:
*ceṣīṣṭa*, *cāyiṣīṣṭa*;
*dāsīṣṭa*, *dāyiṣīṣṭa*.
*vadhiṣīṣṭa*, *ghāniṣīṣṭa*; *grahīṣīṣṭa*, *grāhiṣīṣṭa*;
*drakṣīṣṭa*, *darśiṣīṣṭa*.
And in the sense of "to be done tomorrow":
*cetā*, *cāyitā*;
*dātā*, *dāyitā*.
The killer, the one who caused to be killed; the grasper, the one who caused to be grasped; the seer, the one who caused to be seen.

The *iṭ* augment would cause the elision of the causative suffix (*kārita*) when the quality of becoming long (*ijvadbhāva*) applies: *kāriṣyate*, *kārayiṣyate*. Similarly, *coriṣyate*, *corayiṣyate*. For roots with the marker *m*, the vowel is always short: *gamiṣyate*.

Regarding *suṭ* [as a prefix] in the sense of adornment (*bhūṣaṇa*) after *sam*, *pari*, and *upa*: Pāṇini 6.1.138 states that when the root *kṛ* follows *sam*, *pari*, or *upa* in the sense of adornment, the augment *suṭ* is inserted at the beginning. Thus:

*saṃskartā*, *saṃcaskāra*, *samaskārṣīt*; *pariṣkartā*, *paricaskāra*, *paryaṣkārṣīt*. It is maintained that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs even when there is no intervention by the augment *aṭ*.

*upaskartā*, *upacaskāra*, *upāskārṣīt*. The same should be stated for *samavāya* (conjunction). It is also seen in senses other than ornamentation and conjunction, as in "this is refined" (*saṃskṛtam*) and "this is impermanent. Regarding the prefix *upa-*, the suffix *suṭ* should be prescribed in the senses of effort (*pratiyatna*), transformation (*vikṛta*), and supplying an ellipsis (*vākyādhyāhāra*). [Examples: *asipatrasyopaskurute* (he polishes the sword-blade); *upaskṛtaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats what has been prepared), meaning he eats what has been transformed; *upaskṛtaṃ jalpati* (he prattles on), meaning he prattles by supplying an ellipsis. Thus ends the seventh section (*pāda*) in the verbal section (*ākhyāta*) of the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.

At the end of a word, the first [consonant] of the *dhuṭ* [class] is substituted. (Kātantra 3.8.1) For *dhuṭ* sounds occurring at the end of a word, the most similar first [consonant] of their respective class is substituted. Examples: *tvannāthaḥ*, *ṣaṇmukhāni*, *jñānabhuṭṭīkanam*, *tacchrutam*, *kakubbhāsaḥ*; these would possess the characteristics of the first consonants of their classes (*varga*). However, because the rule *aleṭ*, *aleḍ*, *āsīt*, *āsīd*, or [the absence of sandhi] at the pause (Kātantra 2.3.62) is an exception (*bādhaka*), the first and third [consonants] are used.

The mention of *pada* is for the purpose of including even a non-initial *liṅga* (consonant); consequently, it would not apply at the end of a verbal root (*dhātu*), as in *vadati* and *edhate*. Why [specify] *dhuṭām* (of the *dhuṭ* consonants)? [Consider] *ahan* and *apacam*. [In these cases,] there is the release [of the aspiration] of the *ra* and *sa* sounds. (Kātantra 3.8.2)
The *visarjanīya* occurs for the *repha* (r) and the letter *sakāra* (s) when they stand at the end of a word, as in *abibhaḥ* and *pacāvaḥ*.
Why "at the end of a word"? [Observe] *bibharti* and *āsmahe*; it is for this very reason that the rule is commenced.

How is it that in *abhinastvam*, *abhinattvam*, *aruṇastvam*, and *aruṇattvam*, the *repha* occurs even though the original form (*prakṛti*) does not contain a *repha*? [Answer: At the end of a word, the substitution of *repha* may optionally occur for the root *dadh-* even when it is not originally a *repha*.

*Ghaḍhadhabhebhyas tathor dho 'dhaḥ.* (Kātantra 3.8.3) After *gha*, *ḍha*, *dha*, *bha*, and *bha*, the *tha* of the suffixes *ta* and *thas* becomes *dha*, but not after the root *dhā*. Examples: *adugdha*, *adugdhāḥ*; *alīḍha*, *alīḍhāḥ*; *abuddha*, *abuddhāḥ*; *alabdha*, *alabdhāḥ*. Why does it say "not after *dha*" (*adhaḥ*)? [Because otherwise it would apply to] *dhattaḥ*, *dhatthaḥ*.
*ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ se*. (Pāṇini 8.2.41) The substitution of *k* occurs for *ṣ* and *dh* when followed by *s*. [Examples: *pekṣyati*, *pipikṣati*, *lekṣyati*, *lilikṣati*.
Why is it said "when followed by *s*" (*se*)? [Counter-examples: *pinaṣṭi*, *leḍhi*.
The *ṭa*-class [substitutes] for the *ta*-class after the *ṣa*-class and the *ṭa*-class. (Kāt.
3.8.5) After the *ṣa*-class and the *ṭa*-class, the *ta*-class is replaced by the *ṭa*-class; as in *vapuṣṭaram*, *vapuṣṭā*, *dveṣṭi*, *dviṣṭaḥ*, *piṇḍḍhi*, *kuṣṇāti*, *īṭṭe*, *līḍhaḥ*, *alīḍhvam*.
Why "after the *ṭa*-class, [the *ṭa*-class]"? To establish forms such as *vaktā* and *papaktha*.
How is *madhulittaraḥ* derived? It is from *madhulit*, because it is the final member [of a compound].
When the suffix *ḍha* follows, there is elision of the *ḍha* and lengthening of the penultimate vowel (Kāt.
3.8.6). When *ḍha* follows, the *ḍha* is elided and the penultimate vowel is lengthened, as in *līḍhaḥ* and *mūḍhaḥ*.

How is it that *leḍhā* and *droḍhā* are formed? Because the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) takes precedence, once the *guṇa* substitution has been applied, there would only be the elision of the *ḍh*.
Due to the fact that the mention of the "penultimate vowel" (*upadhā*) is based on a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), the rule for *ṛ* would not apply; thus we have *vṛhū*, *vṛḍhaḥ*;
*dṛhū*, *dṛḍhaḥ*.

*sahivahor od avarṇasya* (Kāśikā 3.8.7): When *ḍha* follows the roots *sah* and *vah*, there is elision of *ḍha*, and the vowel *o* (*au*) replaces the *a*-vowel [of the root]. Thus: *soḍhā*, *voḍhā*.
How is it that [the forms] *ūḍhaḥ* and *ūḍhavān* occur? Because the *saṃprasāraṇa* [substitution] is both internal (*antaraṅga*) and obligatory (*nitya*).
What is the purpose of mentioning *varṇa* (phoneme)? [It is so that] in *udavoḍhām*, even though there is lengthening of the vowel in *sic*, [the substitution] does not occur.

*Kāt_3.8.8*: "In place of the third [consonant] of *dhuṭ* sounds, when followed by fourths. In the case of verbal roots containing *dhuṭ* sounds, the third [consonant] occurs only when followed by fourths: *dogdhā*, *dviḍṭhi*, *cakāddhi*, *labdhā*.
Because of the restriction "only in the case of four [consonants]," it is suspected that [the rule] applies to both [voiced and voiceless].
*Aghoṣeṣv aśiṭāṃ prathamaḥ* (Kātantra 3.8.9):
when voiceless consonants follow, the first of the *dhuṭ* suffixes that do not contain *ś*, *ṣ*, or *s* occurs; as in *dhokṣi*, *bhettā*, *yuyutsate*, and *āripsate*.
What is meant by "only when not preceded by an *aśit*"? It exists. [The rule] *bhṛjaḥ svarāt svare dviḥ* (Kāt. 3.8.10) states:
after a vowel of the root *bhṛj*, there is reduplication before a following vowel. Thus: *bhṛjī*, *babhrajje*, *babhrajjāte*, *babhrajjire*.
This is the opinion of the Ādyavyākaraṇa school:
"There is lengthening of the vowel before *va* and *ma*" (Kāt 3.8.11).
A long vowel occurs before the suffixes *va* and *ma*: *pacāmi*, *pacāvaḥ*, *pacāmaḥ*; *dīvyāmi*, *dīvyāvaḥ*, *dīvyāmaḥ*.
What does "of this" (asya) refer to? It refers to *dadhvaḥ* and *dadhmaḥ*; if there were a long vowel [in place of the short], then the elision (*lopa*) would not occur.
How then is it explained in the case of *pacamānaḥ* and *apacam*? Because of the association (*sāhacarya*) with the first two vowels, namely *v* and *m*.
[The rule applies] to those ending in vowels before the suffix *san*: Kātantra 3.8.12.

For verbal roots ending in vowels, a long vowel occurs when the suffix *san* follows: *cikīrṣati*, *juhūṣati*, *cicīṣati*, *śiśrayiṣati*, and *bibhaviṣati*. Because these forms are not affected by *guṇa* substitution, the specification "for roots ending in vowels" is stated merely for the sake of convenience.

*Kāt_3.8.13*: "Of the penultimate vowel of *han* and *iṅ-gam*. [The compound] *iṅ-gamaḥ* is formed from *iṅaḥ* and *gamaḥ*. When the suffix *san* follows, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of *han* and *iṅ-gam*. Examples: *jighāṃsati*, *adhijigāṃsate*.
Why specify "*iṅo gama*" (of *iṅ* and *gam*)? [Consider: *saṃjigaṃsate*.
One should say *titāṃsati* or *titaniṣati*. [Pāṇini 6.4.15 states:

"In place of a short vowel (*nāmin*) before *r* or *v*, when followed by a consonant, provided that *kṛ* or *cur* do not follow. Here, the suffix ending in *t* is not a qualifier; rather, when *r* or *v* follows a consonant, there is lengthening of the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel of the root if it is a *nāmin*, but not in the case of *kṛ* or *cur*. Examples: *cikīrṣati*, *bubhūrṣati*, *dīvyati*, *mīvyati*, *kūrdate*, *khūrdate*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "from a verbal root" (*dhātu*)? [Consider: *kurkuraḥ* ("a dog").

How is it that *kurkurīyate* occurs? Because it is a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*). What is the purpose of [specifying] "of a vowel-bearing base" (*nāmin*)? [Consider: *kartā* ("agent"), *bhavyam* ("to be").
Why does it say "except for *ṛ* and *kurchu*"? [Consider: *nṛtyati*.

Why does it say "except for *ṛ* and *kurchu*"? [Consider: *kuryāt*; because of the rule "with respect to the prescription of a long vowel, [the substitute] is not like the original" (*na sthānivat*), [we have] *churyate*. How is it that from the root *rī* in the sense of "scraping," we have *riyatuḥ*?

In the case of the root *vī* in the sense of procreation, as in *vivyatuḥ*, there is a prohibition of reduplication. What is the purpose of the condition "after a consonant"? [Consider] *kirati* and *lunāti*. [Furthermore,] for the *s* of this [root], when followed by the suffix *dau* of the imperfect (*hyastanī*), *t* is substituted. (Kāt. 3.8.15)
In the *hyastanī* (imperfect) tense, when the suffixes *ta* and *tha* follow, the augment *s* is inserted after the root vowel; for example, *acakāt* and *anvaśāt*.

Why specify "in the *hyastanī*"? [To exclude cases such as] *abhaitsīt*, because the suffix *īṭ* is included by the mention of that [suffix]. It should be stated that in the *hyastanī* tense, before the suffix *si*, the augment is optional: *acakāstvam* or *acakāttvam*.

The augment *aṭ* is applied to the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) before the suffixes of the past tense (*hyastanī*), the present tense (*adyatanī*), and the conditional (*kriyātipatti*). In the presence of the past tense (*hyastanī*) and the following suffixes, the augment *aṭ* is added to the beginning of the root: *akarīt*, *akārṣīt*, *akariṣyat*.
Why is it said "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [To show that it does not apply when the root is part of a compound: *nyaviśata*.
*Vṛddhi* is the substitute for the initial vowel of roots beginning with *svara*. (Kāśikā 3.1.46):

For roots beginning with *svara*, when followed by the *hyastanī* (imperfect) and other tenses, *vṛddhi* occurs in place of the initial vowel due to phonetic proximity (*āntaratamya*). Examples: *aidhata*, *aidhiṣṭa*, *aidhiṣyata*. How is it that [the forms] *aijyata*, *aupyata*, and *auhyata* are derived? Because the *aḍ*-augment is internal (*antaraṅga*), *vṛddhi* occurs after the *yaṇ*-substitution, the *saṃprasāraṇa*, and the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) have taken place; or else, the *yaṇ*-substitution and the others are themselves internal operations.
The substitution of *a* for an *a*-vowel [of roots beginning with *a*]. Kāt_3.8.18:

For roots beginning with a vowel, the initial *a*-vowel becomes *ā* when followed by the suffixes of the past tense (*hyastanī*) and so forth; as in *āṭat*, *āṭīt*, *āṭiṣyat*, *āpnot*, *āpat*, *āpsyat*.

Some maintain that the *a*-vowel has all points of articulation (*sarvamukhasthāna*), and because of its closest similarity (*antaratama*) even in part, the mention of "vowel" (*avarṇa*) is made so that not all *vṛddhi* substitutions might apply.

Regarding the root *as* (to be): Kāt_3.8.19 states that in the imperfect tense (*hyastanī*), when there is no *guṇa*, the vowel *a* replaces the [final] *a*-vowel of *as*; thus we have *āstām* and *āsan*. In *vyatyāsta*, even though another [element] follows, the replacement of the *a*-vowel by *ā* is not obstructed by the elision [of the *s*], because it depends solely upon the root *as*. Regarding the root *i* (to go): Kāt_3.8.20 states [that *ya* is substituted for the suffix *liṭ*].
In the following cases, when *ya* follows an *a*-vowel that occurred yesterday (i.e., in the preceding syllable), the substitution of *ā* for the *a* occurs: *āyan*, *adhyāyan*.
Even the *vṛddhi* substitution is superseded by the *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*) which depends solely upon the presence of the vowel *i*.
Why say "when *ya*"? [Consider: *agāt*.

*na māṃāsmayoge*. (Pāṇini 6.4.74) In the presence of *mā* and *mā sma*, the augment *aṭ* does not occur before the aorist (*hyastanī*) and other tenses. For example: *mā bhavān karot* ("May you not do"), *mā sma karot* ("May you not have done"), and *jugupsata smainam aduṣṭabhāvaṃ maivaṃ bhavān akṣatasādhuvṛttaḥ* ("Do not despise this man of pure character; may you not, O one of unimpaired virtuous conduct, act thus"). This is the established view. [Examples: *mā bhavān kārṣīt*, *mā sma kārṣīt*. The mention of *mā sma* is for the purpose of excluding cases where [the root] is joined with a consonant cluster (*saṃyukta*).
Due to association (*sāhacarya*), there would be no *mada*; do not say "you did not see.

*Kāt_3.8.22*: After a verbal root ending in a vowel (*nāmī*), in the forms of the precative (*āśīḥ*), the imperfect (*adyatanī*), and the periphrastic perfect (*parokṣā*), the letter *dha* is replaced by *ḍha*. Examples:
*ceṣīḍhvam*, *kṛṣīḍhvam*, *adhyagīḍhvam*, *samasthiḍhvam*, *tuṣṭuḍhve*, *cakṛḍhve*.
The mention of the suffix *anta* (the ending) is for the sake of including those forms that previously had the name *anta*; by this, [we obtain] *prāvariṣīḍhvam*, *alaviḍhvam*, and *luluviḍhve*.

The rule "of a root" (*dhātoḥ*) is for the sake of making the application non-obligatory because it is based on a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*); therefore, the optionality is established for these roots with the augment *iṭ*: *prāvariṣīḍhvam* / *prāvariṣīdhvam*, *alaviḍhvam* / *alavidhvam*, and also *didīyiḍhve* / *didīyidhve*.
[In the case of] *marj*, [the substitute] *mārj* [is applied]. (Kāt. 3.8.23)
For this root *marj*, the substitute *mārj* occurs: *mārṣṭā*, *mārṣyati*, *amārṭ*, and the root *marj* is present [in these forms].
Why "for *marj*"? [Observe: *mṛṣṭaḥ*. It should be stated that [the substitution] optionally occurs before a vowel that lacks *guṇa*: *parimṛjanti* or *parimārjanti*.
*dhātvādeḥ ṣaḥ saḥ*. (Pāṇini 6.1.64) The *ṣakāra* at the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) becomes *sakāra*. For example: from the root *ṣaha*, *sahate*; from *ṣic*, *siñcati*.
What is the purpose of specifying "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*)? [Consider] *ṣaṭ*, *ṣaṇḍaḥ*. What is the purpose of specifying "of the initial" (*ādeḥ*)? [Consider] *laṣitum*.
How is it that [the word] *ṣaṇḍīyati* is formed? Because it is a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*), and since the root is initiated by a *ya*-suffix, the *ṣakāra* is not part of the root itself.

Based on the grammatical indication in *ṣṭhivuklamvācamāmani* (Kātantra 3.6.67), it is held that after the root *ṣṭhivu*, the letter *ṣ* may optionally be followed by *ṭha*, *ka*, or *pa*. By this, forms such as *ṭeṣṭhīvyate* and *teṣṭhīvyate* are established. It must be stated, however, that this does not apply to the root *ṣvakka*: one says *ṣvakkate*. The roots are taught with an initial *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*) for the purpose of causing the change of *s* to *ṣ* when it stands in the place of a phonetic cause (*nimitta*). In this context, those roots beginning with *sa* and followed by a vowel or a dental (*dantya*) are taught with an initial *ṣ*; these include *ṣmiṅ*, *ṣvidi*, *ṣvadi*, and *ṣvap*, excluding *sṛp*, *sṛj*, *stṝ*, *styai*, *sīkṛ*, and *sekṛ*.
*Kāt_3,8.25*: *ṇo naḥ* (The substitute *na* takes the place of *ṇ*).
The *ṇ* at the beginning of a verbal root becomes *n*. For example: *ṇīñ* (*nayati*), *ṇam* (*namati*).
Why "at the beginning of a verbal root"? [Observe that] *kvaṇati* does not apply.
How is it that *ṇakārīyati* occurs? Because it is a nominal verb (*nāmadhātu*).

Here too, in the case of a root taught with an initial *ṇ* (ṇopadeśa), the spelling with *n* is for the purpose of ensuring the substitution of *ṇ* when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*), even in non-compound forms.
All roots beginning with *n* are taught as having an initial *ṇ*, with the exception of *nṛt*, *nand*, *nard*, *nak*, *nāṭ*, *naṭ*, *nṝ*, *nāth*, and *nādh*.
According to the rule *nimittāt pratyayavikārāgamasthaḥ saḥ ṣatvam* (Kāt. 3.8.26), that *s* which stands in place of a suffix, a modification, or an augment becomes *ṣ* when following such a cause.

This undertaking has the final sound as its object: when following a *nimitta* (causal trigger), a suffix (*pratyaya*), a modification (*vikāra*), or an augment (*āgama*) situated after a vowel (*nāman*) undergoes the change to *ṣ*. First, regarding vowels: *cicīṣati*, *lulūṣati*, *sarpiṣyati*, *dhanuṣyati*.
Regarding consonants: *śakṣyati*, *vivakṣati*.

In *cikīrṣati*, [the *k*] resides in a *vikāra* (substitute); in *siṣeva* and *suṣvāpa*, [the *s*] resides in an *āgama* (augment). In *pariṣkaroti*, [the designation of the whole as the beginning] occurs even though it is in a separate word due to the rule of "behaving like that which possesses the designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) based on explicit statement (*vacana*).
What is the purpose of the rule "occurring after a suffix, a substitute, an augment, or a [verbal] element"? [Examples: *sṛp* (to creep): *sisṛpsati*. *sekṛ* (to sprinkle): *sisekiṣate*.
This is an elaboration of that very word *api* (also).

Likewise, after a prefix, in the case of the roots *su*, *sū*, *styai*, *stu*, and *stobh*, the augment *aṭ* occurs even when there is an intervening vowel: *abhiṣuṇoti*, *abhyaṣuṇot*; *abhiṣuvati*, *abhyaṣuvat*; *abhiṣyati*, *abhyaṣyat*; *abhiṣṭauti*, *abhyaṣṭaut*; *abhiṣṭobhate*, *abhyaṣṭobhata*.

In the case of the roots *sthā*, *sīd*, *sic*, *sañj*, and *svañj*, [the augment *iṭ* is inserted] even when there is an intervening *aṅ* and reduplication: *abh-i-ṣṭhā-syati*, *abhya-ṣṭhāt*, *abhita-ṣṭhau*.
With the army (*senā*), one marches against: *abhi-ṣeṇayati*, *abhya-ṣeṇayati*, *abhya-ṣeṇayat*, *abhi-ṣiṣeṇayiṣati*.
He wards off: *abhi-ṣedhati*, *abhya-ṣedhat*, *prati-ṣiṣedhayiṣati*, *praty-a-ṣedhat*, *prati-ṣiṣedhiṣati*.
He sprinkles, he sprinkled, he will sprinkle.
He clings, he clung, he will cling.
He embraces, he embraced, he will embrace.
[The rule applies] after *sa-* and *adhi-*.
[Examples: niṣīdati, nyaṣīdat, niṣiṣatsati. Why "not after *prati-*"? [Counter-examples: pratisīdati, pratyasīdat, pratisiṣatsati.
Also after *prati* with the root *stambh*:
*pratiṣṭabhnāti*, *pratyaṣṭabhnāt*, *pratitaṣṭambha*.
Likewise: *abhiṣṭabhnāti*, *abhyaṣṭabhnāt*, *abhitaṣṭambha*.

The suffix *kta* with the prefix *ava-* is used in the sense of "relying on" (*aurjityanikaṭāśrayeṣu*), as in: "the wrestler’s reliance" (*mallasyāvaṣṭambhaḥ*), "the army has halted" (*avaṣṭabdhā senā*), and "he remains leaning on his staff" (*daṇḍam avaṣṭabhya āste*).
Why [is the restriction] "in these cases"? Consider: *avastabdho vṛṣalaḥ*; the meaning here is that he is shriveled by the cold.
Furthermore, the suffix *kta* with the prefix *ava-* is used in the sense of "eating" (*bhojane*) when combined with the root *śvan*.

*viṣvaṇati*, *avaṣvaṇati*, *vyaṣvaṇat*, *avāṣvaṇat*, *viṣaṣvāṇa*, *avaṣaṣvāṇa*; the meaning is that he eats with sound. Other [forms] should be understood in the same way. *Kāt_3.8.27*: *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*. After a cause [of change], the *s* of the roots *śās*, *vas*, and *ghas* undergoes the change to *ṣ*. Examples: *śiṣyate*, *uṣyate*, *jakṣatuḥ*.

The rule begins with the words *avikārastha* ("situated in that which is not a modification"). According to Pāṇini 8.3.61 (*stauti-inantayoḥ sani*), when the suffix *san* follows the roots *stu* and *in*, a *s* situated in a suffix, a modification, or an augment that follows a cause [of doubling] becomes *ṣ*, provided it occurs after the roots *stu* and *in* when *san* has undergone the change to *ṣ*. Thus: *tuṣṭūṣati*, *siṣedhayiṣati*, *suṣvāpayiṣati*.
Why does it say "in the case of *stauti* and *aniti*"? [Consider] *sisikṣati* and *susūṣati*. Why does it say "when the state of *ṣa*-hood has occurred"? [Consider] *tiṣṭhāsati* and *suṣupsati*.
How is it that in *soṣupiṣate*, the *ṣa*-hood occurs later in the intensive (*cekrīyita*) form? [Answer: Because the *san* suffix follows after the *ṣa*-hood has already taken place.

In *arthān prati-iṣiṣati*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* would indeed occur because the element *san* follows a cause (*nimitta*) that is not part of a reduplicated syllable (*anabhyāsa-stha*). However, it is not desired for the roots *svid*, *svad*, and *sah* when they are followed by the suffix *in*; thus, we have *sisvedayiṣati*, *sisvādayiṣati*, and *sisāhayiṣati*. By this very same principle, another case is also excluded: likewise, the substitution would not occur after the root *sic* when the *yaṅ* suffix (*cekrīyita*) is applied, as in *sesicyate*.
In the case of the root *śru* with the suffix *sya*, [we have] *abhiśoṣyate*.
In the case of *sedhati* meaning "to go," [we have] *abhisedhayati gām*, which means "he causes the cow to go.
Other [roots] should be understood in the same way.

When there is elision by *luk*, [an operation] caused by a suffix does not take place. (Kāt. 3.8.29) When there is elision by *luk* before a suffix, whatever operation would apply to the base (*prakṛti*) does not occur. The analysis of the compound is: "that which has its elision effected by *luk*. Examples: *aṅgāḥ*, *vaṅgāḥ*, *kaliṅgāḥ*; *pañca*, *kati*; *dugdhe*—here, when the *vikaraṇa* suffix is elided by *luk*, there is no *guṇa* substitution. The word *luki* is used instead of *luglope* for the sake of distinguishing between the two types of elision; therefore, it is determined that when a suffix is elided, the operations conditioned by that suffix still apply. Examples: *abhitta*, *acchitta*. Why say "caused by a suffix"? Consider *parasyāna us*: *udaguḥ*, *aduḥ*.
How many [vowels] are there here? Five.
The rule for vowels (*svaravidhi*) applies when reduplication has occurred due to a cause for reduplication. Kāt_3.8.30:

When a suffix beginning with a vowel follows as a cause for reduplication, and reduplication has been performed either before or after the base, a rule concerning the vowel takes effect in place of that vowel—as in *papatuḥ*, *āṭiṭat*, *jagmatuḥ*, *iyāya*, *nināya*, *ninayitha*, *lulāva*, *lulavitha*, *ninyatuḥ*, *cakratuḥ*.

What is the purpose of the rule "the prescription regarding accent" (*svaravidhi*)? [Consider] *asūṣupat*: when there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel following the *s*, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs afterwards.
What is the purpose of the word "accent" (*svara*)? [Consider] *jeghrīyate*. What is the purpose of the phrase "caused by reduplication" (*dvirvacananimitta*)? [Consider] *dudyūṣati*.
That without which something does not occur is its cause (*nimitta*).
By that rule—"there is reduplication after the suffix *san* when preceded by a vowel"—the form *aririṣati* is established.

How is it that [the forms] *iyeṣa* and *uvoṣa* are formed? There is no status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (substitution of the original element), because of the statement "when [the preceding vowel] is not homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*).

That which is an *anubandha* is non-functional (*aprayogī*). [Kāt. 3.8.31] It is called an *anubandha* because it is "bound on" (*anubadhyate*); "non-functioning" means not being employed (*aprayuktiḥ aprayogaḥ*). That which is an *anubandha* is non-functional; it is not to be pronounced. For example: *iṅ*, as in *adhīte*;
*ḍukṛñ*, as in *kurute*; and others likewise.

*Śiṭ* refers to the *śādi* [consonants]. According to Kāt_3.8.32, the phonemes beginning with *śa* and ending with *ha* are designated by the technical term *śiṭ*. Instances where *śiṭ* is employed include Kāt_3.3.10: *śiṭparo ’ghoṣaḥ*, and others such as these.
The *saṃprasāraṇa* [substitution] consists of *y*, *v*, and *ṛ*, which have the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) as their cause.

(Kāt. 3.8.33) The term *iś-ūś-ṛś* is a *dvandva* compound; the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation. Those *y*, *v*, and *ṛ* whose production has the semi-vowels as their cause are designated by the technical term *saṃprasāraṇa*.
The rules governing *saṃprasāraṇa* include such passages as: "There is *saṃprasāraṇa* of a semi-vowel that follows a vowel" (Kāt. 3.4.1), and so forth.
What is meant by "having internal causes" (*antaḥsthānimitta*)? [In the case of] *sthitaḥ* and *sthitavān*, that long vowel would not be the final [element].

[The rule] *ar pūrve dve sandhyakṣare ca guṇaḥ* (Kāt. 3.8.34) designates as *guṇa* the letter *ar*, the two preceding vowels, and the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*). This is with respect to the first [vowel], namely *ai*, and with respect to the other, namely *au*.
The *guṇa* substitutes for the final vowels of roots and verbal suffixes, as in the rule "there is *guṇa* for the root and the suffix at their junction" (Kāt. 3.5.1), and so forth.
Regarding *ār* and those that follow, there is *vṛddhi*. According to Kāt.
3.8.35, the two diphthongs following *ā*—namely *ār*, *ai*, and *au*—are designated by the technical term *vṛddhi*.
The rules for *vṛddhi* substitution include "vṛddhir ādau saṇe" (Kātantra 2.6.49) and others.
Thus, in the *Daurgasiṃhī-vṛtti*, the eighth section (*pāda*) on verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) is completed.
The section on verbal roots is hereby finished.
The above has not been translated or proofread.
Now, regarding the word *kṛta*:
these [words] are established like trees and the like; they are not created by an author (*kṛtin*), but are *kṛta* (established).
They were created by Kātyāyana for the sake of awakening and re-awakening [the understanding of] grammatical forms.
Regarding the rule *siddhir ijvad ñṇānubandhe* (Kāt_4.1.1):

when a *kṛt* suffix marked with the indicatory letters *ñ* or *ṇ* follows a verbal root, the accomplishment of the grammatical operation as if it were *ij*-vowel substitution is extended [to that root].

In the case of the substitution of *ij*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel and *vṛddhi* for *nāmin* vowels; for the root *han*, there is *gha*; for roots ending in *j* or *dh*, there is shortening; for *kuṭādi* roots, there is *guṇa*.
For roots ending in long *ā*, there is the suffix *āyi*, according to the rule *inīci*.
The short vowel does not occur for roots with *m* as an indicatory letter (*mānubandha*) before the suffix *ic*, either by rule or by explicit statement.
Examples: *pāṭhaḥ*, *pāṭhakaḥ*; *kāraḥ*, *kārakaḥ*; *ghātaḥ*, *ghātakaḥ*; *janaḥ*, *janakaḥ*; *vadhaḥ*, *vadhakaḥ*; *utkoṭaḥ*, *utkoṭakaḥ*; *pāyaḥ*, *pāyakaḥ*.
The mention of "established" (*siddhi*) is for the sake of auspiciousness, because [the author of this section] is a different person [from the author of the preceding rules].
*Hanteḥ taḥ*:

In place of the *n* of the root *han*, a *t* is substituted when a *kṛt* suffix with the markers *ñ* or *ṇ* follows; for example, *ghātaḥ* and *ghātakaḥ*. How is the form *bhrauṇahatyam* established? It is established by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

*Kāt_4.1.3*: "For a root ending in *am* that has an *iṭ* augment, [the rule] does not apply, except for the roots *vam*, *kam*, and *cam*. Only the presence of *iṭ* is remembered here; for a root ending in *am* that has an *iṭ* augment and excludes *vam*, *kam*, and *cam*, the grammatical operation prescribed by *iṭ* does not take place. Examples: *aśami*, *atami*. Furthermore, because of the treatment as having undergone *iṭ*-augmentation (*iḍvad-bhāva*) when followed by suffixes marked with the *ñ* or *ṇ* indicatory letters (*ñānubandhe*), we have: *śamaḥ*, *śamakaḥ*, *śamī*; *tamaḥ*, *tamakaḥ*, *tamī*.

What is the purpose of the restriction *seṭ*? [Examples where it does not apply: *avāmi*, *akāmi*, *ācāmi* (from the root *cam* preceded by *āṅ* due to its specific mention), *vāmaḥ*, *kāmaḥ*, and *ācāmaḥ*. How is *āmaḥ* formed? It is from the root *am* meaning "disease" belonging to the *curādigaṇa*; the vowel is lengthened by the suffix *ini*. Regarding *viśrāmaḥ*: because the rule concerning the prefix *vi-* with the root *śram* is not explicitly stated as being restricted to *nañ*-prefixed forms, it is not invariably limited, and thus *viśrāmaḥ* is valid.

How is it that *udyama* and *yama* belong to the *caurādika* group and have the marker *mān* [indicating the *manin* suffix], while *uparama* is also seen? And [the forms] with the elision of suffixes (*pratyayaluk*) belong to the *an* class. (Kātantra 4.1.4)

Regarding the rule *pratyaye luk*: for those verbal roots whose single portion [the suffix] is elided by a suffix (*pratyayaluka*), that which would otherwise apply—namely, for those roots ending in vowels other than *ā* (i.e., those not ending in *ā*) and excluding the elision of *n*—does not take place when that very same suffix follows. For example: *samidhitā*, *samidhakaḥ*; *adṛśadi*, *dṛśadakaḥ* (with the suffix *yin*). In *loluvaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*, where there is elision of the suffix before a vowel (*tasya lug aci*), there should be neither lengthening of the penultimate vowel nor *guṇa*. If it were stated simply "for those from which the suffix is elided" (*pratyayasya lug yebhyaḥ*), then a prohibition would apply to the elision of the suffixes *inan* and *inu*, as in *bhedyād* and *vetti*.
What is meant by "an-ām"? [The suffix] *ghañ* after the root *indh* results in *edhaḥ*;
*manin* after *und* results in *odman*;
and [the suffix] after *rañj* results in *rāgaḥ*.

How is it that for *kṛñ* there is the suffix *śa*? Because a quality (*guṇa*) is characterized by its occurrence in a specific grammatical configuration (*saṃnipātalakṣaṇatva*). It is like the case of the *sārvadhātuka* suffixes. According to Pāṇini’s rule *Kāt_4.1.5*, when a *kṛt* suffix with the indicatory letter *ś* follows, the operation is as if it were a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; thus we have forms such as *juhūṣati* and *pacamānaḥ*. Furthermore, according to *Kāt_4.5.77*, *śa* is added after *kṛñ*: *kriyā*. Whatever has been stated for a particular element applies to it precisely because of that specific mention (*śrutatvāt*).

Now, regarding *guṇa*: Kāt_4,1.6 states that when a *kṛt* suffix with *ṅ* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) follows, *guṇa* does not occur; for example: *bibhyat*, *vidan*, *sunvan*, *katīha madhu lihānāś cinvānāḥ*. Kāt_4,1.7 states that [the substitution of] *yaṇ* occurs for *ke* (the locative singular ending), except in the case of *yoktra*.

When a *kṛt* suffix follows that has a *kān* augment, the operations of a semivowel (*yaṇ*) take place, with the exception of what has been stated [in the previous rule]. For example: *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*, *gṛhītvā*, *iṣṭiḥ*. If the status of being like a semivowel were not present, there would be neither the absence of *guṇa* nor *saṃprasāraṇa*. Why is it said "with the exception of what has been stated"? [Consider: *kṛtaḥ*, *jitaḥ*, *smṛtaḥ*; otherwise, the insertion of the vowel *i*, the lengthening, and the *guṇa* substitution would not occur. [The rule applies] to the *kṛt* suffixes following *jāgṛ*, as well as those beginning with *aś* and *tṛn*. (Kātantra 4.1.8)

The grammatical operation that occurs when *yaṇ* follows a *kṛt* suffix after the root *jāgṛ* does not occur after the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvip*. [This applies to] *yaṇ* [in the case of] *āśis* and *ye*: *jāgarakaḥ*, *jāgaritaḥ*, *jāgartiḥ*.
Why "after a *kṛt* suffix"? [Observe: *jāgṛyāt*.
Why "not after *śatṛ* and *kvip*"? [Observe: *jāgrat*, *jāgṛviḥ*; [the suffix] *kvip* is applied after the roots *kṝ*, *gṝ*, and *jāgṛ*.

Kāt_4.1.9: After a root ending in a consonant (*arudādi*), beginning with *kṣudh* and excluding *kliś* and *gudh*, as well as after *mṛḍ*, *mṛdu*, *vad*, *vas*, and *grah*, the suffix *ktvā* is *guṇī* (undergoes *guṇa*) when it is *seṭ* (followed by the augment *iṭ*). The suffix *in* is used here to express the intended meaning that "that which occurs in a certain element belongs to that element. Examples: *śayitvā*, *devitvā*, *śraṃsitvā*.
Why mention *ktvā*? [To exclude forms like] *nikucitiḥ*.
There would also be a restrictive rule (niyama) stating that for roots beginning with *śīṅ*, the *niṣṭhā* suffixes alone are *seṭ*. What is the purpose of the term *seṭ*? [Consider] *kṛtvā*.

Why is it said "for roots beginning with *rud* and *kṣudh*"? [In the rule] *rudavidamuṣāṃ sani* [Kāt. 3.5.16], the root *vid* associated with *rud* has the meaning of "knowing" (*jñāna*). Thus: *ruditvā*, *viditvā*, *muṣitvā*, *kṣudhitvā*, *kuśitvā*, *kliśa* / *kliśū*—*kliśitvā*, *gudhitvā*; or [the suffix may not be added] because of the presence of the prefix *vi-* or *upa-*.

Having softened (mṛḍitvā), having crushed (mṛditvā), having spoken (uditvā from the root *vad*), and having dwelt (uṣitvā from the root *vas*—the latter due to its inclusion in the *yajādi* group)—in these cases, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule *kṣudhivasoś ca* (Kātantra 4.6.87).
Having taken (*gṛhītvā*).
According to Kātantra 4.1.10, the suffix *ktvā* is used after the roots *skand* and *syand*.
In these two cases, the *ktvā* suffix undergoes *guṇa*: from *skand*, *skantvā*; from *syand*, *syantvā*.
This repetition of the term *ktvā* is for the purpose of excluding forms with the augment *iṭ*; thus, *guṇa* does not apply in *praskadya* and *prasyadya*.

The *ava* of a root beginning with a consonant and having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter optionally undergoes *guṇa* before the suffix *ktvā* when it is *seṭ*. (Kāśikā 4.1.11) That which has *u* and *i* (*vī*) as its penultimate letters is called *vyupadha*. For a root beginning with a consonant, having *u* or *i* as its penultimate letter, and ending in the vowel *a*, the *ktvā* suffix is optionally *seṭ* and undergoes *guṇa*: *dyutitvā* or *dyotitvā*;
*likhitvā* or *lekhitvā*.
Why [is it said] "after a consonant, etc."? [Examples: *eṣitvā*, *oṣitvā*.
Why [is it said] "after *ava*"? [Example: *devitvā*.
It should be stated that [the rule applies] also after *sam*: *ruruciṣate*, *rurociṣate*; *lilikhiṣati*, *lilekhiṣati*.
*Kāt_4.1.12*: For these roots—*tṛṣ*, *mṛṣ*, *kṛś*, *vañc*, *luñc*, and those ending in *ṛ*—the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* and undergoes *guṇa*. Examples: *tṛṣitvā*, *tarṣitvā*;
*mṛṣitvā*, *marṣitvā*.
The root *kṛś* means "to make thin": having made thin, *kṛśitvā* or *karśitvā*.
*Vacitvā*, *vañcitvā* (having deceived).
*Lucitvā*, *luñcitvā* (having plucked out). *Ṛt* is a verbal root found in the Sūtras; [from it come] *ṛtitvā* or *artitvā* (having gone).
Kāt_4.1.13: For roots ending in *th* or *ph* that have an *anuṣaṅga*, the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes *guṇa* when it is marked with *s*. Examples: *śrathitvā* or *śranthitvā*;
*grathitvā* or *granthitvā*.

*guphitvā*, *gumphitvā*. [The rule applies] to those [roots] ending in *-an* that are followed by a suffix beginning with *i* (*anuṣaṅgin*). Why [is this specified]? [Because otherwise, forms like] *kothitvā* and *rephitvā* would not allow for the optional application [of the suffix -tvā] when there is a prefix (*vyupadhātva*). [This applies to] roots ending in *j*, *n*, or *n*, provided they are *aniṭ* (lacking the augment *iṭ*) before the suffix -ktvā. (Kātantra 4.1.14)
For roots ending in *j*, *n*, or *ṇ* that lack an *iṭ* augment and possess a *anuṣaṅga* (nasal), the *guṇa* substitution optionally occurs in the *ktvā* suffix: *bhaktvā* or *bhaṅktvā*;

*raktvā* or *raṅktvā*; *naṣṭvā* or *naṃṣṭvā*. In the case of *masji* and *naś*, the augment *n* is inserted before a consonant beginning with a *dhuṭ* sound, according to the rule "of *masji* and *naś* before a *dhuṭ*."

What is the purpose of the restriction "of those [roots] that do not take *iṭ*"? [Consider] *añjitvā*. According to Pāṇini 7.2.15 (*śīṅpūṅdhṛṣikṣvidisvidimidāṃ niṣṭhā seṭ*), the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of roots beginning with *śīṅ* takes *iṭ* and undergoes *guṇa* substitution; thus: *śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*.
In *pavitaḥ* and *pavitavān*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule *pūkliśor vā* [Kāt 4.6.89].
Similarly, in *dharṣitaḥ* and *dharṣitavān*.

In *kṣveditam*, *meditam*, *prakṣveditaḥ*, *prasveditaḥ*, and *prameditaḥ*, the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied after roots with an initial vowel (*ādi-anubandha*) in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the passive/objective action (*ādikarman*), according to the rule *ādanubandhād bhāvādikarmaṇor vā* [Kāt 4.6.92].
What is the purpose of the word *seṭ*? [Examples: *pūtaḥ*, *dhṛṣṭaḥ*.
Because of the mention of the option (*vā*) in the subsequent rule, it is understood that here [the suffix] is obligatory.
[The suffix *kta* is added after the root] *mṛṣ* in the sense of "forgiveness. (Kāśikā 4.1.16)

When the root *mṛṣ* meaning "to endure" (*kṣānti*) is present, the suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle suffix *kta*) takes the augment *iṭ* and undergoes *guṇa* substitution: *marṣitaḥ*, *marṣitavān*.
Why say "in the sense of endurance" (*kṣamāyām*)? [Observe: *apamṛṣitaṃ vākyam āha* ("he spoke an incorrect sentence").
[The rule] *bhāvādikarmaṇor vodupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.21) applies.

After a verbal root that has *u* as its penultimate letter, the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktavatu*) optionally undergo *guṇa* substitution when expressing the state (*bhāva*) or the initial action (*ādikriyā*), provided the root is capable of taking the *iṭ* augment. For example: *dyotitam anena*, *dyutitam anena*;

*pradyotitaḥ*, *pradyutitaḥ*. Regarding the initial action, the *kta* suffix may denote the agent; by virtue of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), there may be *guṇa* for roots ending in *an*, as in *gudhitam*.
The *hlād* [root] becomes short when long. According to Kāt. 4.1.18, the long vowel of *hlād* becomes short before any *niṣṭhā* suffix; thus, *prahlannaḥ* and *prahlannavān*.
However, *prahlattiḥ* is desired when the suffix *ktin* follows.

Regarding *chādi-* before the suffixes *gh*, *man*, *traN*, and *kvip*: Pāṇini 6.4.19 states that when *chādi-* occurs before these suffixes, a long vowel becomes short. Thus we have *uraśchadaḥ* (breast-armor) and *pracchadaḥ* (covering). Because it is traditionally established (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*) that this shortening applies only when there is a single prefix before the *gh*-suffix, we have *samupacchādaḥ* (a complete covering). From the roots *arci*, *śuci*, *ruc*, *husṛp*, *chād*, and *chardi*, the suffix *is* is applied; thus, "that which covers" is *cchadiḥ*, and the forms *cchadiṣī* and *cchadīṃṣi* [are derived].
The word *man* means deception (*chadma*).
From the root *chad*, with the suffix *kvip*, we derive *chattram*, meaning "that by which one is covered. Thus, *tanucchattram* means "the thin covering" (i.e., the skin).

When a non-indeclinable (*anavyaya*) stem ending in a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is an *upapada* (an accompanying word), and a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in an affix marked with the indicatory letter *kh* follows, a short vowel (*hrasva*) occurs [in place of the final vowel of the *upapada*]. Examples: *vadhuṃmanyā dāsī* ("a maidservant who considers herself a bride"), *grāmaṇiṃmanyo dāsaḥ* ("a slave who considers himself a village headman"), *vṛddhaṃmanyā*, *kāliṃmanyā*, and *hariṇiṃmanyā*. This rule supersedes the application of *pumvadbhāva* (masculine stem substitution) which would otherwise apply when a single entity is intended as both agent and object, because this rule is subsequent [in the order of the grammatical system]. Some maintain that the explicit mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) is for the sake of ease in understanding [the scope of the rule], as in the example *vāṅmanyā* ("one who considers herself speech").

What is the purpose of the restriction "of a secondary word" (*upapada*)? [Example: *paṭvī priyaṃvadā* ("she who speaks kindly is clever"). What is the purpose of the restriction "of that which is not an indeclinable" (*anavyaya*)? [Example: *divāmanyā rātriḥ* ("the night is considered as day").
*Kāt_4.1.21*: For a monosyllabic stem ending in a *nāmin* vowel, the suffix *am* is applied, and it functions like a primary suffix (*pratyayavat*).

The suffix *am* occurs after a nominal stem (*nāman*) that is not an indeclinable (*avyaya*), consists of a single syllable (*ekasvara*), and follows a verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in a suffix marked by the phoneme *kh* as its indicatory letter (*anubandha*). Furthermore, this suffix functions like the suffix itself; by virtue of its proximity, it behaves like the second case singular (*dvitīyaikavacana*). For example: *ravikaras taruṣu kiśalayam iva*, where it is understood that [the tree] is "red" (*rakta*).
