Examples include: *nāvamanyaḥ* ("one who does not despise a boat"), *naramanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself a man"), *gāmamanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself a cow"), and *śriyamanyaḥ* ("one who considers himself prosperity"). Why specify "nominal stem" (*nāmina*)? Consider: *jñammanyā* ("one who considers herself wise").

What is the purpose of the term *ekasvarasya* (of that which has a single vowel)? [Consider the example: *senānimanyaḥ*. *Kāt_4,1.22*: "The letter *m* becomes the final element (*anta*) of a non-indeclinable (*anavyaya*) upapada ending in a short vowel, as well as of the word *aruṣ*, when followed by a verbal root ending in an affix having *kh* as its *it*-marker. Examples: *nāḍiṃdhamaḥ*, *aṅgamejayaḥ*, *aruṃtudaḥ*. The elision of the *s* [in *aruṃtudaḥ*] occurs according to *saṃyogāder dhuṭaḥ* [Kāt_2,3.55].
Why [is it specified] "of that which does not end in -m"? [Consider: *sukaraḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is easy to make").
Regarding the rule *satyāgadāstūnāṃ kāre* (Pāṇini 8.3.115): when the word *kāra* follows, the final element of *satya* and the others becomes *-m*.

One who makes something true is called *satyaṃkāraḥ*; likewise, *agadaṃkāraḥ* (one who makes medicine) and *astuṃkāraḥ* (one who says "so be it"). Even for words where the suffix *kāra* follows an upapada, they maintain that the *ghañ* suffix applies; thus, the act of making true is *satyaṃkāraḥ*. Similarly, elsewhere the addition of the letter *m* is observed: *lokaṃprīṇaḥ* (one who pleases the world), *bhrāṣṭramindhaḥ* (one who kindles a frying pan), *agnimindhaḥ* (one who kindles fire), *bhadraṃkaraṇam* (making auspicious), *uṣṇaṃkaraṇam* (making hot), and *madhyaṃdinam* (midday). Also, *śyainaṃpātā* (the hawk’s swoop) and *tailaṃpātā* (the oil’s flow) refer to a game.

*gile 'gilasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.70). When *gila* follows, the augment *m* is added as a final element (*anta*) to a word other than *gila* itself. [This occurs] when the suffix *kap* is applied to the root *gir*. For example:
*timi-gila*, meaning "the swallower of whales."
In this way, [the suffix *ka* is applied] to *ripuṃgila*.
Why [is it said] "of one who does not swallow" (*agilasya*)? [To show that it is not applied] to *gilagila*.
There is a fish named *timira* which is a hundred *yojanas* in width.
"There is even the *timiṃgilagila* (the swallower of the *timiṃgila*), and there is even the one who swallows that [swallower], O Rāghava.

*Kāt_4.1.25*: After a prefix (*upasarga*), the augment *m* is inserted before the letter *bh* of the root *labh*, when the suffixes *khal* or *ghañ* follow, but not after the prefixes *su-* or *dur-*. For example: *īṣatpralambhaḥ* (an easy deception), *supralambhaḥ* (well-deceived), and *duṣpralambhaḥ* (difficult to deceive).
In the case of the suffix *ghañ*, there are *pralambhaḥ* and *vipralambhaḥ*.
Because of the restriction that [the suffix applies] only after a prefix (*upasarga*), in *īṣallabhaḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* does not apply; rather, *lābhaḥ* occurs.
Why [is it said] "after *asu-* and *dur-*" (*asudurbhyām*)? [To show that it does not apply here: *sulabhaḥ*, *durlabhaḥ*.
By that [rule], it is intended that [the suffix] occurs only after the two [words] *atisulabha* and *atidurlabha*.
How are they *atisulabha* and *atidurlabha*? First there is the compound with *ati*, and then [the suffix] by [the rule] *āṅo yi* (Pāṇini 7.1.26).
The augment *m* is inserted before the *bh* of the root *labh*, following the prefix *āṅ*, when a suffix beginning with *y* follows; thus, *ālambhyā gauḥ*.

[When the prefix] *upa* [is used], it is for the purpose of praise (*praśaṃsā*). According to Pāṇini 4.1.27, the augment *m* is inserted before the *bh* of the root *labh*, following the prefix *upa*, when a suffix follows, provided that "praise" is understood; thus, *upalambhyāni dhanāni*, meaning "the riches are to be praised."
What is the purpose of [the rule] "in the sense of praise"? [Consider: *upalabdhuṃ śakyam* (capable of being perceived), *upalabhyam* (perceivable).

How [is it that] *ālabhya* (to be touched/attained) and *upalabhyate* (is perceived)? Because of the specific restriction [of the rule] regarding the suffix *yak* after the root *labh*. Or, by the rule *vā kṛti rātreḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.72). *Kātantra 4.1.28*.

When a *kṛt* suffix ending follows, the final syllable of *rātri-* optionally becomes *-m-*. Thus: *rātriṃcaraḥ* or *rātricaraḥ*, *rātrimaṭaḥ* or *rātryaṭaḥ*; [the suffix] *ac* is applied because [the words] belong to the *pacādi* group.
In the case of *rātriṃmanyaḥ*, the substitution is obligatory because it depends on the preceding word (*upapada*).
Furthermore, there are the forms *puraṃdaraḥ*, *vācaṃyamaḥ*, *sarvaṃsahaḥ*, and *dviṣaṃtapaḥ*. (Kātantra 4.1.29)

These are derived as irregular formations (nipātana) ending in the suffix *aṇ*: "he splits the city" (*puraṃ dārayati*) thus [becomes] *puraṃdara*, Indra; "he restrains speech" (*vācaṃ yacchati*) thus [becomes] *vācaṃyama*, which refers specifically to a vow; "he endures everything" (*sarvaṃ sahate*) thus [becomes] *sarvaṃsaha*; "he torments the enemy" (*dviṣaṃ tāpayati*) thus [becomes] *dviṣaṃtapa*.
Whatever is not established by the general grammatical rules is all established through these irregular derivations.
"He splits the private parts" (*bhagaṃ dārayati*) thus [becomes] *bhagaṃdara*, referring to a disease, by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone.

*dhātoḥ to 'ntaḥ pānubandhe* (Kāt_4,1.30). From the rule *hrasvāruṣor mo 'ntaḥ* (Kāt_4,1.22), the word *hrasvaḥ* (short vowel) is understood to carry over. When a *kṛt* suffix with *p* as its *anubandha* follows, a short-vowel-final root takes *t* as its final augment (*anta*). Examples: *agnicit*, *somasut*, *prakṛtya*, *itvaraḥ*. Why specify "of a root"? To prevent this from applying to a subordinate word (*upapada*); e.g., *grāmaṇīḥ*, *senāni kulam*.

Regarding the form *vṛtrahabhyām*, [the rule] "that which is external is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*)" applies. Why is it specified "of that which ends in a short vowel"? [Consider] *ānīya* and *āpūya*.
How is it that [in forms like] *upetya*, since an action depends upon its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the grammatical operation pertains only to the suffix?
The inclusion of the term *anta* [in the rule] is for the sake of clarity.
*Kāt_4.1.31*: A *ya* suffix following a *kṛt* suffix after [stems ending in] *o* or *au* is treated like a vowel (*svaravat*). For example: *lavyam*, *avaśyalāvyam*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] *odaudbhyām*? [Consider: *ceyam*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] *kṛt*? [Consider: *upoyate*, *prauyata*. Here, because of the mention of *kṛt*, it is understood that elsewhere there is a general [application].
[The rule] *jikṣyoḥ śakye* [is stated] at Kāśikā 4.1.32.

A *kṛt* suffix prescribed after the roots √ji and √kṣi when the sense is "capable" (*śakye*) becomes *svaravat* (as if it possessed its own accent). For example: that which is capable of being conquered is *jayyam*; that which is capable of being destroyed is *kṣayyam*. Why is it said "when the sense is capable"? [Consider: *jeyam*, *kṣeyam* (that which is to be conquered/destroyed, where the sense is not "capable").
Why is it said "after √ji and √kṣi"? [Consider: that which is capable of being gathered is *ceyaḥ* (where the root is √ci, not √ji).

*Krīñas tadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.1.82). The meaning of that [root] is the exchange of goods (*dravyavinimaya*). A *kṛt* suffix following the root *krī* (to buy) which occurs in that sense becomes as if it were accented (*svaravat*). Example: *krayyā gauḥ*. The meaning is: "A cow brought down to the market because someone will buy it. Why say "in that sense"? Consider: *kreyaṃ me dhānyam nāsti krayyam*. This means: "The grain is not for sale," i.e., it has not been spread out for purchase.

Regarding *lopo 'pṛktasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.67): after the prefix *vi*, there is elision (*lopa*) of an *apṛkta* [suffix] consisting of a single phoneme that is not joined with another letter, provided it bears the technical name *kṛt*. For example, with *kvip*: *ghṛtaspṛk*;
with *viṇ*: *ardhabhāk*.

[The suffixes] *vic* and *kīlālapāḥ*. Why [is it specified] "after [the root] *kṛta*"? Consider: one tells that he has gone (*upeyivāṃsam ācaṣṭe*), [forming] *upeyivayatīti* with *kvip*, [resulting in] *upeyivaḥ*, *upeyivau*. Why [is it specified] "of that which is not a single consonant" (*apṛktasya*)? It is for the sake of eliding the mere *v* characterized by the vowel *i*—having set aside the specific indicatory letters (*anubandha*) of *kvip* and the others; therefore, it would not apply here: *jāgṛviḥ*, [formed] with *kvi* after the roots *kṝ*, *gṝ*, and *jāgṛ*.

When *y* or *v* is followed by a consonant other than *y*, their elision occurs. For example: *knūyī*, *knūtaḥ*, *knūtavān*, *didivān*, *siṣivān*. Why specify "when followed by a consonant"? [Observe: *kṣmāyitā*, *devitā*.
What is meant by "aya"? [The forms] *praknūyya* and *pradīvya*.

How then are *kaṇḍūḥ* and *lolūḥ* explained? In certain cases, even when the substitution depends on the phonetic form (*varṇāśraye*), there is the application of the rule regarding the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopalakṣaṇam*). As in *labdhā* and *labdhūm*, this *v* is a labial.
*niṣṭheṭīnaḥ*. (Pāṇini 7.2.47) When the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows, if the augment *iṭ* is present, there is elision of the root *in*. For example: *hāritaḥ*, *hāritavān*; *lakṣitaḥ*, *lakṣitavān*.
Why specify "when *iṭ* is present"? [Consider: *saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ("the animal has been slaughtered").
By the rule *iv-antardha-* [Kāt 3.7.33] and others, there is optionally the augment *iṭ* before the suffix *san*.

Since the *iṭ* is remembered as being optional (*veṭ*) for monosyllabic roots, it is applied in *saṃjñapita*; however, in *pācita*, because the *in* suffix was elided prior to that, there is no *iṭ* after the monosyllabic root *pac*.
*Kāt_4.1.37*: The elision of *in* does not occur before the suffixes *ālu*, *iṣṇu*, *āyya*, *anta*, and *itnu*. Examples: *spṛhayāluḥ*, *pāvayiṣṇuḥ*, *spṛhayāyyaḥ*.
[The suffix] *āyya* is applied after the roots *śru*, *dṛś*, *ksi*, *spṛh*, and *grah*.
The suffix *jhac* is applied after the roots *gaṇḍi*, *maṇḍi*, *jani*, and *nandi*.

The suffixes *ina* and *itnu* are applied after the roots *stan*, *kṛṣ*, *puṣ*, *gad*, and *mad*. When the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu*), the augment *y* is added before the suffix *ap*. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.1.38)

When the suffix *yap* follows, a root preceded by a light vowel (*laghu-pūrva*) undergoes this [substitution], even when there is an intervention of a single phoneme, because of the specific rule; as in *praśamayya* and *vigaṇayya*. Why "preceded by a light vowel"? Consider: *saṃpradhārya gataḥ*.
It should be stated that it is optional when *āp* (the feminine suffix) follows: *prāpya gataḥ* or *prāpayya gataḥ*.

Because the substitute *iṅ* is *lākṣaṇika* (derived from a rule), [the rule does not apply]: *adhyāpya gataḥ*. *Kāt_4.1.39*: For the roots *mī*, *mīnāti* and others, as well as *dī*, *dā*, *mā*, *gā*, *yati*, *pibati*, *sthā*, *syati*, and *jahāti*, the vowel *ā* is substituted when the suffix *yaP* follows. Examples: from *mīñ*, *pramāya*; from *ḍumiñ*, *parimāya*; from *dīṅ*, *upadāya*.

[This rule] is solely for the purpose of overriding the substitution of *ī* for [the roots] *dā* and others: *pradāya*, *pradhāya*, from *meṅ* and *māṅ*: *pramāya*, *pragāya*, *prapāya*, *prasthāya*, *so avasāya*, *avahāya*.
*Kṣi* becomes long before *yap*. (Kāt. 4.1.40) A long vowel occurs for the root *kṣi* when *yap* follows: *prakṣīya*, *upakṣīya*.
How is it that [the form] *prakṣītya* is derived? Because the root *kṣi* is defined as "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*).

And regarding the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*): by Pāṇini 7.2.41, "In the case of the past passive participle, there is lengthening of the vowel of the root *kṣi*. Thus we have *prakṣīṇaḥ*, *prakṣīṇavān*, and *prakṣīṇam*—meaning "that in which one has perished"—as in "this is the student's *prakṣīṇam* (exhausted portion)."

The term *dīrgha* (long) indicates that [the rule] is non-permanent (*anitya*) because it is preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*). Consequently, it would not apply in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); for example, *kṣitam anena* ("he has destroyed by this") or *prakṣitaś chātro bhavatā* ("the student was ruined by you").
Furthermore, regarding abuse (*ākrośa*) and dejection (*dainya*), there is an option (*vā*): *kṣitāyuḥ* or *kṣīṇāyuḥ*. And in the sense of dejection: *kṣitakaḥ* or *kṣīṇakaḥ*.

This one has been crushed; this poor fellow is exhausted. Here too, [the rule] applies only to the agent (*kartṛ*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the root *sphāy-*: *sphī-*. According to Pāṇini 6.1.42, the substitute *sphī-* occurs for *sphāy-* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes; thus, *sphītaḥ*, *sphītavān*.

Regarding the root *sphāy-*: by the force of its indicatory letter (*it*), this substitution is non-obligatory; thus we have *sphātaḥ* and *sphātavān*. Here, however, [the suffix] *iṭ* is prohibited. *Kāt_4.1.43*:

*pyāyaḥ pīḥ svāṅge* ("*pyāy-* becomes *pī-* when referring to one's own limb"). One's own limb is called *svāṅga*. When the root *pyāy-* refers to a part of one's own body, it becomes *pī-* before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes; thus: *pīnaṃ mukham* ("a swollen face") and *pīnavat mukham* ("a face that has become swollen").

What is meant by "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*)? [Examples are: *pyānaḥ svedaḥ* (profuse sweat), *pyānā buddhiḥ* (expanded intellect), *pyānaṃ mukhaṃ śālāyāḥ* (the wide opening of the hall), *pyānaḥ śothaḥ* (swollen swelling).
How then do you explain *pīno bāhū rathyāyāṃ patitaḥ* (the swollen arm fallen on the road) or *pīnaṃ mukhaṃ pratimāyāḥ* (the swollen face of the statue)?
It would indeed be so [if they were one's own limbs].
A non-fluid, corporeal limb belonging to a living being, which is not produced by modification, is [the substratum].
Even if it does not reside in that [limb], it is seen there; and because of that, the whole is designated as such.
For example: "The boy is fat" due to his connection with a fat limb; or "phlegm is fat," or "wind is fat"—these are based on analogy.

*Āpīna* [is substituted for *āpyāna*] before *andhu* and *ūdhas*: *āpīno 'ndhuḥ* ("a well that has been filled"), *āpīnam ūdhaḥ* ("a full udder"). [The rule] "only before *andhu* and *ūdhas*" applies to the prefix *āṅ*. *Śṛtam* [is a substitute] in the sense of cooking (Kāśikā 4.1.44).

The form *śṛtam* is irregularly derived from both the roots *śrāti* and *śrapayati*, in the sense of cooking; however, because this irregular formation is intended to apply only to milk (*kṣīra*) and sacrificial oblation (*havis*), we have *śṛtaṃ kṣīram* ("cooked milk") and *śṛtaṃ haviḥ* ("cooked oblation").
It would not apply when there is another agent, as in: "The milk was boiled by Devadatta for Yajñadatta.
Why specify "of milk and sacrificial oblation" (*kṣīrahaviṣoḥ*)? [Consider: "the thickened gruel" (*śrāṇā yavāgūḥ*), "the boiled gruel" (*śrapitā yavāgūḥ*).
There is *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution for the root *prastyaḥ*. (Kātantra 4.1.45)

When the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows the root *styai* preceded by *pra*, the semivowel undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*): *prastītaḥ*, *prastītavān*. From the compound *pra-styai*, [we have] *prasaṃstīnaṃ* and *prasaṃstīmavān*; because the vocalization is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the suffix *matup* would indeed occur optionally once the vocalization has been applied. [The root] *śyai* [is used] in the sense of becoming liquid or dense to the touch. (Kātantra 4.1.46)

The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs for the root *śyai* when followed by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*), provided the meaning refers to becoming liquid and solid (*dravaghana*) or to touch (*sparśa*). Examples: *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* (melted butter), *śīto vāyuḥ* (cool air). The meaning is "having become liquid and then solidified/hardened. Touch (*sparśa*) is a specific quality perceivable by the sense organ of the skin. Why specify "becoming liquid and solid" and "touch"? [Consider: *saṃśyāno vṛścikaḥ* (a shriveled scorpion); the meaning here is "contracted by cold. Also after *prati*. (Kātantra 4.1.47)

The *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution occurs for the root *śyai-* when preceded by *prati* in the *niṣṭhā* (past participle) suffix: *pratiśīnaḥ*, *pratiśīnavān*. This [root] preceded by *prati* refers specifically to a disease. *Kāt_4.1.48*:

After *abhi* and *ava*, the *saṃprasāraṇa* substitution optionally occurs for the root *śyai-* in the *niṣṭhā* suffix: *abhiśīnaḥ* / *abhiśyānaḥ*; *avaśīnaḥ* / *avaśyānaḥ*. This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) applying in both cases.
*na vejyor yapi*. (Kāt.
4.1.49) When *yap* follows, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* for these two roots, *veñ* and *jyā*; thus, *pravāya* and *prajyāya*.
These two are included in the group beginning with *yaj*.

And from *vye*. According to Kāt_4.1.50, when the suffix *yap* follows, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) for the root *vye*; thus, *pravyāya*, *upavyāya*. This [root] belongs to the *yajādi* group.

*Kāt_4.1.51*: After *sam* and *pari*, the semivowel of the root *vyeñ* optionally undergoes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) when followed by the suffix *yap*; thus, *saṃvyāya* or *saṃvīya*, and *parivyāya* or *parivīya*. Others maintain that this optionality does not apply after *sam*.

That [vowel] which is long and final [becomes lengthened]. (Kāt_4.1.52) That *saṃprasāraṇa* vowel becomes long if it is final: as in *hūtaḥ*, *saṃvītaḥ*, *prastītaḥ*, *mitrahūḥ*, and *saṃvīya*. Because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), it overrides the addition of the augment *t*.

The mention of "final" is for the sake of clarity, and the mention of "that" is to ensure that the cognition remains undivided; by this, the *saṃprasāraṇa* is established in place of the vowel together with its following consonant.
In the presence of *kvip*, [the vowel] of the root *veñ* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* and becomes long: *ūḥ*, *uvau*, *uvaḥ*. Why specify "in the presence of *kvip*"? [Consider: *utaḥ*, *utavān*.

Regarding *dhyā* and *āp*: Pāṇini 6.1.26 states that the semivowels of the roots *dhyai* and *āp* undergo *saṃprasāraṇa* when followed by the suffix *kvip*, and this *saṃprasāraṇa* becomes long, resulting in *dhīḥ* and *āpīḥ*.
By virtue of this explicit statement (*vacanāt*), the *saṃprasāraṇa* is established.

"Before a *kvip* suffix, before a *dhuṭ* sound, and before a suffix that does not cause *guṇa*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of a stem ending in a fifth-class consonant (*pañcamānta*). Examples: *praśān*, *pratān*, *śāntaḥ*, *śāntavān*, *śāntiḥ*, *śāntvā*.
Why say "before a *dhuṭ* sound"? [Consider: *avamatya*.

What is the purpose of [the condition] "not having a suffix" (*aguṇa*)? [Consider the example: *gantā*. Why is it that the rule for lengthening applies here? Because the designation (*saṃjñā*) is based on a prior technical name. Thus, after the root *kram* followed by the suffix *ktvā*, there is optionally [lengthening]: *krantvā* or *krāntvā*.
[The rule] *chvoḥ śūṭau pañcame ca* (Kātantra 4.1.56) [applies].

In place of *cha* and *va*, the sounds *ś* and *ūṭ* respectively occur before a *kvip* suffix, a *dhut* consonant, a non-*guṇa* vowel, and a fifth (nasal) consonant: *viś* from *viś* (as in *goviṭ*), *praś* from *prach* (as in *pathiprāṭ*), *div* from *div* (as in *akṣadyūḥ*), *pṛṣṭaḥ*, *pṛṣṭvā*, *dyūtaḥ*, *dyūtvā*, *dudyūṣati*, *viśnaḥ*, and *praśnaḥ*.

The suffix *man* occurs after all verbal roots (*sarvadhātubhyaḥ*). In *syomā*, because it is an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), *yatva* (the substitution of *ya*) takes precedence. The double recitation of *ch* is either for the sake of emphasis or to indicate the absence of even that which is occasioned by a specific condition.

*Kāt_4.1.57*: For these roots—*śri*, *vi*, *mā*, *ji*, *vṛ*, and *tṛ*—the vowel *u* (denoted by *uḍ*) is substituted for the *v* together with the preceding vowel (*upadhā*), when followed by a *kvip* suffix, a consonant (*dhuṭ*), a non-guṇa vowel, or a fifth letter (nasal). Thus: from *śriv*, *śrūḥ*, *śruvau*, *śruvaḥ*;
from *av*, *ūḥ*, *uvau*, *uvaḥ*.
mava, mūḥ, muvau, muvaḥ;
jvara, jūḥ, jurau, juraḥ;
tvara, tūḥ, turau, turaḥ.
śrūtaḥ, śrūtavān, śrūtiḥ;
ūtiḥ, mūtiḥ, jūrtiḥ;
tūrtiḥ.
In the case of *man* and *śromā*, there is elision of the final vowel and the following consonant; thus, *om*.
According to Kātantra 4.1.58, the *r* and *l* are also to be elided.

The letters *cha* and *va* following the letter *ra* are elided when followed by a *kvip* suffix, a *dhut* consonant, or a fifth-class vowel that does not undergo *guṇa*. Thus: *mūrchā*, *mūḥ*, *murau*, *muraḥ*.
Similarly, *dhurvī*: *dhūḥ*, *dhurau*, *dhuraḥ*.
Regarding *mūrtiḥ* and *mūrtaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇatva* for the nasal is not desired.
In this context, the recurrence of the rule regarding the fifth vowel when there is no *guṇa* does not apply.

According to Kātantra 4.1.59 (*vanatitanotyādipratiṣiddheṭāṃ dhuṭi pañcamo 'c cātaḥ*), for the root *van*, for roots beginning with *tan*, and for those whose *iṭ* is prohibited, the fifth vowel is elided before a *dhuṭ* suffix when there is no *guṇa*; furthermore, an *at* (the short *a*) is substituted for the final vowel (*ā*) as far as possible. Thus: *vanu*, *vataḥ*, *vatavān*, *vatiḥ*, *vatvā*.
The roots beginning with *tan* extend up to *man*, [ending] with *tataḥ*, *tatavān*, *tatiḥ*, and *tatvā*.
And for those from which *iṭ* is prohibited: *hataḥ*, *hatavān*, *yataḥ*, *yatavān*.
For *ṛṇu*, *ghṛṇu*, and *tṛṇu*, there is no lengthening; thus we have *ṛtam*, *ghṛtam*, and *tṛtam*. Those for whom *iṭ* exists in certain cases are also called *aniṭ* (non-*iṭ* roots).

Furthermore: According to *Kāt_4.1.60*, when the suffix *yap* follows, the fifth vowel (the penultimate) is elided in the case of roots whose insertion of the augment *iṭ* is prohibited, such as *van*, *tan*, and *ṣan*. For example: *vana* → *pravrátya*; *tan* → *pratátya*; *ṣan* → *prasátya*; *han* → *prahrátya*; *man* → *pramátya*.
Why specify "of these"? [Consider: *prabháṇya*.

Or *maḥ*. According to Kāt_4,1.61, for roots whose *iṭ* augment is prohibited, the letter *m* may optionally be elided when the suffix *yap* follows; this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) where [otherwise] it would have applied. Examples: *prayamya*, *prayatya*, *praṇamya*, *praṇatya*.
According to Kāt_4,1.62, [the elision does not occur] in the case of the suffix *tik*, and there is lengthening [of the vowel].

In the *tiki* suffix, the long vowel does not occur for those roots such as *van* and *tan* that are prohibited from taking the *iṭ* augment, nor does the fifth letter [the nasal] become elided: *vanyāt*, *vantiḥ*; *tanyāt*, *tantiḥ*; *yamyāt*, *yantiḥ*; *vadhyāt*, *hantiḥ*. Under *mani*:
according to Kāt_4.1.63, the fifth letter becomes elided under *mani*: *odman*, *odmanī*.
From *indh* with the suffix *ghañ*. According to Kātantra 4.1.64, when *ghañ* follows *indh*, the fifth vowel is elided; thus, *eḍhaḥ*.
[The word] *syadaḥ* [is formed] in the sense of speed. Kātantra 4.1.65.

In the word *syada*, derived from the root *syand* with the suffix *ghañ*, the absence of lengthening is prescribed when the meaning is "speed"; thus, from *syandū*, we have *syadaḥ*. Furthermore, the forms *avoda*, *himaśratha*, and *praśratha* are to be treated as irregularly formed (*nipātayitavya*). From the root *und* preceded by *ava*, we have *avodaḥ*.
From the root *śranth* preceded by *hima* and *pra*, we have *himaśrathaḥ* and *praśrathaḥ*.
Regarding the root *rañj* in the senses of "state" (*bhāva*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

According to Pāṇini 3.3.18 (*ranjer bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*), when the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed after *rañj* in these two senses, the fifth vowel (the penultimate *a*) is elided. Thus, *rañjanam* becomes *rāgaḥ*.
In the sense of state (*bhāve ghañ*), it is *rāgaḥ*, meaning that by which one is colored (*rajyate 'nena iti rāgaḥ*).
What is the purpose of the phrase "in the case of the agent and the instrument"? [Example: *raṅgaḥ* ("color"), from the sense "that in which one colors.

And in the case of the suffixes *vuṣ*, *ghin*, and *ṇi*: according to Kātantra 4.1.67, when the suffixes *vuṣ* and *ghin* follow the root *rañj*, the fifth vowel is elided; *vuṣ* is used in the sense of an artisan (*śilpin*), as in *rajakaḥ* (a dyer) and *rajakī* (a female dyer).
By the rule *yuja-bhaja-etc.*, the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇiṅ* are applied, resulting in *rāgī*.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, the suffix *yuṭ* is also included, as in *rajanam* and *rajanī*.
Regarding the root *vṛṃh*, [the suffix *ghinuṇ* is applied] optionally before a vowel that does not take *iṭ*. (Kāśikā 4.1.68)

In the case of the root *vṛṃh*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel (*svara*) that does not take the augment *iṭ* (*aniṭ*), the fifth letter (the nasal *ṃ*) may optionally be elided. Thus: *varhakaḥ* or *vṛṃhakaḥ*; *varhaṇam* or *vṛṃhaṇam*; *varhati* or *vṛṃhati*.

Why "when not taking the augment *iṭ*" (*aniṭi*)? Consider *vṛṃhitavyam*. Why "beginning with a vowel" (*svare*)? Consider *vṛṃher man dṛśyate*: *parivṛṃhmā* and *parivṛṇḍhiḥ*; [also] the suffix *ktin* in the feminine.

How is it that *vṛhyate*, *vṛṃhyate*, *varhitā*, and *vṛṃhitā* are formed? According to the view of those who maintain that these are distinct verbal roots (*prakṛti*), the augment *iṭ* would also occur before consonantal-initial suffixes. *Kāt_4.1.69*: *yamamanatanagamāṃ kvau*. When the suffix *kvip* follows, the fifth letter [the nasal] of these [roots] is elided, and *ā* is substituted for the final vowel (*āt*). Thus, from *yam*, we have *saṃyat*.
*manas*, *saṃmat*; *tanu*, *parītat*: the lengthening of a short vowel. *gamḷ*, *jagat*.
The *sic* affix is seen after *han* when used in the middle voice; it is also seen after *yam* in the sense of hinting.
However, in the case of marriage, there is an option (*vibhāṣā*) regarding both *sic* and *āśis*; likewise for *gam*. [Example:
*āhata*.
He took a maiden as his wife by means of a ritual; he united with her.
May he be united, may he be united.
May he be united, may he be united.

*Kāt_4.1.70*: Before the suffixes *viṭ* and *vani*, the fifth vowel (the penultimate vowel) becomes *ā*. In *viṭ*: *abjāḥ* ("born from the water"), *goṣāḥ* ("winning cattle")—here there is the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the root *san*. In *vanip*: *vijāvā* ("procreating"), *agregāvā* ("going at the head"). From the root *oṇṛ*, we have *avāvarī* ("one who causes to sound"). In *vano ra ca*: *ghuṇa* ("a wood-boring insect") becomes *ghvāvā*. In *kvanip*: they desire that the vowel *ā* be nasalized as well.

Before an affix beginning with *dh*, *kh*, *s*, or *n*, the fifth vowel (the penultimate vowel) of these [roots] becomes *a*. Examples: *khātaḥ*, *khātiḥ*; *sātaḥ*, *sātiḥ*; *jātaḥ*, *jātiḥ*. Also before the suffix *san*: *siṣāsati*.
Or [the following]:
according to Pāṇini 6.1.72, the vowel *ā* optionally replaces the fifth vowel (*e*) of these roots when *ya* follows: *prakhāya*, *prakhanya*, *prasāya*, *prasanya*, *prajāya*, *prajanya*.
Likewise: *khāyate*, *khanyate*, *cākhāyate*, *caṃkhanyate*.
The suffix *jā* is always applied in the sense of "being born," as in *jāyate*.

By virtue of the rule of restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), when the suffix *ghyaṇ* is applied, *ya* does not occur; thus we have *khānya*, *sānya*, and *janya*. Regarding the root *tan*, it should be stated that *yaṇ* is optionally applied; hence both *tāyate* and *tanyate* are formed.

*Kāt_4,1.73*: When *tiki* follows the root *san*, the fifth vowel (*a*) optionally becomes *ā*. Thus: *sanutāt*, *sātiḥ*, *santiḥ*. Because the word "optionally" (*vā*) is repeated, there is also elision (*lopa*), resulting in *satiḥ*.
*Kāt_4,1.74*: In the case of the roots *sphur* and *sphul*, when *ghañ* follows, the *o* of the suffix is replaced by *ā*.
In these two cases, when the suffix *ghañ* follows, the vowel *o* optionally becomes *ā*: *visphāraḥ*, *visphoraḥ*, *visphālaḥ*, *vispholaḥ*.

Regarding the root *hā* (to abandon), when the suffix *ktvā* follows, the rule from Pāṇini 7.2.56 does not apply; instead, the vowel *i* is substituted for the final vowel of *jahāti*: *hitvā gataḥ* (having abandoned, he went).
Why [is it specified] "except for *hā*"? [Because in] *hāṅ*, [the form] *hātvā* [is desired].

[The rule] *dyatisyatimāsthāṃ ty aguṇe* (Pāṇini 7.4.40) states: after these roots, when followed by an affix beginning with *t* that does not have *guṇa*, *iṭ* is inserted; thus: *ditaḥ*, *ditavān*, *ditiḥ*, *ditvā*.
So: *avasitaḥ*, *avasitavān*. *Mā*: *mitaḥ*, *mitavān*. *Sthā*: *sthitaḥ*, *sthitavān*.
What is the purpose of the condition "not having a suffix" (*aguṇa*)? [Examples: *dātā*, *mātā*, *sthātā*.
[This refers to] the mention by means of the *tip* suffix. Why [is it not so in the case of] *dheṭ*? [Because in] *dhītaḥ*, *dhītavān*, [the *iṭ* augment intervenes].

*sanu*, *sātaḥ*, *sātavān*. Regarding *chā* and *śā*: according to Kāśikā 4.1.77, after *chā* and *śā*, an *it*-augment is optionally applied before an affix beginning with *t*. Thus: *avacchitaḥ*, *avacchātaḥ*; *avacchitiḥ*, *avacchātiḥ*; *niśitaḥ*, *niśātaḥ*; *niśitiḥ*, *niśātiḥ*.

In the sense of a religious vow (*vrata*), the substitution of *śit* for the root *śyai* is obligatory by virtue of the rule of optional application (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*); thus we have *saṃśito brāhmaṇaḥ*. Otherwise, it is already established by the rule for *śiñ*.
For the root *dhā*, there is the substitution of *hi*. (Kāt.
4.1.78) The substitution of *hi* occurs for the root *dhā* before an affix beginning with *t* that does not involve *guṇa*; thus: *hitaḥ*, *hitavān*, *hitiḥ*, *hitvā*.

Why mention *dadhāti*? [Because] *dheṭ*, *dhītaḥ*, and *dhītavān* do not undergo [the substitution] due to the influence of being different roots (*dhātu*). For *car* and *phal*, *ut* replaces the vowel *a*. (Kātantra 4.1.79)

In these two cases, when followed by a word beginning with *t*, the *u* of *ud* occurs as the guṇa-less vowel; thus: *cūrtaḥ*, *cūrtiḥ*, *praphultaḥ*, *praphultiḥ*. [And] *da* becomes *dha*: Kātantra 4.1.80.

For a root designated as *dā* (excluding *dhā*), when followed by an affix beginning with *t* that does not take *guṇa*, *dad* is substituted [for the root]. Examples: *dattaḥ*, *dattavān*, *dattiḥ*, *dattvā*.
Why "designated as *dā*"? Consider *avadātaḥ*. Why "excluding *dhā*"? Consider *dhā* (to suck), as in *dhītaḥ* and *dhītavān*.

In the case of *dā*, there is *natvam* (the substitution of *n*); in the case of *dhā*, there would be *dhatvam* (the substitution of *dh*), because that which is characterized by a *saṃnipāta* (a specific grammatical combination) serves as a cause when a phoneme is being apprehended.

[The rule] "after a prefix ending in a vowel, *taḥ*" (Kāśikā 4.1.81) means: after a prefix ending in a vowel, for a root designated as *dā*—excluding *dheṭ* and *vṛh*—when followed by a suffix beginning with *t* that lacks *guṇa*, the substitution of *t* occurs. Thus: *prattam*, *nīttam*, *parīttam*. In some instances, there is the lengthening of a short vowel of a *nāmin* (a vowel followed by a consonant) before *das*: *ti*.
Why does it say "having a vowel" (*svarāt*)? [Consider] *nirdattam* and *durdattam*. Whether this substitute has a vowel or lacks a vowel, there is no fault whatsoever.

How is it that we have *nidattam*, *avadattam*, or *pradattam*? These are either *prādi*-compounds with the verbal root *dā-* in the sense of the object of the action (karmakartari), or they are indeclinables (*nipāta*). Furthermore, according to Pāṇini 6.1.82, *jagdhi* replaces *ada-* before the suffix *yap*.

When followed by a *yap* suffix beginning with *t*, or by a vowel lacking *guṇa* (*aguṇa*), the root *ad-* becomes *jagdhi-*. Examples: *jagdhaḥ*, *jagdhavān*, *jagdhiḥ*, *jagdhvā*, *prajagdhya gataḥ*. How is it that [the word] *annam* is formed? It is due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *ado 'nanne*. Why does it say "when lacking *guṇa"*? Consider: *attavyam*.

Others say: "When [the substitution of] *gh* for *j* has been established, the rule stating that *yaP* applies because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that internal operations are superseded by *yaP*."
After the roots *pra-nam*, *ā-pracch*, and *pra-div*, the long vowels and other such substitutions do not occur for the fifth class suffixes (*upadhā*) and those following.
Regarding *ghañ* and *al*: *ghasḷ* [is substituted] for *ad*. (Kāt.
4.1.83) In the presence of *ghañ* and *al*, *ghasḷ* is substituted for *ad*; the letter *ḷ* is for the sake of pronunciation; thus, *ghāsaḥ*.
In the presence of a prefix, *ad* becomes *al*, as in *vighasaḥ*; and it should be stated that [the suffix] *aci* applies, as in *praghasaḥ*.

The suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu* are termed *niṣṭhā*. According to Pāṇini 1.1.26 (*ktaktavantū niṣṭhā*), the suffixes *kta* and *ktavantu* receive the designation *niṣṭhā*. Because the word is eternal (*nitya*), there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) in the grammatical description regarding those [suffixes] which are yet to come into being; for example: *śīrṇaḥ* (decayed), *śīrṇavān* (one who has decayed), *bhinnaḥ* (split), *bhinnavān* (one who has split).

The *niṣṭhā* suffixes, such as those beginning with *niṣṭhā* [Pāṇini 1.1.26], and the suffix *ktvā* ending in *m*, are indeed indeclinables (*avyaya*) because they belong to the category of *kṛt* suffixes and are not numerals (*asaṃkhya*). Thus ends the first quarter on *kṛt* suffixes in the commentary of Daurgasimhi.

"From a verbal root (dhātuḥ). [Pāṇini 3.1.91] The term "from a verbal root," ending in the ablative case, is repeated here without qualification; it should be understood as a governing heading (*adhikāra*). [Examples: *kartavyam* ("to be done"), *karaṇīyam* ("to be performed").
Why say "from a verbal root"? [Counter-example: *kumbhatā* ("the state of being a jar").
In the case of *kumbhaṃ karoti*, the suffixes such as *tavya* do not apply to the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
According to the rule *yuṣmadi madhyamaḥ* [Kāt 3.1.6], that which is joined with the locative case is not an *upapada*.

The general rule (*utsarga*) would not apply in the domain of *sic* and *san*; furthermore, since the word *dhātoḥ* is understood from the rule *dhātos to 'ntaḥ pānubandhaḥ* [Kāt 4.1.30], [if one were to apply it here], the form *dudyūṣati* would fail to establish the long vowel *ū*.

The term *upapada* is that which is joined with the locative case. According to Kātantra 4.2.2, within this rule, that which is indicated by the locative case under the governing heading of "roots" (*dhātu*) receives the technical designation *upapada*. This includes such rules as Kātantra 4.3.1, *karmaṇy aṇ*, and 4.3.5, *nāmni sthaś ca*, and so forth.
Why is the word "stated" (*ukta*) used? It is so that the designation does not apply merely to anything ending in the locative; otherwise, one would have to form *stamberamaḥ* and *kurucaraḥ*.
If that [word] is a noun (*nāman*). Kāt_4.2.3:
If that *upapada* is a noun, it is placed before the verbal root; for example, *kumbhakāraḥ* (pot-maker) and *grāmasthaḥ* (village-dweller).
Why specify "if it is a noun"? [Consider: *bhoktum icchati* (he wishes to eat).
The compound of that with that [is formed]. (Pāṇini 2.2.19) A compound occurs between that nominal upapada and that verbal root ending in a *kṛt* suffix, as in *godah*, *jalajam*, and *krodhajam*.

Just as the prefixes beginning with *pra* are established as *upasargas* indicating action and are therefore established even prior to the verbal root, so too the particles beginning with *urī* are established prior to the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* when used in connection with an action, as in *prakṛtya*, *urīkṛtya*, and *urarīkṛtya*.

Likewise, having made [it] white (*śuklīkṛtya*), having made [it] crackle (*paṭapaṭākṛtya*): because the names [of these formations] possess their literal meaning, the compound is indeed established. These three *yogās* (rules), as they are stated, along with the two that will be mentioned later, serve merely for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*). This [rule] regarding the verbal root (*dhātu*) is also [included] because of its connection with the *vāsarūpa* principle.
[The rule: "Not with an indeclinable (*avyaya*) when followed by a suffix marked with *ṇ* (*anām*). (Kātantra 4.2.5)

The prior occurrence of a compound with that [word]—provided it is a name or a secondary derivative (upapada), ends in an indeclinable or a primary suffix (kṛt), and excludes those ending in -am—is not permitted. For example: *kṛtvā alam*, *alam kṛtvā*, *bhoktum kālaḥ*, and *kālo bhoktum*.
Why "of that" (*tasya*)? [Consider: *prakṛtya*. Why "excluding those ending in -am" (*anam*)? [Consider: *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati*.

Or, for those beginning with the third case. From the rule *upadaṃśes tṛtīyāyām* (Kātantra 4.2.6) onwards, whatever words serve as *upapadas* are those beginning with the third case; for these, even when combined with a word ending in the accusative suffix (*amanta*), the prior compound (*prāgbhāva-samāsa*) is optionally not formed: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats with radish as a side-dish), or *mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*; *bhrāṣṭrād apakarṣaṃ dhānā bhakṣayati* (he eats roasted grains, drawing them from the frying pan), or *bhrāṣṭrāpakarṣaṃ dhānā bhakṣayati*. Why say "for those beginning with the third case"? [Consider: *samartho bhoktum* (capable of eating).

*kṛt* (Kāt_4.2.7): This is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). Because it ends in the nominative case, it is connected only with the suffixes to be formed (*sādhya*). Therefore, the suffixes to be mentioned hereafter should be understood as having the technical designation *kṛt*. [As stated in Kāt_4.6.46: "The *kṛt* suffixes [denote] the agent. Examples: *pācakaḥ* (cook), *paktvā* (having cooked); likewise others as well. *vāsarūpo 'striyām* (Kāt_4.2.8).

The analysis of the compound is: "that which has no similar form (*asamānarūpa*). With the exception of those prescribed under the heading of feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), a *kṛt* suffix having the same form as its base is an optional sublater (*bādhaka*). Even when the exception (*apavāda*) is made optional, the sublation remains established; however, since there is no gain for the general rule (*utsarga*), its status as a sublater is rendered optional.

The rule *svarādi* (Kāt. 4.2.10) is an exception (*apavāda*) to that domain; thus, the suffixes *tavya* and *anīya* apply: *ceyam*, *cetavyam*, *cayanīyam*. Likewise, from roots such as *nandi*, the suffix *yu* applies: *nandanaḥ*, *nandakaḥ*, *nandayitā*; so it is with others as well. Why specify "of different form" (*asarūpa*)? Otherwise, in the case of the suffix *ghyaṇ*, the suffix *yu* would not apply: *kāryam*. And in the domain of *kavi*, the suffix *aṇ* would not apply: *godaḥ*. Since the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is not used in actual application, there is indeed similarity of form (*sārūpya*).

Why does it say "not in the feminine"? [Because] in *cikīrṣā*, the suffix *ktin* would not occur; likewise, in *īṣaṇā* and *śranthanā*, only the suffix *yu* occurs. The word *vā* (or) expresses a restriction (*vyavasthā*); thus, regarding the meanings of *kta*, *yu*, *tun*, *khala*, and *artha*, the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply. [The suffixes] *tavya* and *anīya* [are used]. (Kāt_4.2.9)

The suffixes *tavya* and *anīya*, following a verbal root, are designated as *kṛt*. Thus, *kartavyam* and *karaṇīyam*. Because they are *kṛtya* suffixes, they may express either the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); however, the suffix *elima* is desired to express the agent who is simultaneously the object (*karmakartṛ*). For example: *bhidelimā māṣāḥ* ("the beans are easily split") and *pacelimās taṇḍulāḥ* ("the rice grains are easily cooked").
In the word *vāstavya*, the suffix expresses the agent and the vowel lengthening occurs due to its being a conventional form (*rūḍhi*).
Regarding the rule *svarād yaḥ* (Kāt_4.2.10):
the suffix *ya* occurs after a verbal root ending in a vowel (*svara*), as in *ceyam* and *cetavyam*.
The inclusion of the term *svarāt* is merely for the sake of clarity.
And [the suffix *ya*] follows a root ending in *śak*, *sah*, or a labial (*pavarga*).
(Kāt. 4.2.11) The suffix *ya* occurs after roots ending in *śak*, *sah*, or a labial: *śakyam*, *sahyam*, *japyam*, *labhyam*.
And [the suffix *ya*] follows the roots *āp* and *khan*, with the vowel *i* being substituted [for the final vowel of the root]. (Kāt. 4.2.12)
The suffix *ya* occurs after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, as well as after the root *khan*; for these two, the final vowel becomes *i*. Thus: *deyam*, *dheyam*, *kheyam*.

Since the substitution of *e* for *ai* (in *dhe-*) has been applied, this [substitution of *i*] is considered non-eternal (*anitya*), according to the principle that "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to that which is internal (*antaraṅga*).
However, the suffix *ya* occurs after the roots *yam*, *mad*, and *gad* when they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). (Kātantra 4.2.13)
But when these [roots] are without a prefix (*upasarga*), the forms are *yāmyam*, *madyam*, and *gadyam*.
Why "without a prefix"? [To exclude cases such as] *prayāmyam*, *pramādyam*, and *pragādyam*.
The mention of *yama* is for the purpose of restriction.

After the root *car*, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *yañ* occurs; and also after *car* when preceded by *āṅ*, provided it does not mean "to study" (*agurau*). Examples: *caryam*; *ācaryo deśaḥ* ("a region to be traversed").
Why specify "after *āṅ*" (*āṅi*)? [Consider: *abhicāryam*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "agurau" (not when meaning "teacher")? [Example: *ācāryo guruḥ* ("the teacher is a guru"). The term *paṇya*, *avadya*, and *varya* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the senses of "to be sold," "blameworthy," and "restriction," respectively. According to Kāśikā 4.2.15: *paṇya* is irregularly formed in the sense of "that which is to be sold"; *paṇyam* means "merchandise for sale," whereas *pāṇyam* means something else.

The form *avadyam* is a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*) derived from the root *vad* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, used in the sense of "blameworthy"; thus, *avadyam* means "blameworthy," while *anudyam* means something else. Furthermore, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *vad* when forming a name (as in *vadya*). From the root *vṛ*, the form *varyā* occurs when "non-restraint" is understood; otherwise, the form is *vṛtyā*.

The opinion is that [this is so] because of the feminine gender indication: *vāryā* means "sacrificial priests. *Vahyam* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). According to Kāt_4.2.16, *vahyam* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātita*) in the sense of an instrument; *vahyam* means "a cart."
The other [term] is external. *Arya* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātita*) in the sense of "master" and "vaiśya. According to Kāt_4.2.17:
*arya* is prescribed as a term for a master and for a vaiśya; thus, *aryaḥ svāmī* (the master is noble) and *aryo vaiśyaḥ* (the vaiśya is noble).

The other [word] is *ārya*. Regarding *upasaryā* in the sense of "fit for breeding": according to Pāṇini 4.2.18, that which has reached its time (*kāla*) is designated as *kālyā*. "Breeding" (*prajana*) means the act of procreation, that is, conception. If she has reached the time for breeding, the form *upasaryā* is prescribed by nipātana; it is derived from the root *sṛ* with the prefix *upa*, meaning "she who is approached. Thus, *upasaryā* refers to a cow, meaning one in her season (*ṛtumatī*).
Another [word] is to be introduced:

*ajaryam* when used with *saṃgata*. According to Kāśikā 4.2.19, *ajaryam* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word when *saṃgata* is the agent; it is called *ajaryam* because it does not decay (*na jīryati*), thus "an undecaying association."
What is the meaning of *saṃgata*? For example: *ajaritā kambalaḥ* ("a woolen blanket that has not been worn").

*Kāt_4.2.20*: *nāmni vadaḥ kyap ca*. When a noun (*nāman*) is the upapada, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *vad*, and by the word "and" (*ca*), the suffix *ya* is also applied. Examples: *brahmaṇo vadanam* (the speaking of Brahman) becomes *brahmodyam* and *brahmavadyam*; a discourse spoken regarding Brahman is *brahmaṇodyā* and *brahmavadyā*.
What is meant by "in the sense of a name" (*nāmni*)? For example, *vādyam* (to be spoken) and *anuvādyam* (to be repeated).

Regarding the rule *bhāve bhuvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.107): when a word meaning "name" (*nāmni*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *bhū* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, *brahmabhūyam gataḥ* means "he has attained the state of Brahman," that is, *brahmatvam*.
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in a name"? [Examples: *bhavya*, *prabhavya*.
The inclusion of the term *bhāva* is for the sake of the subsequent rules and for the sake of ease here.
*hanas ta ca* (Kāśikā 4.2.22).

When a noun (*nāman*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *han* (to kill) to denote an abstract state (*bhāva*), and the letter *t* is substituted for the final letter [of the root]. For example: *brahmaṇo hananam* (the killing of a Brahmin) becomes *brahmahatyā*. Why is it specified "denoting an abstract state"? Consider: *śvaghātyo mṛgaḥ* (a deer that can be killed by a dog). Why is it specified "when a noun is used as an *upapada"*? Consider: *ghātaḥ* (a blow) and *upaghātaḥ* (an injury).

The suffix *ghyaṇ* is not seen after the root *han*; even when *yap* is present, there is no *t* at the end because *kyap* has an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). According to Pāṇini 3.1.115 (*vṛdṛjuṣīṇśāsustuguhāṃ kyap*), *kyap* occurs after these roots. The phrase "in the sense of a name and in the sense of an action" (*nāmni bhāve ca*) is no longer applicable; for these [roots], *kyap* occurs: from *vṛñ*, *vṛtya*; but from *vṛṅ*, *vāryā ṛtvijaḥ* (the priests who are to be chosen).
From the root *dṛś*, *dṛśya*;
from *juṣ*, *juṣya*;
from *iṇ*, *itya*; but from *iṅ*, *upeya*.
The vowel *u* as an *anubandha* in the root *śās* is for the sake of ease [of pronunciation]; thus, [the forms] are *śiṣyaḥ* and *stutyaḥ*, and *guhyaḥ*.
As for *avaśyastutyaḥ*, the re-mention of the suffix *kyap* [indicates that it applies even when the prefix *avaśyam* is present].

How so? [The word *saṃvṛta* means] "not to be warded off by other elephants," like the innate nature (*svabhāva*) of embodied beings; thus, due to this association, the root *vṛ* takes the suffix *in* elsewhere as well. According to Pāṇini 3.1.120 (*ṛdupadhāc cākḷpicṛteḥ*), the suffix *kyap* occurs after a root ending in *ṛ* that has *ṛ* as its penultimate letter, excluding the roots *kḷp* and *cṛ*. Thus we have *vṛtyam* and *vṛdhyam*.
What is the purpose of excluding *kḷp* and *cṛt*? [The answer is: they are to be optionally applied (*vikalpyam*) or excluded (*vicartyam*).
The marker *ṛt* with a following *t* (tapara) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation.
[The rule] *bhṛño 'saṃjñāyām* (Kāśikā 3.1.25) applies. *Kāt_4,2.25*.

The suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *bhṛ* (to support) when not forming a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*). Thus, there are the forms *bharaṇam*, *bhṛtyam*, or [the agent] *bhṛtyaḥ*—so called because he is supported (*bhriyate*). Why "when not forming a technical name"? Consider *bhāryā* as the name of a Kṣatriya woman, or *bhāryā* as a wife.
But surely, even when it is a technical name, the suffix *kyap* does occur in the feminine; is that not so? No, for that [usage] is prescribed in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
The suffix *kyap* is optionally applied after the root *grah* following the particles *api* and *prati*. (Kāt. 4.2.26) Thus, one has *apigṛhyam* or *apigrāhyam*, and *pratigṛhyam* or *pratigrāhyam*.
And [the suffix *kyap* is also applied] after the words *pada* and *pakṣya*. (Kāt. 4.2.27)
The suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *grah* when the meanings "wing" (*pakṣya*) or "word-group" (*padapakṣya*) are to be expressed.

A *pragṛhya* word is one that is not euphonically combined with a following vowel; an *avagrahya* word is one for which an *avagraha* (separation) is made. For example: *arjunagrahyā senā* ("an army whose wing is Arjuna").

Due to the word *ca* ("and"), [the suffix *ka* is applied] in the sense of "not independent" (*asvairiṇi*) and "external" (*bāhyāyām*). For example: *gṛhyakā ime*, meaning "these are domesticated"; *avaruddhakāḥ*, meaning "those who are confined. *grāmagṛhyā strī*, meaning "a woman external to the village.
[The suffix *ka* is applied] after the roots *nī* and *pūñ* when preceded by *vi*, in the senses of "kalka" (a medicinal paste) and "muñja" (a type of grass), respectively. (Kāśikā 4.2.28)

When *ava* is the prefix, the suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *nī* and *pū*, in the senses of "medicinal paste" (*kalka*) and "muñja grass" (*muñja*) respectively: *vinīyaḥ* for a medicinal paste, and *vineyam* for anything else;
*vipūyaḥ* for muñja grass, and *vipavyam* for anything else.
After the roots *kṛ*, *vṛṣ*, and *mṛj*, the suffix *kyap* is optional. (Kātantra 4.2.29)

The suffix *kyap* occurs optionally after the roots *kṛñ* and others: *kṛtyam*, *kāryam*, *vṛṣyam*, *varṣyam*, *mṛjyam*, *mārgyam*. After the roots *duh* and *śaṃs*, *kyap* also occurs: *duhyam*, *dohyam*, *śasyam*, *śaṃsyam*, according to the rule "the suffixes *kṛtya*, *yu*, and *t* occur even in other instances" (Kātantra 4.5.92). Likewise, in the word *mṛṣodyam*, it is precisely *kyap*.
Likewise, from the roots *sṛj* and *sṛj*, only the suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after the prefix *pra-* and *samava-* respectively: *pāṇisargyā* and *samavasargyā* (a rope).
Similarly, after the root *bhṛ* with the prefix *sam*, the suffix *kyap* occurs: *saṃbhṛtyaḥ* and *saṃbhāryaḥ*.
Likewise, from the roots *tak*, *cat*, *pat*, *śas*, and *yaj*, only the suffix *ya* occurs: *takyam*, *catyam*, *patyam*, *śasyam*, and *yajyam*.
Likewise, from the root *guh*, [the suffix] *ghyaṇ* occurs as well: *guhyam*, *gohyam*.
Likewise, after the root *ji*, the suffix *kyap* occurs only before a consonant: *jityā* [is used for] a plough (*hali*); a great plough is called a *hali*.
[The suffix *kyap* occurs] after *sūrya-ruci* and *avyathin* in the sense of the agent (Kāśikā 4.2.30).

These are irregularly formed (nipātyante) in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). From the root *sū* in the sense of impelling (*preraṇe*): "he impels the worlds" or "he moves," thus *sūryaḥ*; "he shines," thus *rucyaḥ*; "he does not tremble," thus *avyathyaḥ*.

Regarding *bhidya* and *uddhya* in the sense of a river (*nade*): according to Pāṇini 4.2.31, these two are irregularly formed in the sense of the agent when referring to a river; "it breaks the banks," thus *bhidyaḥ* a river; "it releases water," thus *uddhyaḥ* a river.
"How is the river to be divided?"—this is an instance where the object (*karman*) is intended to be expressed.

Regarding the asterisms *puṣya* and *siddhya*: according to Pāṇini 4.2.32, these two are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when the asterism is the agent (*kartṛ*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). [In the sense of] "it nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) undertakings" or "undertakings flourish in it (*puṣyanti asmin*)," it is *puṣya*; [in the sense of] "it accomplishes (*sādhayati*) undertakings" or "undertakings succeed in it (*sidhyanti asmin*)," it is *siddhya*; thus, *puṣya* itself [is used].

*Kāt_4,2.33*: *yugya* is an irregularly formed word (*nipātana*) when it means a vehicle (*patra*). It is called *yugya* because it is joined (*yujyate*) by this, or because it is itself joined; thus, it is *yugya*.
*Kāt_4,2.34*: [The suffix *yat* is applied] after *kṛṣṭapacya* and *akūpya* when they are technical names (*saṃjñā*).

These two [suffixes] are applied as irregular forms (*nipātyete*) when they denote a technical name (*saṃjñā*). "They ripen by themselves in what has been ploughed" (*kṛṣṭe pacyante svayam eva*); thus, *kṛṣṭapacyāḥ* refers to rice-grains. That which is protected is *kupya*, meaning something other than gold and silver.
The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after stems ending in *ṛ*, diphthongs (*ṛvarṇa*), or consonants. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.2.35)

The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after verbal roots ending in *ṛ*-vowels or consonants: *kṛ* → *kāryam*, *śṛ* → *śāryam*, *pākyam*, *vākyam*. The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of causing the root to behave like one ending in *ij* (i.e., *guṇa*), and the letter *gh* is for the purpose of providing a general designation (*ghañ*). [The suffix *ghyaṇ* also occurs] after the roots *āsū*, *yu*, *vap*, *rap*, *lap*, *trap*, *dabh*, and *cam*. (Kātantra 4.2.36)

The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after the root *su-* preceded by *ā*, and after roots such as *yu-*, etc. [Examples: *āsāvyam*, *yāvyam*, *vāpyam*, *rāpyam*, *lāpyam*, *apatrāpyam*. Here, the root *dambh-* has undergone the elision of its nasal (*na-lopa*). [Examples: *avadābhyam*, *ācāmyam*. [The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs] after a root ending in *u* when necessity (*avaśyaka*) is implied. (Kāśikā 4.2.37) Necessity is "that which must be" (*avaśya-bhāva*). When necessity is understood from a root ending in *u*, the suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs. [Examples: *nāvyam*, *lāvyam*. "It must be cut" (*avaśya-lāvyam*). In the case of a *kṛtya* suffix, there is the elision of the *m* of *avaśyam*; otherwise, it is simply *lavyam*.

After the roots *pā* and *dhā*, when they have the senses of "mental recitation" (*mānasa-āmidhena*) respectively, the suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs according to their respective order. [Thus] *pāyya* means "measure," which—by virtue of the explicit statement—abandons its own primary sense; anything else is *peya*.
That which "places the fire" is *dhāyyā*; it is a *sāmidhenī*, a mantra for placing the fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*).

By way of metaphorical extension (*upacāra*), [the term] also applies to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); for example, "they recite the *dhāyyā*s" (where the *dhāyyā*s are the priests). *Kātantra 4.2.39*: When *pra* or *āṅ* are the preceding words (*upapada*), the suffix *ghyaṇ* is applied to the root *ni*, provided that the resulting word is neither a consensus (*saṃmata*) nor non-eternal (*anitya*). This suffix bears the same accent (*svaravat*) as the root. For example, *praṇāyyaś cauraḥ* ("a thief who is not approved of"), meaning one who is disapproved of (*asaṃmata*).
The *ānāyya* is the *dakṣiṇāgni*; that which is brought forth and established from the *gārhapatya* fire is called *ānāyya* by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), though it is not permanent.
This is because of the statement "even elsewhere," as in: "A father may teach the Veda to his eldest son, and to a pupil who is worthy of instruction (*praṇāyya*).
[The term *saṃcikuṇḍapa* applies] to a sacrifice. (Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 4.2.40)

The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after the root *ci* preceded by *sam*, and after the root *pā* preceded by *kuṇḍa*, when a sacrifice (*kratu*) is to be expressed; and that [suffix] bears the accent of the vowel [of the prefix]. That which is gathered together is the *saṃcāyya* sacrifice. That which is drunk from cups (*kuṇḍa*) is the *kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice; for that is indeed a Soma sacrifice, and "sacrifice" (*kratu*) is used here by implication. Alternatively, because of the expression "Soma is drunk in this," it may denote the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
And there is also the *rājasūya*. (Kātyāyana 4.2.41)

When a sacrifice (*kratu*) is the meaning to be expressed, *rājasūya* is also derived as an irregular form (*nipātyate*). From the root *ṣuñ* in the sense of "pressing" (*abhiṣava*), it refers to a sacrifice where the king is to be pressed, or where the king is consecrated; thus, it is the *rājasūya* sacrifice.

Regarding *sāṃnāyya* and *nikāyya*: Pāṇini 4.2.42 states that these two are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) in the senses of "oblation" (*havis*) and "dwelling" (*nivāsa*) respectively. *Sāṃnāyya* refers specifically to a particular oblation, whereas other [milk-based offerings] are simply *saṃneya*.
*Nikāyya* means "dwelling"; *niceya* is something else.

*Paricāyya* and *upacāyya* [are used] in the sense of fire (*agni*). According to Pāṇini 4.2.43, these two are irregularly formed (nipātita) in the sense of fire; it is he who is piled around (*paricīyate*), thus *paricāyya* refers to the fire.

That which is piled up (*upacīyate*) is called *upacāyya*, as in "the fire-altar" (*agni*). According to Pāṇini 3.1.130, both *citya* and *agnicityā* are also [irregularly formed] in the sense of "fire. That which is piled up is *citya* (the fire-altar), and the piling of the fire is *agnicityā*, denoting the action itself.
The form *samūhya* is established by [the suffix] *-ūhya*; this [root] is also used in the sense of "carrying" (*vahati*) in certain instances, and *saṃvāhya* indeed occurs in the sense of "fire.

Or else, it is *amāvasyā*. [Kāśikā 4.2.45: In the sense of "together" (*saha*), after the prefix *amā* preceding the root *vas*, the suffix *ghyaṇ* is applied in the sense of a locus of time (*kālādhikaraṇe*), and the absence of lengthening is prescribed by nipātana (irregular derivation). Thus, because the moon and sun dwell together (*sahavasataḥ*) in this [time], it is *amāvasyā*, or *amāvāsyā*, the lunar day (*tithi*). Whatever is not produced by a general rule is all established through nipātana.
Those are the *kṛtya*s. According to Kāt_4.2.46, those suffixes beginning with *tavya* bear the technical designation *kṛtya*.

The applications (*pradeśa*) of the *kṛtya*s include such rules as Kāt_4.6.47: "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, *khala*, and *artha* suffixes [are used] in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). And so forth.

The suffixes *vuṇ* and *tṛc*. According to Pāṇini 3.1.133 (*dhātoḥ parau vuṇtṛcau*), the suffixes *vuṇ* and *tṛc* occur after a verbal root; since *kṛt* suffixes denote the agent, we have *pācakaḥ* (a cooker) and *paktā* (one who cooks).

How is it that *galecopakaḥ* (one who squeezes at the throat) is formed from "he is squeezed at the throat" (*gale cupyate*), and *pādahārakaḥ* (one who carries by the feet) from "he is carried by the feet" (*pādābhyāṃ hriyate*)? [These are formed with the suffix *vuṇ*].
*Ac* is added after *pac* and others (*pacādibhyaś ca*).
All verbal roots (*dhātu*) are recited among the *pac*-class and so forth; from those *pac*-class roots, the suffix *ac* occurs, as in *pacaḥ*, *paṭhaḥ*, and *bhavaḥ*.
The mention of the *pac*-class is for the purpose of overriding an overriding rule; therefore, in cases such as *śvapacaḥ* and *jārabharaḥ*, the suffix *aṇ* would not occur.

Who would not be [called] *deva*, *sarpa*, or *meṣa*? In this same way, others are also to be understood. *Kāt_4.2.49*: After the group of nouns beginning with *nandi*, the suffix *yu* occurs. From the verbal roots *nandi*, *vāsi*, *madi*, *dūṣi*, *sādhi*, *śobhi*, and *vardhi*, when followed by the suffix *in*, the suffix *yu* is applied provided they do not form a proper name (*asaṃjñāyām*). Thus: from *nandayati* comes *nandanaḥ*; likewise, *vāsanaḥ*, *madanaḥ*, *dūṣaṇaḥ*, *sādhanaḥ*, *śobhanaḥ*, and *vardhanaḥ*.

The suffix *ana* is applied after verbal roots ending in *i*, *n*, or *ṛ*, provided they do not already end in *nin*, when used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*). Examples include: *sahanaḥ* (enduring), *tapanaḥ* (scorching), *damanaḥ* (subduing). Likewise: *jalpanaḥ* (prattling), *darpaṇaḥ* (proud), *ramaṇaḥ* (delighting), *candanaḥ* (gladdening), *saṃharṣaṇaḥ* (exhilarating), *saṃkarṣaṇaḥ* (drawing together), *janārdanaḥ* (afflicting people), *madhusūdanaḥ* (slayer of Madhu), *pavanaḥ* (purifying), *lavaṇaḥ* (salting). The change of *n* to *ṇ* occurs here due to the specific inclusion of these names in the list. Other examples are: *vibhīṣaṇaḥ* (terrifying), *cittavināśanaḥ* (destroying the mind), and *kuladamanaḥ* (subduing a family).
This suffix may also be applied to roots preceded by an object (*karman*) even in cases where *aṇ* would otherwise apply.

The suffix *ṇin* follows roots beginning with *grah* [Kāśikā 3.1.134]. The suffix *ṇin* occurs after those roots enumerated in the list of names beginning with *grah*: *grāhī* (one who seizes), *sthāyī* (one who stands), *nirakṣī* (one who looks out), *viśrāvī* (one who hears).

After the roots *yāci*, *vraj*, *vad*, and *vas*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, [the suffix *ṇin* is applied]: *ayācī* (one who does not beg), *avrājī* (one who does not wander), *avādī* (one who does not speak), *avāsī* (one who does not dwell).

However, after a word ending in a vowel (svarānta), when the suffix *aci* follows, it is added after a word denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). Examples: *akārī gharmasya bālātapaḥ* ("the morning sun has made the heat"); *viṣayī deśe* ("he is familiar with the country"); *vibhāvī*, *abhibhāvī* in the sense of "having become" (*bhūte 'rthe*); *paribhavī*, *paribhāvī*. In some cases, shortening occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). How is it that [words like] *utsāhī*, *udvāhī*, *saṃmardī*, and *niveśī* are formed? They are established by means of the root *iṇ* in the sense of "existence" (*astyartha*). Likewise: *adhyāhārī*, *saṃvyāhārī*, *aparādhī*, *uparādhī*.
The suffix *ka* is applied after roots ending in a nasal (*nāmī*) with a penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), as well as after the roots *prī*, *kṛ*, *gṛ*, and *jñā*.

[Kātantra 4.2.51] After the roots *prīṇāti*, *kirati*, *girati*, and *jānāti*—provided they end in a nasal with a penultimate vowel—the suffix *ka* occurs: *vikṣipaḥ*, *vilikhaḥ*, *priyaḥ*, *utkiraḥ*, *giraḥ*, *gilaḥ*, and *jñaḥ*.
However, when there is a prefix (*upasarga*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied to roots ending in *ā*. [Kātantra 4.2.52]

When a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ḍa* occurs after a verbal root ending in long *ā*. Thus: *suglaḥ*, *sumlaḥ*. [In the case of] *prahvaḥ*, if the suffix *ḍa* were applied, there would be neither vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) nor the substitution of *u*; however, because it is subsequent, the suffix *aṇ* applies [in *gosandāya*], and this [suffix *ḍa*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that *ṇa*. After the roots *dheḍ* (to suck), *dṛśi* (to see), *pā* (to drink), *ghrā* (to smell), and *dhmā* (to blow), the suffix *śa* occurs. (Kātantra 4.2.53)

The suffix *śa* occurs after these [roots] when preceded by prefixes (*upasarga*) or secondary words (*upapada*): *uddhayaḥ*, *utpaśyaḥ*, *utpibaḥ*—the latter being from the root *pibati* due to association; the letter *ṭ* in the root *dheṭ* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation; *ujjighraḥ*, *uddhamaḥ*. How is *paśyaḥ* formed? Because of the rule stating "also elsewhere.
Likewise, one who smells about is *vyāghraḥ*.

*Kāt_4.2.54*: For the roots *sāhi*, *sāti*, *vedi*, *udeji*, *cetī*, *dhṛ*, *pṛ*, *limp*, and *vind*, when there is no prefix (*upapada*), the suffix *śa* is applied. Because these [roots] lack a prefix, the suffix *śa* occurs: from *sāhayati* comes *sāhayaḥ*; likewise, *sātayaḥ*. From *vidi* in its general sense, *vedayaḥ*; from *udejṛ*, *udejayaḥ*; from *cetī*, *cetayaḥ*; from *dhṛñ* or *dhṛṅ*, *dhārayaḥ*; from *pṛ*, *pārayaḥ*; from *limpati*, *limpaḥ*; and from *vindati*, *vindaḥ*. [Objection]: Why is it not *viduḥ* for the root *vidi* in the sense of "part" (*avayava*)? [Response]: Because of the association (*sāhacarya*) with the other forms, or because of the specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) that results in *vinduḥ*.
[Objection]: How then are the gods called *nilimpāḥ*? [Response]: Because of the rule stating "it also occurs elsewhere."
Likewise, in the case of *govindaḥ* (from *gāṃ vindati*), the suffix *aṇ* would not apply in the case of *aravinda*.
[The forms] *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* are established by the rule *dadadadhor acā*.
[The suffix] *ṇa* optionally applies after roots beginning with *jval*, as well as after *du*, *nī*, and *bhū*. (Kātantra 4.2.55)

The suffix *ṇa* is optionally applied after the roots *jval*, *dunoti*, *nayati*, and *bhavati*, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus: *jvalaḥ* and *jvālaḥ*; *calaḥ* and *cālaḥ*. The roots beginning with *jval* and ending with *kas* are included because of the formation of the *vṛt* list. [Examples: *davaḥ* and *dāvaḥ*; *nayaḥ* and *nāyaḥ*—though some do not accept these; *bhavaḥ* and *bhāvaḥ*. Why "provided they are not preceded by a prefix"? [Counter-examples: *prajvalaḥ*, *pradavaḥ*, *praṇayaḥ*, *prabhavaḥ*. After the root *sru*, it is so when preceded by *sam* or *āṅ*. (Kātantra 4.2.56)

When *sam* or *āṅ* are the preceding words (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied to the root *sru*; it is not remembered [in other grammatical traditions] as being optional. Thus: *saṃsrāvaḥ*, *āsrāvaḥ*. Why specify "when *sam* or *āṅ* are present"? [Because otherwise we would have] *sravaḥ*, *parisravaḥ*.
[The suffix *ṇa* is also applied] to the roots *hṛ* and *su* when preceded by *ava*: Kāśikā 4.2.57.
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after the roots *hṛ* and *sā* when *ava* is the prefix: *avahāraḥ*, *avasāyaḥ*. Why "when *ava* [is the prefix]"? [To show that it does not apply otherwise: *haraḥ*, *viharaḥ*.
[The suffix *ṇa* also occurs] after *dih*, *lih*, *śliṣ*, *śvas*, *vyadh*, *atīṇ*, and *śyai*. (Kātantra 4.2.58)

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after these roots: *dih* (to smear), *lih* (to lick), *śliṣ* (to embrace)—the mention of *ke* being for the sake of the specific rule; *śvas* (to breathe), *vyadh* (to pierce), *i* (to go)—with a prefix, the mention of *śyai* is a restrictive rule to prevent [the suffix] from applying to *bādh*; *ava-śyai* (dew), *dai* (to give), *dhā* (to place).
*Pratyāya* is also seen. *Avatāra* is included because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule.
Or after the root *grah*, [the suffix] *ṇa* optionally occurs. (Kāt_4,2.59) After the root *grah*, *ṇa* optionally occurs: *grāhaḥ* "an aquatic creature," *grahaḥ* "the sun and so forth.
But after [the root *grah*] with the prefix *ud*, [the suffix] *ak* occurs. (Kāt_4,2.60)
When *gṛha* is to be expressed as the meaning, the suffix *tvac* occurs; thus, from the root *grah*, one forms *gṛham* (house) and *gṛhāḥ* (houses).

Regarding the rule *Kāt. 4.2.61*: "When a craftsman (*śilpin*) is to be expressed, the suffix *vuṣ* occurs. Due to the specific mention [in the rule], this applies only to the roots *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*. Thus: *nartakaḥ* (male dancer), *nartakī* (female dancer); *khanakaḥ* (digger), *khanakī* (female digger); *rajakaḥ* (dyer), *rajakī* (female dyer).

*Śilpa* means skill in knowledge; and because it is mentioned in connection with something inferior, [the suffix] *thakan* is applied. According to Pāṇini 4.4.62: the suffix *thakan* occurs after the root *gai* when a person skilled in an art (*śilpin*) is to be expressed; thus, *gāthaka*.

And *ṇyuṭ*. According to Pāṇini 4.2.63, the suffix *ṇyuṭ* also occurs after the root *gāyati* when a person skilled in an art (*śilpin*) is to be expressed; thus, *gāyanaḥ* (masculine) and *gāyanī* (feminine).
These two suffixes are also seen even when the person is not a professional artist.

*Haḥ* [is used] for *kāla* (time) and *vrīhi* (rice). According to Kātantra 4.2.64, the suffix *ṇyuṭ* occurs after the root *jahāti* when the meanings are "time" or "rice": *hāyanaḥ* means "a year," as it leaves behind (passes) all states; *hāyanāḥ* means "rice," as it leaves behind water.
Why specify "for time and rice"? [Otherwise, it would apply to] *hātā*.

The suffix *aka* occurs after a verbal root when a benediction (*āśis*) is implied. According to Pāṇini 3.3.170 (*āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*), when a benediction is understood, the suffix *aka* is applied to the root. For example: *jīvatāt*, *jīvakaḥ*;
*nandatāt*, *nandakaḥ*.

*Kāt_4.2.66*: After the roots *pru*, *sru*, *sṛ*, and *lū*, the suffix *aka* occurs in the sense of one who performs an action well (*sādhukārin*). Thus: *sādhu prāvakaḥ* (one who flows well), *srāvakaḥ*, *sārakaḥ*, *lāvakaḥ*.
Skillful performance (*sādhukaraṇa*) is indeed craft (*śilpa*).
This [term] is for the sake of the elaboration of the feminine form. Why say "one who acts well"? [Consider: *protā*.
Thus ends the second quarter on *kṛt* suffixes in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by Daurgasimhi.

*Karmaṇy aṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1): When a word denoting an object (*karman*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root. For example: "one who makes a jar" (*kumbhaṃ karoti*) is a *kumbhakāraḥ* (potter); likewise, *kāṇḍakāraḥ* (reed-maker), *śaralāvaḥ* (reed-cutter), and *vedādhyāyaḥ* (Veda-student).

However, in cases such as "he sees the sun," "he hears the Himalayas," or "he goes to the village," there is no formation of a compound because of a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), and thus only the sentence remains. Furthermore, in the case of "he makes a large pot," the formation does not occur because the meaning is dependent on another factor (*sāpekṣatvāt*).

In the expression *aghaṭaṃ ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes what was not a jar into a jar"), the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed after roots ending in the * cvi*-suffix when there is reference only to the prior state (*prāgavasthā*). [The rule] *hvāvāmaś ca* (Kātantra 4.3.2) states that *aṇ* occurs after these [roots], with the object (*karman*) as the governing word (*upapada*).
*Kāpavādaḥ*,
*svargahvāyaḥ*, *tantravāyaḥ*, *dhānyamāyaḥ*.
The root *vā* is intransitive.

In the case of the roots *mīnāti* and *minoti*, when a suffix marked with *k* follows and *vṛddhi* is to be applied, there is an absence of the form *mā*. [Kāśikā 4.3.3] After the roots *śīli*, *kāmi*, and *bhakṣi-ācari*, the suffix *ṇa* occurs when a direct object (*karman*) is present as an upapada. *Śīli* and *bhakṣi* end in *in* in the *curādi* class; for *kāmi*, the substitution of *inaṅ* applies. Thus: *māṃsaśīlā*, *māṃsakāmā*, *māṃsabhakṣā*.

She practices what is auspicious; thus she is a woman of auspicious conduct (*kalyāṇācārā*). For the suffix *aṇ* is indeed applied to feminine nouns to form the suffix *ī*. It is called *śīla* because it is practiced (*śīlyate*); she whose practice is meat is "meat-practicing" (*māṃsaśīlā*).

Just as there is no *aṇ* suffix in the case of "waiting for the auspicious" (*kalyāṇapratīkṣā*) or "enduring suffering" (*duḥkhakṣamā*) according to their respective definitions, so it is here as well.

If it were thus, then because there is an approach (*abhigama*) to water (*ambhas*) for this [person], it would be *ambho'bhigama*; yet one intends [the term] to be *ambho'bhigāmī*. If there is a designation even in a compound, then the statement "it is difficult" applies. [The rule] *āto 'nupasargāt kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3): when a word ending in *ā* is an object (*karman*) and an upapada, the suffix *ka* occurs after a verbal root that does not have a prefix (*anupasarga*). Examples: *godah* ("cow-giver"), *aṅgulitraḥ* ("finger-protector").

What is the purpose of the restriction "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*)? [Examples: *gosaṃdāyaḥ* ("one who binds cows"), where the suffix *aṇ* is applied because there is no intervention by prefixes. [Examples:
*brahmajyaḥ* ("one who harms a Brahmin") and *mitrahvaḥ* ("one who abandons a friend"), where the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule "also after other [roots]" (*anyato ’pi ca*).
[And: *stha-* [is added] in names (*nāmni*), according to Pāṇini 4.3.5.

When a noun is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ka* occurs after the root *sthā* and after roots ending in long *ā*; the restriction "provided it is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) does not apply here. For example: one who drinks with the neck (*kaccha*) is called *kacchapa*; one who drinks with two [hands] is called *dvipa*; one who stands on level ground is *samastha*; one who stands in a village is *grāmasaṃstha*. Regarding the rule *tundaśokayoḥ parimṛjāpanudoḥ* (Kātantra 4.3.6): when *tunda* and *śoka* are present as the objects (*karman*) serving as *upapadas*, the suffix *ka* occurs after the roots *parimṛj* and *apanud* respectively. One who wipes his belly (*tunda*) is *tundaparimṛjaḥ*, which denotes specifically a lazy person; another is simply *tundaparimārjaḥ*.

It dispels sorrow; thus, *śokāpanudaḥ* means one who causes joy, except in the case of *śokāpanodaḥ*, which refers specifically to a preacher of the Dharma (*dharmakathaka*). Regarding *pra* and *dājñaḥ*: by rule Kāt_4.3.7, the suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *dā* (to give) and *jñā* (to know) when *pra* is used as a prefix and an object (*karman*) is present. Thus, *prapāpradaḥ* (one who provides water) and *pathiprajñaḥ* (one who knows the way).
In this context, "wood" (*dāru*) is understood [by the term *dāruka*], not the word-form itself, due to its association with it; thus, one who suckles at the breasts is called a *stanapradhāya*.

Regarding *sami khyaḥ*: by Pāṇini 3.2.9 (*Kāt_4,3.8*), the suffix *ka* is applied to the root *cakṣiṅ* when the prefix *sam* is present as an upapada and it has an object; for example, one who enumerates cattle is a *gosaṃkhyaḥ*. This specific mention is made because of the presence of the prefix (*sopasargatvāt*).

"Vibhuja" means that which splits the roots; thus, *mūlavibhuja* refers to a chariot. "Nakhamuca" refers to bows, according to the traditional usage (*abhidhāna*). In this case, the suffix *ka* is applied as before.
Likewise, there are sesame seeds to be hidden from crows, called *kākaguhā*; it is also seen used with the object of the action (*karman*).
[The suffix] *ṭak* is applied after the root *guh*. (Kātantra 4.3.9)

When a word denoting an object (*karman*) follows as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the root *gā* when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). For example: one who sings sweetly is a *madhuragī*; one who sings the *sāman* is a *sāmagī*. Why specify "not preceded by a prefix"? Consider *sāmasaṃgāyaḥ*.
The inclusion of the six indicatory markers (*anubandha*) beginning with *nad-* is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).
Kāśikā 4.3.10: *surāsīdhvoḥ pibateḥ*.

When *surā* or *sīdhu* are the objects [of the action] and serve as co-occurring words (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭac* is applied to the root *pibati* provided it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Examples: *surāpī*, *sīdhupī*.
Why specify "when *surā* or *sīdhu* are the objects"? [Consider: *kṣīrapā brāhmaṇī* ("a Brāhmaṇī who drinks milk").
Why is it said "after the root *pā* (to drink)"? [Answer: A woman who drinks liquor (*surāpā*).

Why is it said "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*)? [Answer: A place for distributing liquor (*surāprapāyaḥ*). [The suffix] *ac* is added after the root *hṛ* (to carry) when it does not mean "carrying away" or "lifting up. (Kāśikā 4.3.11)

The rule "provided it is not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) is not traditionally recorded [in this context]. When *harati* occurs with an object as its subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied provided that "age" is understood and it does not involve "lifting. Lifting (*udyamana*) is the act of raising upward; other than that is non-lifting (*anudyamana*). The mention of "age" implies that here age is understood even when it is merely possible that lifting might occur. Examples include: *kavacaharaḥ kṣatriyakumāraḥ* ("a young Kṣatriya boy who takes up armor"), *asthiharaḥ śvā* ("a dog that carries bones"), *aṃśaharo dāyādaḥ* ("an heir who takes his share"), and *vātaharaṃ tailam* ("oil that removes wind"). However, in the case of lifting, we have *bhārahāraḥ* ("one who carries a load").
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *aṇ*.

[The rule] "when *āṅ* is present, in the sense of habitual action" (Kāśikā 4.3.12) means that when *āṅ* is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*) and habitual action is understood, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *hṛ*. Habitual action is an activity independent of [immediate] results; thus, one whose habit it is to gather flowers is a *puṣpāhara* Vidyādhara.
What is the purpose of the condition "having that as its habitual nature" (*tācchīlya*)? [Consider: *bhārāharaḥ* ("one who carries a load").

And [the suffix] *arha*. According to Kāśikā 4.3.13, the sense of habitual nature (*tācchīlya*) and the prefix *āṅ* are not traditionally taught [in this context]; when the object is the governing word (*upapada*), the suffix *ac* occurs after the root *arh*, as in *pūjārhā strī* ("a woman worthy of honor").

Kāśikā 4.3.14: *dhṛñaḥ praharaṇe cādaṇḍasūtrayoḥ*. When a word expressing a weapon (*praharaṇa*), with the exception of *daṇḍa* and *sūtra*, is present as the object (*karma*) in composition, the suffix *ac* is applied after the root *dhṛ*. For example, "he holds a thunderbolt" (*vajraṃ dharati*) results in *vajradharaḥ*; likewise, *cakradharaḥ*.
Why specify "with the exception of *daṇḍa* and *sūtra*"? [To exclude cases such as] *daṇḍadhāraḥ* (staff-bearer) and *sūtradhāraḥ* (thread-holder).

Due to the prohibition [of the suffix *a*] by the preceding rule (*sūtra-pratiṣedha*), even when there is no taking up [of a weapon], we have *bhūdharaḥ* ("earth-bearer") and *jaṭādharaḥ* ("matted-hair wearer").

*Kātantra 4.3.15*: "After the root *grah*, [the suffix *a*] is optionally used when these are present as objects: *dhanus*, *daṇḍa*, *tsaru*, *lāṅgala*, *aṅkuśa*, *yaṣṭi*, and *tomara*. When these are present as objects, the suffix *a* is optionally applied after the root *grah*. Thus: *dhanur gṛhṇāti* ("he grasps a bow") → *dhanurgrahaḥ* or *dhanurgrāhaḥ*; *daṇḍagrahaḥ* or *daṇḍagrāhaḥ*; *tsarugrahaḥ* or *tsarugrāhaḥ*; *lāṅgalagrahaḥ* or *lāṅgalagrāhaḥ*; *aṅkuśagrahaḥ* or *aṅkuśagrāhaḥ*; *yaṣṭigrahaḥ* or *yaṣṭigrāhaḥ*; *tomaragrahaḥ* or *tomaragrāhaḥ*.

*ghaṭagrahaḥ*, *ghaṭīgrahaḥ*—the suffix *ac* is applied because they belong to the *pacādi* group; likewise, *ghaṭagrāhaḥ* and *ghaṭīgrāhaḥ* are formed with the suffix *aṇ*. Similarly, *sūtragraha* is used in the sense of "holding," whereas elsewhere *sūtragrāhaḥ* is used. This section is for the purpose of illustrating the various forms of the *pacādi* group. [Kātantra 4.3.16] *stambakarṇayo ramijapoḥ*.

When *stamba* and *karṇa* are used as preceding members (*upapada*), the suffix *ac* is applied respectively after the roots *ram* and *jap*: one who delights in thickets is a *stamberama*, an elephant; one who whispers into the ear is called a *karṇejapa*, specifically a slanderer. Likewise, the suffix *aluk* (non-elision) occurs after a locative case ending. Kātantra 4.3.17: "After roots preceded by *śam*, when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood, the suffix *ac* is applied.
After roots preceded by *śam*, when a name is implied, the suffix *ac* occurs: one who makes happiness is *śaṃkara*; one who becomes happiness is *śaṃbhava*; *śaṃvara*; *śaṃvada*.

By the *bahuvrīhi* compound *śaṃpūrvo yebhyo dhātubhyaḥ*, the suffix *ṭa* [prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.20] is superseded even in the case of roots such as *kṛñ* when used with causes (*hetu*) and so forth; thus, there is a female ascetic named Śaṃkarā.
Regarding the rule *śīṅo 'dhikaraṇe ca* (Kātantra 4.3.18):
