when a word denoting a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the *upapada*, the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *śī* (to lie); for example, one who lies in the sky is a *khaśaya*.

From the word *ca* (and), [the suffix] is applied when the side (*pārśva*) and so forth function as the instrument: *pārśvena śete* (he sleeps on his side), *pārśvaśayaḥ*; likewise, *pṛṣṭhaśayaḥ* (one who sleeps on his back) and *udaraśayaḥ* (one who sleeps on his belly).
*Digdhena saha śete* (he sleeps with one smeared [with poison]), *digdhasahaśayaḥ*: thus there are two types of compounds.
When the agent is "face-up" (*uttāna*) and so forth: *uttānaḥ śete*, *uttānaśayaḥ*.

*careṣ ṭaḥ*. (Pāṇini 4.4.19) When *cara-* is used [as a verb], the suffix *ṭa* occurs when a word denoting a location (*adhikaraṇa*) is present as an accompanying word (*upapada*). For example: "he moves among the Kurus" (*kuruṣu carati*) results in *kurucaraḥ*; likewise, *kurucarī*. Because of the inclusion of the letter *ca*, it also occurs in other cases: "he moves for alms" (*bhikṣāṃ carati*) results in *bhikṣācaraḥ* and *bhikṣācarī*; "he moves with an army" (*senayā carati*) results in *senācaraḥ* and *senācarī*; "he moves having taken [something]" (*ādāya carati*) results in *ādāyacaraḥ*.

Regarding *puro’grato’greṣu sarteḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.20): when these words are used as upapadas, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus, from "he moves forward" (*puraḥ sarati*), we have *puraḥsaraḥ* and *puraḥsarī*; *agrataḥsaraḥ* and *agrataḥsarī* (the suffix *tas* is added here because they belong to the *ādyādi* group); and *agresaraḥ* and *agresarī*.
Due to the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*), the word ending in *e* is treated as an indeclinable, or alternatively, the elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending does not occur.

*Pūrve kartari* (Kāt. 4.3.21). When the word *pūrva* is used as an accompanying word (*upapada*) expressing the agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *sṛ*. Thus, "one who goes first" is *pūrvasaraḥ*, or *pūrvasarī*. Why [is it] "first"? Because the agenthood is simply not intended to be expressed. Why say "when expressing the agent"? [Consider: "that which goes first" is *pūrvasāraḥ*.

*Kṛño hetutācchīlyānulomyeṣv aśabdaślokakalahagāthāvairacāṭusūtramantrapadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.2.20). When the words *aśabda* and so forth are used as objects (*karma*) in composition with the root *kṛ*, the suffix *ṭa* is applied provided that the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), "habitual character" (*tācchīlya*), or "conformity" (*ānulomya*) is understood. Here, "cause" (*hetu*) is taken in the sense of a well-known causal power, because the root *kṛ* is not used here in its causative form (*ṇijanta*). Example for "cause": *vidyā yaśaskarī* ("learning brings fame"). Example for "habitual character": *śrāddhakaraḥ* ("one who habitually performs ancestral rites").
*Ānulomya* means compliance or conformity; [it refers to] one who carries out what is said.
Why say "in the absence of *śabda*, etc."? [Consider: *śabdakāraḥ*, *ślokakāraḥ*, *kalahakāraḥ*, *gāthākāraḥ*, *vairakāraḥ*, *cāṭukāraḥ*, *sūtrakāraḥ*, *mantrakāraḥ*, *padakāraḥ*.

The non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding cause (*hetu*) and compliance (*ānulomya*) remains established; the exclusion [of these from the rule] is for the sake of [including cases of] habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

How is it that potters and others are designated as "those whose habit is the making of jars and so forth"? [It is] because of such designations. Furthermore, [the suffix -in is applied] after the words *tad* (that), *ādi* (beginning), *anta* (end), *ananta* (endless), *kāra* (maker), *bahu* (many), *bāhu* (arm), *ahan* (day), *divā* (by day), *vibhā* (light), *niśā* (night), *prabhā* (splendor), *bhās* (light), *citrakartṛ* (painter), *nāndī* (auspicious song), *kim* (what), *lipi* (writing), *livis* (script), *bali* (offering), *bhakti* (devotion), *kṣetra* (field), *jaṅghā* (shank), *dhanus* (bow), *arus* (wound), and in the case of numerals. (Kātantra 4.3.23)

This [sūtra] is for the purpose of excluding *ahetu* and others; when words such as *tad*, *ādi*, and so forth are used as upapadas (governing words) with the root *kṛ*, the suffix *ṭa* occurs. This word *tyac* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). "One who does that" is *tatkaraḥ*; because it is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), the form is *taskaraḥ* (thief), where the *sakāra* is substituted for the *takāra*. Likewise: *yatkaraḥ*, *ādikaraḥ*, *antakaraḥ*, *anantakaraḥ*, *kārakaraḥ*, *bahukaraḥ*, *bāhukaraḥ*, *ahaskaraḥ*, *divākaraḥ*, *vibhākaraḥ*, *niśākaraḥ*, *prabhākaraḥ*, *bhāskaraḥ*, *citrakaraḥ*, *kartṛkaraḥ*, *nāndīkaraḥ*.
*kiṃkaraḥ*, *lipikaraḥ*, *livikaraḥ*, *balikaraḥ*, *bhaktikaraḥ*, *kṣetrakaraḥ*, *jaṅghākaraḥ*, *dhanuṣkaraḥ*, *aruṣkaraḥ*.

[The suffix] *kara* is added after *eka*, *dvi*, *tri*, *catur*, and after words expressing "what" (*kim*), "how much" (*yad*), "that" (*tad*), or "many" (*bahu*) when used in the feminine; however, the suffix *āp* (forming feminines in *-ā*) must be applied.
Because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], forms such as *rajanīkaraḥ*, *kṣapākaraḥ*, and *kṣaṇadākaraḥ* are also to be understood.
In the case of *bhṛti* (wages), when the word for the action is used as an upapada. Kāt_4.3.24:

When the word for the action (*karmaśabda*) is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ*, provided that *bhṛti* (wages) is understood. *Bhṛti* means the price for work. [Examples: *karmakaraḥ bhṛtakaḥ* (a hired laborer); *karmakarī dāsī* (a female slave). Why "in the case of *bhṛti*"? [Counter-example: *karmakāraḥ* (a worker).
The mention of *śabda* is for the sake of indicating the meaning of the suffix; [it serves to show that] it would be the object (*karman*).
Regarding *iḥ* after *stamba* and *śakṛt*:

Kāt_4.3.25 states that when *stamba* and *śakṛt* are present as objects, the suffix *i* occurs after the root *kṛ*. Thus, *stambakari* refers specifically to rice (*vrīhi*), whereas *stambakāra* refers to something else.

Only a calf is denoted by the term *śakṛtkari*; another [animal] is a *śakṛtkāra*. Regarding the root *harati* (to take), when *dṛti* and *nātha* are the objects (*karma*) as subordinate words (*upapada*), the substitution of *iṛ* for the root vowel occurs, provided the agent (*kartṛ*) is an animal (*paśu*). According to Pāṇini 3.2.25: *dṛtināthayoḥ paśau*, when *dṛti* and *nātha* are the objects, the substitution of *iṛ* occurs after *harati* when the agent is an animal: *dṛtihariḥ* "a leather-bag-carrying animal" and *nāthahariḥ* "a master-carrying animal."
Regarding *phale*, *mala*, and *rajas* [as upapadas] for the root *grah*:

Kāt_4.3.27 states that when these actions serve as upapadas, the suffix *ir* is applied to *grah*. Thus, one who "takes fruit" is *phalegrahiḥ*; the change to *e* occurs by virtue of a specific rule (*sūtranipātana*).
One who "takes impurity" is *malagrahiḥ*; one who "takes dust" is *rajograhiḥ*.

*Kāt_4,3.28*: When *deva* and *vāta* are the objects (*karman*) serving as upapadas, the suffix *ir* is applied to the root *āp*. Thus, "one who attains the gods" is *devāpiḥ*; "one who attains the winds" is *vātāpiḥ*. This is because it is a conventional term (*rūḍhi*) for these specific [beings]. *Kāt_4,3.29*: When *ātman*, *udara*, and *kukṣi* are the objects, the suffix *khi* is applied to the root *bhṛ*.

When these verbal roots are used with an object as an *upapada*, the suffix *khi* is applied to the root *bhṛ*. Thus: *ātmānam eva bibharti* (he supports himself alone) becomes *ātmambhariḥ*; likewise, *udarambhariḥ* (one who fills his belly) and *kukṣimbhariḥ* (one who fills his stomach). *Kāt_4.3.30*: When an object is an *upapada*, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *ej* (to move). Thus: *aṅgam ejayati* (he moves his limbs) becomes *aṅgamejayaḥ*; *janam ejayati* (he agitates people) becomes *janamejayaḥ*. Because the suffix has *kh* as its *anubandha*, the final letter *m* is substituted for the root-final vowel (*mo 'ntaḥ*). Since the suffix has *ś* as its *anubandha*, it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* affix; consequently, by the rule regarding *iṇ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84), the *guṇa* substitution occurs for the vowel *i*.

*Kāt_4.3.31*: After the root *dheṭ* ("to suck"), the suffix *khaś* occurs when these [words] are used as objects (*karman*). When one says "he sucks a bitch," it becomes *śunindhayaḥ*; "he sucks breasts," *stanandhayaḥ*; likewise, *muñjandhayaḥ*, *kūlandhayaḥ*, *āsyandhayaḥ*, and *puṣpandhayaḥ*.
Regarding *muñja* and the others, some do not accept [the application of this rule].

Because it would otherwise be meaningless in its primary sense (*prakṛti*), the *ṭ* of the root *dheṭ* is understood to serve the purpose of [marking] the *nadādi* group; thus we have *śunindhayī* and *stanandhayī*. *Kāt_4.3.32*: *nāḍī-kara-muṣṭi-pāṇi-nāsikāsu dhmaś ca*. When these are used as objects (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the roots *dhamati* and *dheṭ*. Thus: *nāḍindhamaḥ*, *nāḍindhayaḥ*, *karaṃdhamaḥ*, *karaṃdhayaḥ*. Some do not accept these forms. Likewise: *muṣṭindhamaḥ*, *muṣṭindhayaḥ*, *pāṇindhamaḥ*, *pāṇindhayaḥ*; some do not accept these. And: *nāsikandhamaḥ*, *nāsikandhayaḥ*.

According to some, the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *dham* (to blow) when preceded by the objects *śunī*, *stana*, *ghaṭī*, *khārī*, and *vāta*: *śunindhamaḥ*, *stanandhamaḥ*, *ghaṭindhamaḥ*, *khāriṃdhamaḥ*, *vātandhamaḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 3.2.35 (*vidhvarustileṣu tudaḥ*), the suffix *khaś* is applied after the root *tud* (to strike/pierce) when these are the objects:
*vidhuntudaḥ*, *aruntudaḥ*, *tilantudaḥ*.

*Kāt_4.3.34*: When *asūrya* and *ugra* are used as objects (*karman*) as subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *dṛś*. [Examples: *na sūryaṃ paśyanti* (they do not see the sun) → *asūryaṃpaśyāni mukhāni* (faces that do not see the sun), *asūryaṃpaśyā rājadārāḥ* (the king’s wives who do not see the sun). The meaning is that they do not see even the sun; because the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with *dṛś*, its composition with *sūrya* occurs due to semantic intelligibility (*gamakatva*). [Another example: *ugraṃpaśyaḥ* (one who sees the fierce).
*tapaḥ* [is added] after *lalāṭe*. Kāt_4,3.35:

When *lalāṭa* is the object (*upapada*), the suffix *khaś* occurs after the root *tap*; thus, "one who heats his forehead" is *lalāṭaṃtapaḥ*. *pacaḥ* [is added] after [the root *pac*] when the objects are measures of *mita*, *nakha*, and *parimāṇa*. Kāt_4,3.36.

When these actions are used as upapadas, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *pac*. Examples include: *mitampacā brāhmaṇī* (a Brahmin woman who cooks a little), *nakhaṃpacā yavāgūḥ* (gruel that cooks [its own] nails), *prasthaṃpaco māṇavakaḥ* (a boy who cooks a *prastha*), and *droṇaṃpacā sthālī* (a pot that cooks a *droṇa*). Here, only measures (*parimāṇa*) such as *prastha* and so forth are denoted; time and number are not included. Therefore, expressions such as *māsaṃ pacati* (he cooks for a month) or *ekaṃ pacati* (he cooks one) remain merely syntactical sentences.
[The suffix *khaś* is also applied to the roots *udruj* and *udvah* when *kūla* is the upapada. (Kātantra 4.3.37).

The suffix *khaś* occurs after the roots *udruj* and *udvah* when the word *kūla* is an accompanying word (*upapada*). Examples: *kūlamudrujā nadī* (a river that erodes its bank), *kūlamudvahaḥ samudraḥ* (the ocean that carries away its banks).
Furthermore, *vahaṃliha*, *abhraṃliha*, *paraṃtapa*, and *iraṃmada* are also [formed with] this suffix as irregular forms (*nipātana*).

According to Pāṇini 3.2.38, these are derived by adding the suffix *khaś*. Examples: *vahaṃliha* (a cow licking the carriage-pole), *abhraṃliha* (wind licking the clouds), *paraṃtapaḥ* (one who torments enemies), and *iraṃmadaḥ* (an elephant, so called because it intoxicates with its vital energy).

From the word *ca* [in the rule], those who drive the wind are *vātamaja* deer; those who abandon the herd are *śardhaṃjahā* beans. Regarding the root *vad-* (to speak), the suffix *kha* occurs when *priya* or *vaśa* are the objects [of the action]. According to Pāṇini 3.2.38: when *priya* or *vaśa* are present as the object (*karman*) in composition, the suffix *kha* occurs after the root *vad-*. Thus: *priyaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks kindly) and *vaśaṃvadaḥ* (one who speaks according to another's will).

The suffix *kha* is introduced here for the sake of subsequent rules and for the sake of brevity in the grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*). Regarding the rule *sarvakūlābhrakarīṣeṣu kaṣaḥ* (Kāśikā 4.3.40): when these [words] are present as objects (*karman*) in composition, the suffix *kha* occurs after the root *kaṣ*. Thus: *sarvaṃkaṣaḥ khalaḥ* ("a wicked person who scrapes away everything"), *kūlaṃkaṣā nadī* ("a river that erodes its banks"), *abhraṃkaṣo giriḥ* ("a mountain that scrapes the clouds"), and *karīṣaṃkaṣā vātyā* ("a whirlwind that scatters dried cow-dung").

*Kāt_4,3.41*: After the root *kṛ*, when these words—*bhaya*, *arti*, and *megha*—are present as objects (*karman*), the suffix *kha* occurs. For example: "one who causes fear" (*bhayaṃkaraḥ*), "one who causes fearlessness" (*abhayaṃkaraḥ*). It is accepted that the rule applies to the end of the compound containing *bhaya*. Examples: *ṛtiṃkaraḥ* ("one who causes distress"), *meghaṃkaraḥ* ("one who causes clouds"). *Kāt_4,3.42*: And after the root *kṛ*, when *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra* are present as objects, the suffix *aṇ* also occurs. (The suffix *kha* also applies here. Thus: *kṣemakāraḥ*, *priyakāraḥ*, *madrakāraḥ*. (With *aṇ*: *kṣemaṃkaraḥ*, *priyaṃkaraḥ*, *madraṃkaraḥ*.)

When these actions are used as upapadas, the suffix *kha* occurs after the root *kṛ*, and the suffix *aṇ* also occurs: *kṣemaṃkaraḥ*, *kṣemakāraḥ*, *priyaṃkaraḥ*, *priyakāraḥ*, *madraṃkaraḥ*, *madrakāraḥ*.

Although the rule would have been established by the word "optionally" (*vā*), the explicit mention of *aṇ* is for the purpose of superseding the suffix *ṭa* even in cases such as those beginning with "cause" (*hetu*).
Why say "when these"? [Consider: *bhadrakāraḥ*.

Regarding the suffix *kha* after the root *bhū* when the word *āśita* is used as an upapada, in the sense of either an action (*bhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*): Pāṇini 3.4.43 states that when the word *āśita* is present as an upapada, the suffix *kha* occurs after the root *bhū* in the sense of an action or an instrument. Thus, *āśanam* (the act of eating) is *āśitam*; *āśitasya bhavanam* (the becoming of one who has eaten) is *āśitaṃbhava*.
That by which one becomes satiated is *āśitaṃbhavā*, as in "a bundle of five [grains] that causes satiety."

Pāṇini 3.2.46 states: *nāmni tṛ-bhṛ-vṛ-ji-dhāri-tapi-dami-sahāṃ saṃjñāyām*. When a nominal is used as an upapada, the suffix *kha* occurs after these roots—*tṛ*, *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, *ji*, *dhṛ*, *tap*, *dam*, and *sah*—provided they form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example: that which crosses by means of a chariot is called *rathaṃtara*, the name of a *sāman*;
she who supports the universe is *viśvaṃbharā*, the earth. Similarly, *avalih* [is derived from *ava-lī*].
A maiden who chooses her own husband is called *patiṃvarā*.

One who has conquered wealth is *dhanaṃjaya*, namely Arjuna. That which supports wealth (*vasu*) is *vasuṃdharā*, the earth; [here] the vowel is shortened due to the specific designation. One who torments the enemy is *śatruṃtapaḥ*.

One who tames or subdues an enemy is *ariṃdamaḥ*. One who endures an enemy is *śatruṃsahaḥ*. The designation and the action are understood as a name (*saṃjñā*) according to their possibility; the term "in a name" (*nāmni*) is used merely for the sake of clarity.

And *gama*. (Kāt_4.3.45) When a word is present as an upapada, the suffix *kha* is added to *gama* to form a proper name (*saṃjñā*). For example: *sutaṃgamaḥ*; "he goes by means of his arms" (*bhujābhyāṃ gacchati*), thus *bhujaṃgamaḥ*; "he goes measuredly" (*mitaṃ gacchati*), thus *mitaṃgamaḥ* (an elephant); "paths that go before" (*pūrvaṃgamāḥ*); "words that reach the heart" (*hṛdayaṃgamāḥ*).
(Kāt_4.3.46) [The suffix *kha* is added to *gama* after the words] *uras* and *vihāyas*, and [the forms] *ura-* and *vi-* [are substituted for *uras* and *vihāyas* respectively].

When *uraḥ* and *vihāyasaḥ* are used as subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *kha* is applied after the root *gam*, provided a name (*saṃjñā*) is being formed; in those cases, *uraḥ* and *vihaḥ* are substituted respectively. Thus, "one who goes by means of the chest" is *uraṅgamaḥ*; "one who goes through the sky" is *vihaṅgamaḥ*.
The suffix *ḍa* is also applied even when it is not a name. (Kātantra 4.3.47)

When *nāman* is the upapada, the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *gam*, whether it denotes a proper name (*saṃjñā*) or not; and in the case of *uras* and *vihāyas*, they are respectively replaced by *uru* and *vi*. Examples: *bhujagaḥ*, *turagaḥ*, *plavagaḥ*, *patagaḥ*, *antagaḥ*, *atyantagaḥ*, *adhvagaḥ*, *dūragaḥ*, *pāragaḥ*, *sarvagaḥ*, *sarvatragaḥ*, *pannagaḥ*, *grāmagaḥ*, *gurutalpagaḥ*, *sugaḥ*, *durgaḥ*, *nirgo deśaḥ*, *agaḥ*, *tīragaḥ*, *pīṭhagaḥ*, *uragaḥ*, *vihagaḥ*. Also: *vihaṅga*, *turaṅga*, and *bhujaṅga*. (Kātantra 4.3.48)

These words ending in the suffix *ḍa* are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*) only when they denote a name (*saṃjñā*). For example: "he goes through the air" (*vihāyasā gacchati*) becomes *vihaṅga*; "he goes quickly" (*turaṃ gacchati*) becomes *turaṅga*; "he goes by means of his arms" (*bhujābhyāṃ gacchati*) becomes *bhujaṅga*. By virtue of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], we also have: "he goes by flying" (*pataṃ gacchati*) becomes *pataṅga*; "he goes by leaping" (*plavena gacchati*) becomes *plavaṅga*; "he goes by gliding" (*praveṇa gacchati*) becomes *pravaṅga*. Furthermore, [the suffix *ḍa* is applied] even from other [bases] as well (Pāṇini 4.3.49).

The suffix *ḍa* is also applied after other words, whether they denote a conscious being (*saṃjñā*) or not, when a noun (*nāman*) follows as an upapada: "he moves in the water" (*vāri carati*) is *vāricaraḥ*, a swan;
"he lies on a mountain" (*girau śete*) is *giriśaḥ*; "he strikes at boars" (*varān āhanti*) is *varāhaḥ*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *khan* (to dig) when it is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in *parikhā* ("moat"). It is also seen [used] after the root *han* (to kill) when it denotes the object, provided that the meaning is either "blessing" (*āśis*) or "motion" (*gati*). (Kātantra 4.3.50)

The suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *han* when it signifies an object (*karman*), a benediction (*āśis*), or motion (*gati*). For example: *śatruṃ vadhyāt* (may he slay the enemy) becomes *śatruhaḥ*;

*krośaṃ hanti* (he slays [the distance] of a *krośa*) becomes *krośahaḥ*. The mention of "object" (*karman*) is for the sake of clarity, as the suffix applies only when the root is used intransitively with respect to that object.

[The suffix] *ḍa* occurs after the root *han*, when *kleśa* or *tamas* are the object (*karman*) in composition with *apa*. (Pāṇini 3.2.51) When *kleśa* or *tamas* are the objects in composition, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *han* following *apa*; thus: *kleśāpahaḥ* ("dispeller of afflictions"), *tamo'pahaḥ* ("dispeller of darkness").

How is it that [the forms] *sukhāpahaḥ*, *duḥkhāpahaḥ*, *jvarāpahaḥ*, *vātapittakaphāpahaḥ*, and *viṣāgnidarpāpahaḥ* are formed? They are established by the rule "also from other [words]" (*anyato 'pi ca*). The prescription of *ḍa* here is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*).

How is it that *dārvāghāṭaḥ*, *cārvāghāṭaḥ*, and *varṇasaṃghāṭaḥ* are formed? They will arise from the root *ghaṭ*. [In *cārvāghāṭaḥ*: he strikes what is beautiful (*cāru*), thus *cārvāghāṭaḥ*; likewise *varṇasaṃghāṭaḥ*. But then *dārvāghāṭaḥ* would also follow; however, it is indeed desired when not used as a technical name (*asaṃjñāyām*). [The suffix] *ṇin* is applied after the words *kumāra* and *śīrṣa*. (Kāśikā 4.3.52)

The word *śīrṣa* is a synonym for *śiras*. When the words *kumāra* and *śīrṣa* are used as co-occurring objects (*upapada*) with the verb *han*, the suffix *ṇin* is applied; thus, *kumāraghāṭī* and *śīrṣaghāṭī*. Regarding the rule *ṭag lakṣaṇe jāyāpatyoḥ* (Kātantra 4.3.53): because it denotes a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the term "characteristic" is used here. When the words *jāyā* and *patnī* are used as co-occurring objects with the verb *han*, the suffix *ṭak* is applied to the agent who possesses that characteristic; thus, *jāyāghna* (one who kills his wife) is a Brāhmaṇa, and *patighnī* (one who kills her husband) is a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*).

And also when the agent is not a human being (Kāśikā 4.3.54): when the object is used as a co-occurring word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṭak* occurs after the root *han*, even when the meaning of the verbal root involves an agent who is not a human being. Examples: *jāyāghnas tilakaḥ* (a mole that kills its wife), *patighnī pāṇirekhā* (a palm-line that kills the husband), *śleṣmaghnaṃ trikaṭukam* (trikaṭuka that destroys phlegm), *pittaghnaṃ ghṛtam* (ghee that destroys bile), *vātaghnaṃ tailam* (oil that destroys wind).
Why say "when the agent is not a human being"? [Consider: *ākhughātaḥ śūdraḥ* (a Śūdra who kills rats), *brāhmaṇaghāto vṛṣalaḥ* (a Vṛṣala who kills a Brāhmaṇa).

And how is it that *cauraghāta* means "an elephant" and *śasyaghāta* means "a bull"? It is because of the word *api* [in the rule]. Furthermore, there are such cases as *kṛtaghna* meaning "ungrateful" and *śatrughna* meaning "hero.
[The suffix *ghañ* is used] after the words *hasta*, *bāhu*, and *kapāṭa* when expressing capability (*śakti*). (Kātantra 4.3.55)

When these verbal roots are used as upapadas and the sense of "capability" (śakti) is understood, the suffix *ṭak* occurs after the root *han*. Thus, according to some, there are *hastighnaḥ* ("one capable of killing an elephant") and *bāhughnaḥ* ("one capable of killing with the arms"); also *kapāṭaghnaḥ* ("one capable of breaking a door").

However, in the case of *nagara*, because of a specific rule even when it does not refer to an elephant, we have *nagaraghno 'gniḥ* ("a fire that destroys a city"), whereas *nagaraghātaḥ* refers to an elephant.
Furthermore, *pāṇighaḥ* and *ghaṭāḍhaḥ* are formed with this suffix when referring to an artisan (*śilpin*). (Kātantra 4.3.56)

These two [terms] are irregularly formed (nipātita) when the agent is a craftsman (śilpin). One who strikes with the hands or strikes at the hands is a *pāṇigha*. One who strikes with a *tāḍa* is a *tāḍagha*.
Why "when the agent is a craftsman"? [Because otherwise we have] *pāṇighātaḥ* and *tāḍaghātaḥ*.
[The suffix *gha*] is applied after [the root *han*] when preceded by *rāja-* due to the governing rule, as in *rājagha* (“one who kills a king”). *Kāt_4.3.57*:

When the sense of “the transformation of something into that which it was not” (*abhūtatadbhāva*) is present, the suffix *khyuṭ* is added to the root *kṛ* (to do/make) when words such as *nagna* (naked), *palita* (gray-haired), *priya* (dear), *andha* (blind), *sthūla* (fat), *subhaga* (fortunate), and *āḍhya* (wealthy) are used as upapadas, provided the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*). When the sense of “the transformation of something into that which it was not” is expressed, the suffix *khyuṭ* occurs after *kṛ* with *nagna* and the others as subordinate words, in the sense of the instrumental factor. For example: *anagno nagnaḥ kriyate ’neneti nagnaṃkaraṇaṃ dyūtam* (“that by which one who is not naked is made naked is the instrument of making naked,” i.e., gambling); likewise, *palitaṃkaraṇaṃ tailam* (“oil that makes [hair] gray”), *priyaṃkaraṇaṃ śīlam* (“conduct that makes [someone] dear”), *andhaṃkaraṇaḥ śokaḥ* (“grief that makes [someone] blind”), *sthūlaṃkaraṇaṃ dadhi* (“curd that makes [something] fat”), *subhagaṃkaraṇaṃ rūpam* (“beauty that makes [someone] fortunate”), and *āḍhyaṃkaraṇaṃ vittam* (“wealth that makes [someone] rich”).

The rule beginning with *anagnīkaraṇam* applies by the principle of *tadantavidhi* (extension to that which ends in such). Why is it said "when there is the becoming of what was not previously so" (*abhūtatadbhāve*)? [Consider: *āḍhyam karoti tailena* ("he makes rich by means of oil"), which means he anoints him; because here the "becoming of what was not previously so" is not intended in the sense of production (*utpāda*), but rather the manifestation (*vyakti*) is intended, the suffix *cvi* does not apply in such cases. The same applies in subsequent instances: *nagnīkaroti* ("he makes naked")—here the *yuṭ* augment also does not occur, as there is no distinction [in the application of the rule].
*bhuvaḥ khiṣṇukhukañau kartari* (Pāṇini 3.2.58): After the root *bhū*, the suffixes *khiṣṇu* and *khukañ* are added when denoting the agent.

When words such as *nagna* (naked) and others are used as upapadas, the suffixes *khiṣṇu* and *khukañ* are applied after the root *bhū* in the sense of the agent, to express the attainment of a state that was previously non-existent: *nagnambhaviṣṇuḥ*, *nagnambhāvukaḥ*;
*palitambhaviṣṇuḥ*, *palitambhāvukaḥ*;
*priyambhaviṣṇuḥ*, *priyambhāvukaḥ*.
*andhaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *andhaṃbhāvukaḥ*; *sthūlaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *sthūlaṃbhāvukaḥ*;
*subhagaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *subhagaṃbhāvukaḥ*.
*āḍhyaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *āḍhyaṃbhāvukaḥ*;
*anagnaṃbhaviṣṇuḥ*, *anagnaṃbhāvukaḥ*, and so forth. By the rule of application to that which ends in such suffixes (*tadantavidhi*), this does not occur with forms ending in *cvi*: *āḍhyībhavitā*.

Because it expresses a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*), there is no transformation into that which was not previously so; thus, the suffixes *uṇ* and *ukañ* do not apply even when the object is another.

The letter *i* is for the sake of euphony (*sukha*), as is the case with the rule "after the root *kṛ*, in the sense of the agent. After the root *bhaj*, the suffix *viṇ* applies [by Pāṇini 3.2.62]. (Kāśikā 4.3.59)
When a word denoting an object (*karman*) is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *viṇ* is applied after the root *bhaj*; for example, *ardhabhāk* ("sharing half") and *pādabhāk* ("sharing a quarter").
According to some, it is also applied after a prefix (*upasarga*), as in *ardhaprabhāk*.
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), it is applied after the prefix *saha*; [Kātantra 4.3.60].

When a word is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *viṇ* is observed after the root *sah* in the Vedic language (*chandas*) when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is intended; this [suffix] is also employed in common usage (*loka*). For example: *turāṣāṭ* and *turāsāhaṃ purodhāya*. And [the suffix *viṇ* occurs] after the root *vah*. (Kātyāyana 4.3.61) When a word is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *viṇ* occurs after the root *vah* in the Vedic language when a technical name is intended. Examples: *praṣṭhavāṭ* and *praṣṭhauhī*. Regarding *vah*, there is the rule that the vowel *au* replaces the *ā* of *vah*; this also follows the previous [analogy].

When *anas* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffix *viṇ* occurs after the root *vah*, and the final syllable of *anas* becomes *ḍa*. Thus, "one who carries a cart" is *anaḍvān*; [the feminine form] *anaḍuhī* is established by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). *Kāt_4,3.63*: After the root *duh*, the suffix *ka* occurs, and the final consonant is replaced by *gha*.
When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *ka* occurs after the root *duh*, and *gha* is substituted for the final letter; thus, *brahmadughā gauḥ* ("a cow that milks the Veda").

It is remembered by the wise that a cow which properly milks all desires (*kāmadughā*) is truly a cow when correctly employed; however, when wrongly employed, that very same [word] proclaims the "cow-ness" (the state of being a mere animal) of the speaker.
*Kāt_4.3.64*: When *nāman* is the upapada, the suffix *viṭ* occurs after the roots *vi*, *krami*, *gam*, *khan*, and *sanij*. Thus:
*agregāḥ*, *udadhikrāḥ*, *goṣāḥ*, and likewise *viṣakhāḥ*.
"O Indra among kings, may these lotuses together bestow prosperity upon you.
It is held that those [words] well-known in the world as technical designations (*saṃjñā*) in Vedic literature (*chandasi*) are employed [in secular usage].
In the mantra [of Pāṇini 5.1.71]: 'The suffix *viṇ* is applied after the words *śvetavāh*, *ukthaśas*, *puroḍāś*, and *avayaj*. (Kātantra 4.3.65)
From these [prefixes], *viṇ* occurs in a mantra: *śvetavāḥ*, Indra, who is drawn by white [horses].
Or, one recites hymns (*ukthāni*) with hymns (*ukthaiḥ*), thus [he is] *ukthaśāḥ*, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

It is offered before him, thus *puroḍāḥ*; the substitution of *ḍ* for *d* occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), or it is that which is seen before; and the form ending in *a* is also irregularly derived, as in "his lower lip is always purified by the *puroḍāśa*."

The forms *avayajate* and *avayāḥ* [are derived from the root *yaj*]. When a pause (*virāma*) follows, or when a consonant begins the following word, the final syllable of these [words] becomes *-us*: *śvetavobhyām*, *puroḍobhyām*, *ukthaśobhyām*; however, in the absence of the dental *-d*, it is *puroḍāśābhyām*.
But when a vowel begins the following word, they remain as *śvetavāhau*, *ukthaśaṃsau*, and *avayājau*.
In the case of *mantra*, it is understood according to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) because it is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*); thus, it is held that they are employed in common worldly usage.

*Āto mankvanibvanibvicaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.74) The suffixes *man*, *kvanip*, *vanip*, and *vic* occur after a verbal root ending in long *ā*. [Accordingly, the forms *mantra*, *karman*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, and *pācaka* are derived.]
*Man*: "He gives beautifully" is *sudāmā*.
"He stands like a horse" is *aśvatthāmā*.
With the suffix *kvanip*: *supīvā*, *sudhīvā*.
*vani-p*, *ghṛtapāvā*, *bhūridāvā*;
*vi-c*, *kīlālapāḥ*. [These suffixes] are also seen after other roots. (Kāśikā 4.3.67)
These suffixes are also seen after other verbal roots: *man*, as in *suśarmā*;
*kvanip*, as in *prātaritvā*.
*vanip*, *vijāvā*.
From the roots *ric*, *riśa*, and *ruśa* in the sense of "injury," [we derive] *reṭ* and *roṭ*.
The inclusion of the root *dṛś* is for the sake of following actual usage.

*Kvip* also [is applied]. According to Pāṇini 3.2.76 (*dhātoḥ kvip ca*), the suffix *kvip* is also seen after a verbal root. For example: *ukhāyāḥ sraṃsate* (it falls from the pot) becomes *ukhāsrat*;
*parṇāni dhvaṃsate* (it falls from the leaves) becomes *parṇadhvat*.
*diva*, *akṣadyūḥ*;
*kruṅ*, *pratyaṅ*, *ūḥ*, *kīḥ*, *gīḥ*, *lūḥ*. After the root *bhraṃś*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) when it means "falling away" (*vahe*). (Kātantra 4.3.69)

When *vah* ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is the governing word (*upapada*), the root *bhraṃś* takes the suffix *kvip*; for example, "he falls from the vehicle" (*vahād bhraśyati*) becomes *vaha-bhraṭ*.
According to Kāśikā 4.3.70, when a word other than *udaka* is the governing word, the root *spṛś* takes the suffix *kvip*;
for example, "one who touches ghee" (*ghṛtaṃ spṛśati*) becomes *ghṛta-spṛk*, and "one who touches with a mantra" (*mantreṇa spṛśati*) becomes *mantra-spṛk*.

What is the meaning of "anudaka" (not water)? For example: *udakasparśaḥ* (touching water). Regarding *ado 'nanne* (Kātantra 4.3.71): when a word other than "food" (*anna*) is the accompanying term (*upapada*), the root *ad-* takes the suffix *kvip*; for example, *sasyam atti* (he eats grain) becomes *sasyāt*.
"He eats raw [food]," from *āmāt*. Why say "not food" (*ananna*)? [Consider] *annādaḥ* ("eater of food").
*Kaṇādaḥ* is also seen [as a formation].

"And with *kravya*. (Kāt. 4.3.72) When *kravya* is the upapada, the root *ad* takes the suffix *kvip*; because of this repeated mention, it applies to the cooked [meat]. Thus, *kravyāt* ("flesh-eater"). In the case of uncooked meat, the suffix is simply *aṇ*, as in *kravyādā rākṣasāḥ* ("the Rākṣasas are eaters of raw flesh"). This group of four sūtras is for the sake of detailed exposition (*prapañca*).

*Ṛtvij*, *dadhṛk*, *sraj*, *dig*, and *uṣṇih* [are formed with the suffix *kvip*]. (Kātantra 4.3.73) These are irregularly derived forms ending in *kvip*: "one who sacrifices at the proper season" is *ṛtvij*; this is established solely by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). From the root *dhṛṣ* ("to dare"), there is reduplication, resulting in *dadhṛk*.
From the root *sṛj*, after the vowel *ṛ*, there is the suffix *at*; with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the object, it is that which one emits (*srjati*), hence *srak*.
From the root *diś*, with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the object, it is that which one points out (*diśati*), hence *dik*.

It is *uṣṇik* because it is warm (*ūrdhvam snihyati*); by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the elision of the *d* in *ud*, the substitution of *ṣ*, and the substitution of *g* due to its inclusion in the *dṛk*-class.

*Kāt_4.3.74*: After the roots *sū*, *dviṣ*, *druh*, *duh*, *yuj*, *vid*, *bhid*, *chid*, *jin*, and *rāj*, the suffix *kvip* occurs when there is a prefix (*upasarga*), even if there is no prefix, and even when a noun (*nāman*) is present as an upapada. Examples: from *sad*, *upāsīdati*, *upasat*, *sat*, *sabhāsat*. Because of its association with *dviṣ*, the root *sū* here refers to the *sū* beginning with *su-* (to bring forth): *prasūte*, *prasūḥ*, *sūḥ*, *aṇḍasūḥ*.
vidviṭ, dviṭ, mitradviṭ;
pradhruk, dhruk, mitradhruk;
pradhuk, dhuk, godhuk.
*prayuk*, *yuṅ*, *aśvayuk*;
*saṃvit*, *vit*, *vedavit*—these are not seen when the sense is "acquisition" (*lābha*).
*prabhit*, *bhit*, *kāṣṭhabhit*.
*pracchit*, *chit*, *rajjucchit*;
*abhijit*, *jit*, *arijit*;
*praṇīḥ*, *nīḥ*, *senānīḥ*.
*virāṭ*, *rāṭ*, *girirāṭ*.
This is for the sake of the elaboration (*prapañca*).

[The suffixes] *ṭak* and *sak* are applied after the root *dṛś* when it follows an object that is also a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) belonging to the class beginning with *tyad*. (Kātantra 4.3.75)

When *tyad* and other pronouns are used as the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the word to be compared (*upameya*) functions as the object (*karman*), the suffixes *ṭak*, *sak*, and *kvip* are applied to the root *dṛś*. Thus: *sya iva dṛśyate* [he is seen like him] results in *tyādṛśaḥ*, *tyādṛśī*, *tyādṛkṣaḥ*, and *tyādṛk*.
Similarly, *sa iva dṛśyate* [he is seen like him] results in *tādṛśaḥ*, *tādṛśī*, *tādṛkṣaḥ*, and *tādṛk*.
In these cases, when the word *samāna* (same) is used, *sa* is substituted for it; thus, *sadṛśaḥ*, *sadṛśī*, *sadṛkṣaḥ*, and *sadṛk*.

[The suffix *dṛś* is applied] after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*), as in: *anyādṛśaḥ*, *anyādṛśī*, *anyādṛkṣaḥ*, *anyādṛk*. Why specify "after *tyad* and so forth"? [Consider: *vṛkṣa iva dṛśyate* ("it is seen like a tree"). Why specify "when it is a standard of comparison" (*upamāna*)? [Consider: *sa dṛśyate* ("he is seen").
What is the purpose of the term *karmaṇi*? [Consider: *sa iva paśyati* ("he sees like that").

[The rule] *nāmny ajātau ṇinis tācchīlye* (Kāt. 4.3.76) applies: the word *tat* refers to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that very thing is the habitual disposition (*śīla*) of the agent. When a noun denoting a non-genus (*ajāti*) is the subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a verbal root when a habitual disposition is understood. Examples: *uṣṇabhojī* ("one who habitually eats hot food"), *dharmāvabhāṣī* ("one who habitually preaches the Dharma").
What is the purpose of the term "nāmni" (as a name)? [Examples: *upabhoktā* (enjoyer), *saṃbhoktā* (partaker).
How about *udāsārī*, *pratyāsārī*, and *brahmavādī*?
And in the sense of "good," it should indeed be stated that one who gives well is *sādhudāyī* and one who acts well is *sādhukārī*.
What is meant by "in the case of those not yet born"? [The example is: "one who will address the Brāhmaṇas.
A *jāti* (genus) is grasped through its form; it does not possess all genders, and it is to be understood as being taught once. It includes both *gotra* (lineage) and *caraṇa* (Vedic school).
"Before its production and destruction, existence [sattva] is simultaneous with the qualities;
the wise know that genus (*jāti*) to have manifold meanings and not all genders"—
so say others.
In that case, it must necessarily be *kumāravādī* because of the absence of a genus (*ajātitvāt*).

[This applies] when the agent is the object of comparison. According to Pāṇini 3.2.77: "When a word denoting an agent is used as an upapada in the sense of an object of comparison, the suffix *ṇini* occurs after a verbal root, for the purpose of expressing a genus (*jāti*), and not for the purpose of expressing habituality (*tācchīlya*) or frequency (*abhīkṣṇya*). For example: "He cries like a camel" (*uṣṭra iva krośati*) results in *uṣṭrakrośī*.
"He cries like a jackal" is *dhmāṅkṣarāvī*.
Why is it specified "in the sense of the agent"? [Consider: "He eats kodrava grains as if they were śāli rice.
Why is it specified "when there is a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)"? [Consider: "The camel cries."

The agent expressed by the upapada [in the compound] is logically the standard of comparison for the agent of the action denoted by the suffix *ṇini*. This is because, in the sentence "his shouting is like that of a camel" (*uṣṭrasyeva krośanam asya*), there is a state of being figurative (*gauṇatva*) even when there is an internal relationship [between the members].

And [the suffix *ṇini* is applied] after a word expressing a *vrata* (vow) or frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). According to Kātyāyana 4.3.78, *vrata* means a restriction prescribed by scripture; *ābhīkṣṇya* means repetition or constant practice.

When a noun is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied to a verbal root when either a vow (*vrata*) or frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*) is implied. For example: *aśrāddhabhojī* (one who does not eat at a funeral feast) and *alavaṇabhojī* (one who does not eat salt). Regarding the vow: it is a restriction regarding one’s engagement due to a specific purpose; even when food is available, he eats only what is not a *śrāddha* meal, and not a *śrāddha* meal. Regarding frequency: "The Uśīnaras are milk-drinkers" (*kṣīrapāyinaḥ*) or "The Vāhīkas are sour-gruel-drinkers" (*sauvīrapāyinaḥ*). In these cases, since there is no other drink available, their intent is directed toward milk (or sour gruel) regardless of personal preference; thus, frequency is distinct from habitual disposition (*śīla*). In this context, the word *manas* is treated like a masculine noun. (Kātantra 4.3.79)

When an object (*karman*) is the subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *man*. And when this root ends in the suffix *ṇini*, the feminine form of the subordinate word is substituted for it as far as possible, and it becomes like the masculine (*puṃvat*).
[Examples: *paṭuṃ manyate* (she considers herself clever) becomes *paṭumānī*; *paṭvīṃ manyate* (she considers herself clever) becomes *paṭumāninī*.

By the rule *puṃvac ca*, the grammatical rules concerning the masculine form (*puṃvad-ādi-śāstra*) are intended here; by that, forms such as *khaṭvāmāninī*, *brahmabandhūmāninī*, and *droṇīmāninī* are established.
[Regarding] *khaś cātmane* (Kātantra 4.3.80):
when *ātman* is the object of the sense of "thinking" (*manyati*), provided it is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇini* occurs, and *khaś* also occurs.

She who considers herself learned is *vidvanmāninī*, *viduṣimanyā*, or *vidvanmānī*; he who considers himself learned is *vidvanmanyaḥ*. She who considers herself clever is *paṭumāninī*, *paṭvimanyā*, *paṭumānī*, or *paṭumanyaḥ*. Because there is coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇatva*), the suffixes *ṇini* and *kvin* undergo the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*). Here, the word "self" (*ātman*) functions as the object through its meaning; it is for the sake of that [object], and in the sentence it serves the purpose of "pleasure. Due to the distinction in the power of the grammatical factors (*kārakaśaktibheda*), there is a distinction: a single entity may be both agent and object, just as the honey being drunk intoxicates. In this context, the "self" is external, because of the expression "one's own self" (*ātmavacana*).
*Karaṇe ’tīte yajaḥ* (Kātantra 4.3.81).

When a word expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) is used as a subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇini* is applied after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) when it denotes a past action. Examples are *agniṣṭomayājī* and *vājapeyayājī*. The meaning is that one has brought about the fruit called heaven by means of sacrifices known as the *agniṣṭoma*. However, the word "heaven" (*svarga*), being already included within the compound formation (*vṛtti*), is not explicitly employed. If a specific operation is the instrument for a general operation, how could one say, "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," given that Vedic sentences are of non-human origin? Why does the rule specify "past" (*atīte*)? [Consider: *agniṣṭomena yajati* ("He sacrifices with the *agniṣṭoma*"). This is present, not past.

What is the purpose of the term *karaṇe* [“when the instrument is the upapada”]? For example: *grāme yajati sma* (“he used to sacrifice in the village”), because the instrument is not intended to be expressed.

*Karmaṇi hanaḥ kutsāyām* (Kāśikā 4.3.82): When *han* (“to kill”) occurs with a past action and a word denoting the object (*karman*) is present as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇini* is applied provided that contempt (*kutsā*) is understood; e.g., *pitṛghātī* (“patricide”), *mātṛghātī* (“matricide”).

Why is it said "in the sense of reproach"? [Examples such as] *cauraṃ hatavān* ("he has killed a thief") and *daṇḍena hatavān pitṛvyam* ("he has struck his paternal uncle with a staff") are excluded because they involve a dependency [on other factors].
The mention of the word *karman* (object) is for the sake of clarity.
[The suffix] *kvip* is applied after [the roots] *brahman*, *bhrūṇa*, and *vṛtra*. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.3.83)

When *brahman* and other such words are used as upapadas (governing objects), the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *han* in its past sense (*atīta*) when it is in the present tense. Examples are: *brahmahā*, *bhrūṇahā*, and *vṛtrahā*. In this rule, there is a fourfold restriction (*niyama*): only after *brahman* and others; only after the root *han*; only in the past sense; and only with the suffix *kvip*. Consequently, [the suffix does not apply] in cases such as *gāṃ hatavān* ("he killed a cow"), *brahmādhītavān* ("he studied the Veda"), *brahma hanti* ("he kills a Brahmin"), or *brahma hatavān* ("he has killed a Brahmin"); therefore, the suffix *aṇ* is not applied here.
A specific restriction is also observed: [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after *madhu-hā*, *ahi-hā*, *gotra-hā*, *brahma-ghnaḥ*, the killer of Vṛtra, and *brahma-vit*.
[The suffix *kvip* is applied] after the root *kṛ* when followed by the words *su-puṇya*, *pāpa-karman*, and *mantra-pada*. (Kātantra 4.3.84)

When these verbal roots (*karma-upapada*) follow as objects, the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *kṛ* when it is in the past tense (*atīta*). For example: *sukṛt* (one who has done well), *puṇyakṛt* (one who has performed merit), *pāpakṛt* (one who has committed sin), *karmakṛt* (one who has performed an action), *mantrakṛt* (one who has composed a mantra), *padakṛt* (one who has composed a word). In this context, there is a threefold restriction: 1) the roots must be *svādi* (beginning with *su*, etc.), 2) the root must be *kṛ* itself, and 3) the suffix *kvip* occurs only in the past tense. Therefore, in cases such as *mantrān adhītavān* (he has studied the mantras), *karma karoti* (he performs an action), or *karma kṛtavān* (he has performed an action), the suffix *aṇ* does not apply.

The terms *śāstrakṛt* ("author of a treatise") and *sūtrakṛt* ("author of a sūtra") certainly exist [by this rule]. Regarding the word *soma*: Kātantra 4.3.85 states that when *soma* is the object (*karman*) and occurs as a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *suñ* (to press) when it refers to the past. Thus, having pressed the *soma*, one is called *somasut*.

In this case as well, there is a fourfold restriction; therefore, [the suffix] *aṇ* does not apply after *surāṃ sutavān*, *somaṃ vikrītavān*, *somaṃ sunoti*, and *somaṃ sutavān*. After other roots, however, *aṇ* would indeed apply in the absence of *kvip*. [The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after *ci* when *agni* follows. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.3.86)
When *agni* is the upapada and the action is past, the suffix *kvip* occurs after the root *ci* (to pile). One who has piled the fire-altar is *agnicit*.

Here too, the fourfold restriction applies; therefore, [the suffix does not occur] in cases such as "one who has piled flowers," "one who has offered oblations to the fire," "one who piles the fire," or "one who has piled the fire"—hence no *aṇ* suffix is used.

However, when the specific arrangement of bricks for the purpose of the fire-altar is understood, it is indeed seen even with the object [as the upapada]: that which was piled like a hawk is *śyenacit*.
It was piled like a chariot wheel; thus, "rathacakracit.
This set of four sūtras is also for the purpose of elaboration (*prapañca*).
[The suffix] *in* is used in the sense of reproach (*kutsā*). (Kāśikā 4.3.87)

When *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *in* occurs after the root *krī* preceded by the prefix *vi*, provided it refers to the past and contempt (*kutsā*) is implied; for example, *somavikrayī* (a seller of Soma) and *tailavikrayī* (a seller of oil), meaning one who has sold Soma.
This rule is stated to prevent the application of *aṇ*, even though the formation would otherwise be established by the suffix *al*.

The suffix *kvanip* is added to the root *dṛś* (to see). According to Pāṇini 3.2.88, when a past object is used as an upapada, the suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *dṛś* in its sense of the past. For example: *meruṃ dṛṣṭavān* (he has seen Meru) becomes *merudṛśvā*.
This rule serves as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the suffixes *kvip* and others that apply in the past tense.

Regarding *saha* and *rājan* [as upapadas]: Pāṇini 3.2.89 states that when *saha* and *rājan* are used as objects (*karman*) as subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *yudh* (to fight) when referring to the past. Thus: *saha yudhyate sma* (he fought together), *sahayudhvā*;
*rājānaṃ yudhyate sma*, *rājayudhvā*.
When *antarbhūta* (included) [as a prefix], the root *yudh* becomes transitive; the meaning is "he fought with the king.

And from the root *kṛ*: according to Pāṇini 3.4.21 (*saharājñor yoge kṛñaḥ kvanip*), when *saha* and *rājan* are used as co-occurring objects (*upapada*), the suffix *kvanip* occurs after the root *kṛ* when referring to the past. Examples: *saha cakre* ("he did together") and *sahakṛtvā* ("having done together").

Having formed the word *rājakṛtvā*. According to Pāṇini 3.2.97 (*janer ḍaḥ*), when the root *jan* (to be born) occurs with a word ending in the seventh (*saptamī*) or fifth (*pañcamī*) case as its attendant noun (*upapada*), the suffix *ḍa* is applied provided that the action has occurred in the past. Examples: *jale jātam* (born in water) → *jalajam*; *sarasijam* (born in a lake); *buddhijam* (born from intelligence); *buddhijaḥ* (born from intelligence); *saṃskārajaḥ* (born from refinement); *krodhajam* (born from anger); *brāhmaṇajo dharmaḥ* (dharma born of a Brāhmaṇa); *kṣatriyajaṃ yuddham* (war born of a Kṣatriya).

How is it that expressions such as *aśvāj jātaḥ* ("born from a horse") and *hastino jātaḥ* ("born from an elephant") are generally seen with the ablative case (*pañcamī*) even when the action of being born has not yet occurred? This is also seen elsewhere. *Kātantra 4.3.92*: When another word (*upapada*) follows, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *jan-* (to be born) when it denotes the past, provided the action of being born has not yet occurred. Thus: *ajaḥ* ("unborn"), *dvijaḥ* ("twice-born"), *prajā* ("progeny"), *abhijaḥ*, and *parijaḥ*. A girl born after a male is *pumanujā*; one born after a female is *stryanujaḥ*.
Niṣṭhā. (Kāt 4.3.93) The suffix *niṣṭhā* occurs after a verbal root denoting the past; e.g., *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*, *śayitaḥ*, *śayitavān*.
(Kāt 4.3.94) The suffix *ṅvanip* occurs after the roots *su* and *yaj*.
The suffix *ṅvanip* occurs after the roots *su* and *yaj* when used in the past or present; for example, *sutavān* and *sutvā*, as well as *iṣṭavān* and *yajvā*.
The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of preventing *guṇa* substitution.

The suffix *antṛn* is applied after the present stem of the root *jṛ* (to grow old) when it denotes the past. Thus, *jaraṃ* and *jaratī*. The vowel *ṛ* and the consonant *n* are for the sake of pronunciation.
Thus ends the third quarter in the *Daurgasimhī-vṛtti* on the *Kṛt* suffixes.
*Kvansukānau parokṣāvac ca* (Kāt. 4.4.1):

After a verb root signifying the past, the suffixes *kvansu* and *kāna* occur; these two are designated as if they were the *parokṣā* (perfect) tense. Examples: *pecivān*, *pācayāṃcakṛvān*, *oṣāṃbabhūvān*.

*śiśīrvān*, *didīrvān*, *jajāgarvān*, *babhajvān*, *rarajvān*. Because [the form] is seen when the semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) is substituted, there is guna for the root *jāgarti* and the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* (the nasal). *vyatipecānaḥ*, *cakrāṇaḥ*. Why is the heading "past" (*atīta*) stated? The suffix *kvansu* should be prescribed for the roots *śru*, *sad*, *vas*, and *am* immediately following the past tense; as in *upaśuśrāva*, *upāśrauṣīt*, *upāśṛṇot*, *upaśuśruvān*.
*upasasāda*, *upāsadat*, *upāsīdat*, *upasedivān*.
*anūvāsa*, *anvavātsīt*, *anvavasat*, *anūṣivān*. Likewise, from the root *i* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, and from the root *aś*: *īyivān*, *samīyivān*, *upeyivān*, *anāśvān*.
Likewise, from the root *vac* with the prefix *anu*, the suffix *kāna* occurs only in the sense of the agent, as in *anūcāna*.
Although these express something past, they are to be employed as before. These roots, beginning with *śru*, are established in common usage (*bhāṣā*) in this very way.

*Kāt_4.4.2*: "In the sense of the present, the suffixes *śantṛṅ* and *ānaś* occur after a verbal root denoting a present action, [provided they do not have] coreferentiality with a non-nominative (i.e., non-first-case) word, and also when there is a vocative. The meaning is that these suffixes *śantṛṅ* and *ānaś* do not occur when they share coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a word ending in the nominative case; for example: *pacantaṃ pacamānaṃ chāttraṃ paśya* ("See the student who is cooking"), *pacatā pacamānena chāttreṇa kṛtam* ("Done by the student who is cooking"), and so forth.
And in the case of an address (*āmantrita*), as in *he pacan* and *he pacamāna*.
Why [is it said] "of an address that is not in the first case and has the same substratum" (*aprathamakādhikaraṇāmantritayoḥ*)? [Consider: *pacati chātraḥ*.
Because of the non-universality (*anityatva*) of what is indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*), we have *juhoti* and *juhvat*.
Likewise, with the negative particle *mā* used in the sense of prohibition (*ākrośe*), [the suffixes] *śatṛ* and *śānac* are applied: *mā pacan*, *mā pacamānaḥ*.
And when there is a requirement for an action (*kriyāpekṣāyām*), the suffix *ānaś* is also applied: *pacann āste*, *pacamānas tiṣṭhati*.
Or, in the sense of existence (*sattāyām*): *san guṇaḥ*, *asti guṇaḥ*; *vidyamāno brāhmaṇaḥ*, *vidyate brāhmaṇaḥ*.

*Kāt_4,4.3: lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ.* From *ā bhūtāt* [Kāt_4,4.67], the governing rule for the present tense applies; the suffixes *śatṛ* and *ānaś* occur after a verbal root when it denotes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) or the cause (*hetu*) of an action. Examples: *tiṣṭhanto 'nuśāsanti gaṇakāḥ* (The accountants give instructions while standing), *śayānā bhuñjate yavanāḥ* (The Yavanas eat while lying down).
And as for the cause: *arjayan vasati* (He dwells while earning), *adhīyāno vasati* (He dwells while studying).
*Lakṣaṇa* means a characteristic mark; *hetu* means a productive cause.
Why [specify] "of a characteristic mark and a cause"? [Consider: "He cooks and he reads.
Why [specify] "of an action"? [Consider: "That which trembles is an *aśvattha* tree," or "That which floats is light."
*Vetteḥ śantur vaṃsuḥ*.
(Pāṇini 3.2.128) After the root *vid*, the suffix *śatṛ* optionally becomes *vaṃsu*; thus, *vidvān*, *vidvāṃsau*.

[The forms] *vidan*, *vidantau* [are also included]. The mention of the *ti* (the *ti* of *śatṛ*) is for the sake of ease; it indicates that the suffix *śatṛṅ* follows immediately after the root *vid* alone.
*Āna* is designated as *ātmanepada*.

(Kāt_4.4.5) Among these, beginning with *kvansu*, the suffix *āna* is termed *ātmanepada*; by implication, the others are *parasmaipada*. Examples: *adhīyamānam*, *sthīyamānam*, *rocamānaḥ*, *cakrāṇaḥ*, *vyatibabhūvānaḥ*.

Because it is an ātmanepada root, [the suffix -ta] occurs in the sense of the passive or the reflexive, as well as in the sense of the agent after roots such as *ruc*. Regarding the rule *īt tasyāsaḥ* (Kāt. 4.4.6): for that which follows *ās*, namely the suffix *āna*, its initial vowel becomes *ī*; thus, *āsīnaḥ*.

The word *tasya* is used for the purpose of drawing in [the term] *rūpamātra* (the mere form); by that, it applies even to the suffix *śānac*. [Example: *katīhodāsīnāḥ santi* ("How many are there here who are indifferent?").

*Kāt_4.4.7*: *ānmo 'nta āne*. When the suffix *āna* follows an *akāra*, the letter *m* becomes the final element (*anta*) of that which ends in *akāra*. [Examples: *pacamānaḥ*, *yajamānaḥ*, *kriyamāṇaḥ*, *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*.
Kātyāyana 4.4.8: After the roots *pū* and *yaj*, the suffix *śānac* occurs. Thus, from *pū*, we have *pavate* and *pavamānaḥ*.
"He sacrifices," "the sacrificer.

Regarding these two [forms], some say that the statement of the suffix *ānaś* is for the sake of establishing its presence only in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); others say that the suffix *ānaś* must occur in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*); still others say it is for the purpose of elaborating upon the first [category] having a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*). This technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*) refers to the *bahiṣpavamāna* and *mādhyandina* [stotras] in their non-literal sense. [The suffix *ānaś* is used] in the sense of capacity (*śakti*), age (*vayas*), or habitual disposition (*tācchīlya*). (Kātantra 4.4.9)

When meanings such as "capacity" (*śakti*) and so forth are implied, the suffix *śānac* occurs after a verbal root: *katīha nighnānāḥ* ("how many here are striking?"), *katīha kavacam udvahamānāḥ* ("how many here are wearing armor?"), *katīha nṛtyamānāḥ* ("how many here are dancing?"). Because these meanings are specifically prescribed, the suffix *śatṛ* (the present participle marker) would not otherwise apply by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpa*). However, *śatṛ* is applied after the roots *iṅ* and *dhṛ* when there is no difficulty (*akṛcchra*): [Kātantra 4.4.10].

The suffix *śantṛṅ* occurs after the roots *iṅ* (to study) and *dhṛ* (to hold), when no difficulty is implied: *adhīyan pārāyaṇam* (studying the Pārāyaṇa), *dhārayann upaniṣadam* (holding the Upaniṣad).

Since *ānaś* would have applied after *iṅ*, and both [suffixes] would have applied after *dhṛ*, this rule provides an option; furthermore, even the principle of *vāsarūpa* (the optional use of non-identical forms) should not be desired here.
Why "when no difficulty is implied"? [Observe: *kṛcchreṇādhīte* (he studies with difficulty).
*dviṣaḥ śatrau* (Pāṇini 3.2.61). After the root *dviṣ*, the suffix *śatṛṅ* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is in the sense of "enemy" (*śatru*). Examples: *dviṣan*, *dviṣantau*.
Why specify "in the sense of enemy"? [Consider: *dveṣṭi patiṃ bhāryā* ("the wife hates her husband").

*Suño yajñasaṃyoge* (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.4.12). When the root *su* is used in the sense of being connected with the fruit of a sacrifice, the suffix *śantṛṅ* occurs; for example, *sunvanto yajamānāḥ* ("the sacrificers who press [the Soma]").
The mention of "connection" (*saṃyoga*) is for the purpose of indicating an agent who possesses the fruit [of the action].
What is meant by "in connection with sacrifice" (*yajñasaṃyoga*)? [Example: *sunoti surām* ("he presses the liquor").

*Arhaḥ* [is used] in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). According to Pāṇini 3.2.133, when praise is implied, the suffix *śantṛṅ* occurs after the root *arh*; [example: *arhan bhavān vidyām* ("you are worthy of knowledge").
What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of praise" (*praśaṃsāyām*)? [Consider: "The thief deserves death.

From *Kātantra* 4.4.14 up to *Kātantra* 4.4.57, inclusive of the suffix *kvip*, these suffixes are to be understood as occurring after roots when the agent possesses the qualities of "having that habit" (*tacchīla*), "having that duty" (*taddharma*), or "performing that well" (*tatsādhukārī*).

*tṛn*. (Kāt_4.4.15) The suffix *tṛn* occurs after a verbal root when the agent is characterized by that habit, possesses that quality, or performs that action well; it is an exception to *tṛc* and other such suffixes. Examples: *vaditā janāpavādān* ("one who is wont to speak ill of people"); *muṇḍayitāraḥ śrāviṣṭhāyanā ūḍhāṃ vadhūm* ("the Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are those who habitually shave their married brides"). In the example *sādhu gacchati gantā khelam*, the word *sādhu* here has the sense of "skillful" (*kuśala*). (Kāt_4.4.16) The suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after the roots *bhrāj*, *alaṃkṛ*, *bhū*, *sah*, *ruc*, *vṛt*, *vṛdh*, *car*, *prajan*, and *apatrap*.
The suffix *iṣṇuc* occurs after these [roots] when the agent possesses that habit or similar quality; it is an exception to *tṛn*. Examples:

*bhrājiṣṇuḥ* (shining), *alaṃkariṣṇuḥ* (adorned). The word *alam* is used in the senses of ornament, sufficiency, and prevention; here, it also sets aside the suffix *yuc* [which would otherwise apply in the sense of adornment].

*bhaviṣṇuḥ*, *sahiṣṇuḥ*, *rociṣṇuḥ*, *vartiṣṇuḥ*, *vardhiṣṇuḥ*, *cariṣṇuḥ*, *prajaniṣṇuḥ*, *apatrapiṣṇuḥ*. These [words ending in] *-iṣṇu* are [formed] in the Vedic language (*chandas*). [In the Classical language, one says] *dhārayiṣṇuḥ*. It should be stated that [the word] *nirākariṣṇuḥ* [is also formed in this way].
After *mad*, *pat*, and *pac*, [the suffix] *iṣṇuc* occurs when *ud* is the upapada, provided the agent possesses the qualities of habit, etc. Examples: *unmadiṣṇuḥ*, *utpatiṣṇuḥ*, *utpaciṣṇuḥ*.
There is no correspondence in order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*).
After the roots *ji* and *bhū*, the suffix *snuk* occurs when the agent possesses the sense of habitual action and so forth; thus: *jiṣṇuḥ* (victorious) and *bhūṣṇuḥ* (prospering).
After the roots *glā*, *mlā*, *sthā*, *kṣi*, *pac*, and *parimṛj*, the suffix *snu* occurs.
The suffix *snur* occurs after these [roots] when the agent possesses that habit and so forth: *glāsnuḥ*, *mlāsnuḥ*, *sthāsnuḥ*, *kṣeṣṇuḥ*, *pakṣṇuḥ*, *parimārkṣṇuḥ*.
*Kāt_4.4.20*: The suffix *knur* occurs after these—*tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*—when the agent possesses that habit and so forth: *trasnuḥ*, *gṛdhnuḥ*, *dhṛṣṇuḥ*, *kṣipnuḥ*.
The suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* occur after the eight roots beginning with *śam*, when the agent possesses the qualities of habit, etc. (Kātantra 4.4.21).

The suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* are applied to the eight roots beginning with *śam* when the agent has such characteristics [as habitual action, etc.]. Thus: from *śam* comes *śamī* ("one who is calm"); likewise *damī*, *tamī*, *śramī*, *bhramī*, *kṣamī*, *klamī*, and *unmādī*.
Why specify "of the eight"? [To exclude others, e.g.,] *asitā*.

Kāśikā 3.2.158: *yuj-bhaj-bhuja-dviṣa-druha-duha-duṣ-āṅ-kruñc-aty-aṅ-ru-dh-āṅ-yam-aṅ-ya-sṛ-raj-abhi-āṅ-han-ām ca*. The suffix *ghin* occurs after these roots when the agent possesses the qualities of being habitually so (*tacchīla*) and the like. From the root *yuj* (to join), *yuja*, the word is *yogī* (one who is habitually joined in yoga).
Bhaja, one who possesses a share;
bhuja, one who enjoys;
dviṣa, one who hates.
druha, drohī;
duha, dohī;
duṣa, doṣī.
From *ā-krīḍ* comes *ākrīḍī*; from *tyaj* comes *tyāgī*;
from *anu-rudh* comes *anurodhī*.
From the root *yam* with the prefix *ā*: *āyāmī*. From the root *yas* with the prefix *ā*: *āyāsī*. From the root *rañj*: *rāgī*.

*Abhyāṅ han*, *abhyāghātī*. *Sami sṛjipṛcijvaritvarām* (Pāṇini 3.2.142). When *sam* is a prefix (*upapada*), the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* are applied after the roots *sṛj*, *pṛc*, *jvar*, and *tvar* in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīlādi*). Thus: *saṃsargī*, *saṃparkī*, *saṃjvarī*, *saṃtvarī*.

The vowel is short because it is followed by a nasal (mānubandhatvāt). [Kātantra 4.4.24] When *vi* is the upapada, the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* are applied after the roots *kattha*, *śrambhu*, *kaṣa*, and *laṣa* in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīlādiṣu*). Thus: *vivekī*, *vikatthī*, *viśrambhī*, *vikāṣī*, *vilāṣī*.

After the prefixes *pra*, *drum*, *tha*, *vad*, and *vas*, the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* occur when these words function as *upapadas*, in the sense of "having that as one's habitual disposition" (*tacchīla*) and so forth: *pradrāvī* (one who runs away), *pramāthī* (one who crushes), *pravādī* (one who speaks).
Since *vas* means "dwelling," [the form is] *pravasī* (one who dwells abroad).

*pralāpī*. Regarding *sṛ* and *dah*: Kāt_4.4.26 states that when *pari* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* occur after *sṛ* and *dah* in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīlādi*). Examples: *parisārī*, *paridāhī*.

When there is a desire to express existence (*astivivakṣā*), [the suffix] *in* is established; what then is the purpose of [the suffixes] *ghin* and *ṇi*? For example: *prayāmī*, *prayāsī*, *visārī*, *vidāhī*, *vivādī*, *anuvādī*, *saṃvādī*, *vivāhī*, *saṃcārī*, *vyabhicārī*, *vighātī*, *vidrāvī*, *rogī*, and so forth.

This statement is made so that [the suffix] *tṛn* does not apply when there is a desire to express one who has that as a habit (*tacchīla*) and so on. Furthermore, after the roots *kṣip*, *raṭ*, *vad*, *av* and others, and after *devi*, the suffix *vuṇ* also [applies]. (Kātantra 4.4.27)
When *parā* is the prefix (*upapada*), the suffixes *vuṇ* and *ghin* are applied after these [roots] in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
Examples: *parikṣepakaḥ*, *parikṣepī*;
*parirāṭakaḥ*, *parirāṭī*.
The forms *parivādakaḥ*, *parivādī*, and *parivādayati* are likewise used in the sense of "one who reviles.
Regarding *paridevakaḥ* and *paridevī* (from *paridevate*),
some maintain that the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇiṅ* are applied only after the roots *vad* and *dev*.
The inclusion of the suffix *vuñ* is for the purpose of indicating that the rule of non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*).

Kāśikā 4.4.28: The suffix *vuñ* occurs after the following roots when expressing habitual action and so forth: *nind*, *hiṃs*, *kliś*, *khād*, [roots] consisting of more than one syllable, *vināśi*, *vyābhāṣ*, and *asūy*.
From these, *vuñ* is applied: *nindakaḥ*, *hiṃsakaḥ*, *kleśakaḥ*, *khādakaḥ*, *gaṇakaḥ*.

The word *daridrāyakaḥ* [is formed with the suffix *ṇvul*]. Some do not accept [the application of the suffix] after roots with more than one vowel (*anekasvara*). [The suffix *ṇvul* is applied] to form *vināśakaḥ* (one who destroys) from *vi-nāś*, and *vyābhāṣakaḥ* (one who speaks excessively).
[The suffix *ṇvul* is also applied] to form *asūyakaḥ* (one who is envious), according to the rule "after *kaṇḍū* and others, or after [roots] beginning with *asūy* that have more than one vowel."
The repetition of the suffix *vuñ* is intended to ensure that even when the context is the original [rule], the suffixes *ghin* and *ṇi* do not apply. Regarding *Kātantra 4.4.29*:
"After the roots *div* and *kruś*, when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present as an upapada, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīla*)," and so forth.

*Ādevakaḥ* and *paridevakaḥ* are designations used specifically in the sense of "playing. [The suffix *vuñ* is applied after these roots] when preceded by the prefix *pra*. Why mention "upasarga" (prefix)? [To show that it does not apply otherwise: *devayitā*, *kroṣṭā*.

The suffix *yu* is applied after the roots *krudh*, *maṇḍ*, *cali*, and the word *artha*, in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions and so forth (Kātantra 4.4.30). The word *artha* is connected with each [of the preceding terms].
From a root meaning "to be angry": *krodhanaḥ* (one who is prone to anger), *kopanaḥ*.
From roots meaning "to adorn": *maṇḍana*, *bhūṣaṇa*.

From roots meaning "to move": *calana*, *kampana*. From roots meaning "sound": some say that *śabda* is a noun (*liṅga*) ending in *-in* derived from the *cur*-class; [others give] *śabdana*, *ravaṇa*.

How is the suffix *yu* prescribed for the *vidyā* [roots]? It is stated: "after roots that are intransitive (*akarmaka*) by virtue of their verbal form (*abhidhāna*) or the meaning of the word (*śabdārtha*)," and "after the group beginning with *ruc*, provided they begin with a consonant" (Kātantra 4.4.31). From the class of roots beginning with *ruc* that start with a consonant, the suffix *yu* occurs in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Those from which the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is heard in the list belong to the *ruc*-class, excluding those marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ*. Examples are: *rocanaḥ*, *vartanaḥ*, *vardhanaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the phrase "beginning with *ruc*"? [Examples: *bhavitā*, *śayitā*.

What is the purpose of the phrase "beginning with a consonant"? [Example: *edhitā*. Why is the word "beginning" (*ādi*) used? [So that the rule would] also apply here: *jugupsanaḥ*, *titikṣaṇaḥ*, *bhīmāṃsanaḥ*, *bībhatsanaḥ*; for these, too, are among those other than the *ruc*-class which end in a consonant. How is it that [one says] *vastram vasitā* ("he will wear a garment")? Because of specific linguistic usage (*abhidhāna*), here too [the suffix applies] only after intransitive verbs.

From the roots *ju*, *caṅkram*, *daṇḍram*, *sṛ*, *gṛdh*, *jval*, *śuc*, *laṣ*, *pat*, and *pad*, the suffix *yu* occurs in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. *Ju* is a root belonging to the *sūtra* (Vedic) language meaning "to go"; thus, *javanaḥ* ("one who moves swiftly"), *caṅkramaṇaḥ* ("one who paces"), and *daṇḍramaṇaḥ* ("one who runs about").
In the latter two, the *y* is elided by the rule *yasyānaṇi* (Kātantra 3.6.48).
Saraṇa, Gardhana, Jvalana, Śocana, Abhilaṣaṇa, Prapatana, and Prapadana.

The inclusion of roots meaning "to move" (*calanārtha*) is for the sake of [forming] transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), because [otherwise] they would be barred by the suffix *ukañ* prescribed after the roots *pati* and *pad*. This statement is intended to ensure their application; or rather, since the rule of non-identity of forms (*asarūpavidhi*) does not apply to suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*), their co-occurrence is also observed, as in: *vikalpī*, *vikalpana*; *bhāsura*, *bhāsvara*, *bhāsana*; *jāgaritā*, *jāgarūka*; *vardhiṣṇuḥ*, *vardhana*; *apalaṣitā*, *apalāṣukaḥ*, *apalaṣaṇa*. Some maintain that this is for the sake of transitive verbs. [However, the suffix *ukañ* is] not applied to roots ending in *y*, nor to *sūd*, *dīp*, or *dīkṣ*. (Kātantra 4.4.33)

The suffix *yu* does not occur after roots ending in *y*, nor after the roots *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ*, when forming words denoting habitual action (*tacchīla*) and the like. Since roots ending in *y* would otherwise take *yu* by virtue of belonging to the *krudh*-class, and since *sūd*, *dīp*, and *dīkṣ* would take *yu* by virtue of belonging to the *ruc*-class, this suffix is here prohibited. Thus we have: *knopitā*, *kṣmāyitā*, *vayitā*, *sūditā*, *dīpitā*, *dīkṣitā*. As for *arisūdana*, it is formed because the root belongs to the *nandī*-class. In the case of *dīp*, the suffix *yu* is indeed barred. However, the inclusion of *dīp* in the rule is intended to indicate that even the principle of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) applies here; consequently, the suffix *tṛn* may also occur, as in *dīpitā* and *dīpra*.

Likewise, *kāmukaḥ*, *kamanaḥ*, and *kamraḥ*. According to Pāṇini 3.2.158 (*śṝkamagamahanavṛṣabhūsthālaṣapatapadām ukañ*), the suffix *ukañ* is applied after these roots in the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth: *śārūkaḥ*, *kāmukaḥ*, *āgāmukaḥ*, *āghātukaḥ*, *varṣukaḥ*, *prabhāvukaḥ*, *upasthāyukaḥ*, *apalāṣukaḥ*, *prapātukaḥ*, and *prapādukaḥ*.

The suffix *ṣākan* occurs after the roots *vṛñ*, *bhikṣi*, *luṇṭi*, *jalpi*, and *kuṭṭi* in the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. [Examples: *varākaḥ*, *varākī*; *bhikṣākaḥ*, *bhikṣākī*; *luṇṭākaḥ*, *luṇṭākī*; *jalpākaḥ*, *jalpākī*; *kuṭṭākaḥ*, *kuṭṭākī*. However, from the root *vṛñ* [with the suffix *tṛc*], it is *varitā*.

The letter *ṣ* has the sense of "and so forth" (*nadādi*). [Kātantra 4.4.36 states: *pre jusuvor in*. When *pra* is the prefix, the suffix *in* occurs after the roots *ju* (to hasten) and *sū* (to bring forth) in the sense of those who habitually perform such actions (*tacchīlādi*). Examples: *prajavī* (one who hastens), from *ṣu* in the sense of procreation (*prasava*), *prasavī* (one who brings forth).
From these [roots]—*ji*, *iṇ*, *dṛś*, *viś*, *pṛ*, *bhū*, *mā*, *vyath*—the suffix *in* occurs in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. From *ji*: *jayī*;
from *iṇ*: *pratyayī*.
dṛṅ, ādarī;
kṣi, kṣayī;
viśri, viśrayī.
paribhū, paribhavī; ṭuvama, vamī;
abhyama, abhyamī.
"Na vyathate" means "he does not tremble"; thus, he is "avyathī" (one who does not tremble).
This rule is stated so that the suffix *tṛn* may not apply when there is an intention to express one's character (*tacchīla*) and so forth.
[The suffix] *ālu* is applied after the roots *day*, *pati*, *gṛhi*, *spṛhi*, *śraddhā*, *tandrā*, and *nidrā*. (Kātantra 4.4.38)
The suffix *āluc* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth: from *day*, *dayāluḥ*.
The roots *pati-gṛhi-spṛhi* are included in the *curādi* class with the suffix *in*; thus: *patayāluḥ*, *gṛhayāluḥ*, *spṛhayāluḥ*.
The root *dhā* preceded by *śrad* forms *śraddhāluḥ*.
*tandrā* is a root found in the *sūtra*; from it comes *tandrāluḥ*. From *drā* preceded by the prefix *ni-* comes *nidrāluḥ*. One should say *śayāluḥ*.
How is *hṛdayāluḥ* formed? When the intention is to express "one who possesses a heart," the suffix *ālu* is applied as a conventional formation (*rūḍhi*).
The suffix *ru* occurs after the roots *śad*, *sad*, *dhā*, *didhi*, and *das* in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Thus: *śadruḥ*, *sadruḥ*, *dhāruḥ*.
[From *dā*: he gives, bestows, grants, or cuts—*dāruḥ*.

The root *ṣiñ* means "to bind"; [the suffix] *seruḥ* [is applied]. According to Pāṇini 3.2.161 (*sṛghasyado marak*), the suffix *marak* occurs after these roots in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth: from *sṛ*, one who moves or flows is *sṛmaraḥ*; from *ad*, one who eats is *admaraḥ*.
The suffix *ghurac* is applied after the roots *yuk*, *svar*, *pū*, as well as by virtue of the general rule [of *ghurac* application]; thus, *saraṇaḥ* and *sṛtvaraḥ*.
After the root *ghas*, there is the alternative form *ghasḷ*;
[the suffix *ghurac* is applied] after the roots *mid*, *bhās*, and *bhañj*. (Kātantra 4.4.41)

From these [roots], the suffix *ghur* occurs in the sense of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth: *meduraḥ* (fatty) from *mid*, meaning "he becomes fat"; *bhāsuraḥ* (shining) from *bhās*, meaning "he shines. Regarding *bhaṅguram* (brittle wood): since it is stated that this is used specifically in the reflexive passive construction (*karmakartṛ*), where the object itself performs the action, it means "wood that breaks by itself. However, when one breaks something else, the suffix *tṛn* is used: *bhaṅktā* (one who breaks). For the roots *chid*, *bhid*, and *vid*, the suffix *kura* is applied. (Kātantra 4.4.42)

From these [roots], the suffix *kru* occurs in the sense of "having that as its nature" (*tacchīla*), etc.: *chidura*, *bhidura*. As for *vidura*, it means "one who knows. This is because the suffixes for *chid* and *bhid* are prescribed only when the object is also the agent (the reflexive construction).

Some, however, apply them even when the object is not the agent, as in: *doṣāndhakārabhiduraḥ* ("dispelling the darkness of faults") and *dṛptāripakṣacchiduraḥ* ("cutting down the faction of arrogant enemies").

Jāgurūkaḥ. (Kāt 4.4.43) The suffix *ūka* occurs after the root *jāgṛ* in the sense of one who habitually performs that action and so forth; thus, *jāgarūkaḥ*. For roots ending in the *cekrīyita* (intensive) suffix, [the suffix *ūka* occurs] after *yaj*, *jap*, *daṃś*, and *vid*. (Kāt 4.4.44)
The suffix *ūka* occurs after these [roots] ending in the *cekrīyita* (intensive) reduplication when expressing habituality and similar senses: *yāyajūkaḥ*, *jañjapūkaḥ*, *daṃdaśūkaḥ*, *vāvadūkaḥ*.
Furthermore, *sāsahi*, *cācali*, *vāvadi*, and *pāpati*—which also end in the *cekrīyita*—are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) with the suffix *kvi*;
when this [suffix] is followed by a vowel, its elision (*luk*) occurs. (Kātantra 4.4.45)

The elision (*luk*) of that *cekrīyita* suffix occurs when it denotes one who habitually performs an action (*tacchīla*), and so forth, provided that a vowel (*ac*) follows; thus, *loluvaḥ* and *popuvaḥ*. [This rule] is already established for roots ending in a consonant.
Some divide the *yoga* [into two parts], whereby forms such as *bobhavīti* and *rāraṭīti* are established.

Then, *vara* [is added] after *yāti*. (Kāt_4.4.46) After *yāti* ending in an *icekrīyita* suffix, *vara* occurs in the sense of "one who habitually does that" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; thus, *yāyāvaraḥ*.
When *vara* is the object of the suffix and its [the *icekrīyita*'s] elision occurs, there would be elision of the *ya* before a consonant.
The suffix *kvarap* is applied after the roots *kas*, *pis*, *bhās*, *īś*, *sthā*, and *pramad*.
(Kāt_4,4.47) The best among these occurs in the sense of their respective qualities (*tacchīla*) and so forth: *kasvara*, *pesvara*, *bhāsvara*, *īśvara*, *sthāvara*, and *pramadvara*.
The suffix *kvarap* is also applied after the roots *sṛj*, *iṇ*, and *naś*. (Kāt_4,4.48)

The suffix *kvarap* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth: *sṛtvaraḥ*, *jitvaraḥ*, *itvaraḥ*, *naśvaraḥ*. *Kvarap* also occurs in the *nadādi* group: *sṛtvarī*. After the root *gam*, the suffix *ta* is also applied: *gataḥ*. (Kātantra 4.4.49)

The suffix *kvarap* is applied to the root *gam* in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth, and the letter *t* is substituted for the final [letter] of the root; thus, *gatvaraḥ*, *gatvarī*. By Pāṇini 3.2.160 (*dīpikampyajasahiṃsikami-sminamāṃ raḥ*), the suffix *ra* is applied to these roots in the sense of "having that as one's habit" and so forth: *dīpraḥ*, *kampraḥ*; with the prefix *nañ* (negation), from *jasu* in the sense of "releasing," *ajasraḥ*; *hiṃsraḥ*, *kamraḥ*, *smeraḥ*, *namraḥ*.

The suffix *yu* is also seen [after these roots]: *kampanaḥ*, *kamanaḥ*. *Kāt_4.4.51*: After a root ending in the desiderative suffix *san*, after *ā-śaṃs*, and after *bhikṣ*, the suffix *u* occurs in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Thus: *cikīrṣuḥ* (desiring to act), *āśaṃsuḥ* (expecting)—the reading *āṅaḥ śāmi icchāyām* ("after *ā-śās* in the sense of wishing") is the correct one—and *bhikṣuḥ* (a mendicant).
The inclusion of the term *antagrahaṇa* is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that it applies only to [the suffix] *san*.
[The rule] *vindvicchū ca* (Kāt.

4.4.52) states that *vindu* and *icchū* are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) in the sense of "having such a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; because the root *vid* in the sense of "knowing" (*jñāne*) is mentioned [in the rule], *vinduḥ* is derived.
The root *iṣ* means "to desire"; hence *icchu*.

How is it that *vidu*, meaning "a drop" (a synonym for *stoka*), is derived from the root *vid* meaning "to know," since it is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*) formed by the *uṇādi* suffixes? [The rule states:
"After roots ending in *ā* or *ṛ*, and after those whose penultimate vowel is elided, the suffix *ki* is added and the root is reduplicated. (Kātantra 4.4.53).

The suffix *ki* occurs after a root ending in *a*, after one ending in an *ṛ*-vowel, and after one that undergoes elision of its penultimate vowel (*upadhālopin*), when expressing habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth; and by virtue of this suffix, there are two utterances (*ukti*). For example: from *ḍudhāñ*, *dadhiḥ*;
after a root ending in an *ṛ*-vowel: *cakriḥ*, *sasriḥ*;
and after one that undergoes elision of its penultimate vowel: from *janī* (to be born), *jajñiḥ*.
These are established in common usage; others are to be understood from their application.

[Kāśikā 3.2.170] *tṛṣi-dhṛṣi-svapām najiṅ*: the suffix *najiṅ* occurs after these roots in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth—namely, *tṛṣṇak*, *dhṛṣṇak*, and *svapnak*.
Some do not accept [the suffix] after the root *dhṛṣ*.

After the roots *śṝ* and *vand*, the suffix *āru* occurs (Pāṇini 3.2.173): it becomes *āru* after *śṝ* and *vand* in the sense of "having that as one's habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth; thus, *śarāruḥ* ("one who is prone to breaking") and *vandāruḥ* ("one who is prone to praising").

*bhiyo ruglukau ca* (Kāśikā 4.4.56): After the root *bhī*, the suffixes *ruk* and *luk* also occur when the sense of "having that as a habit" (*tacchīla*) and so forth is intended. Thus: *bhīruḥ*, *bhīluḥ*, *bhīrukaḥ*, *bhīlukaḥ*.
[The mention of] *ku* has the same meaning as *bahula* (i.e., it is used irregularly).
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *bhrāj*, *pṛ*, *dhurv*, and *bhās* when expressing habitual action (*tacchīla*) and so forth. Thus: *vibhrāṭ* (shining), *vibhrājau*;
*pūḥ* (a city), *purau*.
*dhūḥ*, *dhurau*;
*bhāḥ*, *bhāsau*.
The rule for *kvip* is stated again in order to override the suffixes used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*).
The suffix *kvip* occurs after the roots *dyuti* and *gam*, as well as two forms; [the forms] *didyut* and *jagat* occur in the sense of habitual action and so forth.
After the root *bhū*, the suffix *ḍu* occurs before the words *viśam* and *preṣ*.
The suffix *ḍu* is applied after the root *bhū* when preceded by the upapadas *vi*, *śam*, and *pra*; thus: *vibhuḥ*, *śambhuḥ*, *prabhuḥ*.

The letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of eliding the final vowel and the following consonant. After the root *dhā* (to suck) with the object as its upapada, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied; [thus: *karmadhaḥ*]. (Kātantra 4.4.60)

The suffix *ṣṭran* occurs after the root *dhā* when it functions as an object (*karman*) in relation to the agent (*kāraka*).
