The letter *ṣ* is for the purpose of [forming] feminine stems such as *nadī*. That which one drinks (*dhayati*) is a *dhātrī*, meaning a wet-nurse (*stanadāyinī*); it is also called the *āmalakī* fruit. Some also desire [the suffix] after the root *dhā*; that which one places (*dadhāti*) for medicinal purposes is a *dhātrī*. Because it is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*), there is no distinction [between the two roots]. [The suffix *ṣṭran* occurs] after the roots *nī*, *dāp*, *śasu*, *yu*, *yuj*, *stu*, *tud*, *si*, *sic*, *mih*, *pat*, *daṃś*, and *nah* when they function as an instrument (*karaṇa*). (Kātantra 4.4.61)
The suffix *ṣṭran* occurs after these roots when they function as instruments (*karaṇa*). From the root *nī* (to lead), *netra*; from *dāp* in the sense of cutting (*lavana*), *dātra*;
and from *śasu* in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*), *śastra*.
*yu*, *yoktram*; *yujir*, *yoktram*;
*ṣṭuñ*, *stotram*.
*tud*, *tottra*;
*ṣiñ*, *setra*; *ṣic*, *sektra*.
*miha*, *meḍhra*;
*patḷ*, *pattram*; *danśa*, *daṃṣṭrā*—these are always feminine. *ādā*.

*naha*, *naddhrī*. According to Pāṇini 4.4.62, the suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after the roots *pūñ* or *pūṅ* when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a part of a plow (*hala*) or a pig (*śūkara*). Thus, there is *halasya potram* (the snout of a plow) and *śūkarasya potram* (the snout of a pig); the meaning is "the mouth."
This is for the purpose of elaborating upon the rule *sarvadhātubhyaḥ ṣṭran* (Pāṇini 3.2.181).

[The suffix] *itran* [is applied] after the roots *ṛ*, *lū*, *dhū*, *sū*, *khan*, *si*, *hṛ*, and *car*. According to Kāśikā 4.4.63, the suffix *itran* occurs after these [roots] in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in *aritram* and *lavitram*.
The root *dhū* means "to shake," as in *dhavitra*; *ṣū* means "to impel," as in *savitra*;
and *khan* and *sah* form *khanitra* and *sahitra*.
The root *car* has the sense of "going"; [the word] *cāritra* [is derived from it].

According to Pāṇini 3.2.184 (*puvaḥ saṃjñāyām*), the suffix *itran* is applied after the roots *pūñ* or *pūṅ* when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood; thus, *pavitram* means the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and *pavitrā* is the name of a river.

Regarding the agent (*kartṛ*) [in the sense] of a seer (*ṛṣi*) or a deity (*devatā*): according to Pāṇini 4.4.65, the suffix *itran* occurs after the root *pū* when the agent is a seer or a deity. Thus, one who purifies is a "purifier" (*pavitra*); this seer is a purifier; this fire is a purifier.
Some, continuing the [previous rule regarding] the instrument (*karaṇa*), desire a connection based on the respective order [of the roots], asking: "What is the difference in the intended meaning?"
The suffix *kta* is applied after verbal roots marked with the indicatory letters *ñ* or *ṇ*, and after those meaning "desire" (*mati*), "knowledge" (*buddhi*), or "reverence" (*pūjā*).

(Pāṇini 3.4.66) Here, *mati* means desire, *buddhi* means knowledge, and *pūjā* means honor. The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the present tense after roots marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* and after those meaning desire, knowledge, or reverence; it applies to the abstract state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*) as appropriate. For example, from the root *ñimidā* (to break), we have *minnaḥ*.
From *ñikṣvidā*: *kṣviṇṇaḥ*.
From a verb meaning "to think": *rājñāṃ mataḥ*, *rājñām iṣṭaḥ*.
From a verb meaning "to perceive": *rājñāṃ buddhaḥ*, *rājñāṃ jñātaḥ*.
Because it has the sense of "worship": *rājñāṃ pūjitaḥ* (honored by kings), *rājñām arcitaḥ* (revered by kings).
According to the rule stating "also elsewhere," there are also [forms such as] *śīlitaḥ*, *rakṣitaḥ*, *kṣāntaḥ*, *ākruṣṭaḥ*, and *juṣṭaḥ*.
*Ruṣṭa* and *ruṣita*, both are said to be "addressed";
likewise *hṛṣṭa* and *tuṣṭa*, as well as *kānta*; and both *saṃyata* and *udyata*.
They say "it will be difficult" (*kaṣṭam*); these are remembered as being like the immortals (*amṛta*) as before.

Likewise, [words such as] *śuptaḥ* (asleep), *śayitaḥ* (having lain down), *āśitaḥ* (eaten), *liptaḥ* (smeared), *snigdhaḥ* (smoothed), and *tṛptaḥ* (satiated) [are formed]. Since the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is paramount, it is stated that even in the present tense, the past and future moments of action certainly exist. Regarding the rule *uṇādayo bhūte 'pi* (Kātantra 4.4.67):
the *uṇādi* suffixes occur not only in the present but also in the past.

Some [words] apply to the present tense: *kāruḥ* (artisan) from *karoti* (he does), and *vāyuḥ* (wind) from *vāti* (it blows). Some apply even to the past: *vartma* (path) from "that which has been traversed" (*vṛttam*), and *bhasma* (ash) from "that which has been reduced to ashes" (*bhasitam*).
Even in the case of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), the understanding of stem and suffix occurs solely by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

"Words such as *gamī* and others will [be used] in the sense of the future. (Kāt. 4.4.68) Words such as *gamī* and so forth are derived from the *uṇādi* suffixes and are correct when referring to the future time; the meaning is that the suffix *in* occurs after roots such as *gam*, which function in the future tense. Examples include: *grāmaṃ gamī* ("one who will go to the village"), *grāmam āgāmī* ("one who will come to the village"), and *bhāvī* ("one who will be"). They are also used in the context of the periphrastic future (*śvastanī*); for instance, *śvo grāmaṃ gamī*. According to the rule *padārthaśvastane*, one would have expected the form *śvo grāmaṃ gantā*.

The suffixes *vuṇ* and *tumun* are used after a verbal root when another action is expressed as the object of that action. (Kāśikā 3.3.10) When another action is expressed as the object of the first action, the suffixes *vuṇ* and *tumun* occur after a verbal root signifying a future time. For example: *pācako vrajati* ("He goes as one who will cook") or *paktuṃ vrajati* ("He goes in order to cook"). The meaning is: "Having thought, 'I shall cook,' he goes. Why is it specified "when another action [is expressed]"? Consider: *bhikṣiṣya ity asya jaṭā* ("His matted hair is because he intends to beg"). In this case, the intention is not subordinate to another action.
What is the meaning of *kriyārthāyām*? [Example: *dhāvatas te patiṣyati daṇḍaḥ* ("As you run, the staff will fall").
The mention of *vuṇ* is for the purpose of excluding suffixes such as *tṛc*; it expresses only the state (*bhāva*).
And [the suffix *tumun* is used] after words expressing a state (*bhāvavācin*). (Kātantra 4.4.70)

When a word denoting an action is used as an adjunct (*upapada*) to another action intended for that purpose, suffixes expressing the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) are added to a verbal root (*dhātu*) signifying a future action. For example: *pākāya vrajati* (he goes for the sake of cooking), *paktaye vrajati*, *pacanāya vrajati*. Since the suffix *-tum* would otherwise necessarily apply here, this rule is stated to show that the principle of "non-identity of form" (*vāsarūpa-vidhi*) does not operate in this section. Furthermore, the suffix *-aṇ* is applied when the object (*karman*) is expressed. (Kātantra 4.4.71)

The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when it denotes a future sense, provided that another action is the purpose of the first action (*kriyārtha*) and that a noun (*karman*) is used as a subordinate word (*upapada*). Examples: *kāṇḍalāvo vrajati* ("he goes to reap stalks"), *godāyo vrajati* ("he goes to give a cow [in sacrifice]"), *gosaṃkhyāyo vrajati* ("he goes to count the cows"), *sāmagāyo vrajati* ("he goes to sing the Sāman chants"), *surāpāyo vrajati* ("he goes to drink liquor").
Regarding the rule *śatṛānau syasaṃhitau śeṣe ca* (Kātantra 4.4.72):
here, the suffix *āna* is understood as being accompanied by *śantṛṅ*.

When a verb root expressing a future sense occurs with another verb denoting an action for the sake of that action (kriyārtha) as its object (karman), or when it stands alone as a remainder (śeṣa), the suffixes *śatṛ* and *ānaś*—joined with the particle *syen*—are applied. Examples: *kariṣyan vrajati* ("he goes intending to do"), *kariṣyamāṇo vrajati* ("he goes while being about to do"). With an object: *kaṭaṃ kariṣyan vrajati* ("he goes intending to make a mat"), *kaṭaṃ kariṣyamāṇo vrajati* ("he goes while being about to make a mat").
And in the case of the remainder (*śeṣa*): *kariṣyan*, *kariṣyamāṇaḥ*, "O *kariṣyan*!", "O *kariṣyamāṇa*!"; [these forms are used].
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the *Daurgasimhī-vṛtti* on the *Kṛt* suffixes.
[The rule] *pada-ruja-viśa-spṛśo ghañ* (Kāt 4.5.1) states that the suffix *ghañ* occurs after these roots;

the *gh* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is for the purpose of applying the substitution of *k* and *g* for *c* and *j* according to *cajoḥ kagau* (Kāt 4.6.56), while the *ñ* as an indicatory letter is for the purpose of causing the root to behave like one ending in *ij*.
*padyate*, *patsyate*, *apādi*, or *pede*; *pādaḥ*.
Likewise, *rogaḥ* (disease), *veśaḥ* (entrance), *sparśaḥ* (touch), as well as *kṣaya-vyādhiḥ* (consumption/disease) and *okaḥ* (abode).
[The root] *sṛ* [is used] in the sense of "stability" and "disease. (Kāt. 4.5.2)

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *sṛ* when denoting a stable object or a disease; thus, that which moves (*sarati*) over a period of time is *sāra*, meaning a stable thing. *Atīsāra* is a disease [where the short vowel becomes long]. That by which they move is *sāra*, meaning strength. That by which they disperse is *visāra*, meaning a fish; this is established as being only in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it is a technical term (*saṃjñāśabda*).

If it is so, then [the word] *pāda* will be derived from the sense "that by which one steps" (*pad-yate ’nena iti pādaḥ*). This is true; however, the inclusion of the term *pada* is for the sake of detailed exposition.
According to Pāṇini 3.3.18 (*bhāve*), the suffix *ghañ* occurs after every verbal root in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*); thus: *pākaḥ*, *pākau*, *pākāḥ*.

In this context, the meaning of *bhāva* (existence) refers to the generality of action (*kriyāsāmānya*), which is termed "accomplished" (*siddhatā*) and is of the nature of a substantive (*sattvabhūta*); therefore, the dual and plural numbers are employed. *Kāt_4.5.4*: "The suffix *ghañ* occurs after a verbal root when a *kāraka* other than the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended, or when *bhāva* is understood, provided that a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is implied. Examples: *Prākāraḥ* ("a rampart"): they build it up (*prakurvanti*). *Prāsaḥ* ("a dart"): it is thrown forth (*prāsyate*). *Āhāraḥ* ("food"): they bring it (*āharanti*). *Prāsādaḥ* ("palace"): eyes and minds find delight in it (*prasīdanti*). *Dārāḥ* ("wife/wives"): they are torn apart by them (*dīryante*). *Jāraḥ* ("lover"): he causes [her] to age by means of him (*jīryate*).
Why does it say "not when [the word] is not an agent" (*akartari*)? [Consider: *nadaḥ* (roaring) refers to the Śoṇa river.
Even when not a technical term (*asaṃjñāyām*), we have *dāyo dattaḥ* (a gift given) and *lābho labdhaḥ* (gain obtained).
The inclusion of the term "kāraka" (participant in an action) is for the purpose of making known that this is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) even when used with force.

Regarding the rule *sarvasmāt parimāṇe* (Pāṇini 3.3.20): "Parimāṇa" (measure) is so called because it is that which is measured. The suffix *ghañ* occurs after any verbal root (*dhātu*) when it denotes a measure, provided that the sense of a "name" (*saṃjñā*) is understood, and [the action] pertains to a factor other than the agent (*kartṛ*) or to the abstract state (*bhāva*). Alternatively, "measure" refers to numbers such as one, *prastha*, and so forth: for example, *ekaḥ taṇḍulaniścāyaḥ* ("one handful of rice"), *dvau śūrpaniṣpāvau* ("two winnowings with a winnowing-basket"), *prasthaniścāyaḥ* ("a handful measured by a *prastha*"), and *droṇāvakṣāyaḥ* ("a measure emptied by a *droṇa*"). Since the suffix *al* (the *kvun* suffix) would otherwise supersede [the application of *ghañ*], the expression "after any [root]" (*sarvasmāt*) indicates that the suffix *ghañ*—which depends on the verbal root—is not superseded, but rather [the *al* suffix is].
Regarding the phrase "dependent on the meaning": by that [principle], there is one *tila* (sesame seed) as the height, two streams (*sruti*) of oil, and the suffix *ktin* itself.
There is one flowing (*sravaṇa*), two starting points (*prasthāna*), and the suffix *yuṭ* is established.
How is there a single determination? Because of the governing context (*apyadhikāra*).

"And after the root *iṅ* and after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs. (Kātyāyana 4.5.6) This is an exception to [the rule for] *ap*. It should be understood that the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "in the sense of an action (*bhāva*), and in the sense of a factor other than the agent (*akartṛ-kāraka*), when a name (*saṃjñā*) is to be formed," applies without distinction here.
Thus, from the root *adhi-i*, we have *adhyayana* ("study") or *adhyāya* ("lesson").

Because one approaches (*upetya*) and studies from him, he is called *upādhyāya*, *upādhyāyā*, or *upādhyāyī*; [this is derived] from the root *iṅ* with the suffix *ghañ*, optionally in the *na*-class and others. Also from roots ending in long *ā*: *dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *ru* when a prefix (*upasarga*) precedes it. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.3.7)
When an *upasarga* (preverb) is the *upapada*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *ru* (to cry out): *saṃrāvaḥ*, *uparāvaḥ*.
Why specify "an *upasarga*"? [Consider: *ravaḥ*.
In the case of *sāṃrāviṇam*, the suffix *inuṇ* is superseded by this rule.

*sami duvaḥ*. When *sam* is the preceding word (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *du* (to burn), as in *saṃdāvaḥ*. Why "when *sam*"? [To show that] *davaḥ* [is not formed in this way].
*Kāt_4.5.9*: When *ut* is the upapada, and also when *sam* is present, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *yu* and *dru*. Thus: *udyāvaḥ*, *uddrāvaḥ*;
*saṃyāvaḥ*, and *saṃdrāvaḥ*—so say some.
What is the purpose of [the word] *udi*? [Examples: *yavaḥ*, *dravaḥ*.
Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of *api*, there would also be *yāvaḥ*, *drāvaḥ*, and *dāvaḥ*.

Likewise, *śāra* means wind; *śāra* also means straight; *nīśāra* means a covering; and it denotes the lengthening of what is short. According to Kātantra 4.5.10, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after these roots when no prefix (*anupasarga*) is present: *śrāyaḥ*, *nāyaḥ*, and *bhāvaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the condition "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? [Examples where it does not apply: *praśrayaḥ*, *praṇayaḥ*, *prabhavaḥ*.
How then are *prabhāvaḥ* (excellent being), *anubhāvaḥ* (consequent being), and *vibhāvaḥ* (departed being) formed?
[They are formed] because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the suffix *ap*, and also because of the word *naya*.
Kāt 4.5.11: After the roots *kṣu* and *śru*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs when *vā* is the accompanying word (*upapada*);
thus, *vikṣāvaḥ* and *viśrāvaḥ*.
Kāt 4.5.12: The root *sraṃs* [takes *ghañ*] in the sense of expansion (*prathana*), provided it does not refer to sound (*aśabda*).

*Prathana* means expansion or width. The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *stṛ* when the word *prathana* (expansion) is to be expressed as the meaning, provided that this expansion does not pertain to sound; for example, "the width of a cloth" (*paṭasya vistāraḥ*). Why is it said "not pertaining to sound"? [Consider] "the expansion of a sentence" (*vākyasya vistaraḥ*).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "spreading" (*prathana*)? [For example: the expansion of grass (*tṛṇasya vistaraḥ*). *Pre* also [is used] except in the context of a sacrifice. Kāt_4.5.13: When *pra* is the upapada, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *stṛ*, provided it is other than in the context of a sacrifice; [thus we have] *prastāraḥ*.

In the context of sacrifice, however, there is *barhis* and *prastara*. And [the suffix] *ghañ* occurs after the root *stṛ* when referring to the names of Vedic meters (*chandas*). For example: *prastārapaṅkti*, *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, and *āstārapaṅkti*.
Before *dru*, *stu*, and *śru*: According to Pāṇini 3.3.49, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after these roots when preceded by the prefix *pra*; thus, *pradrāvaḥ*, *prastāvaḥ*, and *praśrāvaḥ*.
How is *śrāvaḥ* [formed]? Because of the governing rule (*apyadhikārāt*).

Regarding *ni* with *ava* and *ud*: Kāt_4.5.16 states that when *ava* and *ud* are used as subordinate words (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *nī*. Thus, we have *avanāyaḥ* and *unnāyaḥ*.
How is it that *udyato nayaḥ* (the conduct of one who has risen) is called *unnayaḥ*? It is because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) [of the general application of *ghañ*].
Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.17: After the prefixes *niḥ* and *abhi*, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the roots *pū* and *lū* respectively;
thus, *niṣpāvaḥ* and *abhilāvaḥ*. Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.18: In the context of a sacrifice (*yajña*), the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *stu* when preceded by the prefix *sam*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *stu* when preceded by the prefix *sam*, in the context of a sacrifice; thus, *saṃstāva* refers to a place where they gather and praise, whereas *saṃstava* has another meaning.

After the prefixes *ut* and *ni*, [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] to the root *gṛ*. According to Pāṇini 3.3.59 (*unnyor giraḥ*), the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *gṛ* when *ut* and *ni* are the preceding prefixes; thus, *udgāraḥ* (vomiting) and *nigāraḥ* (swallowing).

What is the meaning of *unni*? It is *gara*. Regarding the rule *kiro dhānye* (Pāṇini 3.3.29): when *unni* are used as co-occurring words (*upapada*) and the action pertains to grain (*dhānya*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *kṛ* (to scatter). Thus, we have *utkāra* of grain and *nikāra* of grain.
What is the meaning of *dhānya*? [Examples: *puṣpotkaraḥ*, *puṣpanikaraḥ*.
Why is it said "of the root *kṛ*" (*kirateḥ*)? [Counter-example: *kṛñ* in the sense of harming; [example: *dhānyanikaraḥ*.
[The suffix *ghañ* is applied] after the root *vṛñ* following the word *nau*. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.21)

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *vṛ* when the word *nau* is the preceding member (*upapada*) and "grain" (*dhānya*) is to be expressed; thus, *nīvārāḥ* (wild rice), where the short vowel becomes long.
After the roots *śri* and *pū*, *ghañ* occurs when *ud* is the preceding member; thus, *ucchrayaḥ* (height) and *utpāvaḥ* (winnowing).

How is there the suffix *ucchraya*? Because it is included under the governing rule (*adhikāra*). And [the suffix] *ghañ* applies after the root *grah* when *ud* is the preceding word (*upapada*). According to Kātantra 4.5.23, *ghañ* occurs after the root *grah* with *ud* as the preceding word; thus we have *udgrāhaḥ*. It is also held that this applies even in the common language (*bhāṣā*).

When *ava* and *ni* are used as prefixes (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah* when reproach (*ākrośa*) is implied. For example: *avagrāhas te vṛṣala*, *nigrāhas te vṛṣala*. Why "when reproach"? [Because otherwise: *avagrahaḥ padasya* (the separation of a word), *nigrahaś caurasya* (the arrest of a thief).
Regarding *pra* in the sense of desiring (*lipsā*). Kāt_4.5.25:

When *pra* is the preceding word (*upapada*) in the sense of desiring, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah*. Example: *pātrapragrāheṇa carati bhikṣuḥ* ("the mendicant goes about with a bowl-grasper"). Why "in the sense of desiring"? [Counter-example: *pragrahaḥ* ("seizing" or "holding").

*sami muṣṭau* (Kāśikā 4.5.26): When *sam-* is the prefix, the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *grah-* in the sense of "fist"; for example, *saṃgrāhaḥ* of a wrestler. Why "in the sense of fist"? [Consider: *saṃgrahaḥ*.
In this context, *muṣṭi* (fist) is understood as a specific configuration of the fingers; thus, the form *eka-śākasaṃgrāhaḥ* is established by the rule *sarvasmāt parimāṇe* [Kāt 4.5.5].
Regarding the rule *parau yajñe* [Kāt 4.5.27]:
when *para-* is the preceding word (*upapada*) and the subject pertains to sacrifice (*yajña*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah*, as in *uttara-parigrāhaḥ*.

What is meant by "sacrifice" (*yajña*)? It means "appropriation" (*parigraha*). In the sense of "obstructing rain," [the suffix] *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *grah* when *ava* is the preceding word (Kāśikā 4.4.28). Thus, there is *avagrāha* or *avagraha* in the sense of "obstruction of rain."
In the sense of "rope" (raśmi), when *pra* is the prefix, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *grah*. Thus, one says either *pragrāhaḥ* or *pragrahaḥ*.
Here, "rope" refers to a cord.

And [the suffix *ghañ* is optionally applied] after the root *grah* when preceded by *pra*, provided that *artha* is the upapada and it refers to the balance-string (*tulāsūtra*) belonging to merchants (*vaṇij*). Thus, one says either *tulāpragrāheṇa carati* or *tulāpragraheṇa carati vaṇik* ("the merchant moves with the balance-string").
[The suffix *ghañ* is also applied] after the root *vṛ* in the sense of covering (*ācchādane*). (Kātantra 4.5.30–31)

When *pra* is the prefix (*upapada*) for the root *vṛ* in the sense of "covering," the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs: *prāvāraḥ* (masculine) and *prāvaraḥ* (masculine); this [root] is preceded by *āṅ*. *Kāśikā 4.5.32*: When *āṅ* is the prefix, the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the roots *ru* and *plu*: *ārāvaḥ* (masculine) and *āravaḥ* (masculine); *āplāvaḥ* (masculine) and *āplavaḥ* (masculine).

*Parau bhuvo 'vajñāne* (Kāśikā 4.5.33): When *pari* is the governing preposition (*upapada*), the suffix *ghañ* optionally occurs after the root *bhū* in the sense of "disrespect. Thus: *paribhāvaḥ*, *paribhavaḥ*.
Why "in the sense of disrespect"? [Consider: "being on all sides" (*sarvato bhavanam*) is *paribhavaḥ* [in the sense of pervasion].
Thus it is regarding *hastādāna* (taking with the hand).
According to Pāṇini 3.3.40 (*hastādāne cerasteye*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *ci* in the sense of taking with the hand; for example, *puṣpapracāyaḥ* (the gathering of flowers).
The mention of "taking with the hand" is an indication of proximity; therefore, one may say *vṛkṣāgre phalapracayaṃ karoti* (he performs the gathering of fruits at the top of the tree).
Even because of the governing rule [of the previous sūtra], it would not apply to the act of stealing; for example, "a thief gathers fruit with his hand.

Regarding *kāya* and *nikāya*: Kāt_4.5.35 states that the suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *ci* (cinoteḥ) in the senses of "body" (*śarīra*) and "dwelling" (*nivāsa*), and the letter *k* is substituted for the initial [of the root]. That which is accumulated is the *kāya*, the body; that in which things are accumulated is the *nikāya*, the dwelling.
By extension of the rule, it applies even to heaps of bricks and piles of straw: *citir āśuḥ* ("a pile of bricks"), *ākāyaś citiḥ* ("a straw pile"), *gomayanikāyaḥ* ("a heap of cow dung").

How then is there the form *kāṣṭhanicayaḥ*? It is by intending to express mere plurality. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] to a collection (*saṃgha*) when there is no superposition of one thing upon another. (Kātantra 4.5.36)

A collection (*samūha*) of living beings is called a *saṃgha*. When there is no vertical stacking (*anauttarādharya*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *ci* (to gather) in the sense of a *saṃgha*, and the substitution of *ka* for *ca* occurs; thus we have *vaiyākaraṇanikāyaḥ* (the assembly of grammarians). Why "when there is no vertical stacking"? [Consider] *śūkaranicayaḥ* (a heap of pigs).

Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.37: After the prefixes *pari* and *ni*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the roots *nī* and *iṇ* respectively when used in the sense of gambling (*dyūta*) and non-deviation (*abhreṣa*). Non-deviation means not wavering; that is, acting according to what is appropriate. For example: *pariṇāyena śārīn hanti*, meaning "he kills the dice by leading them all around"; this is the proper method here. Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.38: After the prefixes *vi* and *upa*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *śī* in the sense of rotation (*paryāya*).

The suffix *ghañ* occurs after the root *śī* (to lie down) when the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-* are used as subordinate elements (*upapada*) in the sense of "turn" (*paryāya*). For example: *tava rāja-viśāyaḥ* ("your turn to lie down among the kings") and *tava rāja-upaśāyaḥ* ("your turn to lie down near the kings"); the meaning is "it is your turn to lie down with respect to the king.
By this very indicative [rule], the suffix *ghañ* also occurs after the root *i-* preceded by *pari-* in the sense of "sequence" (*krama*).
The suffix *inuṇ* occurs in the sense of "pervasion" (*abhividhi*) to denote an action (*bhāva*). (Kāśikā 4.3.9)

When pervasion (*abhividhi*) is understood, the suffix *inuṇ* occurs after a verbal root; for example, *sāṃkoṭinam* and *sāṃrāviṇam vartate*. The pervasion is effected by the action itself. From a word ending in *inuṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the same sense (*svārthe*); furthermore, the augment *yuṭ* is also seen, as in *saṃkuṭanam vartate*. *Karmavyatīhāre ṇac striyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.43): When a reciprocal action (*karmavyatīhāra*) is understood, the suffix *ṇac* occurs after a verbal root in the feminine gender to denote the abstract action (*bhāve*). Examples include *vyāvakrośī* and *vyāvabhāṣī*. From a word ending in *ṇac*, the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the same sense (*svārthe*).
In some cases, due to the governing rule (*adhikāra*), there is the augment *vṛddhi* by means of the reciprocal action (*vyatīhāra*).

How is it that [the forms] *vyatīkṣā* and *vyavakruṣṭiḥ* are formed? It is because of the absence of the governing rule for feminine nouns (*astrī-adhikāra*) that there is the optionality of non-identical forms (*vā-asarūpa-tā*).
[The suffix] *al* is applied after the roots *svar*, *vṛt*, *gam*, *i*, and *grah*. (Kātantra 4.5.41)
The suffix *al* occurs after verbal roots ending in vowels, as well as after the roots *vṛ*, *dṛ*, *gam*, and *grah*; it is an exception to *ghañ*. Examples: *kṣayaḥ*, *krayaḥ*, *bhavaḥ*, *lavaḥ*.
Whether it is *vṛṅ* or *vṛñ*, the form is *varaḥ*.
From *dṛṅ*: *daraḥ*.

*gamaḥ* (going), *grahaḥ* (seizing). Due to the restriction "only after *vṛt* and *vṛdh*," the suffix *ghañ* alone is applied after other roots ending in ṛ: *kāraḥ* (doing), *hāraḥ* (taking). After a long vowel, only *ap* is applied: *karaḥ* from *kṝ*, *garaḥ* from *gṝ*.

*Bhītiḥ* and *bhayam* are formed by the suffix *al* alone; they do not include *yuṭ* and the others. In the case of *vaśaḥ* and *raṇaḥ*, the suffix *al* is applied because they are conventional (rūḍhi) words.
[Kātantra 4.5.42: *upasarge 'deḥ*]
When a prefix (*upasarga*) is the preceding word, *al* is substituted for *ad*, as in *praghasaḥ* and *vighasaḥ*.
Regarding *ghañ* and *al*, *ghañ* is replaced by *al*. Why "when a prefix"? [Consider] *ghāsaḥ*.
Nau and na [are prefixes]. Kāt_4.5.43: When *nau* is the upapada, the suffix *al* is applied after the root *ad*, and there is also the substitution of *ṇa*; thus: *nighasaḥ*, *nyādaḥ*.
[The suffix *al* is applied] after the root *mad* when preceded by *pra* or *sam* in the sense of joy. Kāt_4.5.44.

The suffix *al* occurs after the verbal roots *pra-mad* and *sam-mad* when used with an upapada, in the sense of joy: *pramadaḥ* of maidens, *saṃmadaḥ* of cuckoos. According to Pāṇini 3.3.61 (*vyadhajapoś cānupasarge*), the suffix *al* occurs after the roots *vyadh*, *japi*, and *mad* when no prefix (*anupasarga*) is present: *vyadhaḥ*, *japaḥ*, and *madaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? [Examples with prefixes: *āvyādhaḥ*, *upajāpaḥ*, *pramādaḥ*.
*Kāśikā* 4.2.46: After these two roots, *svan* and *has*, the suffix *al* optionally occurs when not preceded by a prefix. Thus: *svanaḥ* or *svānaḥ*; *hasaḥ* or *hāsaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "without a prefix" (*anupasarga*)? [Examples with prefixes: *prasvānaḥ*, *prahāsaḥ*. *Kāt_4.5.47*:

After the root *yama*, when not preceded by a prefix, and in combination with the prefixes *sam*, *ni*, *upa*, and *vi*, the suffix *al* is optionally applied. Thus: *yamaḥ*, *yāmaḥ*; *saṃyamaḥ*, *saṃyāmaḥ*; *niyamaḥ*, *niyāmaḥ*; *upayamaḥ*, *upayāmaḥ*; *viyamaḥ*, *viyāmaḥ*.

Regarding *nau* as an upapada, the suffix *al* optionally occurs after these roots: *gad*, *nad*, and *paṭh*. Thus: *nigadaḥ* / *nigādaḥ*, *ninadaḥ* / *ninādaḥ*, *nipaṭhaḥ* / *nipāṭhaḥ*, *nisvanaḥ* / *nisvānaḥ*. Because of the rule *svanahasor vā* (Kāt 4.5.46), the prefixless form does not apply here.

Regarding *kvaṇo vīṇāyām* (Kāt_4.5.49): when *vīṇā* is the object, the suffix *al* optionally occurs after the root *kvaṇ*, provided there is no preceding word (*upapada*) or no prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus we have *kvaṇaḥ* and *kvāṇaḥ*; likewise, *nikvaṇaḥ* and *nikvāṇaḥ*. Because of the presence of the particle *ca* [in the rule], the mention of *vīṇā* is intended to include cases where there is a prefix; thus we have *prakvaṇo vīṇāyāḥ* and *prakvāṇaḥ*.

The suffix *al* is invariably applied to the root *paṇ* in the sense of "measure. [Kāt_4.5.50] The suffix *al* occurs after *paṇ* when the meaning is "measure," as in *paṇaḥ*; even a measured handful of vegetables and the like is called a *paṇa*.
Why specify "in the sense of measure"? [Consider: *dāsyāḥ pāṇaḥ* ("the hand of a female slave").

*Samudor ajaḥ paśuṣu* (Pāṇini 3.3.69). When *aja-* follows *sam-* or *ud-* as governing prepositions (*upapada*) and denotes animals, the suffix *al* is applied. *Samajaḥ paśūnām* means "a gathering of animals"; that is, a collection.
*Udajaḥ paśūnām* means "the driving forth of animals"; that is, the act of impelling them.

What is the purpose of the phrase "among animals" (*paśuṣu*)? [Examples: *samājaś chātrāṇām* ("a gathering of students"), *udājaḥ khagānām* ("the rising of birds"). Regarding *glaho 'kṣeṣu*: according to Pāṇini 3.3.70 (*Kāt_4.5.52*), the suffix *ali* (the root *ghañ*) is applied after the root *grah-* when it refers to dice (*akṣa*), and the substitution of *la* for *ra* is prescribed; thus, *akṣāṇāṃ glahaḥ* ("the taking up of dice"). Some maintain that *glahi* is a separate verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*); in that case, *praglāhaḥ* would serve as a counter-example formed with the suffix *ghañ*.
Kātantra 4.5.53: After the root *sṛ*, when it signifies "procreation" (the taking of conception), the suffix *al* occurs;
for example, *gavām upasaraḥ* ("the gathering of cows for breeding"), whereas *upasāraḥ* has a different meaning.
Kātantra 4.5.54: After the root *hve* (to call), the suffix *al* occurs with the prefix *hu*, and also with the prefixes *abhi*, *upa*, *ni*, and *vi*.
With these prefixes, the suffix *al* is applied to the root *hve*, and there is the substitution of *hu* for it: *abhihavaḥ*, *upahavaḥ*, *nihavaḥ*, *vihavaḥ*.

When *āṅ* is the prefix and the sense is "battle" (*yuddha*), [the suffix *al* is applied]. According to Pāṇini 3.3.73: when *āṅ* is the prefix, the suffix *al* is applied to *hve* in the sense of battle, and there is the substitution of *hu*; that in which warriors are summoned is *āhavaḥ*.

How is it that *āhāva* means "a place for calling cows to drink"? It is a reservoir of water (*jalādhāra*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied in this sense as well, and there is the substitution of *hur* [for the root *hvā*].

According to *Kātantra* 4.5.56, *anupasargasya*, the suffix *al* occurs after the root *hvayati* when used without a prefix in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*), and there is the substitution of *hur*. Thus, *havaḥ*.
What is the purpose of the restriction "when not preceded by a prefix" (*anupasargasya*)? [Example: *prahvāyaḥ*.
Regarding the rule *hanter vadhiś ca* (Kāt.
4.5.57): when the root *han* is not preceded by a prefix, the suffix *al* occurs in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and *vadhi* is the substitute for *han*; thus, killing is *vadhaḥ*.
And there is also destruction due to [the loss of] authority.
Why [is it specified] "without a prefix"? [To show that] *vighātaḥ* [is not included].
And *ghaṇi* [is used] when referring to a physical form. (Kātantra 4.5.58)

*Mūrtiḥ* means solidity (*kāṭhinyam*). After the root *han*, the suffix *al* occurs when a solid object (*mūrtāv arthe*) is denoted, and *ghan* is the substitute [for *han*]. Thus, there is "solid curd" (*dadhno ghanaḥ*) and "solid curd" (*ghanaṃ dadhi*), because of their non-difference [in nature]. *Kāt_4.5.59*: *prād gṛhaikadeśe ghañ ca*. After the prefix *pra*, the suffix *al* occurs and *ghañ* as well, with *ghan* as the substitute for *han*, when the meaning is "a part of a house. Thus, *praghaṇaḥ* and *praghāṇaḥ*. This refers to that which is outside of a house divided in two by the door and the vestibule. Because of the explicit statement "there too," the substitution of *ṇ* [occurs].
*Antarghana* and *udghana* are irregularly formed [with the suffix *ghañ*] in the senses of "place" (*deśa*) and "over-laying" (*atyādhāna*), respectively.

(Kātantra 4.5.60) These two words ending in *-an* are irregularly derived in the senses of place and over-laying according to their respective order: that in which one strikes within is *antarghana*, a place; that in which one strikes upwards is *udghana*; and that upon which wood is struck is *atyādhāna*. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied] in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) when [the object] is iron, lead, or stone. (Kātantra 4.5.61)

With these prefixes, the suffix *al* is applied to the root *han*, and *ghan* is substituted [for *han*]. For example: "that by which iron is struck" is *ayoghana*; "that by which one is struck apart" is *vighana*; likewise, *drughaṇa*. In the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*), there is the substitution of *ṇ*. *Kāśikā 4.1.62*:
With *pari* as a prefix, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to *han*, and *ghan* is substituted [for *han*]. "That by which one is struck around" is *parigha*.
In Latvian, *palighaḥ* means "a crossbar.

Regarding *nau nimite*: according to Pāṇini 3.3.83 (*nau nimite*), when *nau* is the upapada (governing word), the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *han*, and *ghan* is the substitute for *han*, provided that the object (*nimite*) is something indistinct; [trees] are struck or known without distinction, such as *nighā vṛkṣāḥ* ("trees that are struck") or *nighāḥ śālayaḥ* ("rice plants that are struck").
The term *nimita* [is used] in the sense of "measured" with respect to both height and circumference.
What is the meaning of *nimita*? It means "struck down. [The prefix] *sam-ud-* [is used] in the senses of "counting" (*gaṇa*) and "praise" (*praśaṃsā*). (Kātantra 4.5.64)

The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *han* when preceded by the prefixes *sam* and *ud*, provided that the sense is "praise" (*praśaṃsā*) within the group [of meanings]; furthermore, *ghan* is the substitute for *han*. Thus, *saṃghaḥ* means that in which parts are joined together (*saṃhanyate*), or where they are gathered.
*Udghaḥ* refers to a man who is "raised up" (*utkṛṣṭaṃ hanyate*) or known; the meaning is "praiseworthy.
After the prefix *upa*, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "support" (*āśraya*). (Pāṇini 3.3.81–82).

What [suffix] occurs after the root *han* when "support" (*āśraya*) is understood? The suffix *ghan* and the substitution of *ghni* [for *han*] occur. For example: *kuḍyopaghnaṃ vasati* ("he dwells near a wall"). *Kāt_4,5.66*: When *stamba* is the upapada, the suffix *ac* occurs after *han*, and there is the substitution of *ghan* for *han*. Thus, that by which a clump is struck is called *stambaghnaḥ*. Examples: *stambaghno daṇḍaḥ* ("a staff for clearing clumps"), *stambaghno yaṣṭiḥ* ("a stick for clearing clumps"). There is only the masculine gender; however, some maintain it is feminine, as in *stambaghnā yaṣṭiḥ*.

By virtue of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), the suffix *ka* may also be applied after the roots *sthā*, *snā*, *pā*, *vyadh*, and *han*: *ākhūttham* (the rising of mice), *prasnaḥ* (that in which one bathes), *prapā* (a place where people drink), *āvidhaḥ* (that by which one pierces), *vighnaḥ* (that by which one is obstructed), and *āyudham* (a weapon, that with which one fights). This is established solely through the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence).

From a root having *ṭu* as its *anubandha*, the suffix *athu* is applied: according to Pāṇini 3.3.89 (*Kāt_4,5.67*), the suffix *athu* occurs after a root with *ṭu* as its *anubandha* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) alone; for example, from *ṭu-vepṛ*, we have *vepathuḥ* (trembling).
From the root *ośvi*, *śvayathuḥ*;
from *ṭudu*, *davathuḥ*;
from *ṭuvama*, *vamathuḥ*.

Regarding *vepadava*: because of the rule of optional forms (*vāsarūpa*), [the suffix] *trimac* is applied after a root having *ḍu* as its *anubandha*, in the sense of "accomplished by means of that. According to Pāṇini 4.4.68, the suffix *trimac* occurs after a root having *ḍu* as its *anubandha* when the meaning is "accomplished by means of that" (i.e., by means of the action denoted by the root).
From the root *ḍupacaṣ*: "accomplished by cooking" (*pākena nirvṛttam*) is *paktrimam*.
From the root *ḍukṛñ*: "accomplished by making" (*karaṇena nirvṛttam*) is *kṛtrimam*.
The word *nirvṛttam* [functions] either as an agent (*kartari*) or as an object (*karmaṇi*); the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used accordingly with the word *tena*.
Kātantra 4.5.69: The suffix *naṅ* occurs after these roots: *yāci*, *viśi*, *pracchi*, *yaj*, *svapi*, and *rakṣi*.
[The resulting forms are: *yācñā*, *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*, *yajñaḥ*, *svapnaḥ*, *rakṣṇaḥ*, and *yatnaḥ*.
Kātantra 4.5.70: After the root *dā* (to give), the suffix *ki* occurs when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present.

When a preposition (*upasarga*) is the preceding word, the suffix *ki* occurs after a root belonging to the *dā* class; [the resulting forms are] *ādiḥ* and *nidhiḥ*. Because of the governing rule [of the term] "also" (*api*), there is also *antardhiḥ*. [The suffix *ki* occurs] when the object (*karman*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the preceding word. (Kāśikāvṛtti 3.3.92)

When a word denoting an object (*karman*) follows as an upapada, the suffix *ki* occurs after a root belonging to the *dā* class, and also when the locative (*adhikaraṇa*) is expressed; for example: *vāladhiḥ* (tail) and *jaladhiḥ* (ocean).
There is no intervention by prefixes (*upasarga*s); for example: *payonidhiḥ* (ocean).
In the feminine gender, the suffix *kti* is used. (Kātantra 4.5.72)

The suffix *ktin* occurs in the feminine gender to denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) or an agent other than the subject (*akartari kārake*), when it forms a conventional name (*saṃjñāyām*). Examples are *kṛtiḥ*, *buddhiḥ*, and *iṣṭiḥ* (from the root *yaj*, meaning "that by which one sacrifices"). Likewise, there are *śrutiḥ* and *stutiḥ*. It also occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). Furthermore, *sāti*, *heti*, *yūti*, and *jūti* are formed;

according to Kātantra 4.5.73, these are irregularly derived (*nipātyante*) with the suffix *ktin* in the feminine: *sātiḥ* from either *si* (to bind) or *san* (to obtain); *hetiḥ* from *hi* (to impel); *yūtiḥ* from *yu* (to join); and *jūtiḥ* from *ju* (to hasten).

*Kāt_4.5.74*: After these roots, the suffix *ktin* occurs in the feminine sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Since the root *pac* has the indicatory letter *ṣ*, the suffix *aṅ* would otherwise apply; however, the form is *paktiḥ*.
Likewise, by *Kāt_4.5.84* (*ātaś copasarge*), we have *saṃgītiḥ*, *prapītiḥ*, and *saṃsthitiḥ*.
Furthermore, from the context, *saṃsthā* means "establishment" or "arrangement.

According to Pāṇini 3.1.107 (*vrajyajoḥ kyap*), the suffix *kyap* occurs after the roots *vraj* and *yaj* to form feminine nouns denoting an action (*bhāva*). Thus, there are *vrajyā* and *ijyā*; furthermore, *iṣṭiḥ* is also used in the sense of an action.

*Kāt_4.5.76*: After the roots *samaja*, *ās*, *sad*, *ni-pat*, *śī*, *vṛt*, *car*, *man*, *bhṛ*, and *iṇ*, the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of a feminine noun when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*). Examples: *Samajyā* (an assembly), *āsyā* (a seat). *Niṣadyā* (a place where they sit), from *niṣīdanti asyām*. *Nipatyā* (a place where they fall), from *nipatanti asyām*. *Śayyā* (a bed), from *śerate asyām*; this also applies in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). *Savanaṃ sutyā* (the act of pressing [Soma]). *Vidyā* (knowledge). This also applies in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding *aṭ*, because it is prescribed only after the *cekrīyita* (intensive) form, we have *aṭāṭyā*. Regarding *car* preceded by *pari*, we have *paricaryā*. *Manyā*, *bhṛtyā*, and *ityā*.
Also due to the governing rule [of specific suffixes]: *āsuti*, *bhṛti*, *samiti*.
Why "state" (*bhāva*)? [To exclude] *bhāryā*.
Why "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*)? [To exclude] *saṃvittiḥ*.

Kāt_4,5.77: After the root *kṛ*, there is the suffix *śa*, as well as *kti* and *kyap*. Thus, from "it is done" (*kriyate*) comes *kriyā*; and in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), [there are] *kṛtiḥ* and *kṛtyā*. Kāt_4,5.78: After the root *sṛ*, there is also the suffix *ya*.
The suffix *ya* occurs after the root *sṛ* preceded by *pari*, as in *parisaryā*. Due to the presence of the letter *ca*, it also occurs after the root *jāgṛ*, as in *jāgaryā*.
[This denotes] desire. (Pāṇini 3.3.101)
The form *icchā* is derived as an irregularity (*nipātyate*) from the root *iṣ* according to the rule *iccher iccha*.

[The suffix] *a* follows a word ending in the suffix *śaṃsu*. According to Kātantra 4.5.80, there is the statement that the root *śaṃsu* is without the augment *iṭ* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*); thus, the suffix *a* occurs after the root *śaṃsu* and after roots ending in other suffixes when forming feminine nouns, such as *praśaṃsā* (praise) and *pipatiṣā* (the desire to fall).

*dṛśad* (stone), *dṛśadā*, *aṭāṭā*, *kaṇḍūyā*; some say *kaṇḍūti* as well. [Pāṇini 3.3.103] *guroś ca niṣṭhāseṭaḥ*: According to Kātyāyana 4.5.81, the suffix *ap* occurs after a root containing a heavy vowel (*guru*) when followed by the *niṣṭhā* suffixes (*kta* and *ktvā*) that take the augment *iṭ*; for example, *īhā*, *īkṣā*, *jāgarā*.
Why is it said "of the guru"? [Consider] *nigṛhītiḥ*. Why is it said "of a niṣṭhā [suffix] having the augment iṭ"? [Consider] *nītiḥ* and *rāddhiḥ*.
However, after roots marked with the anubandha *ṣ*, and after [the group of roots] beginning with *bhid*, the suffix *aṅ* [is applied]. (Kāśikā 4.1.82)
From the *bhidādi* group of roots, however, the suffix *aṅ* occurs after those that have a nasal augment (*ṣānubandha*). For example: from *jṛṣ*, *jarā*;
from *ḍupacaṣ*, *pacā*;
from *kṣiṣ*, *kṣiyā*.
The words *ghaṭā* and so forth belong to the *ṣānubandha* group: *ghaṭā*, *vyathā*.

From the specific grammatical instruction (*nirdeśa*) "the root *kṛp* is used in the sense of compassion" (*kṛpāyām*), we have *kṛpā*; from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) "it is an apprehension" (*upalabdhiḥ*), it may also be *kṣāntiḥ*.
From the group of roots specified as beginning with *bhid*—namely, *bhid* in the sense of splitting—we have *bhidā*; *bhittiḥ* is another [form].
*Chidā* means the act of splitting; *chitti* is something else.
*Guhā* refers to a particular part of a mountain; *gūḍhi* is something else. From the root *ṛ* preceded by the prefix *ā*, we have *ārā* meaning a knife; *arti* is something else.
*dhṛṅ* in the sense of falling, *dhārā*, and another [form] *dhṛti*;
*vida*, *vidā*;
*kṣipa*, *kṣipā*.
*gudha*, *godhā*;
*hṛñ*, *hārā*;
*kṛñ*, *kārā*.

*likhā*, *lekhā*, *ratvā* (from *rad* etc.), and *rekhā*. This rule provides for the suffix *yā* after the roots *ūna*, *cūḍa*, *pīḍa*, and *mṛgayati*, which would otherwise have required [the suffixes] *a* and *ā*; thus there should be lengthening (*dīrghatva*) and the substitution of *ḍ* for *t*: *ūnā*, *cūḍā*, *pīḍā*, and *mṛgayā*.
[The forms] *vaśā*, *rujā*, and *mṛjā*—as well as the occurrence of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and so forth, and the specific meanings—result from the force of their inclusion in the *gaṇa* list.

Kātantra 4.5.83: After the roots *bhīṣ*, *cinti*, *pūji*, *kathi*, *kumbi*, *carci*, *spṛhi*, *toli*, and *doli*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied; after *bhī*, when fear is caused by a specific cause, it ends in *ṣ*. Thus: from *bhīṣ* (to terrify), *bhīṣaṇam* (terror) and *bhīṣā* (fear);
from *cit* (in the sense of remembering), *cintā* (thought); from *pūj* (in the sense of honoring), *pūjā* (worship).
From the root *kath* in the sense of a continuous discourse, *kathā*;
from *kub* in the sense of covering, *kumbā*;
from *carc* in the sense of study, *carcā*.
From the root *spṛh* in the sense of longing, *spṛhā*;
from *tul* in the sense of intoxication, *tolā*;
from *dul* in the sense of tossing up, *dolā*.
How is it "measured by a scale" (*tulayā saṃmita*)?

Because of the rule *ātaś copasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106), which states that after a verbal root ending in long *ā*, when preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*) or a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *aṅ* is applied; thus we have *saṃsthā*, *upadā*, and *upadhā*.
It should be stated that [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after a word ending in *antaḥpūrva*: *antardhā*.
How is *śraddhā* derived? It is from the rule *ā śraddhā* (Kāt.
2.1.10). Because of the governing heading *api*, [the suffix is also applied] to form *pramitiḥ*.

The suffix *yu* is applied after the roots *īṣ*, *śranth*, *as*, *vand*, and after those ending in *dikārita*. (Kāśikā 4.5.85) The suffix *yu* occurs after these: from *īṣ* (in the senses of moving, harming, and giving), we have *īṣaṇā*.
Binding, attending upon, and saluting. Knowledge accompanied by aspiration is feeling (vedanā). Causing to do (kāraṇā).

In the *cur*-class (the tenth class), [the suffix *ana* is applied] to *ghaṭṭ* in the sense of "moving," as in *ghaṭṭanā*; however, this does not apply to the *bhūvādika* (first class) root because its formation with *ktin* is not prescribed.

Regarding *kīrti* and *iṣ*, there is also *kti*: according to Pāṇini 3.3.96 (*Kāt_4,5.86*), the suffix *ktin* and the suffix *yu* occur after the roots *kīrti* and *iṣ*, resulting in *kīrtiḥ* and *saṃkīrtanā*.
The root *iṣ* means "to go" or "repetition"; from it are derived *anviṣṭiḥ*, *parīṣṭiḥ*, *anveṣaṇā*, and *paryeṣaṇā*.
With the marker *ṣ* (sānubandha), as in the root *iṣ* meaning "desire," the form is *iṣṭiḥ*.
According to Pāṇini 3.3.108 (*rogākhyāyāṃ vuñ*), the suffix *vuñ* is applied when naming a disease. (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.5.87)
The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a verbal root when it denotes a disease: *pravāhikā*, *pracchardikā*, *vicarcikā*.
Because of the governing rule [of the term] "also" (*api*), there are also *śiro’rdanam* and *śiro’rtiḥ*.
And [it occurs] in the sense of a name (Kāśikā 4.5.88).

The suffix *vuñ* occurs after a verbal root (*dhātu*) when it denotes a name (*saṃjñā*) or an object (*viṣaya*). For example: "that play in which garden flowers are broken" is *udyānapuṣpabhañjikā* (the Garden-Flower-Breaking Play). In the sense of "play," this is always a compound; thus, *puṣpabhañjikā* (Flower-Breaking) is a meaningful name for a type of play. Similarly, there is *vāraṇapuṣpapracāyikā* (the Elephant-Flower-Gathering [Play]). And [the suffix *vuñ* occurs] after a root used in the senses of turn (*paryāya*), worthiness (*arha*), and debt (*ṛṇa*).
According to Kāśikāvṛtti 4.3.89, *vuñ* occurs after such a root: for example, *adyabhavataḥ śāyikā* (the sleeping-turn of today's guest).
Your Honor ought to eat sugarcane.
Regarding debt, you owe me a meal of milk-rice.
From the word "and" (*ca*), it follows that regarding its arising: sugarcane-eating has arisen for me, yet it does not exist; the desire to act and the desire to take have arisen for me.

And [the suffixes] are seen after mere verbal action (bhāvamātra): *kā nāma śāyikā* ("what kind of lying down?"), while others are studying; *kā nāmāsikā* ("what kind of sitting?"), while others are walking. *Kāt_4.5.90*: *praśnākhyānayor iñ ca vā*. When a question or a statement is implied, the suffixes *iñ* and *vuñ* occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*), and by virtue of the word "optionally" (*vā*), they occur according to what is otherwise prescribed. For example: *kāṃ tvaṃ kārim akārṣīḥ*, *kāṃ kārikāṃ*, *kāṃ kṛtiṃ*, *kāṃ kriyāṃ*, *kāṃ kṛtyām* ("what deed did you do?"); [and in response: *sarvāṃ kārim akārṣam*, *sarvāṃ kārikāṃ*, *sarvāṃ kṛtiṃ*, *sarvāṃ kriyāṃ*, *sarvāṃ kṛtyām* ("I did every deed").

*Nañi anyākrośe* (Pāṇini 3.3.112): When *nañ* is used as an upapada and reproach (*ākrośa*) is implied, the suffix *ani* occurs after a verbal root. For example: *akaraṇis te vṛṣala bhūyāt* ("May you be one who does not act, O wretched man!"), and likewise *ajīvanis*. Why "when *nañ* [is used]"? [Consider: *mṛtis te vṛṣala bhūyāt* ("May death be yours, O wretched man!").

The suffix *kvip* is applied after the roots *sam-pad* and others in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) or in the sense of a grammatical participant (*kāraka*), and because the rule "also elsewhere" (*anyatrāpi*) is stated with great frequency (*bahulatvāt*), the forms *saṃpat*, *pratipat*, *vipat*, and *saṃpatti* may all occur; this class beginning with *sam-pad* is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*).

The suffixes *ik*, *iś*, and *tip* are established by the very fact that they indicate [the retention of] the root's own form (*svarūpa*) as the meaning; or, there is a compound with the word *kāra* in the *uṇādi* list, such as "the letter *a*" (*akāraḥ*) or "the letter *ka*" (*kakāraḥ*). Examples include: *evaṃkāraḥ* (the utterance "evam"), *oṃkāraḥ* (the syllable *oṃ*), *cītkāraḥ* (a whistling sound), *śītkāraḥ* (a hissing sound), *sphītkāraḥ* (a puffing sound), *sphutkāraḥ* (a spitting sound), *vaṣaṭkāraḥ* (the sacrificial exclamation *vaṣaṭ*), *svāhākāraḥ* (the exclamation *svāhā*), and so forth.
*Rādiphaḥ*: *repha* is derived from the *auṇādika* (unadi) suffixes.

Regarding *Kāt_4.5.92*, *kṛtya-yuṭo ’nyatrāpi ca*: the *kṛtya* and *yuṭ* suffixes, though prescribed for specific meanings, are observed to occur elsewhere as well—such as in *snānīyaṃ cūrṇam* (bathing powder), *dānīyo brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin worthy of gifts), *samāvartanīyo guruḥ* (a teacher to be attended upon), and *pravacanīya upādhyāyaḥ* (a preceptor fit for instruction). These [suffixes] occur in the sense of instruments (*karaṇa*) and so forth; furthermore, in the case of *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, *upasthānīya*, *janya*, *āplāvya*, and *āpātya*, they occur even when the agent (*kartṛ*) is intended, according to the rule: "In the case of the roots *plu* and *pat* preceded by *āṅ*, there is *yaṇ*."

"Rājabhir bhujyante" (are eaten by kings), "rājabhojanāḥ śālayaḥ" (rice for the king's meal), "rājācchādanāni vāsāṃsi" (clothes for the king's covering)—these [examples] involve the object (*karman*). "Avasecanam" (pouring out), "avaśravaṇam" (flowing down), and "dānam" (giving)—these involve the object. "Praskandanam" (leaping forward) and "prapatanam" (falling down)—these involve the point of departure (*apādāna*).
Here, the word "api" has the sense of "in various instances" (*bahulārtha*).
For the roots *ṣṭhivu* and *ṣivu*, there is optionally a long vowel [in the suffix -ana]: *niṣṭhīvanaṃ* or *niṣṭhevanaṃ*; *niṣīvaṇaṃ* or *niṣevaṇaṃ*.
That which performs (*karoti*) is called *kāraṇaṃ*. The suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter sense of an abstract action (bhāve). (Kāt. 4.5.93)

The suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of a neuter abstract action (*bhāva*): *śayitam*, *sthitam*, "done by you" (*bhavatā kṛtam*), "attained by him" (*prāptam anena*). This rule is stated so that the *kta* suffix may apply in the neuter even when the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarmatva*), since [otherwise] it would be barred by the suffix *yuṭ*. If it were argued that by the principle of "optionality of form" (*vāsarūpa*) the *ghañ* and other suffixes might also occur, [this rule is necessary]. And there is also *yuṭ*: Pāṇini 3.3.114 states that *yuṭ* also occurs in the sense of a neuter abstract action: *sthānam*, *gamanam*.

And [the suffix] *yuṭ* occurs after a verbal root when expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (Kāt_4.5.95) When the instrument or the locus is expressed in the neuter gender, *yuṭ* occurs: *idhmavraścanam* ("a wood-cutter"), *palāśaśātanam* ("a leaf-shatterer").
And when the locus is expressed: *godohanī ghaṭī* ("a jar for milking cows"), *śaktudhānī sthālī* ("a pot for holding barley-meal").

The suffix *gha* occurs after a word ending in a vowel to form a masculine noun when it denotes an instrument or a locus, provided it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*). According to Pāṇini 3.3.117–118 (*Kāt_4,5.96*), the suffix *gha* is applied to form masculine nouns signifying the instrument or the locus from stems ending in vowels. For example: that by which the chest is covered is called *uraśchadaḥ* (a breastplate).
That by which they act is called *karaḥ* (the hand); that by which they hear is called *śaraḥ* (an arrow).

In the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as well: it is called *laya* because things dissolve (*līyante*) in it; *nilaya* because they settle down (*nilīyante*) in it; and *viṣaya* because objects are fixed (*viṣiṇvanti*) in it.
According to Pāṇini 3.3.119 (*gocara-saṃcara-vaha-vraja-vyajana-krama-paṇa-nigamāś ca*), these words ending in the suffix *gha* are treated as irregular forms (*nipātita*).
Thus, *gocara* is derived from "that in which cows move" (*gāvaś caranty asmin*); here, proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is indicated.

Thus, *saṃcara* [is derived from] *car*, "to move"; *vaha* means that by which one carries, as in the case of a bull (*vṛṣabha*); *vraja* is that in which they walk. With the prefix *vi-*, from the root *aj*, *vyaja* is that by which they drive away; *krama* is that by which they step. *Āpaṇa* is that by which they act as merchants (*āpaṇāyante*).

*Nigama* is that by which one enters (*nigacchanti*). By virtue of the word *ca* ("and"), *bhaga* is that which they resort to (*bhajanti asmin*), and *nikaṣa* is that by which they rub (*nikaṣanti anena*).
[The suffix] *ghañ* is applied after the roots *ava*, *tṛ*, and *stuḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.3.120)
When *ava* is the prefix, the suffix *ghañ* is applied after the roots *tṛ* and *stṛ*; this is an exception to [the application of] *gha*.
That by which or in which they descend is *avatāraḥ*. That by which or in which they spread out is *avastāraḥ*.

And from a consonant [suffix]. (Kāt. 4.5.99) After a word ending in a consonant, *ghañ* occurs as an exception to *ap*. [Examples: "That by which they write" is *lekha*; "that by which they know" is *veda*.
"That by which they wipe away" is *apāmārga*; here there is the lengthening of a short vowel.
"Ācāra" means that by which one acts;
"āvāsa" is formed in the same way.
From the inclusion of the word "ca" (and), there are also *adhyāya*, *nyāya*, *udyāva*, *saṃhāra*, *ādhāra*, and *ādhāya*.

*udaṅka* [is formed] when not referring to water. (Kāt_4.5.100) The word *udaṅka* is irregularly derived (*nipātyate*) with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of "not water. It means "that by which one moves upward" (*ūrdhvam añcanty anena*). Thus, *udaṅkaḥ*; *ghṛtodaṅkaḥ*. Why "when not referring to water"? [Consider] *udakodañcanaḥ* ("a water-drawing vessel"); in that case, because it ends in the suffix *gha*, the suffix *yuṭ* applies without distinction.

*Jālam* means a net (*ānāya*). According to Pāṇini 3.3.124, *ānāya* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) term when it refers to a net; it is derived from the sense "that by which things are brought in" (*ānīyante 'nena*), thus *ānāyaḥ* refers to a net for fish.
From the sense "that by which one digs" (*ākhanyate 'nena*), the word *ākhanaḥ* is formed with the suffix *gha*; the form *ākhānaḥ* is also seen, formed with the suffix *ghañ*.

The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *khana* even when preceded by other words; thus, in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), we have *ākharah*, *ā khanikaḥ*, and *ā khanikavakaḥ*, as these suffixes *ḍa*, *ika*, and *ikavaka* are *auṇādika* (belonging to the list of Uṇādi suffixes).

Regarding the rule *īṣad-duḥ-suṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal* (Pāṇini 3.3.126): the meaning of *duḥ* is "difficulty" (*kṛcchra*) or "suffering," while the meaning of the other two [prefixes] is "ease" (*akṛcchra*). When these prefixes—meaning difficulty or ease—are used as *upapadas*, the suffix *khal* is added to the verbal root in the sense of either the abstract state (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).
That which is done with slight effort is "īṣatkaraḥ," as in: "The mat is easy for you to make. That which is done with difficulty and effort is "duṣkaraḥ.
That which is done with ease and without effort is "sukaraḥ."

What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of difficulty or lack of difficulty" (*kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu*)? [Example: *īṣallabhyaṃ dhanam* ("wealth is easily obtained"), meaning "only slightly [difficult] for the miserly.
And regarding the agent and the object: *kartṛkarmaṇoś ca bhūkṛñoḥ*.

According to Kāśikā 4.5.103, when words such as *īṣat* and others are used as upapadas in the sense of difficulty or lack of difficulty, the suffix *khal* occurs after the roots *bhū* and *kṛñ* with respect to both the agent and the object; by virtue of the indicatory letter *kh*, there is immediate proximity only between the suffix and the agent or the object.

One becomes somewhat wealthy (*īṣadāḍhyena bhūyate*), you have become somewhat wealthy (*īṣadāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ bhavatā*), [one has become] difficult-to-wealthy (*durāḍhyaṃbhavam*), [or one has become] self-wealthy (*svāḍhyaṃbhavam*).

One is made somewhat wealthy (*īṣadāḍhyaḥ kriyate*), you are one who makes [someone] somewhat wealthy (*īṣadāḍhyaṃkaro bhavān*), [one is] difficult-to-make-wealthy (*durāḍhyaṃkaraḥ*), [or one is] self-making-wealthy (*svāḍhyaṃkaraḥ*).

When that which is already somewhat wealthy is made [so] to some extent, then [the suffix *kṛt*] does not occur, because here the root *kṛ* has the meaning of "the manifestation of what was previously non-existent" (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*).

According to the rule of respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyāt*), [the suffix] does not occur in the case of *īṣadāḍhyaḥ* (slightly wealthy). [The rule states: "After roots ending in long *ā*, the suffix *yu* occurs when words such as *īṣat* are used as upapadas in the sense of difficulty or ease, provided they are not from the root *daridrā*. (Kātantra 4.5.104). Examples are: *īṣatpānaḥ* (easy to drink), *supānaḥ* (well-drunk), and *duṣpānaḥ* (difficult to drink).
What is the purpose of excluding *adaridrat*? [The answer is: *īṣaddaridraḥ* (slightly poor).
Regarding the rule *śāsuyudhidṛśidhṛṣimṛṣāṃ vā* (Kāśikā 4.5.105):
when words such as *īṣat* and others, which signify difficulty or ease, are used as upapadas, the suffix *yuc* is optionally applied to these roots; thus, *īṣacchāsanaḥ* or *īṣacchāsaḥ*.
Duḥśāsanaḥ, duḥśāsaḥ.
Suśāsanaḥ, suśāsaḥ.
Īṣadyodhanaḥ, īṣadyodhaḥ.
Duryodhana, Duryodha;
Suyodhana, Suyodha;
Īṣaddarśana, Īṣaddarśa.
*durdarśaṇaḥ*, *durdarśaḥ*;
*sudarśaṇaḥ*, *sudarśaḥ*;
*īṣaddharṣaṇaḥ*, *īṣaddharṣaḥ*.
Durdharṣaṇaḥ, durdharṣaḥ;
sudharṣaṇaḥ, sudharṣaḥ;
īṣanmarṣaṇaḥ, īṣanmarṣaḥ.
*durmarṣaṇaḥ*, *durmarṣaḥ*;
*sumarṣaṇaḥ*, *sumarṣaḥ*.

Because of the mention of the option (*vā*) and because the section on feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*) follows, the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply to the subsequent [suffixes].

The suffix *tum* occurs after verbal roots meaning "to desire" (*icchārtha*) when they have the same agent (*ekakartṛka*) as the governing word (*upapada*). According to Kātantra 4.5.106, when verbal roots meaning "to desire" have the same agent as the governing word, only the suffix *tum* is used after the root, and not the suffixes *vuṇ* or *tumun* prescribed by Kātantra 4.4.69 for the case where one action is performed for the sake of another action (*kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām*). Examples: *icchati bhoktum* ("he desires to eat"), *bhoktuṃ kāmayate* ("he desires to eat"). Why specify "having the same agent"? To ensure that the rule does not apply when there are different agents. Otherwise, it would incorrectly apply in cases such as *rājño bhojanam icchati* ("he desires the king's eating") or *icchan karoti* ("desiring, he acts").
What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of desire" (*icchārtheṣu*)? [Consider: *pācako vrajati* ("The cook goes").

And [it applies] when words expressing time (*kāla*), occasion (*samaya*), time-limit (*velā*), and ability (*śakti*) are used as upapadas. According to Pāṇini 3.3.167 (*Kāt_4.5.107*), when these are uttered as upapadas, only the suffix *tumun* occurs after the verbal root.

It is time to eat; it is the proper time to eat; it is the occasion to eat; it is the hour to eat; one is capable of eating; one is able to eat; one is the master of eating; one is sufficient for eating; one is fit for eating.

This is because the sense of "for the purpose of that" (*tādarthya*) is understood from the roots *bhū* or *vṛt*, as in: "the mind is for eating," "the desire is to go," "the ear is for hearing," "the eye is for seeing," "the bow is for fighting," or "the fool is for speaking.
However, the actual utterance depends upon the speaker.

Likewise, from the sense of capability (*śakti*): "he is able to eat" (*śaknoti bhoktum*), "he is capable of eating" (*pārayati bhoktum*), "he dares to eat" (*dhṛṣṇoti bhoktum*), "he knows how to eat" (*jānāti bhoktum*), "he is weary of eating" (*glāyati bhoktum*), "he strives to eat" (*ghaṭate bhoktum*), "he begins to eat" (*ārabhate bhoktum*), "he undertakes to eat" (*ālabhate bhoktum*), "he sets out to eat" (*prakramate bhoktum*), "he exerts himself to eat" (*utsahate bhoktum*), "he deserves to eat" (*arhati bhoktum*), "he exists [to eat]" (*asti bhoktum*), "he is found [to eat]" (*vidyate bhoktum*). Since the suffix *tum* is established by the rule *kriyāyāṃ kriyārthāyām* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), the suffix *vuṇ* should also be understood as being used here for the sake of expression. Furthermore, the suffix *tṛc* is used in the sense of "deserving" (*arhatau*) according to Kātantra 4.5.108.

The suffix *tṛc* occurs after a verbal root that is distinguished by the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*). For example: "You are indeed the one who ought to marry the maiden" (*kanyāyāḥ khalu bhavān voḍhā*); "You are indeed the student of the treatise" (*adhyetā khalu bhavāñ śāstrasya*); and "provided there is practical application" (*prayogataś ceti*). The mention [of the word *arhe*] is so that the locative case (*saptamī*) [used in the rule for the suffix *tṛc*] may serve as an exception to [the general locative used in the rule for the suffix *liṅ*]. Thus: "You should indeed marry the maiden" (*bhavān khalu kanyām udvaheta*), which means you are worthy (*arhaḥ*) or capable (*śaktaḥ*).

The *kṛtya* suffixes may also be used after a root meaning "to be able" (*śak*). (Kāt_4.5.109) The act of being able is *śak*. The *kṛtya* suffixes occur after a verbal root characterized by the sense of "ability" (*śakti*) and after one characterized by the sense of "fitness" (*arhati*). For example: "A maiden must indeed be married by you"—*voḍhavyā*, *vahanīyā*, *vāhyā*, or *uhyet*. [They are also used] in the senses of command, permission, and the arrival of the proper time. (Kāt_4.5.110)

When meanings such as "commanding" (*praiṣa*) and so forth are implied, the *kṛtya* suffixes occur after a verbal root: "You have been commanded by him; the village must be gone to (*gantavyaḥ*), it is to be gone to (*gamanīyaḥ*), it is to be gone to (*gamyaḥ*).

"Permission" (*atisarga*) means consent: "Having been permitted by the teacher, you must make the mat (*kartavyaḥ*), it is to be made (*karaṇīyaḥ*), it is to be made (*kāryaḥ*), it is to be made (*kṛtyaḥ*).
"The time has arrived for you to make the mat": "The mat must be made by you, it is to be made, it is to be made, it is to be made."
It must also be stated that [the suffix *ṇini*] applies in the sense of "a mat should be made within a muhūrta" (*ūrdhvaṃ muhūrtāt kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ*).

This statement is intended to show that [the suffix *ṇini*] set forth with the fifth and seventh case endings would otherwise supersede [the application of *ṇini*] to servants (*praiṣya*) and the like.
According to Kātyāyana 4.5.111, the suffix *ṇini* is applied in the senses of "necessity" (*āvaśyaka*) and "indebtedness" (*adhamarṇa*).

When the sense of "inevitability" (*avaśya-bhāva*) is implied, and when the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) is the agent, the suffix *ṇin* is added to the verbal root; for example: *avaśya-dāyī* ("one who will certainly give") and *avaśya-kārī* ("one who will certainly do").
Regarding the debtor: *śataṃ dāyī* ("one who owes a hundred"), *sahasraṃ dāyī* ("one who owes a thousand"), and *dāyī me śataṃ bhavān* ("may you be one who owes me a hundred").
[The suffixes] *ti* and *kṛt* are used to form names (*saṃjñā*) in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). (Kātantra 4.5.112)
When a benediction (*āśis*) is implied within a name (*saṃjñā*), the suffixes *ti* and *kṛt* occur after a verbal root: *tanu-tāt* (may he extend) becomes *tantiḥ*;
*devāya enam deya-t* (may this be given to the god) becomes *Devadattaḥ*, and likewise *Yajñadattaḥ*.
From *vīro bhūyāt* (may he become a hero), one gets *Vīrabhūtiḥ* and *Mitrabhūtiḥ*; from *agnir asya bhūyāt* (may fire be his portion), one gets *Agnibhūtiḥ*.
Terms and words are to be derived in whatever manner is appropriate.

Regarding the rule *dhātusaṃbandhe pratyayāḥ* (Kātantra 4.5.113): when there is a connection between the meanings of verbal roots—characterized by the relationship of qualifier and qualified—the suffixes designated as *kṛt* are valid, provided they abandon their own time [of application] and occur at the time of the qualified root-meaning; however, the *tya*-suffixes (*ti*, etc. are not so, because they are prescribed for that which is yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
This sūtra, however, is intended solely for the sake of ease.

[In the example] "The son of this [man] will be an Agniṣṭoma-sacrificer," the suffix *ṇini* occurs with reference to the past (bhūte), as in "Agniṣṭomayājī. Its correctness is established through its connection with the word "janitā" ("will be born"). Similarly, in the cases "the mat made [is] to be tomorrow" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ śvo bhavitā*) and "there was a future duty" (*bhāvi kṛtyam āsīt*), the suffix *ṇini*, though prescribed for the future, is established as valid in the past.
The sense of "made" is obtained from the context; the explicit mention of the suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇam*) is for the sake of generality.

"He was possessed of cows" (*gomān āsīt*) and "he will be possessed of cows" (*gomān bhavitā*): in these cases, the suffix *man* [forming *gomān*] occurs in the present tense; when connected with "was," it is established as referring to the past, and with "will be," it refers to the future. Thus ends the fifth quarter on primary suffixes (*kṛt*) in the commentary of Daurgasimhi. [The suffix] *ktvā* is optionally used after a verb when followed by the particles *alam* and *khalu*, which express prohibition. (Kāśikāvṛtti 3.4.18)

When the words *alaṃ* and *khalu*, which have the sense of prohibition, are used as accompanying words (*upapada*), the suffix *ktvā* optionally occurs after a verbal root: *alaṃ kṛtvā* (having done enough), *khalu kṛtvā* (having indeed done);
*alaṃ bhojanena* (enough with eating), *khalu bhojanena* (indeed enough with eating).
Why [specify] "of *alaṃ* and *khalu*"? [Consider: *mā kārṣīḥ* (do not do).

What is the purpose of the rule "pratiṣedhārthayoḥ" (in the case of words having the sense of prohibition)? [Consider: *alaṃkāro niṣkasya*, *khaludānaṃ kanyāyāḥ*. Here, the word *khalu* is used in the sense of certainty. Regarding the root *meṅ* (Kāt. 4.6.2): the suffix *ktvā* optionally occurs after the root *mā* (*mayate*). This must be stated for the sake of expressing an action not prior in time (*apūrvakālārtha*). Examples: *apamāya yācate*, *apamitya yācate*. Although the form *apamītvā* is not desired, the suffix *ktvā* does not occur after *yāc* because it is not so prescribed; furthermore, due to the specific usage (*abhidhānāt*), one says *apamātuṃ yācate* (he begs after having borrowed) or *yācitvāpamayate* (he borrows after having begged).

*Kāt_4.6.3*: When there are two verbal roots having a single agent, the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the root expressing the action that takes place at the earlier time. The state of having a single agent is intended here through the non-differentiation of the power (*śakti*) and the possessor of the power (*śaktimān*). Examples: *bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten, he goes"); because the dual number is not restrictive, or because it is relative to another [action], one may say *bhuktvā pītvā vrajati* ("having eaten and drunk, he goes"). Why specify "having a single agent"? Consider: *gurau bhuktavati śiṣyo vrajati* ("the teacher having eaten, the student goes"). Why specify "earlier time"? Consider: *pacati ca paṭhati ca* ("he cooks and reads").
How is it that one laughs while closing the eyes, or sleeps while opening the mouth? This is because a specific duration of time, such as a moment (*muhūrta*), is intended [to be expressed].

How is it that suffering arises upon seeing the dead, or pleasure might arise upon seeing a loved one? Since these involve different agents, this must be reflected upon. And [this applies] in the case of the connection between the higher and the lower. (Kātantra 4.6.4)

When there is a connection between a posterior action and a prior one, or a prior action and a posterior one, the suffix *ktvā* occurs after the verbal root. For example: *aprāpya nadīṃ parvataḥ* ("the mountain [is reached] without having reached the river"). Here, by its connection with the posterior [action of reaching] the river, the mountain situated in the prior location is qualified. Or: *atikramya parvataṃ nadī* ("the river [is reached] after having crossed the mountain"). Here, by its connection with the prior [action of crossing] the mountain, the river situated in the posterior location is qualified. Since the root *bhū* (to exist/to occur) is possible in all such cases, the rule is stated because the fact of having a single agent and the fact of temporal priority are difficult to understand [without it].

The suffix *ṇam* is used after a verbal root denoting an action occurring prior in time when two actions share the same agent; furthermore, *ktvā* may also be used in this sense. When there is repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), the word is reduplicated. For example: *bhojaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* ("he goes after eating repeatedly") or *bhuktvā bhuktvā vrajati* ("having eaten again and again, he goes").
The rule "the word is reduplicated" (*dviś ca padam*) is stated merely for the sake of clarity.
"Reap, reap!"—this is seen from common usage.

When one says, "He goes after he eats," the suffix *ktvā* does not occur because the sequence is already expressed by the word *tataḥ*; furthermore, the suffix *ṇam* would not apply due to the absence of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*).
However, in the case of "He goes after he eats again and again," the suffix *ṇam* does occur because the repetition is expressed by the word *punaḥpunaḥ*.

When one says, "Having eaten this, he goes; therefore, he has studied," the suffix *ktvā* is used for the sequence between eating and going, whereas the sequence between going and studying is expressed by the word *tataḥ*. *Kāt_4.6.6*: When these words—*agre*, *prathama*, and *pūrva*—are used as upapadas, the suffix *ṇam* optionally occurs after a verbal root. *agre bhojaṃ vrajati* (he goes while eating first), *agre bhuktvā vrajati* (having first eaten, he goes); *prathamaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* (he goes while eating first), *prathamaṃ bhuktvā vrajati* (having first eaten, he goes); *pūrvaṃ bhojaṃ vrajati* (he goes while eating first), *pūrvaṃ bhuktvā vrajati* (having first eaten, he goes).
Because the word *tataḥ* expresses sequence in the sense that "one eats first, then one goes.

[Regarding the rule] *karmaṇy ākrośe kṛñaḥ khamiñ* (Pāṇini 3.4.25): when a direct object (*karman*) is present as a governing word (*upapada*) and censure (*ākrośa*) is implied, the suffix *khamiñ* is applied after the root *kṛ*. For example: *cauraṃkāram ākrośati* ("he censures him by calling him a thief"). Here, the root *kṛ* means "uttering," and the object is established solely through the act of censure itself.

What is the purpose of [specifying] *ākrośe*? [It is to show that the suffix does not apply when one] praises after having done something well. The suffix *kh* with its following *an* is for the sake of the Māgadhī dialect. And [it applies] after verbal roots beginning with *svā*. (Kātantra 4.6.8)

When *svādu* (sweet/delicious) is the object, the suffix *khamiñ* is applied after the root *kṛ* when that [word] is used as an upapada; for example: *svādukāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it sweet), *saṃpannakāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it well-prepared), *lavaṇakāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it salty). Why specify "when *svādu* is the object"? [To show that] this form indicates that the word ends in a short vowel; therefore, *svādūkṛtya* means "having made it sweet," as in *svādūkṛtya svādvīṃ kṛtvā yavāgūṃ bhuṅkte* (having made the gruel sweet, he eats it). [The suffix *khamiñ* is applied] after the words *anyathā*, *evam*, *katham*, and *ittham*, provided that the usage is established even without the suffix (*siddhāprayoga*). (Kātantra 4.6.9)

With these prefixes, the suffix *kha* (forming *-kāra*) is added to the root *kṛ*, provided that the sense of "doing" (*karoti*) is established even when not explicitly used—since words such as *anyathā* and others express a manner—and the root *kṛ* is employed to manifest the usage even when [the manner] has already been stated. Examples: *anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats in another way), *evaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats in this way), *kathaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (how does he eat?), *itthaṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (thus he eats).
Why say "provided that the sense of 'doing' is established even when not explicitly used"? [Consider: *anyathā kṛtvā śiro bhuṅkte* (having done otherwise, he eats with his head [down]).
[The suffix is also applied] to *yathā* and *tathā* when expressing envy or a retort. (Kātantra 4.6.10)

Regarding *osyeti* because it is a *sūtra* [Āpiśali 2.1.20]: *asūyā* means intolerance; the suffix *khamiñ* occurs after the root *kṛ* when *yathā* and *tathā* are used in response to that [intolerance], provided that a response of intolerance is understood and the verb *karoti* is already established in usage. For example: *yathākāram ahaṃ bhokṣye, tathākāram ahaṃ bhokṣye; kiṃ tavānena* ("I will eat in such a way, I will eat in such a way; what is this to you?"). Why "in response to intolerance"? [Consider: *yathā kṛtvāhaṃ bhokṣye, tathā kṛtvāhaṃ śiro bhokṣye; kiṃ tavānena* ("Having done it this way I will eat, having done it that way I will eat on my head; what is this to you?"). After the root *dṛś*, the suffix *ṇam* occurs in the sense of totality. (Kātantra 4.6.11)
The suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *dṛś* when the object (*karma*) is qualified by totality (*sākalya*). For example: *kanyādarśaṃ varayati*, which means "he chooses every girl he sees.
It should be stated that this also applies to the root *vid*: *brāhmaṇavedaṃ bhojayati*, which means "he feeds every Brahmin he knows, finds, or considers.
Why specify "totality"? [Because otherwise it would mean] "having seen some Brahmin, he feeds him."

Kāt_4,6.12: *yāvat* [is used] when the meaning is not explicitly stated. When *yāvat* occurs as an accompanying word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* is applied to the roots *vid* and *jīv*. For example: *yāvadvedaṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats as much as he obtains"). The meaning is: "he eats as much as he finds" or "he eats whatever amount he obtains. *yāvajjīvam adhīte* ("he studies for his whole life"). The meaning is: "he studies for as long as he lives. Kāt_4,6.13: [The suffix *ṇam* is applied] to the root *pūr* (to fill) when *carman* (skin/hide) or *udara* (belly) [are the accompanying words].

The root *pūri* is transitive only when it means "to fill. When the words *carman* ("skin") or *udara* ("belly") occur as the object (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* is applied to the root *pūrayati*. Thus: *carmapūraṃ dadāti* ("he gives [something] filling the skin"), *udarapūraṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats filling the belly"). *Kāt_4.6.14*: When the measure of rainfall is to be understood, the suffix *ṇam* is applied to the root *pūrayati* with an object as the *upapada*, and the vowel *ū* of *pūrayati* may optionally be elided. Thus: *goṣpadapūraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained filling a cow's footprint"), or *goṣpadapraṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained filling a cow's footprint").

Kāt_4,6.15: After the root *knopi* (to moisten), when it has an object denoting "clothing" as its attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* occurs, provided that the measure of rain is understood. Examples: *celaknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained so much that it soaked the clothes"), *vastraknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*, *vasanaknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ*.
Kāt_4,6.16: [The suffix *ṇam* occurs] after the root *kaṣ* (to rub) when the words *nimūla* (root-and-all) or *samūla* (with the roots) are used as attendant words.

The suffix *ṇam* is applied to the root *kaṣ* when the words *nimūla* and *samūla* function as the object (*karman*) in composition; thus, *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati* and *samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati*, meaning "he scrapes out by the roots" (scraping it rootless or scraping it with its roots). Regarding the rule *śuṣkacūrṇarukṣeṣu piṣaḥ* (Kātantra 4.6.17): the suffix *ṇam* is applied to the root *piṣ* when these—*śuṣka*, *cūrṇa*, and *rukṣa*—function as the object in composition; thus, *śuṣkapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*, *cūrṇapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*, and *rukṣapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*, meaning "he grinds dryly," "he grinds into powder," and "he grinds coarsely," respectively. This signifies that he grinds [something] until it is dry.
When *jīva* is the object, [the suffix] *ṇam* is applied after the root *grah*. (Kāt.
4.6.18) When *jīva* is the object (*karman*) as a subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* occurs after the root *grah*; for example, *jīvagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti*, which means "he seizes alive.
After the root *kṛ*, [the suffix *ṇam* is applied] when it has not been performed. (Kāt. 4.6.19)
When *akṛta* is the subordinate word (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *kṛ*; *akṛtakāram* means "he does what was not done," that is, he does it for the first time.

After the root *han*, when *samūla* is the subordinate word, [the suffix *ṇam* is applied]; according to Pāṇini 3.4.28, when *samūla* is the subordinate word, the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *han*: *samūlaghātam* means "he kills with the roots," that is, he kills completely.

In the sense of the instrument (karaṇe). Pāṇini 3.4.37: When a word expressing the instrument is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *han*. For example, *pādaghātaṃ bhūmiṃ hanti* means "he strikes the ground with his foot"; that is, he strikes it by means of his foot.
