Similarly, *muṣṭighātaṃ cauraṃ hanti* means "he strikes the thief with his fist"; that is, he strikes the thief by means of his fist.
Indeed, this [rule] sets aside the statement "also after a verb meaning 'to injure' when it has a single object," because the instrument (*karaṇa*) is a specific entity.

Regarding *grah*, *vṛt*, and *vṛ* when the hand is the object: Kāt_4.6.22 states that when the hand is the object and serves as the instrument (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* occurs after these [roots]. For example: *hastena gṛhṇāti* (he grasps with his hand), *hastagrāham gṛhṇāti* (he grasps by the hand).
Thus he takes it by the hand;
he turns it with his hand, he performs the hand-turning.
He turns with his hand, he performs the hand-turning.

After the root *puṣ* (to nourish), the suffix *ṇam* is applied when it has its own meaning (*svārthe*), provided that words denoting "one's own" (*sva*)—namely, self, one's belongings, kinsmen, or wealth—are used as the instrumental upapadas. Examples include: *svena poṣati*, *puṣyati*, or *puṣṇāti* (he nourishes by means of his own); *svapoṣaṃ poṣati* (he nourishes [something] for the sake of his own nourishment). Likewise: *ātmapoṣam*, *ātmīyapoṣam*, *gopoṣam*, *mahiṣīpoṣam*, *pitṛpoṣam*, *mātṛpoṣam*, *vittapoṣam*, and *raipoṣam*.
After the root *piṣ* (to grind), the suffix *ṇam* is applied when the sense is that of affection (*snehane*). (Kātantra 4.6.23–24)

That by which something is made unctuous or moistened is called *snehana*, such as water and the like. When a word expressing "unctor" (*sneha*) is used as an *upapada* in the instrumental case, the suffix *ṇam* is applied to the root *piṣ* ("to grind"). Examples: *udakena pinaṣṭi* (he grinds with water), *udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*; likewise, *tailapeṣam*, *ghṛtapeṣam*. Furthermore, the substitution of *uda-* for *udaka-* is prescribed before the roots *piṣ*, *vas*, *vah*, and *dhi*.
[The suffix *ṇam* is also applied] after the root *bandh* when it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). (Kāśikāvṛtti 3.4.46–47)

The suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *bandh* when a word denoting a location (*adhikaraṇa*) is present as an attendant word (*upapada*). For example: *cakre baddhaḥ* ("bound in a wheel"), *cakrabandhaṃ baddhaḥ* ("bound in a wheel-binding"), *guptibandhaṃ baddhaḥ* ("bound in a prison-binding"), *hastabandhaṃ baddhaḥ* ("bound in a hand-binding").
And it is also used when a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is intended. According to Pāṇini 3.4.46:

the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *bandh*, whether the attendant word denotes a location or not, provided that a proper name is understood. For example: *krauñce krauñcena vā baddhaḥ* ("bound by a curlew on a curlew-mound"), *krauñcabandhaṃ baddhaḥ*.
Thus, there are the *mayūrikābandha* (peacock-band) and the *aṭṭālikābandha* (pavilion-band). These are technical names for specific types of compositions.
[The suffix *ṇini*] is applied after the verbal roots *naś* and *vah*, when the agent (*kartṛ*) is either a living being (*jīva*) or a person (*puruṣa*). (Kātantra 4.6.27)

When *jīva* and *puruṣa* are used as agentive upapadas, the suffix *ṇam* is added after the roots *naś* and *vah*, respectively: *jīvanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* (he perished while living), meaning "the living being perished"; *puruṣavāhaṃ vahati* (he carries while being a man), meaning "the man carries. Why specify "when they are agents"? [Because in these counter-examples: *jīvena naṣṭaḥ* (perished by means of a living being); *puruṣeṇoḍhaḥ* (carried by means of a man). [Also] after the roots *śuṣ* and *pūr* when preceded by *ūrdhva*. (Kātantra 4.6.28)

When *ūrdhva* is used as a preceding word (*upapada*) expressing the agent, the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the roots *śuṣ* and *pūr*. Thus, one says *ūrdhvaśoṣaṃ śuṣkaḥ* (dried while standing upright) and *ūrdhvapūraṃ pūrṇaḥ* (filled while standing upright); the meaning is "having become upright. In cases such as *anyathākāraṃ bhuṅkte* ("he eats in a different manner"), for what purpose is the prescription of *ṇam*? [One might argue that] the accusative case will occur because of its being the object (*vyāpyatvāt*), just as in *odanapākaṃ śete* ("he lies down for the sake of cooking rice").
[To this we reply: the rule "there is no *ghañ* after *grah*" must indeed be stated.

The claim that *goṣpadapram* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) because it means "as much as a cow's footprint" is incorrect. For *taram* and *tamām* are accepted as indeclinables (*avyaya*), and thus even a preceding time [expression] must be understood according to its designation. Furthermore, this is seen in the section on optionality (*vikalpādhikāra*). Otherwise, in the example "the rice is eaten in a different manner" (*anyathākāraṃ bhujyate odanaḥ*), the accusative case would not occur. As in the example, "the rice is eaten after being cooked" (*odanaḥ paktvā bhujyate*), for a *kṛt*-suffix used as an indeclinable denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*); when the primary power (*pradhānaśakti*) is expressed, the secondary power (*guṇaśakti*) appears as if unenjoined. And [this applies] when the object (*karman*) is the point of comparison. (Kātantra 4.6.29)

The suffix *ṇam* is applied to a verbal root when a word expressing a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) occurs as either an agent (*kartṛ*) or an object (*karman*). For example, when the agent is expressed: "He perished like a crest-jewel" (*cūḍaka iva naṣṭaḥ*), [which becomes] *cūḍakanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ*. When the object is expressed: "It was deposited like gold" (*suvarṇam iva nihitam*), [which becomes] *suvarṇanidhāyaṃ nihitam*; or "He cooked like rice" (*odana iva pakvaḥ*), [which becomes] *odanapācaṃ pakvaḥ*. Why specify "standard of comparison"? [Observe: *cūḍako naṣṭaḥ* ("The crest-jewel perished") and *suvarṇaṃ nihitam* ("Gold was deposited").

In the case of *kaṣ* and other such roots, the subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) must be by those very same roots. (Kātyāyana 4.6.30) When *ṇamul* is the object of application in the case of *kaṣ* and others, the subsequent application must be made by those very *kaṣ* and others, and not by any others; furthermore, the subsequent application indeed expresses the state of being prior in time. For example: *nimūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati* ("he scrapes away root and all"). Why "in the case of *kaṣ* and others"? [Consider: *celaknopaṃ vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained so as to soak the clothes").

Regarding the third [rule]: *upadaṃśeḥ* (Kāśikā 4.4.31). When a word ending in the third case is an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the root *daṃś* preceded by the prefix *upa*. For example: *mūlakenopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte* ("He eats with a radish as a side-dish"). Although the radish is connected to the act of eating (*bhuj*) by way of being the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is also pervaded by the act of biting (*upadaṃś*), and thus it becomes an *upapada*. Due to the governing rule of "option" (*vādhikāra*), one may also say: *mūlakenopadaśya bhuṅkte*. Why specify "when there is a third case"? Observe: *mūlakam upadaśya bhuṅkte* ("Having bitten the radish, he eats").

And after a root meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*) that has a single object (*ekakarmaka*), [the suffix] *ṇam* occurs when a word ending in the third case is used as a subordinate element (*upapada*), provided the root is followed by an auxiliary verb (*anuprayoga*) and shares the same object. For example: *daṇḍenopaghātaṃ daṇḍopaghātaṃ gāḥ kalayati* ("he drives the cows, striking them with a stick"). Why say "having a single object"? Consider: *daṇḍenāhatya bhūmiṃ gopālako gāḥ sādayati* ("the cowherd, having struck the ground with a stick, makes the cows sit down").

And in the case of the seventh [case-ending], there is *ṇam* after a verbal root when the words denoting the instrument (*pramāṇa*) and proximity (*pratyāsatti*) are present as either third-case or seventh-case upapadas; this is not according to the respective order [of the rule], provided that the relationship [between the action and the instrument] is not intended to be expressed. For example: *dvyaṅgulenotkarṣam*, *dvyaṅgula utkarṣam*, *dvyaṅgulotkarṣaṃ gaṇḍikāṃ chinatti* ("he cuts the joint with an excess of two fingers").
*keśair grāham*, *keśeṣu grāham*, *keśagrāhaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight seizing by the hair").

*Kāt_4,6.34*: When *upapīḍa*, *uparodha*, and *upakarṣa* follow [the roots], the suffix *ṇam* occurs after these verbs when preceded by *upa*, provided that a word ending in the third case or the seventh case is used as a co-occurring word (*upapada*). Examples: *pārśvābhyām upapīḍam*, *pārśvayor upapīḍam*, or *pārśvopapīḍam* he lies down;
*vrajenoparodham*, *vraje uparodham*, or *vrajoparodham* he causes the cows to settle in the cow-pen.

*pāṇinopakarṣam*, *pāṇāv upakarṣam*, *pāṇyupakarṣam*—he eats the roasted grains, pulling them [to himself] with his hand. [The suffix] *ṇam* is used after a verbal root when an ablative (*apādāna*) is the attendant word (*upapada*), provided that there is a sense of haste (*parīpsā*). Kāt_4.6.35: *parīpsā* means the desire to reach something completely; it signifies urgency. When an ablative is the attendant word, the suffix *ṇam* occurs after the root if haste is implied: *śayyāyā utthāyam*, *śayyotthāyam*—he runs, rising from his bed.
He drinks water by drawing it from a hole; this is *randhropakarṣam* (drawing out from a hole).
Why [is the word] *parīpsāyām* ("in the sense of haste") used? Because [otherwise] one would say: "Having risen from his seat, he goes.
And [the suffix *lyap* is applied] after a word ending in the second case. (Kātantra 4.6.36)

When a word ending in the second case is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇam* is added to the verbal root when a sense of haste (*parīpsā*) is implied: *loṣṭaṃ grāhaṃ*, *loṣṭagrāhaṃ yudhyante*—they fight with such haste that they do not even take care of their weapons.

[Kāśikā 4.6.37] Regarding a non-permanent part of one's own body (*svāṅge 'dhruve*): "one's own limb" is *svāṅga*; when a word denoting a non-permanent part of one's own body ends in the second case as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇam* is added to the verbal root: *bhruvau vikṣepaṃ*, *bhrūvikṣepaṃ jalpati*—he speaks while tossing his eyebrows.

"Blind in one eye" (*akṣiṇī kāṇam*); "blind-eyed" (*akṣikāṇam*) is used as a laughable term. Why [is it specified] "not permanent" (*adhruva*)? [For example,] he speaks while holding his head up. That limb by which a living being does not die when it is severed is "not permanent."

And when there is *parikliśyamāne* (Kāt_4,6.38): when the word *uraḥ* (chest), ending in the second case, is used as a co-occurring word (*upapada*) meaning "being afflicted on all sides," the suffix *ṇam* occurs after the verbal root. For example: *urāṃsi pratipeṣaṃ*, *uraḥpratipeṣaṃ yudhyante* ("they fight crushing each other's chests"); the meaning is that they fight having pressed their entire chests together. [The suffix *ṇam* also occurs] after the roots *viśi*, *pati*, *pad*, and *skandi* when the sense is either "pervading" (*vyāpyamāna*) or "repeated practice" (*āsevyamāna*). (Kāt_4,6.39)

When a word ending in the accusative case is used as a secondary word (*upapada*) signifying that which is being pervaded (*vyāpyamāna*) or practiced (*āsevyamāna*), the suffix *ṇam* is added to these verbal roots.

Because [the suffix] is explicitly stated, the "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) refers to the complete connection of substances with actions such as eating (*viśyādi*), and this is the sense of desire (*īpsā*). Therefore, the substance is reduplicated.
"Practice" (*āsevā*), however, means intentness or frequency (*tātparya*, *ābhīkṣṇya*), and that belongs to the action alone.

The doubling occurs for words such as *viś* ending in the suffix *ṇamul*: *gehaṃ geham anupraveśam āste* (he sits entering house after house), which is equivalent to *geham anupraveśam anupraveśam āste*.
*Gehaṃ geham anuprapātam āste*, which is equivalent to *geham anuprapātam anuprapātam āste*.
*Gehaṃ geham anuprapādam āste*, which is equivalent to *geham anuprapādam anuprapādam āste*.
"He sits jumping from house to house; he sits jumping from house to house.

In this compound, the distributive sense (*vīpsā*) and the sense of repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*) are expressed by the power of the word itself, as in *gehānupraveśam*, *gehānuprapātam*, *gehānuprapādam*, and *gehāvaskandam āste*. Why specify "when [the action] is being pervaded or repeated"? [Consider: "Having entered the house, he eats."

The suffix *ṇam* is already established for the sense of frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*); this [sūtra] is for the purpose of providing an option regarding the formation of a compound with an *upapada*. *Kāt_4.6.40*: "After the roots *tṛṣ* (to thirst) and *as* (to eat), when another action is implied, [the suffix *ṇam* occurs] in connection with words denoting time ending in the second case. When words ending in the second case expressing time are used as *upapadas*, and another action is understood, the suffix *ṇam* is applied after the roots *tṛṣ* and *as*. For example: *dvyahaṃ tarṣam* (thirsting for two days) or *dvyahatarṣam* (having made them thirsty for two days), he makes the cows drink.

Regarding *dvyaham abhyāsam*, *dvyahābhyāsaṃ gāḥ pāyayati* ("He makes the cows drink [water] with a two-day interval"): the act of making the cows drink is interrupted by both the thirst occurring today and the practice (*abhyāsa*) consisting of the thirst that will occur after two days have passed. Why say "when there is thirst and [the state of] being thirsty" (*tṛṣyasvoḥ*)? [Consider: *dvyaham upoṣya bhuṅkte* ("Having fasted for two days, he eats"). Why say "when there is another action" (*kriyāntare*)? [Consider: *ahar abhyasyeṣūn gataḥ* ("He went [to the target], practicing his arrows day after day"). Here, by means of the practice, the arrows and the times are pervaded, but the act of going is not interrupted.
What is the purpose of the condition "at [specific] times"? [Example: *yojanam abhyasya gāḥ pāyayati* ("Having practiced for a yojana, he makes the cows drink").
The mention of "action" (*kriyā*) is for the sake of ease.
[The rule] *nāmny ādiśigrahoḥ* (Kāt. 4.6.41) [is stated].

When a word denoting a name is used as a secondary word (*upapada*) ending in the accusative case, the suffixes *ṇam* and *ktvā* are applied after the root *ā-diś* (to point out) and *grah* (to seize). [Examples: *nāmāny ādeśam*, *nāmādeśam dadāti* (he points out the names);

*nāmāni grāham*, *nāmagrāham āhvayati* (he calls by name). After the root *kṛ* (to do), when an indeclinable is the secondary word, the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇam* are applied provided there is a description of something not as intended. (Kātantra 4.6.42)

*Yatheṣṭam* is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). When an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is the subordinate term (*upapada*), the suffix *ṇam* (as well as *ktvā*) is applied to the root *kṛ*, provided that the sense of "speaking in a manner other than desired" is implied. For example: "O Brāhmaṇa, a son has been born to you. [If this is said in a low voice: *nīcaiḥkāram*, *nīcaiḥkṛtya*, or *nīcaiḥ kṛtvā*—he speaks thus. For "high" (*uccais*) is what should be spoken when it is pleasant. [Conversely: "O Brāhmaṇa, your daughter is pregnant. [If this is said in a loud voice: *kiṃ tarhi vṛṣaly uccaiḥkāram*, *uccaiḥkṛtya*, or *uccaiḥ kṛtvā*—he speaks thus. For "low" (*nīcais*) is what should be spoken when it is unpleasant. Why does the rule specify "speaking in a manner other than desired"? Consider: "O Brāhmaṇa, a son has been born to you," [and he says] *uccaiḥ kṛtvācaṣṭe* ("he speaks loudly"). [In this case, since the speaker's intention is not contrary to his own desire, the suffix is not applied.]
The mention of *ktvā* is for the purpose of providing an alternative to the compound (*samāsa*).

[Kātantra 4.6.43: When the word *tiryak* is used as an *upapada*, the suffix *ṇam* occurs after the root *kṛ*, and *ktvā* also occurs, when completion (*apavarga*) is implied. Thus: *tiryakkāram*, *tiryakkṛtya*, *tiryak kṛtvā gataḥ*; the meaning is "having gone after completing [the action]."
What is the meaning of *apavarga*? For example: *tiryakkṛtvā kāṣṭhaṃ gataḥ* ("having placed the wood crosswise, he went").

[The rule] *svāṅge tasi* (Pāṇini 3.4.64): when a word ending in the suffix *tas* is designated as a *svāṅga* (body part) and serves as the *upapada*, the suffix *ṇamul* is applied after the root *kṛ*. Examples: *mukhataḥkāram*, *mukhataḥkṛtya*, or *mukhataḥ kṛtvā āste* ("he remains having placed [it] on his face").

What is meant by "one's own limb" (*svāṅga*)? [Examples include: *sarvataḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* (having done it all over, he went), and because of the governing rule for indeclinables (*avyaya*), *mukhataḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* (having placed it on his face, he went).
And after the root *bhū*, when the word *tūṣṇīm* is the attendant word (*upapada*), [the suffix] *ṇam* occurs, as well as *ktvā*.
(Kātantra 4.6.45) When a word ending in the suffix *tas* refers to one's own limb, and the word *tūṣṇīm* is the attendant word, the suffix *ṇam* occurs after the verbal root *bhū*, as well as *ktvā*.
He remains in a state of speech, having become speech, having become speech;
he remains in a state of silence, having become silent, having become silent.
How does he eat? In various ways, having made it varied, having made it varied.

*vinākāram*, *vinākṛtya*, and *vinā kṛtvā gataḥ* are merely adverbs (*kriyāviśeṹṣaṇa*). Alternatively, because the meaning is already expressed by the name itself, it may form a compound. However, in the case of *nānā kṛtvā kāṣṭhāni gataḥ* ("having split the wood, he has gone"), no compound is formed because of its dependency on an external object (*sāpekṣatva*). Similarly: *nānābhāvam*, *nānābhūya*, *nānā bhūtvā āste*; *vinābhāvam*, *vinābhūya*, *vinā bhūtvā gataḥ*. Likewise: *anvagbhāvam*, *anvagbhūya*, *anvag bhūtvā āste*. A compound is formed only when there is conformity (*ānukūlya*), as that is what is expressed; therefore, [it is used] in the sense of "having become favorable, the enemy remains."

*kartari kṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.67). The suffixes designated as *kṛt* should be understood to denote the agent (*kartṛ*). One who performs is an agent (*kartṛ*), such as *kāraka*, *pacaḥ*, or *nandanaḥ*. This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is either supplementary to sentences that are otherwise self-sufficient, or—because it is indicated by the employment of the suffix *khyuṭ*—it does not apply only optionally.

*Kṛtya*, *kta*, and suffixes having the sense of *khala* occur after verbal roots in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). This [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding one; it should be understood that *kṛtya* suffixes, the suffix *kta*, and those with the sense of *khala* occur in the sense of the abstract action and the object. Examples: *śayitavyaṃ bhavatā* (you must lie down), *bhoktavya odano bhavatā* (the rice is to be eaten by you), *āsitaṃ bhavatā* (you have sat), *kṛtaḥ kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat was made by you). [Examples of the sense of the abstract action: *īṣadāḍhyaṃbhavaṃ bhavatā* (you have become somewhat wealthy), *īṣatkaraḥ kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat is easy to make for you), *īṣatpānaṃ bhavatā* (the drinking is easy for you), *īṣatpānaḥ somo bhavatā* (the Soma is easy to drink for you).
By implication, these occur in the sense of the abstract action after intransitive roots, and in the sense of the object after transitive roots.

"The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) as well as [the action] at the beginning of an activity" (Kātantra 4.6.48). The *kta* suffix prescribed for the initial stage of an action should be understood to denote the agent (*kartṛ*) case-role, as well as [the action itself], according to what is appropriate. For example: *prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ bhavān* ("You have begun making the mat") and *prakṛtaḥ kaṭo bhavatā* ("The mat has been begun by you"); *prasupto bhavān* ("You have fallen asleep") and *prasuptaṃ bhavatā* ("Sleep has been entered upon by you"). The prefix *pra-* indicates the initial stage of the action. Among the many moments of the action, the moment of its commencement has already passed. Regarding the future mat, the word "mat" (*kaṭa*) is used there because it serves that purpose (*tādarthya*). "And [the suffix *kta* is used] after roots meaning 'to go' (*gatyartha*), after intransitive roots (*akarmaka*), and after *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *ās*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*" (Kātantra 4.6.49).

The suffix *kta* should be understood as occurring in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) after verbs meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*) that are intransitive (*akarmaka*), as well as after verbs beginning with *śliṣ*, and by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*), as otherwise prescribed. Examples:

*gato grāmaṃ bhavān* ("You have gone to the village"), *prāpto grāmaṃ bhavān* ("You have reached the village"); *gato grāmo bhavatā* ("The village was gone to by you"), *prāpto grāmo bhavatā* ("The village was reached by you"); *gatam anena* ("It was gone by him"), *prāptam anena* ("It was reached by him"). After intransitive verbs: *śayito bhavān* ("You have lain down"), *śayitaṃ bhavatā* ("Lying down was done by you").

Verbs such as *śliṣ* and others, when accompanied by prefixes (*upasarga*), are transitive (*sakarmaka*). *Śliṣ* has the meaning of embracing: "You have embraced the teacher" (*āśliṣṭo guruṃ bhavān*) or "The teacher was embraced by you" (*āśliṣṭo gurur bhavatā*).
"You have lain upon the bed" (*adhiśayitaḥ khaṭvāṃ bhavān*) or "The bed was lain upon by you" (*adhiśayitā khaṭvā bhavatā*).
"You have attended upon the teacher" (*upasthito guruṃ bhavān*) or "The teacher was attended upon by you" (*upasthito gurur bhavatā*).
You have served the teacher; the teacher has been served by you. You have resided for the sake of dwelling; the teacher has been resided with by you.
The young man is born after the young woman; the young woman is born after the young man.
"You have climbed the tree," "The tree has been climbed by you. "You have grown old with the low-caste woman," "The low-caste woman has been grown old with by you.
[In these cases, the agentive suffix *ktvā* is used. The terms *dāśa* and *goghna* are used when [the action] is directed toward the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). (Kāśikāvṛtti 4.6.50)
These two [words] are irregularly formed (nipātita) in the sense of the recipient (saṃpradāna).

From the root *dāśṛ* "to give," one who gives to someone is a *dāśa*; one to whom a cow is killed when he has arrived is a *goghna*, namely a guest (*atithi*). Due to this irregular formation (*nipātana*), the suffixes *ac* and *ṭak* are applied. Those such as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are worthy of the guest-offering (*arghya*) are also called so because they possess that fitness.

*bhīmādayo 'pādāne* (Kāśikā 4.2.51): these are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). *Bibheti asmāt* ("he fears from this") results in *bhīmaḥ*; likewise, *bhīṣmaḥ*.
Also: *caruḥ*, *praskandanaḥ*, *prapatanaḥ*, *samudraḥ*, and *sruvaḥ*.
This etymological derivation belongs to the *uṇādi* class and is formed in whatever manner is appropriate.
According to Kātantra 4.6.52, "other than those two," the *uṇādi* suffixes occur in other *kārakas* besides the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the point of departure (*apādāna*).

Since the *uṇādi* suffixes are included under the category of *kṛt* suffixes, they are primarily understood to denote the agent (*kartṛ*); however, they are also stated to denote the object (*karman*) and other *kārakas*.

One who acts is a *kāru* (artisan); one who blows is *vāyu* (wind); that which is ploughed is *kṛṣi* (agriculture); that which is stretched is a *tantu* (thread). [The suffix] *kta* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after roots meaning "staying" (*dhrauvya*), "motion" (*gati*), and "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*). (Pāṇini 3.4.76) * Dhruva* means immovable; it is a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). The state of being *dhruva* is *dhrauvya*. Because they consist of an action whose nature is immobility, roots with this meaning are called intransitive (*akarmaka*). *Pratyavasāna* means eating.

The *kta* suffix should be understood as denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after roots meaning "to remain" (*dhrauvya*), "to go" (*gati*), and "to consume" (*pratyavasāna*), as well as in accordance with its other established applications: *idam eṣām āsitam* ("this is where they sat"), *ebhir āsitam* ("they have sat here"), *āsito bhavān* ("you have sat").

*Idam eṣāṃ yātam* ("this is where they went"), *iha tair yātam* ("they have gone here"), *grāmas tair yātaḥ* ("the village has been gone to by them"), *grāmaṃ te yātāḥ* ("they have gone to the village").

Since the locus and the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) have not been explicitly stated [as distinct from the action], the nominative case alone is used merely to express the gender and number of the referent.

"This is what was eaten and drunk by them; here rice was eaten and milk was drunk by them. [Objection: Since the root *bhuj* has the sense of "eating," shouldn't the suffix apply even when the agent is expressed? [Response: This is a reading separated [from the previous rule], as in: "How is it that 'the Brahmins have eaten' and 'the cows have drunk'? [This is justified] because of the statement "also elsewhere" (*anyatrāpi*), or because [the word *bhuktam*] belongs to the *arśa-ādi* group [and thus denotes the agent]. [Example: "If the god has rained, the rice has ripened"—here, the cause of the rice has ripened, indicating past time. [The suffix *kta* is applied] after roots ending in *yu* or *vu*, except for those ending in *ā*. (Kātantra 4.6.54)

In place of these [roots], the substitutes *ana*, *aka*, and *anta* occur respectively: *nandanaḥ*, *pācakaḥ*, *gaṇḍayantaḥ*, *maṇḍayantaḥ*. [The suffix] *jhac* is applied after the roots *gaṇḍi*, *maṇḍi*, and *jani*.

How is it that there are *bhujyuḥ* and *mṛtyuḥ*? They are formed from the roots *bhuj* and *mṛṅ* with the suffixes *yuk* and *tyuk*, because the rules of the *uṇādi* [section] are manifold and because this falls under the heading of *kṛt* suffixes. That which has wool (*ūrṇā*) is *ūrṇāyuḥ*.
In a future compound, the *yap* substitute occurs for the *ktvā* suffix after a non-negative (*anañ*) indeclinable when it is compounded with another word ending in *ktvā*.

When a compound is about to be formed with a word ending in the *ktvā* suffix, provided that the preceding member is an indeclinable other than the negative particle *nañ*, the *yap* replacement takes place for the *ktvā* suffix; as in: *praṇamya*, *pradīvya*, *āpṛcchya*, *adhītya*, *upetya*.

The inclusion of the term *bhāvi* (future) is for the purpose of providing instruction; by that [rule], there would not otherwise be the lengthening of vowels and so forth for those beginning with the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) and the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), nor would the suffix *to* be added to the end. Examples include: *khāṭkṛtya*, *kanyām alaṃkṛtya*, *satkṛtya*, *asatkṛtya*, *antarhatya*, *kaṇehatya payaḥ pibati* (he drinks milk until his throat is satisfied), *manohatya payaḥ pibati* (he drinks milk until his heart's content), meaning "he drinks as much as he is satiated."

Having placed before him, having set aside, having gone straight toward, having walked straight, having spoken clearly, having made that [object] his focus, he reflects; having become invisible, having treated with contempt, having made subordinate, having made secondary, having realized directly, having made the middle, having made a footstep, having made a pause, having taken to heart, having kept in mind, having taken in hand, having placed in the palm, having made favorable, having made a secret doctrine, having made a means of livelihood.

And *anukaraṇa* (imitation) [is compounded] with *kṛta*; *alaṃ* [is compounded] with words expressing respect for ornaments or lack thereof, whether good or bad; *antara* [is compounded] with *agrahaṇe* (non-grasping); *kaṇe* and *manas* [are compounded] with *tṛpti* (satisfaction); *puras* and *astaṃ* [are compounded]; *accha* [is compounded] with roots meaning "to go" (*gaty-artha*) and with *vad* (to speak); *adas* [is compounded] when not used as an instruction (*anupadeśe*); *tiras* [is compounded] with *antardhi* (concealment), and it retains its own accent (*sa-tiras*); *upāja* and *anvāja* [are compounded]; *sākṣāt* and the others [beginning with *prabhṛti*] are optionally [compounded] with *kṛñ*; *madhye*, *pade*, and *nivacane* [are compounded]; *uras* and *manas* [are compounded] except when they mean "placing upon" (*anatyādhāne*); [the compounds] *haste* and *pāṇau* are obligatory when referring to marriage (*udvāhe*); *prādhvam* [is compounded] in the sense of binding (*bandhane*); *upaniṣad* [is compounded] in the sense of comparison (*aupamye*) and livelihood (*jīvikā*);
and [these] are all [compounded] when preceding [the verb]. What is the purpose of the word "compound" (*samāsa*)? [To show that these are not compounds: *tiraḥ kṛtvā*, *upāje kṛtvā*.
What is meant by *anañ*? It means "not having performed.
This is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusion), and therefore it would not apply to that which has a numeral [as a prefix], as in *paramakṛtvā*.
[The rule] *cajoḥ kagau dhuḍghānubandhayoḥ* [Kātantra 4.6.56 applies].

The sounds *ca* and *ja* become *ka* and *ga*, respectively, when followed by a *dhuṭ* consonant or an affix having *gh* as its *anubandha*. However, because the relationship with the cause [of the substitution] is not intended to be significant, there is no one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*). Thus we have *paktā*, *bhoktā*, *pākaḥ*, and *bhogaḥ*. In the cases of *rugnaḥ* and *bhugnaḥ*, although the substitution of *na* is obligatory, it is superseded by the substitution of the *ca*-class (the sound *ga*) due to its being *antaraṅga* (more internal). The mention of *dhuṭ* is for the purpose of excluding the application of this rule to *kṛt* affixes that do not have *gh* as their *anubandha*.
*Kāt_4.6.57*: For *nyaṅku* and the others, *c* and *j* become *k* and *g*, and *h* becomes *gh*.
[The rule] *nāv añcer uḥ* [states]: *nyaṅkuḥ*. Thus, for words beginning with *nyaṅku*, *c* and *j* become *k* and *g*, and *h* becomes *gh*. *Nyaṅkuḥ*.
From the roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *tṝ*, *car*, *tṛ*, *tan*, *masj*, and *śīṅ*, the suffix *u* is applied; thus, *madguḥ*.
From *prathi*, *mrad*, and *bhrasj*, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and the elision of the *s*; thus, *bhṛguḥ*.
According to the rule *sphāyitañcivancīty āde rak*, the suffix *rak* is applied; thus, *takram* and *vakram*.
*Asuṅ*: that in which one dwells is called *okaḥ*.
[The suffix] *ghañ* is applied after the roots *sañj* and *sṛj* with the prefix *vi-* to form *vyatiṣaṅgaḥ* (connection) and *avasargaḥ* (release).

The suffix *yat* is added according to the *pacādi* group, as in *śvapākaḥ*, *māṃsapākaḥ*, *kapotapākaḥ*, and *ulūkapākaḥ*. The suffix *an* is added after the root *pac* when it means "action" (*karman*), as in *dūre pacyate svayam eva* (it ripens by itself at a distance) and *phale pacyate svayam eva* (it ripens by itself on the fruit); here, due to the irregularity of the *gaṇa*, there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel and the elision of the locative case ending (*aluk*), resulting in *dūrepākaḥ*, *phalepākaḥ*, and some say *kṣaṇepākaḥ*. The suffix *ac* is added to the root *mih* to form *meghaḥ*, which refers specifically to a cloud.
*avadāghaḥ*, *nidāghaḥ*;
from *arh-* [with the suffix *ghañ*], *arghaḥ*.
When used as a technical term (*saṃjñā*) with the suffix *ghañ*, [the forms are] *avadāghaḥ*, *nidāghaḥ*, and *arghaḥ*; otherwise, [they are] *avadāhaḥ*, *nidāhaḥ*, and *arhaḥ*.
Not [the substitution of *k* and *g* occurs] for the roots *vraj-* and *aj-* following a guttural (*kavarga*) and so forth. (Kāt.
4.6.58) For the roots *vraj-* and *aj-* following a guttural and so forth, the *ca-ja* sounds do not become *ka-ga*. Examples: *kūjaḥ*, *kharjaḥ*, *garjaḥ*, *parivrājaḥ*, *udājaḥ*, *ājyaṃ ghṛtam*.

It should be stated that [this applies] to *vañc-* in the sense of "going": *vañcyate* means "merchants have gone to trade" (*vañcyaṃ gatā vaṇijaḥ*), which means they have gone to where they ought to go (*gantavyaṃ gatā*).
What is the purpose of [specifying] "in the sense of having gone" (*gatāv*)? [Consider: *vaṅkyam kāṣṭham* ("the wood is crooked"). Here, the root *vanci* means "crookedness.

[The suffix] *ghyaṇ* is applied in the sense of necessity (*avaśyake*). According to Pāṇini 4.6.59, when necessity is understood, the substitutions of *ka* for *ca* and *ga* for *ja* do not occur before *ghyaṇ*: *avaśyapācyam* ("that which must necessarily be cooked"), *avaśyabhojyam* ("that which must necessarily be eaten").

What is the purpose of the term *āvaśyaka* (necessary)? [Example: *pākya odanaḥ* (rice that must be cooked). Regarding the rule *pravacarci-ruci-yāci-tajām* (Kātantra 4.6.60): this statement is for the sake of excluding the sense of necessity (*anāvaśyaka*). For these roots, when the suffix *ghyaṇ* follows, the substitutions *k* and *g* do not occur for the letters *c* and *j*. *Pravācyaḥ* refers to a specific recitation; since the book containing it is also called by that name, it pertains to the domain of words. From the root *ṛc* in the sense of praise: *arcyah* (to be praised).
*rocyaḥ*, *yācyaḥ*, *tyājyaḥ*. How is [the word] *śocyaḥ* formed? Because it ends in the suffix *in* with the causal sense (*hetu*).
[The rule] "after the root *vac*, when not meaning 'sound'" (Kātantra 4.6.61).

The suffix *ghyaṇ* does not occur after the root *vac* when it does not refer to a word (*aśabda*), [forming] *vācyam*. Why "not referring to a word"? [Consider] *vākyaṃ*, which is a collection of words (*padasamudāya*).
[Otherwise, one might also have] *vakravākyaracanāramaṇīyaḥ*.

*Kāt_4.6.62*: After the prefix *ni* or *pra*, the substitution of *go* for the root *yuj* does not occur when the suffix *ghyaṇ* is applied in the sense of "being able" (*śakye*). For example: *niyoktuṃ śakyaḥ* ("capable of being employed") results in *niyojyaḥ* "a servant"; likewise, *prayojyaḥ*. Why say "in the sense of being able"? [Consider: *niyoktum arhati* ("deserves to be employed") results in *niyogyaḥ*; *prayogyaḥ* "a master."

*bhuja* [takes *ghyaṇ*] in the sense of food (Kāt_4.6.63). When *bhuja* is used in the sense of eating, the *go* [substitution of *u* for *o*] does not occur before the suffix *ghyaṇ*: *bhojyam annam* (food to be eaten), *bhojyaṃ payaḥ* (milk to be drunk).
Why "in the sense of food"? [Consider: *bhogyaḥ kambalaḥ* (an enjoyable blanket), *bhogyā bhūḥ* (enjoyable land).

*bhujanyubjau* [are used] for the meanings of "hand" (*pāṇi*) and "disease" (*roga*). (Kātantra 4.6.64) The forms *bhuj* and *nyubj*, ending in the suffix *ghañ*, are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*) for the respective meanings of "hand" and "disease. In the case of *bhuja*: it is that by which one enjoys (*bhujyate 'nena*), thus it is the hand (*pāṇi*). In the case of *nyubja*: it is that in which one lies down bent over (*nyubjitaḥ śete 'smin*), thus it is a particular disease (*rogaviśeṣa*). The suffix *ghañ* is applied here according to the rule *vyañjanāc ca* (Kātantra 4.5.99). Why specify "for the meanings of hand and disease"? [Otherwise, one might derive] *bhogaḥ* (enjoyment) and *nyudgaḥ*. Regarding the latter, it is desired that the *g* be substituted for the *d* when the suffix *ghañ* follows.
In the case of *dṛk*, *dṛśat*, and *dṛkṣa*, there is *sa* for the [stem] *samāna*. (Kāt.
4.6.65) For *samāna*, *sa* occurs before *dṛk* and the others; this is due to the explicit statement regarding the suffixes *kvip*, *ṭak*, and *śak*.
Thus: *sadṛk*, *sadṛśaḥ*, *sadṛkṣaḥ*.

Due to the division of the rule (yogavibhāga), compounds such as *sapakṣaḥ* ("on the same side") and *sajyotiḥ* ("under the same sky") are formed with the desired meaning, using the following words as the second members: *pakṣa*, *jyotis*, *janapada*, *rātri*, *nābhi*, *bandhu*, and *patnī*.

Alternatively, with the word *rūpa* and others, we have *samāno rūpaḥ* ("having the same form"), which becomes *sarūpaḥ*; and [the following words may also be used]: *nāman*, *gotra*, *sthāna*, *varṇa*, *vayas*, *dharma*, *jātīya*, *udara*, and *udarya*.
The term *sabrahmacārī* ("fellow student") is always [formed in this manner].

Kāt_4,6.66: For this word *idam*, the substitute *ī* occurs before *dṛg* and the following [suffixes]; thus, *īdṛk*, *īdṛśaḥ*, *īdṛkṣaḥ*; by virtue of non-distinction (*abhedabalāt*), this applies to all [forms].
Kāt_4,6.67: For the word *kim*, the substitute *kī* occurs [before the same suffixes].
What kind [is it] among the eyes and so forth? *kīdṛk*, *kīdṛśaḥ*, *kīdṛkṣaḥ*.
What is its measure? *iyān*, *kiyān*; because of the rule beginning with *sadyas* [the suffix *yat* is applied]. *adas* becomes *amūḥ*. (Kātantra 4.6.68)
In the case of *ado dṛg-ādiṣu*, it becomes *amūdṛk*, *amūdṛśaḥ*, *amūdṛkṣaḥ*.
Some [grammarians] hold that *amūkādṛk*, *amūkādṛśaḥ*, and *amūkādṛkṣaḥ* are simply erroneous forms (*tadāyatna*).
[The rule] *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* [applies]. (Kātantra 4.6.69)
The suffix *dṛk* and others occur after a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) before the verb *bhū*: *tādṛk*, *tādṛśaḥ*, *tādṛkṣaḥ*.
In the form *bhavādṛk*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) occurs because it is an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation.
In the form *anyādṛk*, the suffix *kvip* and *ṭakśac* are applied to the root *dṛś* even after the word *anya*, because of the explicit statement "after a pronominal."

Regarding this measure (*parimāṇa*) of it—whether it be "as much as" (*yāvān*), "so much" (*tāvān*), or "this much" (*etāvān*)—the suffix *vantu* is applied and the vowel *ā* is substituted due to its being present at that very moment (*sadya-āditvāt*). According to Pāṇini 5.2.70: *viṣvag-devayoś cāntyasvarāder adry añcatau kvau*. When the suffix *kvip* follows the verb root *añc*, the word *adri* is substituted for the final vowel and the following consonant of the words *viṣvak*, *deva*, and pronouns. Thus, from *viṣvak añcati* (he moves everywhere), one forms *viṣvadryaṅ*; likewise, *devadryaṅ*.

*yadryañ*, *tadryañ*, *sarvadyañ*, *adryañ*, *amudryañ*. According to *Kāśikāvṛtti* 4.3.71, for these [words]—*sadhri*, *sam*, *tiri*, and *ayaḥ*—the substitutes *sadhri*, *sam*, *tiri*, and *i* respectively occur when followed by the suffix *kvip* in the sense of *añc* (to bend). Thus: that which bends together is *sadhryañ*; that which bends equally is *samyañ*; that which bends across is *tiryañ*.

"Or *dha* for *ruha*. Kāt_4.6.72: When *kvip* follows, *dha* optionally replaces [the final *a*] of the root *ruha*. Thus, from *vīruhati*, we have *vīrut*, *vīrudhau*, *vīruṭ*, *vīruhau*; [here] there is lengthening of the short *i* of *vi*.
By means of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), this applies only to the prefix *vi-*; therefore, [we have] *bhūruṭ*, *bhūruhau*."
From the root *mo*. According to Pāṇini 8.2.63, the *m* of a verbal root becomes *n* when followed by the suffix *kvip*; for example, from *śam*, we have *praśān*;
from *tam*, we have *pratān*.

Furthermore, there is the elision of the *n* in *adanta*. Due to the status of being "as if in its original place" (*sthānivadbhāva*) when *kvip* follows, the elision of the *n* at the end of the stem would not occur for a word ending in *n*.
Alternatively, the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of excluding [the application of the rule] to [stems] other than roots.
And [the elision occurs] after *vam* and *uś*. (Kātantra 4.6.74)
In the case of the roots *vam* and *par*, the *m* becomes *n*. [Examples: *jaganvān*, *ganmā*; the suffix *man* is added after all roots.
Before a vowel, a root ending in *ā* remains as such.
(Kātantra 4.6.75) A root ending in *n* remains as it is before a following vowel; the meaning is that the long *ā* is not elided. [Examples: *praśāmau*, *pratāmau*, *jagmuṣaḥ*, *jagmuṣī*.
[The suffix *yat*] occurs only when the vowel [of the root] is dependent on that [nasal]; thus, in the case of *praśān atra*.
Why "vowel"? [Consider] *praśānbhyām*.
And those [forms] which are desired: *praśāmam icchati*, *praśāmyati*, *praśāme hitam*, and *praśāmyam*.
The augment *iṭ* is placed at the beginning of the suffixes *vans* and *vas* after roots ending in *ṛ*,

*ī*, *ṅ*, *ha*, or a single vowel. By the rule of restriction (*srādiniyama*), since the status of being like the periphrastic future (*parokṣāvad-bhāva*) would otherwise have already established the presence of *iṭ*, this rule serves as a restriction.
*ārivān*, *īyivān*, *jakṣivān*, *ādivān*, *pecivān*, *dadivān*, *papivān*.

In the case of *daridrāṃ cakṛvān*, the suffix *ām* must be applied. By the very mention of *ārtyādi* (beginning with *ṛ*), when there is reduplication (*dvirvacana*), those roots consisting of a single vowel (*ekasvara*) are to be understood; singularity is not [intended] because of the mention of the root *iṇ*.

What is the meaning of "of these"? [The examples are] *babhajvān* and *jajāgarvān*. Regarding the rule *gamahanavidaviśadṛśāṃ vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.68): since this option (*vibhāṣā*) was not previously established, the suffix *iṭ* optionally occurs after these roots in the *vansac* suffix. Thus we have *jagmivān* or *jaganvān*, *jaghnivān* or *jaghanvān*, and *vividivān* or *vividvān*. Due to association with many verbal bases that possess suffixes (*sārvadhātuka*), the root *vid* here is understood in the sense of "to find" (*lābha*).
*viviśivān*, *viviśvān*; *dadṛśivān*, *dadṛśvān*; and *dāśvān*, *sāhvān*, *mīḍhvān*. (Pāṇini 6.1.12)
These are treated as irregular forms (nipātana): there is reduplication and the absence of the augment *iṭ* for the root *sah*, lengthening for *miha*, and the substitution of *ḍha*;
indeed, by virtue of the principle of "tantra" (systematic extension), all these rules apply to every verbal form.

*Kāt_4.6.79*: The augment *iṭ* does not occur after the root *śri*, roots ending in *u*, or the roots *vṛñ* and *vṛṅ* (ending in *ṛ*), when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix marked with the *kān* indicatory letter (*kānubandha*). Examples: *śritaḥ*, *śritavān*, *śritvā*;
*yutaḥ*, *yutavān*, *yutvā*.
rutaḥ, rutavān, rutvā;
lūnaḥ, lūnavān, lūtvā;
vṛtaḥ, vṛtavān, vṛtvā.

*kīrṇaḥ*, *kīrṇavān*, *kīrttvā*. [The suffix] should apply even when there is a modification due to the explicit statement, for the sake of establishing forms such as *śeśriyitaḥ* and *loluvitaḥ*. Others maintain that the rule regarding "monosyllabic roots" (*ekasvara*) continues to apply; according to them, it must indeed be stated [as an exception] for the root *ūrṇu*: *prorṇutaḥ*, *prorṇutavān*.

And when followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*) or the *kṛt* suffixes, [the rule applies]. According to Kāt_4.6.80, the augment *iṭ* does not occur before a voiced sound or before those suffixes designated as *kṛt*: *īśvaraḥ*, *dīpraḥ*, *śarmā*, *dīptiḥ*, *jāgartiḥ*, *buddhiḥ*.
With the suffix *tik*: *tantih*, *santiḥ*.

How is it that *nigṛhītiḥ*, *nipaṭhitiḥ*, *nikucitiḥ*, *ālocitiḥ*, and *upasnihitiḥ* [are formed]? Because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) concerning the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the suffix *iṭ* occurs after roots such as *grah*.

As for *apacitiḥ*, it is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*) and removal (*niṣkṛti*). How is it that *śastraṃ* [is explained]? It is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the traditional rule (*āgama*).
The word *patra* refers to a vehicle, according to the rule *yugyaṃ patre* (Kātantra 4.2.32).
Regarding the rule *veṣusahalubharuṣariṣāṃ ti* (Kātantra 4.6.81), the augment *iṭ* is optionally applied before an affix beginning with *t* that is not a sārvadhātuka; thus we have *eṣṭā* or *eṣitā*.
Soḍhā, sahitā; lobdhā, lobhitā;
roṣṭā, roṣitā.

*reṣṭā*, *reṣitā*. Why is the vowel *u* used as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*)? [To show that the suffix -ta is not used] with the root *iṣ* "to go," as in *eṣitā nityam* (he constantly desires). And [the suffix -ta is not used] after the roots beginning with *radh* (Kātantra 4.6.82).
The word "iti" does not apply here because it is stated separately.

By the mark of the *ṭānubandha*, the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs before a non-sārvadhātuka suffix beginning with a consonant and not starting with *ya*, after roots such as *radh* and others: *ratsyati* or *radhiṣyati*;
*naṅkṣyati* or *naśiṣyati*.
The *āvṛtkaraṇa* [of the root] indicates that it belongs to the *radhādi* group; thus, in forms such as *rarandhiva* and *rarandhima*, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory by the rule *srādiniyamāt*.
According to *Kātantra* 4.6.83, *svaratisūtisūyatyūdanubandhāt*:

after the roots *svarati*, *sūti*, *sūyati*, and those having *ū* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), the initial *iṭ* is optionally applied to a following *asārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant and not starting with *y*. Thus, we have both *svartā* and *svaritā*.
*sota*, *savita*.
But when followed by *tu*, it is always *savitā*.
*nigoḍhā*, *nigūhitā*.
The forms *vidhotā* and *vidhavita* are established through the roots *dhuñ* and *dhūñ*.
In the case of *svariṣyati*, because it is subsequent [to the preceding rule], there would be no option, due to the statement regarding fixed application (*vyavasthita-vibhāṣā*).
Likewise, in the case of *svṛ* and *sūṅ*, there would always be [the substitution] when followed by an affix marked with *kān*, as in *svṛtvā* and *sūtveti*.
From the rule *apatiniṣkuṣoḥ* [Kāt 4.6.90], it is understood that the suffix *iṭ* occurs after the root *niṣkuṣ*.
According to the rule *asārvadhātukasya vyañjanāder ayakārādeḥ* [Kāt 4.6.71], we have *niṣkoṣṭā* and *niṣkoṣitā*.

Furthermore, according to *udanubandhapūkliśāṃ ktvi* [Kāt 4.6.84], [the suffix *iṭ* occurs after roots with *u* as an indicatory vowel, after *pū*, and after *kliś* when followed by the suffix *ktvā*].
After a root ending in *u*, the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ* following the roots *pū* and *kliś*. For example: from *śam*, *śāntvā* or *śamitvā*;
from *pū* or *pūñ*, *pūtvā* or *pavitvā*;
and from *kliś*, *kliṣṭvā* or *kliśitvā*.
The option (*vibhāṣā*) applies when [the suffix] has *ū* as its *anubandha* and for the root *kliś*; it does not apply at all when [the suffix] has *kā* as its *anubandha* after the root *pu*.
According to Kāt_4.6.85, *iṭ* follows the roots *jṝ* and *vraśc*: *jaritvā*, *jarītvā*, and *vraścitvā*.

Because it is based on its specific characteristic (*lākṣaṇikatva*), [the rule applies] after *jṝ* as *jīr* (by *jṝṣ*); and because of the statement regarding *vraśc*, the augment *iṭ* is obligatory. The repetition of the mention of *iṭ* is for the purpose of excluding it in subsequent rules.
[The root] *lubh* [takes *iṭ*] in the sense of delusion (*vimohana*). (Kāt. 4.6.86)
After the roots *muh* "to delude" and *lubh*, the suffix *ktvā* optionally takes the augment *iṭ*; thus, *lubhitvā*.
However, when expressing greed (*gārddhya*), it is *lubdhvā* or *lubhitvā*.
This also applies after the roots *kṣudh* and *vas*. (Kātantra 4.6.87)

By means of the word *ca* ("and"), the rule "after *lubh* [the suffix *iṭ* is added] when there is delusion" (*vimohana*) is drawn forward for the sake of what follows; furthermore, after the roots *kṣudh* and *vas*, the suffix *iṭ* occurs before the suffix *ktvā*. This [rule] sets aside the prohibition [of *iṭ*].

And also in the case of the *niṣṭhā* suffixes: Kātantra 4.6.88 states that after the roots *kṣudh* and *vas*, as well as *lubh*, the suffix *iṭ* occurs before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes when there is delusion. Thus: *kṣudhitaḥ*, *kṣudhitavān*; *uṣitaḥ*, *uṣitavān*; *lubhitaḥ*, *lubhitavān*.

In the case of *gārddhya* (greed), even the optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) is set aside by the prohibition (*vyāvṛtti*); thus we have *lubdhaḥ* and *lubdhavān*. Regarding *pū* and *kliś*, [the rule states]: "After the roots *pū* and *kliś*, the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs before the *niṣṭhā* suffixes. Thus we have *pavitaḥ* and *pavitavān*, as well as *pūtaḥ* and *pūtavān*.

*klīś*, *klīśū*: *kliśitaḥ*, *kliśitavān*, *kliṣṭaḥ*, *kliṣṭavān*. *Kāt_4.6.90*: "The augment *iṭ* does not occur after these roots—excluding those marked with *ḍ* or *ī* as an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), nor those ending in a vowel (*u*), nor those having *v* as an indicatory letter (*veṭ*), nor *pat* and *niṣkuṣ*—when followed by a *niṣṭhā* suffix. Thus, from these roots (excluding *pat* and *niṣkuṣ*), the *niṣṭhā* suffix does not take *iṭ*: *uḍḍīnaḥ*, *uḍḍīnavān*.
*śūnaḥ*, *śūnavān*;
*dīpī*, *dīptaḥ*, *dīptavān*;
*olasjī*, *lagnaḥ*, *lagnavān*.

If, by the force of the suffix *iṭ* having an indicatory letter *i*, there were nasalization (*natva*) even in the absence of *iṭ*, then what would be the purpose of [the suffix] having an indicatory letter *ī*? Alternatively, it might serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for an optional *iṭ*; thus, the roots *ḍī* and *śvī* should be prescribed [with an indicatory *ī*].
And regarding the optional *iṭ*: *guhū*, *gūḍhaḥ*, *gūḍhavān*;
*śamu*, *śāntaḥ*, *śāntavān*.
Why specify "except for *pati* and *niṣkuṣ*" (*apatiniṣkuṣoḥ*)? [Examples: *patitaḥ*, *patitavān*, *niṣkuṣitaḥ*, *niṣkuṣitavān*.

How is it that [the forms] *daridritaḥ* and *daridritavān* are formed? One must remember here that [the root] has only one vowel (*ekasvara*), or else it is because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) [of roots] ending in *pati* and *niṣkuṣ*. And [this applies] also to [roots] having *ā* as an indicatory letter (*ādanubandha*). (Kātantra 4.6.91)
Furthermore, the augment *iṭ* does not occur after a root containing the vowel *ā* when the suffix *niṣṭhā* follows: from *ñimidā*, *minnaḥ*, *minnavān*;
from *ñikṣvidā*, *kṣviṇṇaḥ*, *kṣviṇṇavān*.

The letter *ca* (in the rule) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned; by virtue of it, there is an option for the roots *jap* and *vam*: *japtaḥ* or *japitaḥ*, *vāntaḥ* or *vamitaḥ*.
After the prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, the suffix *kta* is optionally added after the root *śvas*; [the forms are] *viśvastaḥ*, *viśvasitaḥ*, *āśvastaḥ*, and *āśvasitaḥ*.

This prohibition applies when the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) is expressed; however, it will be stated later that in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the beginning of an action (*ādikarman*), the suffix may optionally be applied.
Regarding "optionally in the case of the abstract action or the beginning of an action" (Kātantra 4.6.92).

Due to the connection with the prefix *ā*, the augment *iṭ* optionally occurs after the root in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and in the initial action as well as in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*): *minnam* or *meditam anena*; *praminnaḥ* or *pramedito bhavān*. Because the rule contains the option *veṭ*, the analysis of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) is established as indicating that the prohibition applies only to that which has the same meaning as the optional rule. Therefore, in the rule *gamahanavidaviśadṛśāṃ vā* (Kāt. 4.6.77), since the root *vid* is understood there in the sense of "to obtain" by association (*sāhacarya*), the prohibition would not apply to the root *vid* in the sense of "to know"; thus we have *viditaḥ* and *viditavān*.

Kātantra 4.6.93: The suffix *iṭ* is not applied after the roots *kṣubh*, *vah*, *svan*, *dhvani*, *phaṇ*, and *kaṣ* when followed by the *kta* suffix, provided they occur in the senses of "churning," "intense," "mind," "darkness," "effortless," "difficulty," and "sound," respectively. In these respective senses, *iṭ* does not occur before *kta*: - From *kṣubh* (in the sense of churning): *kṣubdhaḥ* means "churned" or "agitated"; *mantha* refers to barley meal (*saktu*) mixed with liquid substances. - From *vāhṛ* (in the sense of effort): *vāḍham* means "intensely. Here, repetition, excess, and acceptance are understood, but not the sense of "speed. Thus: *kṣubdhaḥ manthaḥ* ("the churned mixture"), meaning it has been stirred; *vāḍham* ("very much"). In this context, the intensification through repetition and the act of assent are intended, rather than the meaning of "quickness."
*svāntam* means the mind (*manas*), in the sense of being undistracted from external objects. *Dhvāntam* means darkness (*tamas*).
The root *phaṇ* means "to go"; thus, *phāṇṭam* refers to a liquid medicinal substance that has been extracted by a physician immediately, without the application of effort.

"Kaṣa-śiṣa": fire is *kaṣṭa*, a mountain is *kaṣṭa*; because it is a cause of hardship (*kṛcchra-hetutvāt*), even a dense forest is called *kṛcchra*, and *kṛcchra* also means suffering (*duḥkha*). Even when the primary sense is present, the secondary sense may also be expressed.

The root *ghuṣ* occurs in the *bhvādi* class with the meaning "to sound" (*ghuṣiraśabda*), as in *ghuṣṭā rajjuḥ* ("the rope was sounded") and *ghuṣṭaṃ śarīram* ("the body was sounded"). However, in the *curādi* class, it occurs with the meaning "to make known" (*viśabdane*); in this case, the augment *iṭ* would apply, as in *avaghuṣitaṃ vākyam āha* ("he spoke a word that made itself known"). Because of the prohibition [of *iṭ*] when meaning "to make known," the *in* suffix applies optionally in the *curādi* class; thus, the following is established: *mahīpālavacaḥ śrutvā jughuṣuḥ puṣpamānavāḥ* ("having heard the king's words, the flower-boys shouted"). Alternatively, since roots have multiple meanings, the *bhvādi* root itself may be used even in the sense of "making known"; the meaning is that they manifested their own intention through sound.

What is the purpose of the phrase "in *mantha* and so forth"? [Examples are: *kṣubhitaḥ*, *vāhitaḥ*, *svanitaḥ*, *dhvanitaḥ*, *phaṇitaḥ*, *kaṣitaḥ*, *ghuṣitaḥ*. Likewise, even when there is a different substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), as in: *manthena kṣubhitam*, *bhṛśena vāhitam*, *manasā svanitama*, *tamasā dhvanitam*, *anāyāsena phaṇitam*, *kṛcchreṇa kaṣitam*, *śarīreṇa ghuṣitam*. How is it that [the form] *udghuṣṭaṃ kokilayā* occurs? It is because the sense of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*) is being qualified.

"How was the ocean agitated?"—it will be understood through this comparison. Regarding *lagna*, *mliṣṭa*, and *viribdha* in the senses of "clinging," "indistinct," and "tone": Pāṇini 6.1.204 states that words beginning with *lagna*, ending in the suffix *kta*, are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) in the respective senses of "clinging" and so forth. Thus, from the root *lage*, we have *lagna* in the sense of "clinging" (*sakta*), while *lagita* has a different meaning.

*Mlecha* means indistinct; *mliṣṭam* is indistinct, while *mlecchitam* is something else. Regarding *rebhṛ*: *viribdhaḥ* refers to a tone (*svara*), where *svara* here means sound (*dhvani*); *virebhitam* is something else. Others, however, cite *viribhitam* as a counter-example, considering *ribhi* to be a root found in the *sūtra*. *Dhṛṣṭaḥ* means "bold" (*viśastaḥ*); because the root *dhṛṣ* has an indicatory letter *ā*, and the root *śas* has an indicatory letter *u*, there is a prohibition against the suffix *iṭ* by the rule "veṭ. This word is conventionally established in the sense of boldness alone; other forms such as *dharṣitaḥ* or *viśasitaḥ* are used either due to the non-constancy of the negative particle (*nañ*) or as synonyms.

*Parivṛḍha* and *dṛḍha* are the [irregular] forms for the meanings of "lord" (*prabhu*) and "strong" (*balavat*), respectively (Pāṇini 4.6.95). These two forms are established as irregular substitutes for the senses of "lord" and "strong": the root *vṛh* preceded by *pari-* undergoes the absence of the augment *iṭ* and the elision of the nasal (*na*-lopa); likewise for the root *dṛh*. Some maintain that *vṛh* and *dṛh* are alternative verbal roots (*prakṛtyantara*). Thus, *parivṛḍhaḥ* means "lord," and *dṛḍhaḥ* means "strong"; it also refers to one who is stout. However, the term *dṛḍha* specifically denotes only one who is strong.

How is it that [the form] *parivṛḍhayya* is formed? Since there is no compound with *parivṛḍha*, the suffix *yap* would not occur; this is true. However, the fact that the root *saṃgrāma* is listed in the *gaṇa*-list [of roots ending in *yuc*] in the rule *tat karoti* indicates that the suffix *in* occurs after a mere nominal stem.
Thus, both *apacāyitaḥ* and *apacitaḥ* are established by means of the roots *cāy* and *ci*, which function in the sense of "honoring."

"How was the *pārāyaṇa* performed by the Brahmin? The quality (*guṇa*) was performed by the student. [In these cases,] it will occur because the root *vṛt* is included within the sense of "performing" (*anarthavṛtti*). Even for that which ends in the suffix *-in*, it should be understood that [the form] *vartitaḥ*—meaning "the quality was performed by him"—must occur; this is the opinion [of some]. Others, however, prescribe *vṛttam* after the root *i* (in the sense of studying). *Kāt_4.6.96*: After the roots *ṛd* preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *ni*, and *vi*, the augment *iṭ* does not occur in the *kta* suffix. Thus: *samarṇṇaḥ*, *nyarṇṇaḥ*, *vyarṇṇaḥ*.
Others say that [the rule] applies when there is no occurrence of the particle *niṣṭhā*.

Regarding *abhi* in the sense of proximity: Kāśikāvṛtti 4.6.97 states that after *abhi*, the suffix *iṭ* does not occur before the root *ṛd* in the *kta* participle when the meaning is proximity; for example, *abhyarṇā senā*, which means "the army is near."
Some say [the prefix *ati-*] is not excessively long because of the mention [in the rule].

Regarding the rule *vā ruṣyamatvarasaṃghuṣāsvanām* (Pāṇini 7.2.28): after these roots, the suffix *kta* optionally does not take the augment *iṭ*. For example, *ruṣṭaḥ* or *ruṣitaḥ*. Since the root *ruṣ* belongs to the class beginning with *veṣu-saha-lubha-ruṣ-* (which is marked as having optional *iṭ*), the prohibition [of *iṭ*] would have applied by default; however, this rule makes it optional.
The root *am* means "to go," and not the root *am* meaning "disease" because it ends in an *in*-affix; thus we have *abhyāntaḥ* and *abhyamitaḥ*.

Regarding *tūrṇaḥ* and *tvaritaḥ*, the prohibition [of the suffix -na] would have applied by the rule "after a root with an initial augment *ā*. [However, this does not apply here. He spoke a sentence that was either *saṃghuṣṭam* or *saṃghuṣitam*.

*saṃghuṣṭau* and *saṃghuṣitau* mean "tamed. Even when preceded by *sam*, the root *ghuṣ* is used in this [specific sense] alone because it is subsequent [in the rules]. Regarding the root *svan* preceded by *ā*: *āsvāntaḥ* and *āsvanitaḥ* refer to a drum; *āsvāntam* and *āsvanitām* refer to the mind. Because it is subsequent [in the rules], even when denoting the mind, this [suffix] alone is used.
*Kāt_4.6.99*: After the root *hṛṣ* when it refers to body hair (*loman*), the augment *iṭ* is optionally absent in the past passive participle (*kta*). Thus: *hṛṣṭāni*, *hṛṣitāni* (body hairs);
*hṛṣṭam*, *hṛṣitam* (made to bristle) by the body hairs.

The hair is "hṛṣṭa" (erect) or "hṛṣita" (thrilled). Regarding the root *hṛṣ* with the indicatory vowel *ū* (*hṛṣū*), it is *aniṭ* (does not take the *iṭ* augment) in the *niṣṭhā* suffix due to its *udittva* (having *u* as an indicatory letter). However, the root *hṛṣ* meaning "to be pleased" (*tuṣṭau*) is *seṭ* (takes the *iṭ* augment); this option applies to both roots.
The word *loman* refers to body hair (*aṅgaja*) and head hair (*mūrdhaja*), as in the rule: "Having touched body hair or nails, one must perform purification.
The root *hṛṣ* occurs in the sense of [erecting] body hair; thus, it has body hair as its agent.

Why is the word *lomasu* used [in the rule]? Consider *hṛṣṭaś chāttraḥ*, which means "the student is delighted" (having a different meaning), and *hṛṣitaś chāttraḥ*, which means "the student is thrilled" (having the intended meaning).

The word *loma* is an illustration [for other cases]; it may also refer to astonishment (*vismaya*) or obstruction (*pratighāta*). In the case of *hṛṣṭo hṛṣitaś chāttraḥ*, the meaning is "astonished. In the case of *hṛṣṭā hṛṣitā dantāḥ*, the meaning is "obstructed" (i.e., set back).
The words *dānta*, *śānta*, *pūrṇa*, *dasta*, *spaṣṭa*, *channa*, and *jñapta* are formed with the suffix *na*. (Pāṇini 7.2.100)
These suffixes are optionally applied as follows: *dāntaḥ* (tamed) and *damitaḥ*;
*śāntaḥ* (calmed) and *śamitaḥ*. The root *pūrī* belongs both to the *divādi* and *curādi* classes; [its past passive participles are] *pūrṇaḥ* and *pūritaḥ*.
*dasu*, *dastaḥ*, *dāsitaḥ*.
*spaṣṭaḥ*, *spāśitaḥ*.
*chad* (in the sense of covering), *channaḥ*, *chāditaḥ*.

In the senses of killing (*māraṇa*), satisfying (*toṣaṇa*), and sharpening (*niśamana*), there is knowledge (*jñā*) and the suffix *mān* follows; thus we have *jñaptaḥ* and *jñapitaḥ*. Regarding the prohibition of *iṭ*, the elision (*luk*) of the root *in* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*), because since the root *jñap* optionally takes *iṭ*, a permanent prohibition would otherwise apply. *Kāt_4.6.101*: After a root-final *r*, the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) becomes *n*, except after the roots *pṝ*, *mūrch*, *mad*, *khyā*, and *dhyai*. Thus: *śīrṇaḥ*, *śīrṇavān*.

In *gurī*, *avagūrṇaḥ*, and *avagūrṇavān*: if there were also the hearing of the vowel *ṛ* [in the rule], then [the substitution of] *na* would not occur in *kṛtam* because of the intervention by a portion of the vowel *ṛ*; nor in *caritam* because of the intervention by the augment *iṭ*, which is a constituent part of the suffix *niṣṭhā*; nor in *kārttiḥ* (meaning "the offspring of Kṛta"), because of the principle that "that which is external is unestablished with respect to that which is internal. What is the purpose of the prohibition? [It applies to] *pṝ*, as in *pūrtaḥ*.

*mūrchā* (feminine), *mūrtaḥ* (masculine). When [the suffixes] *kta* and *ktavatu* follow the roots *mad*, *khyā*, and *dhyai*, [the substitution of *na* for *t* is applied]: *mattaḥ*, *khyātaḥ*, *dhyātaḥ*.
And [the substitution of *na* occurs] after the root *do* (*dā*), and [the *da* of the root is replaced by *sa*]. (Kātantra 4.6.102)

After the letter *d*, the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) becomes *n*, and the *d* itself [becomes *n*]. Examples: *minnaḥ*, *minnavān*. From Pāṇini 8.2.58 (*āto ’ntaḥsthāsaṃyuktāt*): After an *ā* that is not joined with a semivowel (*antaḥsthā*), the *t* of the past passive participle becomes *n*. Examples: *glānaḥ*, *glānavān*; *viśrāṇaḥ*, *viśrāṇavān*; *mlānaḥ*, *mlānavān*.

Because of the governing context of the verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), [the suffix] *niṣṭhā* is applied as "departed" (*niryātaḥ*) or "one who has departed" (*niryātavān*). Also, from roots beginning with *lū* and those marked with the secondary suffix *o*: Pāṇini 8.2.45 states that the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following roots such as *lūñ* and those having *o* as their *it*-augment becomes *n*. Thus, from *lūñ*, we have *lūnaḥ* (cut) and *lūnavān* (one who has cut).
jyā, jīnaḥ, jīnavān; rujo, rugnaḥ, rugnavān;
bhujo, bhugnaḥ, bhugnavān.
The roots *svād* and others have an indicatory vowel *u*. The root *ṣūṅ* (meaning "birth of living beings") forms *sūnaḥ* and *sūnavān*.
From *dūṅ* (due to the non-universality of what is prescribed for the *gaṇa*), we have *dūnaḥ* and *dūnavān*.
From *pūñ* in the sense of "destruction," we have *pūnā yavāḥ*, meaning "the barley has perished"; why say "in the sense of destruction"? [Because] *pūtaṃ dhānyam* means "the grain has been shaken."
The suffix *dugv* is applied after [roots ending in] long vowels (*dīrgha*), as well as after *vidū*, *vidūn*, *vigū*, and *vigūn*.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to include other unstated cases.
Furthermore, the suffix *ktin* is applied after roots ending in *ṛ* and those beginning with *lū* and others: *kīrṇiḥ*, *gīrṇiḥ*, *lūniḥ*, *pūniḥ*, *dhūniḥ*.
And [the suffix] *lyap* [is applied], up to and including *lvādibhyaḥ*, because of the formation of *vṛt*.
Also after *hājyāglābhyaḥ*: *hāniḥ*, *jyāniḥ*, *glāniḥ*. After *vraśc*, there is *ka* as well: *Kāt_4.6.105*.

The *t* of the *niṣṭhā* [suffixes] following the root *vraśc* becomes *n*, and there is the substitution of *ka* at the end [of the word]. Since only *vraśc* is explicitly mentioned [in the rule], this applies even when the penultimate letter is *ś*; thus, when the *dhakāra* [consonant] is present and the final letter is elided, the substitution of *ka* occurs, which supersedes the rule for *ṣatva*. Examples: *vṛkṇaḥ*, *vṛkṇavān*. From the root *kṣi* when it ends in a long vowel: Pāṇini 8.2.46 states that the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following *kṣi* ending in a long vowel becomes *n*. Examples: *kṣīṇaḥ*, *kṣīṇavān*.
What is the purpose of the condition "after a long vowel"? [Consider: *kṣitāyur jālmaḥ* ("the wretch whose life is exhausted"), *kṣitakas tapasvī* ("the poor man who has perished").

*Kāt_4.6.107*: *śyo 'sparśe*. When the root *śyai* (to congeal) occurs in the sense of not being in contact with a solid substance (*asparśe*), the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix is replaced by *n*. Thus: *śīnaṃ ghṛtam* ("congealed ghee"), *śīnavad ghṛtam* ("ghee that has congealed").

In the term *asparśa*, this negative particle (*nañ*) is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). Although *sparśa* (touch) is subordinate [as a member of the compound], it is not the cause for the substitution of *na* for *ta* (*natva*), nor for the *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization), as is the case with *roga*. Therefore, in *pratiśīna*, the substitution of *na* for *ta* indeed occurs. *Kāt_4.6.108*: After the root *añc* when it does not signify an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure), the *t* of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is replaced by *n*. For example, *samaknaḥ* and *samaknavān*, which mean "adhering closely" (*saṃsakta*).

What is meant by "without an *apādāna*"? For example: *udaktam udakam*, meaning "water drawn up," specifically from a well. *Vyaktam* is a form derived from the root *añj*. As for *añcitaḥ* and *añcitavān*, because they are separated by the augment *iṭ*, the presence of *iṭ* and the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) are not desired in the case of the root *añc* when used in the sense of "honoring."

*Kāt_4.6.109*: When not meaning "desire for victory," the *t* of the suffix *niṣṭhā* following the root *div* is replaced by *n*. Thus, we have *ādyūnaḥ* (one who has gambled) and *ādyūnavān* (one who possesses the state of having gambled).
Why "when not meaning desire for victory"? Consider *dyūtaṃ vartate* ("gambling is taking place"); for the throwing of dice is performed with the desire for victory.

Regarding the root *si* (to bind), it should be stated that [the substitution of *na* for *ta*] occurs when the object functions as the agent (*karmakartṛ*) in the sense of "swallowing" (*grāsa*); for example, *sino grāsaḥ svayam eva*, meaning "the morsel has bound itself.
*Kāt_4.6.110*: After these roots—*hrī*, *ghrā*, *trai*, *und*, *nud*, and *vid*—the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix optionally becomes *n*. Thus: *hrīṇaḥ* or *hrītaḥ*, *hrīṇavān* or *hrītavān*.
*ghrāṇaḥ*, *ghrāṇavān*, *ghrātaḥ*, *ghrātavān*.
*trāṇaḥ*, *trāṇavān*, *trātaḥ*, *trātavān*. *undī*: *samunnaḥ*, *samunnavān*, *samuttaḥ*, *samuttavān*.
*nuda*, *nunnaḥ*, *nunnavān*, *nuttaḥ*, *nuttavān*.
*vida* in the sense of "investigation": *vinnaḥ*, *vinnavān*, *vittaḥ*, *vittavān*.
By the rule of fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), [the substitution of *i* for *u*] is obligatory when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*): *devatrātaḥ*.

Likewise, after roots meaning "to deliberate" (vicārārtha), there is only the option of [the augment] *vibhāṣā*; after roots meaning "to know" (*jñānārtha*), the augment *iṭ* is always [applied]; and after the root *vid*, except when it means "to obtain" (*lābhārtha*) or "to exist" (*sattārtha*), *iṭ* is always applied outside of the sense of "enjoyment" (*bhoga*).
*Kṣai-śuṣi-pacāṃ makavāḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.53). For these three roots, respectively, the *t* of the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) becomes *m*, *k*, or *v*. Thus: *kṣāmaḥ*, *kṣāmavān*;
*śuṣkaḥ*, *śuṣkavān*.
*pakvaḥ*, *pakvavān*.
Between two optional rules (*vibhāṣā*), that which is prescribed is indeed obligatory (*nitya*). "The suffix *ma* optionally [replaces] the root *as*. (Kātantra 4.6.112)

The *niṣṭhā* suffixal *t* of the root *styai* preceded by *pra* becomes *m*: *prastīmaḥ*, *prastīmavān*, *prastītaḥ*, *prastītavān*. When the suffix *mat* follows, there is always vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*). *Nirvāṇaḥ* [is formed] except when referring to wind (Kātantra 4.6.113). The form *nirvāṇa* is thus established provided that the meaning of the verbal root does not concern wind: *nirvāṇo 'gniḥ* ("the fire has gone out"), where it refers to the cessation of burning.

A *bhikṣu* is "extinguished" (*nirvāṇa*) here in the sense of the pacification of passion and so forth. Why [is it] "not blown upon" (*avāta*)? [Because] "the wind has ceased" (*nirvāto vātaḥ*); here, there is a contradiction. How then [can one say] "the lamp is extinguished by the wind"? In this case, the wind is the instrument (*karaṇa*), not the locus (*ādhāra*). Even in the sense of the state [of extinction] (*bhāva*), as in "extinguished by the wind," the wind itself is the agent (*kartṛ*).

*bhitta*, *ṛṇa*, and *adhamarṇa* [are formed] in the senses of *śakala* (fragment), *śodhya* (that which is to be cleared/repaid), and *adhamarṇa* (debtor), respectively. Kātyāyana 4.6.114: Words such as *bhitta* ending in the suffix *kta* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) in the senses of *śakala* and so forth, in their respective order. *Bhitta* and *śakala* are synonyms. From the root *ṛ* "to go," *ṛṇa* means "that which is to be cleared. An *adhamarṇa* is one who is inferior (*adhama*) regarding a debt (*ṛṇa*); this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) applied in that context.
The mention of "debtor" (*adhamarṇa*) is an indicator for the regulation of time and other such factors; therefore, this [rule] would also apply in the case of the creditor (*uttamarṇa*).

*Vid* means "wealth" (*vitta*); it is called "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) because it is enjoyed. By metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), even when it is understood as "wealth," it is still referred to as "wealth. [The forms] *phulla*, *kṣība*, *kṛśa*, and *ullāgha* occur after a verbal root that is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). (Kātantra 4.6.115)

These words ending in the *kta* suffix are treated as irregular (*nipātana*) provided they do not follow a prefix: from the roots *dala* and *phalā* in the sense of "falling apart," there is the substitution of *la* for the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix, as in *phullaḥ*.
Others also desire the substitution of *la* for the *t* of the *ktavatu* suffix, as in *phullavān*.

From the roots *kṣībṛ* and *kṛśi*, and also from *lagh* preceded by *ud*, there is the elision of the *t* of the *niṣṭhā* suffix itself and the absence of the augment *iṭ*: *kṣībaḥ*, *kṛśaḥ*, *ullāghaḥ*.

Why does [the rule] specify "after a prefix other than an *upasarga*"? [Consider: *praphultaḥ*, *prakṣībitaḥ*, *prakṛśitaḥ*, *prollāghitaḥ*. How is it that *saṃpraphullaḥ* and *utpraphullaḥ* are established? [They are] established by the root *phulla* in the sense of "blooming," with the suffix *ac*.
But how is *parikṛśaḥ* established? [The answer is: it would be established by a specific statement; otherwise, it would be a different form altogether.
There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] for *ūṭ* following a vowel (*avarṇa*). Pāṇini 6.1.89: *vṛddhir eci*.
After a vowel—whether belonging to a verbal root (*dhātu*) or not—a *vṛddhi* [substitution] occurs for the following *ūṭ*. [Examples:
*śavaḥ*, *śauḥ*, *śāvau*, *śāvaḥ*.
dhāvu, dhautaḥ, dhautavān (←gh°). avanam, ūtiḥ. paṭotiḥ.
[The forms] *janāvati*, *janauḥ*, [and] *janāvau* [are derived by this rule].
Why [is it said] "ūṭ"? [Consider] *adyoḍhā* and *katoḍhā*.
Since the result would have been established by the term "au," the mention of "vṛddhi" is for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
Thus, in the commentary by Daurgasimhi, the sixth quarter (pāda) of the Kṛt suffixes is completed.
Thus, the Kātantra is finished.
